It is also possible that it is the predicate of an implied subject, as if it were said: "Who is it who knows the secret and what is more hidden?" It is said: "He is Allah." "Al-husna" is the feminine form of "al-ahsan", and a feminine singular adjective may be used with a broken plural, and what made this acceptable is that these names came as closing rhymes. The superlative quality (al-ahsaniyya) lies in their including meanings that are at the utmost of goodness, of sanctity, of magnificence, and of lordship, and acts that cannot proceed except from Him. They mentioned that these are the names concerning which the Messenger of God said: "Indeed God has ninety-nine names; whoever counts them enters Paradise." At-Tirmidhi related it with a chain of narration.

**Surah Ta-Ha, peace be upon him, 135 verses, Meccan**

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

(p-222) ﴿Ta-Ha.﴾ ﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you to make you wretched,﴾ ﴿but as a reminder to those who fear,﴾ ﴿a revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens.﴾ ﴿The Most Merciful sat Himself upon the Throne.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens, whatever is on the earth, whatever is between them, and whatever is beneath the soil.﴾ ﴿And if you speak aloud, He knows the secret and what is more hidden.﴾ ﴿God, there is no god but Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ ﴿When he saw a fire and said to his family, "Stay here, for I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I will bring you a brand from it, or find guidance at the fire."﴾ ﴿Then when he came to it, he was called: "O Moses!"﴾ ﴿"I am your Lord, so take off your sandals. You are in the sacred valley of Tuwa."﴾ ﴿"And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed."﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I am God. There is no god but Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance."﴾ ﴿"The Hour is coming. I am almost concealing it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for."﴾ ﴿"So do not let one who does not believe in it and follows his desires turn you away from it, lest you perish."﴾ ﴿"And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?"﴾ ﴿He said, "It is my staff. I lean on it, beat down leaves for my sheep with it, and I have other uses for it."﴾ ﴿He said, "Throw it down, O Moses."﴾ ﴿So he threw it, and suddenly it was a moving serpent.﴾ ﴿He said, "Take hold of it and do not fear. We will return it to its original form."﴾ ﴿"And draw your hand to your side; it will come out white without harm, as another sign,"﴾ ﴿"so that We may show you some of Our greatest signs."﴾ ﴿"Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, expand my chest for me,﴾ ﴿and make my affair easy for me,﴾ ﴿and untie the knot from my tongue,﴾ ﴿that they may understand my speech,﴾ ﴿and appoint for me a minister from my family:﴾ ﴿Aaron, my brother.﴾ ﴿Strengthen my back through him,﴾ ﴿and make him a partner in my task,﴾ ﴿that we may glorify You much﴾ ﴿and remember You much,﴾ ﴿for You are ever Seeing of us."﴾ ﴿He said, "You have been granted your request, O Moses."﴾ ﴿And We had already bestowed favour upon you another time,﴾ ﴿when We inspired your mother with what is inspired:﴾ ﴿"Place him in the chest, then cast it into the river, and let the river throw it onto the bank, where an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his will take him." And I cast upon you love from Me, so that you might be reared under My eye.﴾ ﴿When your sister walked and said, "Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?" So We returned you to your mother, that her eye might be refreshed and she would not grieve. And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress and tested you with many trials.﴾ (p-223)

*Al-thara* (الثَّرى): moist earth, and its dual is *tharayan*. It is said *tharraytu al-turbata* (ثَرَّيْتُ التُّرْبَةَ), meaning I moistened the soil. *Thariya al-ardu tathra tharan* (ثَرِيَتِ الأرْضُ تَثْرى ثَرًى) means the land became moist after dryness, so it is *thariyyah*. *Athrat* (أثْرَتْ) means the soil became abundant, so it is *muthriyah*. And a land is *tharan*, meaning possessing moist soil. Ibn al-A'rabi said: it is said that "so-and-so is near to *al-thara* and far from *al-nabt*," referring to one who promises and does not fulfil. It is also said: "I see the *thara* of anger in the face of so-and-so," meaning its trace. It is also said: "*al-thara* is between me and so-and-so," when the connection between you two has been cut off. Jarir said:

*So do not dig up between me and you the moist earth; indeed, what is between me and you is enriching.*

*Anasa* (آنَسَ): to find. The Arabs say: "Did you *anasta* so-and-so?" meaning did you find him. It is also said it means to sense, which is close to finding. Al-Harith ibn Hillizah said:

*I perceived a sign, and a hunter startled it, in the afternoon when evening had drawn near.*

*Al-qabas* (القَبَسُ): a burning ember of fire that is placed on the top of a stick, reed, or the like. It is a verbal noun in the sense of an object, like *al-qabd* and *al-nafd*. It is said: *qabastu minhu naran, aqbisu*, and *faqbasani* means he gave me a *qabas* from it. From this comes *al-muqbasah*, that in which a brand is carried, from a potsherd or other things. And *iqtabastu minhu naran* and *ilman*, meaning I acquired it. Al-Mubarrad said: *aqbastu al-rajula ilman* and *qabastuhu naran*. Al-Kisa'i said: *aqbastuhu naran* and *ilman*, and I also used *qabastuhu* for both.

*Al-khal'* (الخَلْعُ) and *al-na'l* (النَّعْلُ) are both known; the former is removing the latter from the foot. It is said: *al-na'l* is that which protects the foot from the ground, whether made of leather, iron, wood, or something else.

*Tuwa* (طُوًى): the name of a place.

*Al-sa'y* (السَّعْيُ): walking quickly, and it may also be used for work.

*Radiya yardaa radan* (رَدِيَ يَرْدى رَدًى) means he perished, and *ardahu* means he destroyed him. Duraid ibn al-Simmah said:

*They called out and said, "The horses have destroyed a horseman!" So I said, "I seek refuge in God from that destruction."*

*Tawakka'a ala al-shay'* (تَوَكَّأ عَلى الشَّيْءِ) means he leaned heavily upon it while walking or standing, and from it comes *al-ittika'*. *Tawakka'tu* and *ittaka'tu* have the same meaning. This root was already mentioned in Surah Yusuf in the words ﴿*muttaka'an*﴾ (Yusuf: 31), and it is explained here because the two patterns differ, although the root is one.

*Hashsha ala al-ghanam* (هَشَّ عَلى الغَنَمِ), in the form *yahushshu* with a *damma* on the *ha'*, means he beat the leaves of the tree so that they would fall. *Hashsha ila al-rajul*, in the form *yahisshu* with a *kasra*, as Tha'lab said, means he welcomed him and showed joy towards him. The basic meaning of this root is softness; it is said: *rajul hashsh*, a gentle man. *Al-ghanam* (الغَنَمُ) is known; it is a collective noun and feminine.

*Al-ma'ribah* (المَأْرُبَةُ), with a *damma*, *fatha*, or *kasra* on the *ra'*, means need, and its plural is *ma'arib*. *Al-irbah* also means need.

*Al-hayyah* (الحَيَّةُ): the snake. It applies to the male and female, the small and the large. Its root was mentioned earlier, and it is repeated here because of the specific meaning intended. The saying of people, *hawwa'* for one who catches snakes, is from the pattern of *huwwah*; the two roots are different, like *sibt* and *sibatr*.

*Al-azr* (الأزْرُ): the back, as al-Khalil said. Abu 'Ubayd said: *azarahu* means he strengthened him. *Al-azr* also means strength. The poet said:

*With a bow-shaped land whose vegetation has strengthened the straying plants, passing by armies that are victorious and defeated.*

(p-223) *Al-qadhf* (القَذْفُ): throwing and casting. *Al-sahil* (السّاحِلُ): the shore of the sea, which is its side free of water. It is so named because the water *yasḥaluhu*, that is, peels it off, so it is an active participle in the sense of a passive. Abu Tammam said:

*It is the sea, from whichever direction you come to it: its depth is the known and its shore is generosity.*

* *

(In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Ta-Ha.﴾ ﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you to make you wretched,﴾ ﴿but as a reminder to those who fear,﴾ ﴿a revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens.﴾ ﴿The Most Merciful sat Himself upon the Throne.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens, whatever is on the earth, whatever is between them, and whatever is beneath the soil.﴾ ﴿And if you speak aloud, He knows the secret and what is more hidden.﴾ ﴿God, there is no god but Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾)

This surah is Meccan without disagreement. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to stand on one foot, alternating between his two feet while praying, and this verse was revealed. This is what Ali said. Al-Dahhak said: The Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions prayed, and he prolonged the standing when the Qur'an was revealed to him. The Quraysh then said: "It was revealed to him only to make him wretched." Muqatil said: Abu Jahl, al-Nadr, and al-Mut'im said: "You are indeed wretched by abandoning our religion," so this verse was revealed.

The connection of this surah with the end of the preceding one is that when God mentioned the facilitation of the Qur'an in the language of the Messenger (ﷺ), that is, in his tongue, and among the reasons given was His saying ﴿*that you may give good news thereby to the pious and warn thereby a people contentious*﴾ (Maryam: 97), He confirmed this with His saying ﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you to make you wretched,﴾ ﴿but as a reminder to those who fear.﴾ The *tadhkirah* (التَّذْكِرَةُ, reminder) is good news and warning. What the polytheists claimed, that it was sent down for wretchedness, is not so; rather it was sent down only as a reminder.

Apparently ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ belongs to the disjoined letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah), like *Ya-Sin*, *Alif-Lam-Ra*, and similar ones. This matter was discussed at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

From Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', and 'Ikrimah, the meaning of ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ is "O man." It is said this is in Nabataean, it is said in Abyssinian, and it is said in Hebrew. It is said it is a Yemeni dialect of 'Akk, and it is said of 'Ukl. Al-Kalbi said: If you say to a man of 'Akk, "O man," he will not respond until you say "Ta-Ha." Al-Suddi said the meaning of ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ is "O so-and-so." Al-Tabari cited, for the meaning "O man" in the dialect of 'Akk, the words of one of their poets:

*I called "Ta-Ha" in battle, but he did not respond, so I feared for him that he would be turning away.*

And the words of another:

*Indeed, folly is "Ta-Ha" among your traits; may God not bless the cursed people.*

It is also said it is one of the names of the Messenger, and it is said it is one of the names of God. Al-Zamakhshari said: Perhaps 'Akk altered *ya hadha* (يا هَذا, "O this one") in their speech, as if they in their dialect changed the *ya* into *ta*, saying *ya-ta*, and they abbreviated this and limited it to *ha*. The trace of this artifice is evident and not hidden in the verse cited as evidence:

*Indeed, folly is "Ta-Ha" among your traits; may God not sanctify the morals of the cursed people.*

End of quotation. It had been mentioned earlier that it is said that *taha* in the dialect of 'Akk means "O man," and then he made a conjecture about 'Akk with what no grammarian would say: that they changed the *ya* into *ta*. This does not occur in the language of the Arabs, changing *ya*, the vocative particle, into *ta*, and likewise omitting the demonstrative in the vocative and retaining the particle of attention. It is also said: *ta* is an imperative verb whose root is *ta'*, and the hamza was lightened by changing it into an *alif*, and *ha* is the object, referring to the earth, meaning: "Tread the earth with your two feet and do not alternate," since he used to alternate until his feet swelled. A group including al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Abu Hanifah, and Warsh in his chosen reading recited ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ with the *ha* pronounced. It is said its original form was *ta'* and the hamza was dropped on the basis of its change in *yata'u*, in the manner of *la hunaka al-martaʿu buniya al-amru 'alayhi*; the silent *ha* was added, and continuity was treated as pausing. Or its original form was *ta'*, and its hamza was changed into a *ha*, so it became ﴿Ta-Ha﴾. 'Amr ibn Fa'id and al-Dahhak recited *Ta-wi*.

Talhah recited *ma nuzzila 'alayka*, with a *nun* bearing a *damma* and a *zay* bearing a *kasra* with a *shaddah*, in the passive voice, and *al-Qur'an* in the nominative. The majority recited ﴿*ma anzalna ʿalayka al-Qur'an*﴾. The meaning of ﴿*li-tashqa*﴾ is: "that you may be exhausted through excessive grief over them and over their disbelief, and be distressed that they should believe," as in His saying ﴿*Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief*﴾ (al-Shu'ara': 3). *Al-shaqa'* (الشَّقاءُ) comes in the sense of fatigue, and from it the proverb: "More tired than a breaker of a colt, and more wretched than a breaker of a colt." Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, nothing is upon you except to convey and remind, and it is not decreed upon you that they must believe, after you have not fallen short in delivering the message and the good exhortation. It is also said that what is intended is the refutation of what Abu Jahl and others said, mentioned earlier in the account of the occasion of revelation.

*Li-tashqa* and *tadhkirah* are a reason for the phrase ﴿*ma anzalna*﴾. The preposition *li-* is used with *li-tashqa* because the agent differs: the subject of ﴿*ma anzalna*﴾ is God, and the subject of *li-tashqa* is the Messenger (ﷺ). But since the agent in ﴿*anzalna*﴾ and ﴿*tadhkirah*﴾ is one, for *tadhkirah* is the verbal noun of *dhakkara*, and the one who reminds is God, who is also the one who sent it down, the verb is transitive to it and it is put in the accusative. There is disagreement over whether the agent must be one, and the majority require it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, is it not permissible to say, "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you should be wretched," like His saying ﴿*lest your deeds be voided*﴾ (al-Hujurat: 2)? I say: Yes, but it is an incidental accusative (*nasbah tari'ah*), like the accusative in ﴿*and Moses chose his people*﴾ (al-A'raf: 155). As for the accusative in ﴿*tadhkirah*﴾, it is like that in *darabtu Zaydan*, because it is one of the five objects, which are fundamental and the rules for others. End of quotation.

It is not agreed that when the preposition is omitted, *an tashqa* is in the accusative. Rather there is disagreement on this: is it in the accusative, with the verb transitive to it after dropping the particle, or is it in the genitive by dropping the preposition while retaining its governance?

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿*illa tadhkirah*﴾ may be in the accusative as a substitution (*badal*) for the position of ﴿*li-tashqa*﴾, and it may be in the accusative by supposing a verb whose estimate is: "But We sent it down as a reminder." End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari rejected Ibn 'Atiyyah's first analysis, saying: If you say, can *tadhkirah* be a substitute for the position of *li-tashqa*? I say: No, because the two kinds differ; but it is in the accusative as an exception that is disconnected (*istithna' munqati'*), in which *illa* means *lakin* ("but"). End of quotation. By "the two kinds differ" he means that the accusative of *tadhkirah* is a true accusative and not incidental, while the accusative in *li-tashqa* after the removal of the preposition is incidental. What we say is that *li-tashqa* has no position at all, so a substitution from it cannot be imagined.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that the meaning of "We sent down" (inna anzalna) to you [the Qur'an] is for the bearing of the hardships of conveying (the message) and of contending with the stubborn enemies of Islam, fighting them, and other kinds of burdens and duties of prophethood. And "We did not send down upon you" this burdensome, toilsome (Qur'an) "except" that it would be "a reminder" (tadhkira). On this interpretation, "a reminder" may be both a circumstantial accusative (hal) and an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), "for whoever fears" (liman yakhsha), meaning for whoever's affair ends in fear. End of quote. This is a far-fetched meaning, distant from the wording. Regarding "illa tadhkira" being a substitute (badal) for the position of "li-tashqa", this is the view of al-Zajjaj. Al-Nahhas said: This is a distant opinion, and Abu 'Ali rejected it on the grounds that a reminder is not a hardship. Al-Hawfi said: It is also possible that "tadhkira" is a substitute for "al-Qur'an", so that the Qur'an itself is the reminder. He and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a verbal noun (masdar), i.e., "but We reminded by it with a reminder." Abu al-Baqa' said: It is not permissible for it to be an object of purpose for the verb "anzalna" mentioned, because that verb has already transitively governed an object, namely "li-tashqa", and it does not govern another object of the same kind. End of quote. Fear (al-khashya) is what prompts faith and righteous deeds.

"Tanzilan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun of a deleted verb, i.e., "it was sent down, a sending down, from the One who created..." Al-Zamakhshari said: There are several possibilities for the accusative of "tanzilan": that it be a substitute for "tadhkira" if the latter is taken as a circumstantial accusative, but not if it is taken as an object of purpose, since a thing is not caused by itself; that it be governed by a hidden "nazala"; that it be governed by "anzalna", since the meaning of "ma anzalna ... illa tadhkira" is "We sent it down as a reminder"; that it be in the accusative of praise and specification; and that it be governed by "yakhsha" as a direct object, meaning: God sent it down as a reminder for whoever fears the sending down of God. This is a good meaning and clear grammar. End of quote. The better view is what we mentioned earlier, that it is accusative by a hidden "nazala". What al-Zamakhshari mentioned about its accusative being otherwise is far-fetched. As for the first, it makes "tadhkira" and "tanzilan" two circumstantial accusatives, and both are verbal nouns, and making a verbal noun a circumstantial accusative is not a regular practice. Moreover, the meaning of "tadhkira" is not the meaning of "tanzil", nor is "tanzil" a part of "tadhkira". If it is a substitute, it would be a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) according to the view of those who hold that the second includes the first, since the sending down includes the reminder and other things. As for his statement that the meaning of "ma anzalnahu illa tadhkira" is "anzalnahu tadhkira", this is not so, because the sense of restriction is lost in the phrase "anzalnahu tadhkira". As for its accusative by way of praise, it is distant. As for its accusative by "liman yakhsha", it is extremely distant, because "yakhsha" is the end of a verse and a closing rhyme, so it is not appropriate for "tanzil" to be the object of "yakhsha". His statement about it, "and this is a good meaning and clear grammar," is a non-Arabic idiom and a distance from grasping eloquence.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read "tanzilun" in the nominative, as "huwa" is implied, and this reading indicates that "yakhsha" is not connected to "tanzilun" and that it is disconnected from what precedes it. Its accusative is by an implied "nuzzila", as we mentioned. It is evident that it is connected to "tanzil", and it may be in the position of a qualifier, so it is connected to a deleted element. In the phrase "mimman khalaqa" there is exaltation and magnification of the status of the Qur'an, since its sending down is attributed to the One whose acts and attributes these are, and a belittling of what they worship, and an invitation to souls to reflect and consider. In "mimman khalaqa" there is also an iltifat (shift), since it moves from the first-person pronoun, which appears in "ma anzalnahu", to the third person, and this is part of the art of variation in speech, which is commendable because it does not remain in one pattern. The attribution of these qualities to the third-person form, and the exaltation through the attribution of sending down to the singular pronoun of the one magnifying himself, and then its attribution to the One specially characterized by the attributes of greatness, in which no one shares with Him, together achieve magnification from both aspects.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that "anzalna" is a quotation of the words of Jibril, peace be upon him, and the angels descending with him. End of quote. This is a far-fetched possibility; rather the apparent meaning is that it is a report from God, exalted is He, about Himself. "Al-'ula" is the plural of "al-'ulya", and describing "the heavens" as "high" is a proof of the greatness of the power of the One who originated them, since it is impossible for their like in height to exist from anyone other than Him, exalted is He. The apparent reading is that "al-Rahman" is nominative as the predicate of an implied subject, its estimate being "He is al-Rahman". Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is also possible that it is a substitute for the hidden pronoun in "khalaqa". End of quote. I hold that such a thing is not permissible, because a substitute takes the place of what it substitutes, and "al-Rahman" cannot take the place of the pronoun, since the pronoun refers back to "man", the relative, and "khalaqa" is the relative clause, and the linking element is the pronoun, so the noun cannot take its place for lack of a link. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that "al-Rahman" be nominative as a beginning (mubtada'), saying it would be a subject pointed to by its article as referring to "man khalaqa". It is narrated by Jinah ibn Hubaysh from some of them that he read "al-Rahmani" with a kasra. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a qualifier of "man khalaqa", meaning the relative "man". The view of the Kufans is that incomplete nouns which are not complete without their relative clauses, such as "man" and "ma", may not be described, except that "alladhi" and "allati" may be described, so they may be described. According to their view, "al-Rahman" cannot be a qualifier of "man". Therefore it is best that "al-Rahman" be a substitute for "man". "Al-Rahman" in the Qur'an has taken the course of a proper name in governing the operators. On the reading with a genitive, the estimate is "He 'ala al-'arshi istawa". On the nominative reading, if it is a substitute as Ibn 'Atiyya held, it is the same; or a beginning as al-Zamakhshari stated, then it is in the position of a predicate; or a predicate of an implied subject as is apparent, so "al-Rahman" and the sentence are two predicates of the hidden "huwa". This sentence has been discussed before in al-A'raf.

What is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, of stopping at "'ala al-'arshi" and then reading "istawa" and "lahu ma fi al-samawat" with "istawa" as its subject, is not valid, God willing.

When God, exalted is He, mentioned that He originated the heavens and the earth, and that He "istawa" over the Throne, He mentioned that to Him belongs the dominion of all that the heavens and earth contain, and what is between them, and what is beneath the soil (al-thara). That is, beneath the seventh earth. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b. From al-Suddi: it is the rock beneath the seventh earth. It was said: "wa ma tahta al-thara" means what is in the inner part of the earth, so this would be an emphasis of His saying "wa ma fi al-ard", unless by "fi al-ard" is meant what is upon it, in which case it is not an emphasis. It was said: the meaning is that His knowledge, exalted is He, encompasses all of that, because He is its originator. On this view the estimate is: to Him is the knowledge of what is in the heavens...

When God, exalted is He, first mentioned the origination of the heavens and the earth, and mentioned that all of that and what is in them is His dominion, He mentioned the attribute of knowledge, and that nothing is hidden from His knowledge. The address in His saying, "wa in tajhar bil-qawl" ("And if you speak aloud"), is to the Messenger apparently, or it is intended that his community is addressed. Since addressing people cannot be done except by speaking aloud, the condition was stated with raising the voice, and His knowledge of the secret was linked to the raising of the voice, because His knowledge of the secret includes His knowledge of the open; that is, if He knows the secret, it is more fitting that He knows the open. "The secret" (al-sirr) is the opposite of "the open," as He said, "He knows your secret and your open" [al-An'am: 3]. The apparent view is that "akhfa" is a comparative form, i.e., "and more hidden than the secret."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-sirr" is what you confide to another, and "al-akhfa" is what you conceal within yourself; this is also said by al-Farra'. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "al-sirr" is what one keeps in his soul, and "al-akhfa" is what is hidden from him of what he himself does and does not know. From Qatada: something close to this. Mujahid said: "al-sirr" is what you conceal from people, and "akhfa" than it is the whisper (al-waswasa). Ibn Zayd said: "al-sirr" is the secret of creatures, and more hidden than it is His own secret, exalted is He; al-Tabari rejected this. It was said: "al-sirr" is resolve, and more hidden than it is what has not occurred to the heart. Some of the early scholars held that His saying "wa akhfa" is a past-tense verb, not a comparative, meaning: "He knows the secrets of the servants and has concealed from them what He Himself knows," like His saying: "He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not encompass anything of His knowledge" [al-Baqara: 255], and His saying: "and they do not encompass Him in knowledge" [Ta-Ha: 110]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is weak.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is not as they say. He said: If you ask, how does the response match the condition? I say: its meaning is, if you raise your voice with the remembrance of God, whether by supplication or otherwise, know that He is free of need for your raising it. Either it is a prohibition from raising the voice, like His saying: "and remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and in fear, and without loudness of speech" [al-A'raf: 205], or it is an instruction to the servants that raising the voice is not for God's hearing, but is for some other purpose. End of quote.

"Allah" is the subject, and "la ilaha illa Huwa" is the predicate, and "lahu al-asma' al-husna" is a second predicate. It is also possible that it is the predicate of an implied subject, as if it were said: "Who is it who knows the secret and what is more hidden?" It is said: "He is Allah." "Al-husna" is the feminine form of "al-ahsan", and a feminine singular adjective may be used with a broken plural, and what made this acceptable is that these names came as closing rhymes. The superlative quality (al-ahsaniyya) lies in their including meanings that are at the utmost of goodness, of sanctity, of magnificence, and of lordship, and acts that cannot proceed except from Him. They mentioned that these are the names concerning which the Messenger of God said: "Indeed God has ninety-nine names; whoever counts them enters Paradise." At-Tirmidhi related it with a chain of narration.

**Surah Ta-Ha, peace be upon him, 135 verses, Meccan**

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

(p-222) ﴿Ta-Ha.﴾ ﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you to make you wretched,﴾ ﴿but as a reminder to those who fear,﴾ ﴿a revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens.﴾ ﴿The Most Merciful sat Himself upon the Throne.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens, whatever is on the earth, whatever is between them, and whatever is beneath the soil.﴾ ﴿And if you speak aloud, He knows the secret and what is more hidden.﴾ ﴿God, there is no god but Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ ﴿When he saw a fire and said to his family, "Stay here, for I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I will bring you a brand from it, or find guidance at the fire."﴾ ﴿Then when he came to it, he was called: "O Moses!"﴾ ﴿"I am your Lord, so take off your sandals. You are in the sacred valley of Tuwa."﴾ ﴿"And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed."﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I am God. There is no god but Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance."﴾ ﴿"The Hour is coming. I am almost concealing it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for."﴾ ﴿"So do not let one who does not believe in it and follows his desires turn you away from it, lest you perish."﴾ ﴿"And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?"﴾ ﴿He said, "It is my staff. I lean on it, beat down leaves for my sheep with it, and I have other uses for it."﴾ ﴿He said, "Throw it down, O Moses."﴾ ﴿So he threw it, and suddenly it was a moving serpent.﴾ ﴿He said, "Take hold of it and do not fear. We will return it to its original form."﴾ ﴿"And draw your hand to your side; it will come out white without harm, as another sign,"﴾ ﴿"so that We may show you some of Our greatest signs."﴾ ﴿"Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, expand my chest for me,﴾ ﴿and make my affair easy for me,﴾ ﴿and untie the knot from my tongue,﴾ ﴿that they may understand my speech,﴾ ﴿and appoint for me a minister from my family:﴾ ﴿Aaron, my brother.﴾ ﴿Strengthen my back through him,﴾ ﴿and make him a partner in my task,﴾ ﴿that we may glorify You much﴾ ﴿and remember You much,﴾ ﴿for You are ever Seeing of us."﴾ ﴿He said, "You have been granted your request, O Moses."﴾ ﴿And We had already bestowed favour upon you another time,﴾ ﴿when We inspired your mother with what is inspired:﴾ ﴿"Place him in the chest, then cast it into the river, and let the river throw it onto the bank, where an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his will take him." And I cast upon you love from Me, so that you might be reared under My eye.﴾ ﴿When your sister walked and said, "Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?" So We returned you to your mother, that her eye might be refreshed and she would not grieve. And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress and tested you with many trials.﴾ (p-223)

*Al-thara* (الثَّرى): moist earth, and its dual is *tharayan*. It is said *tharraytu al-turbata* (ثَرَّيْتُ التُّرْبَةَ), meaning I moistened the soil. *Thariya al-ardu tathra tharan* (ثَرِيَتِ الأرْضُ تَثْرى ثَرًى) means the land became moist after dryness, so it is *thariyyah*. *Athrat* (أثْرَتْ) means the soil became abundant, so it is *muthriyah*. And a land is *tharan*, meaning possessing moist soil. Ibn al-A'rabi said: it is said that "so-and-so is near to *al-thara* and far from *al-nabt*," referring to one who promises and does not fulfil. It is also said: "I see the *thara* of anger in the face of so-and-so," meaning its trace. It is also said: "*al-thara* is between me and so-and-so," when the connection between you two has been cut off. Jarir said:

*So do not dig up between me and you the moist earth; indeed, what is between me and you is enriching.*

*Anasa* (آنَسَ): to find. The Arabs say: "Did you *anasta* so-and-so?" meaning did you find him. It is also said it means to sense, which is close to finding. Al-Harith ibn Hillizah said:

*I perceived a sign, and a hunter startled it, in the afternoon when evening had drawn near.*

*Al-qabas* (القَبَسُ): a burning ember of fire that is placed on the top of a stick, reed, or the like. It is a verbal noun in the sense of an object, like *al-qabd* and *al-nafd*. It is said: *qabastu minhu naran, aqbisu*, and *faqbasani* means he gave me a *qabas* from it. From this comes *al-muqbasah*, that in which a brand is carried, from a potsherd or other things. And *iqtabastu minhu naran* and *ilman*, meaning I acquired it. Al-Mubarrad said: *aqbastu al-rajula ilman* and *qabastuhu naran*. Al-Kisa'i said: *aqbastuhu naran* and *ilman*, and I also used *qabastuhu* for both.

*Al-khal'* (الخَلْعُ) and *al-na'l* (النَّعْلُ) are both known; the former is removing the latter from the foot. It is said: *al-na'l* is that which protects the foot from the ground, whether made of leather, iron, wood, or something else.

*Tuwa* (طُوًى): the name of a place.

*Al-sa'y* (السَّعْيُ): walking quickly, and it may also be used for work.

*Radiya yardaa radan* (رَدِيَ يَرْدى رَدًى) means he perished, and *ardahu* means he destroyed him. Duraid ibn al-Simmah said:

*They called out and said, "The horses have destroyed a horseman!" So I said, "I seek refuge in God from that destruction."*

*Tawakka'a ala al-shay'* (تَوَكَّأ عَلى الشَّيْءِ) means he leaned heavily upon it while walking or standing, and from it comes *al-ittika'*. *Tawakka'tu* and *ittaka'tu* have the same meaning. This root was already mentioned in Surah Yusuf in the words ﴿*muttaka'an*﴾ (Yusuf: 31), and it is explained here because the two patterns differ, although the root is one.

*Hashsha ala al-ghanam* (هَشَّ عَلى الغَنَمِ), in the form *yahushshu* with a *damma* on the *ha'*, means he beat the leaves of the tree so that they would fall. *Hashsha ila al-rajul*, in the form *yahisshu* with a *kasra*, as Tha'lab said, means he welcomed him and showed joy towards him. The basic meaning of this root is softness; it is said: *rajul hashsh*, a gentle man. *Al-ghanam* (الغَنَمُ) is known; it is a collective noun and feminine.

*Al-ma'ribah* (المَأْرُبَةُ), with a *damma*, *fatha*, or *kasra* on the *ra'*, means need, and its plural is *ma'arib*. *Al-irbah* also means need.

*Al-hayyah* (الحَيَّةُ): the snake. It applies to the male and female, the small and the large. Its root was mentioned earlier, and it is repeated here because of the specific meaning intended. The saying of people, *hawwa'* for one who catches snakes, is from the pattern of *huwwah*; the two roots are different, like *sibt* and *sibatr*.

*Al-azr* (الأزْرُ): the back, as al-Khalil said. Abu 'Ubayd said: *azarahu* means he strengthened him. *Al-azr* also means strength. The poet said:

*With a bow-shaped land whose vegetation has strengthened the straying plants, passing by armies that are victorious and defeated.*

(p-223) *Al-qadhf* (القَذْفُ): throwing and casting. *Al-sahil* (السّاحِلُ): the shore of the sea, which is its side free of water. It is so named because the water *yasḥaluhu*, that is, peels it off, so it is an active participle in the sense of a passive. Abu Tammam said:

*It is the sea, from whichever direction you come to it: its depth is the known and its shore is generosity.*

* *

(In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Ta-Ha.﴾ ﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you to make you wretched,﴾ ﴿but as a reminder to those who fear,﴾ ﴿a revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens.﴾ ﴿The Most Merciful sat Himself upon the Throne.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens, whatever is on the earth, whatever is between them, and whatever is beneath the soil.﴾ ﴿And if you speak aloud, He knows the secret and what is more hidden.﴾ ﴿God, there is no god but Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾)

This surah is Meccan without disagreement. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to stand on one foot, alternating between his two feet while praying, and this verse was revealed. This is what Ali said. Al-Dahhak said: The Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions prayed, and he prolonged the standing when the Qur'an was revealed to him. The Quraysh then said: "It was revealed to him only to make him wretched." Muqatil said: Abu Jahl, al-Nadr, and al-Mut'im said: "You are indeed wretched by abandoning our religion," so this verse was revealed.

The connection of this surah with the end of the preceding one is that when God mentioned the facilitation of the Qur'an in the language of the Messenger (ﷺ), that is, in his tongue, and among the reasons given was His saying ﴿*that you may give good news thereby to the pious and warn thereby a people contentious*﴾ (Maryam: 97), He confirmed this with His saying ﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you to make you wretched,﴾ ﴿but as a reminder to those who fear.﴾ The *tadhkirah* (التَّذْكِرَةُ, reminder) is good news and warning. What the polytheists claimed, that it was sent down for wretchedness, is not so; rather it was sent down only as a reminder.

Apparently ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ belongs to the disjoined letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah), like *Ya-Sin*, *Alif-Lam-Ra*, and similar ones. This matter was discussed at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

From Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', and 'Ikrimah, the meaning of ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ is "O man." It is said this is in Nabataean, it is said in Abyssinian, and it is said in Hebrew. It is said it is a Yemeni dialect of 'Akk, and it is said of 'Ukl. Al-Kalbi said: If you say to a man of 'Akk, "O man," he will not respond until you say "Ta-Ha." Al-Suddi said the meaning of ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ is "O so-and-so." Al-Tabari cited, for the meaning "O man" in the dialect of 'Akk, the words of one of their poets:

*I called "Ta-Ha" in battle, but he did not respond, so I feared for him that he would be turning away.*

And the words of another:

*Indeed, folly is "Ta-Ha" among your traits; may God not bless the cursed people.*

It is also said it is one of the names of the Messenger, and it is said it is one of the names of God. Al-Zamakhshari said: Perhaps 'Akk altered *ya hadha* (يا هَذا, "O this one") in their speech, as if they in their dialect changed the *ya* into *ta*, saying *ya-ta*, and they abbreviated this and limited it to *ha*. The trace of this artifice is evident and not hidden in the verse cited as evidence:

*Indeed, folly is "Ta-Ha" among your traits; may God not sanctify the morals of the cursed people.*

End of quotation. It had been mentioned earlier that it is said that *taha* in the dialect of 'Akk means "O man," and then he made a conjecture about 'Akk with what no grammarian would say: that they changed the *ya* into *ta*. This does not occur in the language of the Arabs, changing *ya*, the vocative particle, into *ta*, and likewise omitting the demonstrative in the vocative and retaining the particle of attention. It is also said: *ta* is an imperative verb whose root is *ta'*, and the hamza was lightened by changing it into an *alif*, and *ha* is the object, referring to the earth, meaning: "Tread the earth with your two feet and do not alternate," since he used to alternate until his feet swelled. A group including al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Abu Hanifah, and Warsh in his chosen reading recited ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ with the *ha* pronounced. It is said its original form was *ta'* and the hamza was dropped on the basis of its change in *yata'u*, in the manner of *la hunaka al-martaʿu buniya al-amru 'alayhi*; the silent *ha* was added, and continuity was treated as pausing. Or its original form was *ta'*, and its hamza was changed into a *ha*, so it became ﴿Ta-Ha﴾. 'Amr ibn Fa'id and al-Dahhak recited *Ta-wi*.

Talhah recited *ma nuzzila 'alayka*, with a *nun* bearing a *damma* and a *zay* bearing a *kasra* with a *shaddah*, in the passive voice, and *al-Qur'an* in the nominative. The majority recited ﴿*ma anzalna ʿalayka al-Qur'an*﴾. The meaning of ﴿*li-tashqa*﴾ is: "that you may be exhausted through excessive grief over them and over their disbelief, and be distressed that they should believe," as in His saying ﴿*Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief*﴾ (al-Shu'ara': 3). *Al-shaqa'* (الشَّقاءُ) comes in the sense of fatigue, and from it the proverb: "More tired than a breaker of a colt, and more wretched than a breaker of a colt." Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, nothing is upon you except to convey and remind, and it is not decreed upon you that they must believe, after you have not fallen short in delivering the message and the good exhortation. It is also said that what is intended is the refutation of what Abu Jahl and others said, mentioned earlier in the account of the occasion of revelation.

*Li-tashqa* and *tadhkirah* are a reason for the phrase ﴿*ma anzalna*﴾. The preposition *li-* is used with *li-tashqa* because the agent differs: the subject of ﴿*ma anzalna*﴾ is God, and the subject of *li-tashqa* is the Messenger (ﷺ). But since the agent in ﴿*anzalna*﴾ and ﴿*tadhkirah*﴾ is one, for *tadhkirah* is the verbal noun of *dhakkara*, and the one who reminds is God, who is also the one who sent it down, the verb is transitive to it and it is put in the accusative. There is disagreement over whether the agent must be one, and the majority require it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, is it not permissible to say, "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you should be wretched," like His saying ﴿*lest your deeds be voided*﴾ (al-Hujurat: 2)? I say: Yes, but it is an incidental accusative (*nasbah tari'ah*), like the accusative in ﴿*and Moses chose his people*﴾ (al-A'raf: 155). As for the accusative in ﴿*tadhkirah*﴾, it is like that in *darabtu Zaydan*, because it is one of the five objects, which are fundamental and the rules for others. End of quotation.

It is not agreed that when the preposition is omitted, *an tashqa* is in the accusative. Rather there is disagreement on this: is it in the accusative, with the verb transitive to it after dropping the particle, or is it in the genitive by dropping the preposition while retaining its governance?

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿*illa tadhkirah*﴾ may be in the accusative as a substitution (*badal*) for the position of ﴿*li-tashqa*﴾, and it may be in the accusative by supposing a verb whose estimate is: "But We sent it down as a reminder." End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari rejected Ibn 'Atiyyah's first analysis, saying: If you say, can *tadhkirah* be a substitute for the position of *li-tashqa*? I say: No, because the two kinds differ; but it is in the accusative as an exception that is disconnected (*istithna' munqati'*), in which *illa* means *lakin* ("but"). End of quotation. By "the two kinds differ" he means that the accusative of *tadhkirah* is a true accusative and not incidental, while the accusative in *li-tashqa* after the removal of the preposition is incidental. What we say is that *li-tashqa* has no position at all, so a substitution from it cannot be imagined.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that the meaning of "We sent down" (inna anzalna) to you [the Qur'an] is for the bearing of the hardships of conveying (the message) and of contending with the stubborn enemies of Islam, fighting them, and other kinds of burdens and duties of prophethood. And "We did not send down upon you" this burdensome, toilsome (Qur'an) "except" that it would be "a reminder" (tadhkira). On this interpretation, "a reminder" may be both a circumstantial accusative (hal) and an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), "for whoever fears" (liman yakhsha), meaning for whoever's affair ends in fear. End of quote. This is a far-fetched meaning, distant from the wording. Regarding "illa tadhkira" being a substitute (badal) for the position of "li-tashqa", this is the view of al-Zajjaj. Al-Nahhas said: This is a distant opinion, and Abu 'Ali rejected it on the grounds that a reminder is not a hardship. Al-Hawfi said: It is also possible that "tadhkira" is a substitute for "al-Qur'an", so that the Qur'an itself is the reminder. He and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a verbal noun (masdar), i.e., "but We reminded by it with a reminder." Abu al-Baqa' said: It is not permissible for it to be an object of purpose for the verb "anzalna" mentioned, because that verb has already transitively governed an object, namely "li-tashqa", and it does not govern another object of the same kind. End of quote. Fear (al-khashya) is what prompts faith and righteous deeds.

"Tanzilan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun of a deleted verb, i.e., "it was sent down, a sending down, from the One who created..." Al-Zamakhshari said: There are several possibilities for the accusative of "tanzilan": that it be a substitute for "tadhkira" if the latter is taken as a circumstantial accusative, but not if it is taken as an object of purpose, since a thing is not caused by itself; that it be governed by a hidden "nazala"; that it be governed by "anzalna", since the meaning of "ma anzalna ... illa tadhkira" is "We sent it down as a reminder"; that it be in the accusative of praise and specification; and that it be governed by "yakhsha" as a direct object, meaning: God sent it down as a reminder for whoever fears the sending down of God. This is a good meaning and clear grammar. End of quote. The better view is what we mentioned earlier, that it is accusative by a hidden "nazala". What al-Zamakhshari mentioned about its accusative being otherwise is far-fetched. As for the first, it makes "tadhkira" and "tanzilan" two circumstantial accusatives, and both are verbal nouns, and making a verbal noun a circumstantial accusative is not a regular practice. Moreover, the meaning of "tadhkira" is not the meaning of "tanzil", nor is "tanzil" a part of "tadhkira". If it is a substitute, it would be a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) according to the view of those who hold that the second includes the first, since the sending down includes the reminder and other things. As for his statement that the meaning of "ma anzalnahu illa tadhkira" is "anzalnahu tadhkira", this is not so, because the sense of restriction is lost in the phrase "anzalnahu tadhkira". As for its accusative by way of praise, it is distant. As for its accusative by "liman yakhsha", it is extremely distant, because "yakhsha" is the end of a verse and a closing rhyme, so it is not appropriate for "tanzil" to be the object of "yakhsha". His statement about it, "and this is a good meaning and clear grammar," is a non-Arabic idiom and a distance from grasping eloquence.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read "tanzilun" in the nominative, as "huwa" is implied, and this reading indicates that "yakhsha" is not connected to "tanzilun" and that it is disconnected from what precedes it. Its accusative is by an implied "nuzzila", as we mentioned. It is evident that it is connected to "tanzil", and it may be in the position of a qualifier, so it is connected to a deleted element. In the phrase "mimman khalaqa" there is exaltation and magnification of the status of the Qur'an, since its sending down is attributed to the One whose acts and attributes these are, and a belittling of what they worship, and an invitation to souls to reflect and consider. In "mimman khalaqa" there is also an iltifat (shift), since it moves from the first-person pronoun, which appears in "ma anzalnahu", to the third person, and this is part of the art of variation in speech, which is commendable because it does not remain in one pattern. The attribution of these qualities to the third-person form, and the exaltation through the attribution of sending down to the singular pronoun of the one magnifying himself, and then its attribution to the One specially characterized by the attributes of greatness, in which no one shares with Him, together achieve magnification from both aspects.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that "anzalna" is a quotation of the words of Jibril, peace be upon him, and the angels descending with him. End of quote. This is a far-fetched possibility; rather the apparent meaning is that it is a report from God, exalted is He, about Himself. "Al-'ula" is the plural of "al-'ulya", and describing "the heavens" as "high" is a proof of the greatness of the power of the One who originated them, since it is impossible for their like in height to exist from anyone other than Him, exalted is He. The apparent reading is that "al-Rahman" is nominative as the predicate of an implied subject, its estimate being "He is al-Rahman". Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is also possible that it is a substitute for the hidden pronoun in "khalaqa". End of quote. I hold that such a thing is not permissible, because a substitute takes the place of what it substitutes, and "al-Rahman" cannot take the place of the pronoun, since the pronoun refers back to "man", the relative, and "khalaqa" is the relative clause, and the linking element is the pronoun, so the noun cannot take its place for lack of a link. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that "al-Rahman" be nominative as a beginning (mubtada'), saying it would be a subject pointed to by its article as referring to "man khalaqa". It is narrated by Jinah ibn Hubaysh from some of them that he read "al-Rahmani" with a kasra. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a qualifier of "man khalaqa", meaning the relative "man". The view of the Kufans is that incomplete nouns which are not complete without their relative clauses, such as "man" and "ma", may not be described, except that "alladhi" and "allati" may be described, so they may be described. According to their view, "al-Rahman" cannot be a qualifier of "man". Therefore it is best that "al-Rahman" be a substitute for "man". "Al-Rahman" in the Qur'an has taken the course of a proper name in governing the operators. On the reading with a genitive, the estimate is "He 'ala al-'arshi istawa". On the nominative reading, if it is a substitute as Ibn 'Atiyya held, it is the same; or a beginning as al-Zamakhshari stated, then it is in the position of a predicate; or a predicate of an implied subject as is apparent, so "al-Rahman" and the sentence are two predicates of the hidden "huwa". This sentence has been discussed before in al-A'raf.

What is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, of stopping at "'ala al-'arshi" and then reading "istawa" and "lahu ma fi al-samawat" with "istawa" as its subject, is not valid, God willing.

When God, exalted is He, mentioned that He originated the heavens and the earth, and that He "istawa" over the Throne, He mentioned that to Him belongs the dominion of all that the heavens and earth contain, and what is between them, and what is beneath the soil (al-thara). That is, beneath the seventh earth. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b. From al-Suddi: it is the rock beneath the seventh earth. It was said: "wa ma tahta al-thara" means what is in the inner part of the earth, so this would be an emphasis of His saying "wa ma fi al-ard", unless by "fi al-ard" is meant what is upon it, in which case it is not an emphasis. It was said: the meaning is that His knowledge, exalted is He, encompasses all of that, because He is its originator. On this view the estimate is: to Him is the knowledge of what is in the heavens...

When God, exalted is He, first mentioned the origination of the heavens and the earth, and mentioned that all of that and what is in them is His dominion, He mentioned the attribute of knowledge, and that nothing is hidden from His knowledge. The address in His saying, "wa in tajhar bil-qawl" ("And if you speak aloud"), is to the Messenger apparently, or it is intended that his community is addressed. Since addressing people cannot be done except by speaking aloud, the condition was stated with raising the voice, and His knowledge of the secret was linked to the raising of the voice, because His knowledge of the secret includes His knowledge of the open; that is, if He knows the secret, it is more fitting that He knows the open. "The secret" (al-sirr) is the opposite of "the open," as He said, "He knows your secret and your open" [al-An'am: 3]. The apparent view is that "akhfa" is a comparative form, i.e., "and more hidden than the secret."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-sirr" is what you confide to another, and "al-akhfa" is what you conceal within yourself; this is also said by al-Farra'. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "al-sirr" is what one keeps in his soul, and "al-akhfa" is what is hidden from him of what he himself does and does not know. From Qatada: something close to this. Mujahid said: "al-sirr" is what you conceal from people, and "akhfa" than it is the whisper (al-waswasa). Ibn Zayd said: "al-sirr" is the secret of creatures, and more hidden than it is His own secret, exalted is He; al-Tabari rejected this. It was said: "al-sirr" is resolve, and more hidden than it is what has not occurred to the heart. Some of the early scholars held that His saying "wa akhfa" is a past-tense verb, not a comparative, meaning: "He knows the secrets of the servants and has concealed from them what He Himself knows," like His saying: "He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not encompass anything of His knowledge" [al-Baqara: 255], and His saying: "and they do not encompass Him in knowledge" [Ta-Ha: 110]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is weak.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is not as they say. He said: If you ask, how does the response match the condition? I say: its meaning is, if you raise your voice with the remembrance of God, whether by supplication or otherwise, know that He is free of need for your raising it. Either it is a prohibition from raising the voice, like His saying: "and remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and in fear, and without loudness of speech" [al-A'raf: 205], or it is an instruction to the servants that raising the voice is not for God's hearing, but is for some other purpose. End of quote.

"Allah" is the subject, and "la ilaha illa Huwa" is the predicate, and "lahu al-asma' al-husna" is a second predicate. It is also possible that it is the predicate of an implied subject, as if it were said: "Who is it who knows the secret and what is more hidden?" It is said: "He is Allah." "Al-husna" is the feminine form of "al-ahsan", and a feminine singular adjective may be used with a broken plural, and what made this acceptable is that these names came as closing rhymes. The superlative quality (al-ahsaniyya) lies in their including meanings that are at the utmost of goodness, of sanctity, of magnificence, and of lordship, and acts that cannot proceed except from Him. They mentioned that these are the names concerning which the Messenger of God said: "Indeed God has ninety-nine names; whoever counts them enters Paradise." At-Tirmidhi related it with a chain of narration.

[p. 228] ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you? When he saw a fire and said to his family, "Stay here. I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I can bring you a burning brand from it, or find guidance at the fire." When he came to it, he was called: "O Moses! Indeed I am your Lord, so take off your sandals; you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa. I have chosen you, so listen to what is being revealed. Indeed I am God; there is no god but Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance. Indeed the Hour is coming; I am almost keeping it hidden, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for. So do not let one who does not believe in it and follows his own desire turn you away from it, lest you perish. And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?" He said, "It is my staff; I lean on it, beat down leaves with it for my sheep, and it has other uses for me." He said, "Throw it down, O Moses." So he threw it down, and suddenly it was a moving serpent. He said, "Take it and do not fear; We will return it to its original form. And draw your hand to your side; it will come out white, without harm, as another sign, so that We may show you some of Our greatest signs. Go to Pharaoh; indeed he has transgressed."﴾

[p. 229] When the Exalted (ta'ala) mentioned the glorification of His Book and this included the glorification of His Messenger, He followed it with the story of Moses, so that (the Prophet) might take him as an example in bearing the burdens of prophethood, the duties of the mission, and patience in enduring hardships, as the Exalted said: ﴿And We relate to you from the news of the messengers that with it We strengthen your heart﴾ [Hud: 120]. Then He said: ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ This is a rhetorical question (istifham taqrir) that urges attentiveness to what is being conveyed to him and urges following his example. It has been said that "hal" here means "qad" (indeed), i.e., "Indeed the story has reached you," but the apparent meaning is contrary to this, since the surah is Meccan. The apparent meaning is that he had not been informed of the story of Moses before this. It has also been said that it is an interrogative with the meaning of negation: that is, "We did not inform you of the story of Moses before this surah, and now We are relating his story to you so that you may be consoled and take him as an example." Among his story is that when he (peace be upon him) had fulfilled the more complete of the two terms, he asked Shu'ayb for permission to return from Madyan to Egypt to visit his mother and sister, and he granted him permission. The duration of his offense in Egypt had been long, and he hoped that his affair would be forgotten. So he set out with his family and property, and it was in the winter season. He took a route other than the usual one, fearing the kings of the Levant. His wife was pregnant, and he did not know whether she would give birth by night or by day. So he traveled in the wilderness without knowing its paths, and the journey drove him to the side of the western, right-hand slope of Mount Sinai (al-Tur) on a dark, frosty night, extremely cold. His wife went into labor, and he struck his firestarter but it did not produce fire. It has been said that he was a jealous man who would accompany the caravan at night and separate from them by day, so that his wife would not be seen; thus he lost the way.

Wahb said: a son was born to him on the road, and when his firestarter failed to produce a spark, he ﴿saw a fire﴾. The apparent meaning is that "idh" (when) is a temporal adverb related to the narration, because it is a narrative. Al-Zamakhshari (al-Zamakhshari) permitted that it be an adverb of an implied verb, meaning: "a fire, which was such-and-such." He also permitted that it be an object of "udhkur" (remember) implied. As for "﴿Stay here﴾," it means: remain in your place. He addressed his wife, his two sons, and the servant. Al-A'mash, Talha, Hamza, and Nafi' in one narration read ﴿li-ahlihi mkthu﴾ with a ḍamma on the ha' (li-ahlihi-) and likewise in al-Qasas, while the majority read it with a kasra. ﴿Indeed I have perceived (anastu)﴾ means: I sensed. The fire was at a distance and could only be perceived by sight, so some of them interpreted it as "I saw." The verb "ānasa" is more general than "seeing," because you say: "I perceived (ānastu) good from so-and-so." Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-Ins" is clear sight free of any doubt, and from it comes "insan al-'ayn" (the pupil of the eye), because by it a thing is clearly distinguished; and "al-Ins" (humankind) for their being visible, just as "al-Jinn" (jinn) is named for their being hidden. It has been said: it is the perception of something one is comforted by, since that comfort was found from it; so it was certain and definite. He confirmed it for them with the word "inna" in order to settle their hearts. Since bringing a burning brand and finding guidance were expected and anticipated, he framed the matter concerning them on hope and desire, and said "la'alla" (perhaps), and did not state it definitively by saying "I will come to you," so as not to promise what he was not certain he could fulfill. End quote. The apparent meaning is that he really saw light.

Al-Mawardi said: it was a fire to Moses, and it was light to God. It has been said: it was imagined to him that it was a fire. It has been said: this is not permissible, because reporting something that does not correspond to reality is not permissible for prophets, peace be upon them. The word ﴿ʿalā﴾ here is in its original sense of elevation (isti'la'), and its meaning is that the people of the fire ascend the place near it; or because those who warm themselves by it and benefit from it, when they surround it standing and sitting, are overlooking it. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"The dew and the ḥallaq (bird) spent the night upon the fire."

Ibn al-Anbari said: "ʿalā" has the meaning of "ʿinda" (at), and the meaning of "maʿa" (with), and the meaning of "bi" (by). Al-Zajjaj mentioned that he had lost his way to water, so he hoped to meet someone who would guide him on the road or show him the water. ﴿Guidance (hudan)﴾ is in the accusative as a direct object by an implied omitted element, meaning: bearing guidance; or by an implied omitted element, because when the guide is found, guidance—the guidance of the road—has been found. It has been said: "hudan" refers to guidance in religion, said by Mujahid and Qatada, but this is far-fetched, though he sought one who would guide him to the road, he had also found guidance in the absolute sense.

The pronoun in ﴿atāhā﴾ refers to the fire. He came to it and found it blazing in a green, luxuriant tree of jujube (unnab), as said by Ibn ʿAbbas. It has been said: it was a sumrah (acacia) tree, said by ʿAbd Allah. It has been said: it was a ʿawsaj (boxthorn), said by Wahb. It has been said: it was an ʿulayqa (a thorny shrub), from Qatada, Muqatil, and al-Kalbi. Whenever he approached it, it withdrew from him, and when he turned back, it followed him. So he became certain that this was one of God's matters that break habit. He stood bewildered, heard the glorification of the angels from heaven, tranquility (sakina) was cast upon him, and he ﴿was called﴾, and this was God's speaking to him. The majority read ﴿Innī﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, according to the Basrans, by implying "saying" (al-qawl), and according to the Kufans, by treating the calling as speech, since it is a kind of speech. ﴿Anā﴾ is a subject, or a separating pronoun (fasl), or an emphatic for the accusative pronoun. In these grammatical constructions the sentence is formed to affirm knowledge and remove doubt. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿annī﴾ with a fatha on the hamza, and the apparent sense is that the supposition is "bi-annī anā rabbuka" (that I am your Lord). Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is in the sense of "li-ajli" (because of) that "Indeed I am your Lord, so take off your sandals," and "nūdiya" (was called) may be connected by a preposition. Abu ʿAli recited:

"I called by the name of Rabi'a ibn Mukaddam, indeed the one renowned by his name is trustworthy."

End quote. His knowledge that the one who called him was God, the Exalted, came to him either by necessity, through a creation from Him, or by reasoning from the miracle. For the Mu'tazila, this is only possible through the miracle; some of them specified it, and some said: it is not necessary that he know what that miracle is. They said: it is not permissible that it be by necessary knowledge, because that conflicts with the obligation (taklif). The apparent sense is that God's command to him to remove his sandals was due to the greatness of the situation in which he found himself, just as shoes are removed before kings, as the utmost humility. It has been said: they were made of the skin of a dead donkey, so he was commanded to throw them away because they were impure. In al-Tirmidhi, from the Prophet ﴿ﷺ﴾ who said: "Moses, on the day his Lord spoke to him, wore a woolen cloak, a woolen robe, a woolen cap, and woolen trousers, and his sandals were of the skin of a dead donkey." He said: this is a gharib (strange, single-chain) hadith. The "kumma" is a small skullcap. That they were of the skin of a dead donkey, not tanned, is the view of ʿIkrima, Qatada, al-Suddi, Muqatil, al-Kalbi, and al-Dahhak. It has been said: they were of the skin of a slaughtered cow, but he was commanded to take them off to show the blessing of the sacred valley, and so that his feet would touch its soil. It is narrated that he removed his sandals and threw them behind the valley. ﴿Al-Muqaddas﴾ means purified, and ﴿Tuwa﴾ is the proper name of the place, so it is either an appositive (badal) or an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayān).

Al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu al-Sammal, and Ibn Muhayṣ read it with a kasra on the ṭa' with tanwin. The Kufans and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a ḍamma with tanwin. The two men of Haram (Mecca and Medina) and Abu ʿAmr read it with a ḍamma without tanwin. Abu Zayd, on the authority of Abu ʿAmr, read it with a kasra without tanwin. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar and al-Dahhak read "ṭāwī idhhab." Whoever reads with tanwin takes it as referring to a place. Whoever does not use tanwin and puts a ḍamma on the ṭa' may consider it a word deflected from a verb-form such as "Zufar" and "Quthan," or a non-Arabic name, or in the sense of a region. Whoever reads with a kasra and no tanwin, prevents its declension considering it a place. Al-Hasan said: ﴿Tuwa﴾ with a kasra on the ṭa' and tanwin is a verbal noun in which blessing and sanctification were repeated twice; so it is in the pattern of "al-thana'" (praise), and in meaning. This is because "al-thina" with a kasra and short vowel is the thing you repeat, and likewise "al-ṭuwa" in this reading. Qutrub said: ﴿Tuwa﴾ is from "al-layl" (night), meaning an hour, that is, it was sanctified for you during an hour of the night, because he was called at night, so the valley acquired a definite sanctification, that is: "Indeed you are in the sacred valley" at night. Talha, al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Layla, Hamza, and Khalaf in his choice read ﴿akhtartuka﴾ with ... As for reading with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the nun, "ikhtarnāka" with the "we" of majesty.

Al-Sulami, Ibn Hurmuz, and al-A'mash in one narration read "wa-innā" with a conjunction ʿaṭf upon "innī anā rabbuka," because they also used a kasra there; the majority read ﴿wa-anā ikhtartuka﴾ with the first-person singular pronoun, not referring to Himself with majesty. Ubayy read "wa-annī" with a fatha on the hamza and the first-person yā', with ﴿ikhtartuka﴾ in the first person coordinated upon "innī anā rabbuka." The second object of ﴿ikhtartuka﴾, to which it is transitive by "min" (from), is omitted, its estimated meaning being "from your people." The apparent sense is that ﴿limā yūḥā﴾ is connected to "istamiʿ," and "mā" is in the sense of "alladhī" (that which).

Al-Zamakhshari and others said: ﴿limā yūḥā﴾ means "for that which is revealed" or "for the revelation," so he attached the lam to "istamiʿ" or to "ikhtartuka." End quote. Attaching it to "ikhtartuka" is not permissible, because it falls under the category of "al-aʿmāl" (the governance of two verbs over one object), and so it is required, or preferred, to repeat the pronoun with the second verb; it would have been "fa-istamiʿ lahu limā yūḥā," which shows that the governing verb is the second one.

Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari said: when it was said to Moses, may God's blessings be upon our Prophet and upon him: "listen to what is revealed," he stood upon a stone, leaned against a stone, placed his right hand upon his left, laid his chin upon his chest, and stood to listen; all his clothing was wool. Wahb said: the etiquette of listening is: stillness of the limbs, lowering the gaze, attentive hearing, presence of mind, and resolve to act. That is the listening to what God loves. The agent in "yūḥā" is omitted because it is known, and its being the closing word (fāṣila) beautifies it; had it been in the active voice, it would not have been a closing word. The revealed content is His saying: ﴿Indeed I am God﴾ [al-Qasas: 30] to the end. Its meaning is: make Me one (monotheize Me), like His saying: ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56] to the end of the sentences. This came as a clarification and explanation of the ambiguity in His saying ﴿what is revealed﴾. The commentators said: ﴿fa-ʿbudnī﴾ here means "make Me one," like His saying: ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they worship Me﴾, meaning "that they monotheize Me." The better view is that ﴿fa-ʿbudnī﴾ is a term encompassing whatever He obligated him to of worship; then there was joined to it what may fall within that general sense, so He began with prayer, since it is the best of deeds and the most beneficial in the Hereafter. The word "dhikr" (remembrance) is a verbal noun, which may be annexed to the agent, meaning: "that He may remember me," for My remembrance is that I be worshipped and prayed to; or "that he may remember Me in it," because prayer includes remembrances (adhkar); or because "I have mentioned it in the Books and commanded it." It may also be annexed to the object, meaning: "that I may remember you with praise and commendation and make for you a tongue of truthfulness," or "that you may remember Me exclusively, not mixing mention of others with it," or "the pure remembrance of Me and the seeking of My face, that you not show off by it and not intend by it another purpose," or "that you may be one who remembers Me, not forgetful, doing what the sincere do in keeping their Lord's remembrance in mind and devoting their resolves and thoughts to Him," as He said: ﴿Neither commerce nor trade distracts them from the remembrance of God﴾ [al-Nur: 37]; or "for the times of My remembrance," which are the times of prayer, due to His saying: ﴿Indeed prayer has been upon the believers a decreed writing﴾ [al-Nisa': 103]. The lam, according to this view, is like it in His saying: ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra': 78]. It has also been interpreted as the remembrance of prayer after forgetting it, from the saying of the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace: "Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 9–24 (part 2 of 4):

Al-Zamakhshari said: The proper form would have been to say, "for its remembrance" (li-dhikrihā), as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When he remembers it..." Those who try to give this a strained justification say: "When he remembers the prayer, he has remembered Allah," or it is by way of omitting a modifier (taqdir hadhf al-mudaf), i.e., "for the remembrance of My prayer," or because remembering and forgetting are in reality from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. End of quotation. In the hadith, after his saying, "Let him pray it when he remembers it," there is the statement, "for there is no expiation for it except that," and then he recited: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾. Al-Sulami, al-Nakha'i and Abu Raja' read (lil-dhikra) with the definite article and the alif of feminine form, so al-dhikra means "the reminder," i.e., "for My reminding you when I remind you after your forgetting, so establish it." Another group read (li-dhikra) with the alif of feminine form without the definite article. Another group read (lil-dhikr).

When Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the command to worship and to establish prayer, He mentioned what motivates this, namely the resurrection and the return for recompense, so He said: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾, the Hour in which what man has done becomes manifest, and the recompense for that, either reward or punishment. Abu al-Darda', Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Humayd read (ukhfiyha) with a fatha on the hamza, and it is transmitted from Ibn Kathir and Asim, meaning "I make it manifest," i.e., its occurrence is so certain and its existence so assured that it nearly appears, yet it is delayed until the known term. The Arabs say: "khafaytu al-shay'," meaning "I made the thing manifest." The poet said:

"Khafāhunna min īqānihinna ka-annamā
Khafāhunna wadqun min ʿashiyyin mujallabi"

Another said:

"Fa-in tadfinū al-dāʾa lā nukhfihi
Wa-in tūqidū al-ḥarba lā naqʿudi"

On this reading, the lam in ﴿that every soul may be recompensed﴾ (li-tujzā) is connected to ukhfīhā, i.e., "I make it manifest so that every soul may be recompensed." The majority read ﴿ukhfīhā﴾ with a damma on the hamza, which is the imperfect of akhfā meaning "to conceal," and the hamza here is for removal, i.e., "I removed the concealment," which is manifestation; and when you remove manifestation, it becomes concealment, as when you say: "a'jamtu al-kitāb," I removed its non-clarity (ʿujma) from it. Abu ʿAli said: this is of the type of negation (min bāb al-salb), and its meaning is: "I remove its concealment from it, which is its veil," and the lam, according to the reading of the majority... The author of al-Lawami' said: it is connected to ātiyah, as if He said: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾ so that... End of quotation. That is not complete unless we consider ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ as a parenthetical clause. If you make it in the position of a qualifier of ﴿coming﴾, then that is not permitted according to the Basran grammarians, because the active participle does not govern once it is qualified before its object is taken.

It was also said: ﴿ukhfīhā﴾ with a damma on the hamza means "I make it manifest," so the two readings coincide. Akhfā is among the words with contrary meanings (adhdād), meaning both manifestation and concealment. Abu ʿUbayda said: khafiyat and ukhfiyat have the same meaning, and Abu al-Khattab transmitted this, and he is one of the leading linguists, of undoubted reliability. ﴿Akādu﴾ is among the verbs of approximation (af'āl al-muqāraba), but here it is used figuratively. Since the verse is an expression of the intensity of concealing the matter of the Resurrection and its time, and since certainty of its coming together with ignorance of its time is more awe-inspiring to souls, He exaggerated in obscuring its time, saying ﴿I almost conceal it﴾, so that it would not appear at all; yet it must appear.

Another group said: ﴿akādu﴾ means "I want," so the meaning is "I want to conceal it." This was said by al-Akhfash, Ibn al-Anbari and Abu Muslim. Abu Muslim said: among their sayings is, "I will not do that, nor do I almost," meaning, "I do not want to do it." Another group said: the predicate of kāda is omitted, its estimated form being "I almost (do it)," it came for its nearness and the certainty of its occurrence, as it is omitted in the verse of Sabi al-Burjumi:

"Hamamtu wa-lam af'al wa-kidtu wa-laytanī
Tarakta ʿalā ʿUthmāna tabkī ḥalā'iluhu"

meaning: "and I almost did [it]." The speech was complete, then He began a new statement that He conceals it, and al-Nahhas preferred this. Another group said: its meaning is ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ from Myself, as an indication of how intensely it is hidden from created beings, and this is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas.

When some of them noticed the awkwardness of this statement, they said: "ma'nan min nafsī" means "from my own self and from what is with me." Another group said that ﴿akādu﴾ is superfluous, with no effect on the meaning; rather the information is that the Hour is coming and that Allah conceals the time of its coming. This meaning is related from Ibn Jubayr, and they cited the superfluity of kāda with His saying ﴿he almost could not see it﴾ [al-Nur: 40] and with the words of the poet, Zayd al-Khayl:

"Sarīʿun ilā al-hayjāʾi shākin silāḥahu
Fa-mā an yakādu qarnuhu yatanaffasu"

and with the words of another:

"Wa-an lā alūma al-nafsa mimmā aṣābanī
Wa-an lā akāda bi-alladhī niltu anjaḥu"

There is no proof in any of this. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ means "so I do not say it is coming, because of my overwhelming desire to conceal it; and were it not that the information of its coming, with the obscuring of its time, contains kindness, I would not have informed you of it." It was also said: its meaning is ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ from myself, but there is no indication in the speech of this omitted element, and an omitted element without indication is discarded. What misled them is that in the codex of Ubayy it reads ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ from myself, and in some codices ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ from myself, so how would I make you aware of it? End of quotation. This addition is also related from Ubayy; Ibn Khalawayh mentioned it. In the codex of ʿAbd Allah it reads ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ from myself, so how would any created being know it? In some readings it reads "and how would I make it manifest to you." This is to be understood in light of the Arabic custom that when one exaggerates in concealing a matter, he says, "I almost concealed it from myself," while Allah, the Exalted, nothing is hidden from Him. Qutrub and others said this. The poet said:

"Ayyāma tasḥabunī Hindun wa-ukhbiruhā
Mā kidtu aktumuhu ʿannī mina al-khabari"

How could one conceal from himself? Similar to this is the exaggeration; and a man who gives charity and conceals it, so that his left hand does not know what his right hand spends.

The pronoun in ﴿ukhfīhā﴾ refers to "the Hour" (al-sāʿa), and "the Hour" is the Day of Resurrection without disagreement. Here "al-saʿy" means action. The apparent view is that the pronoun in ʿanhā (from it) and bihā (by it) refers to the Hour. It was also said: to the prayer. It was also said that ʿanhā refers to the prayer and bihā, i.e., by the Hour. Those who went far astray were those who held that the pronoun in ʿanhā refers to what preceded, namely the phrase ﴿There is no god but I, so worship Me﴾.

The apparent view is that the address in ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it turn you away﴾ is to Musa, peace be upon him. A prohibition does not imply the possibility of its occurrence from one who has been granted infallibility, so it should be understood as a form of speech where the hearer is someone else for whom such an occurrence is possible. Those who went further astray were those who held that the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) in form, while its meaning is for his community.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: the expression forbids the disbeliever from turning Musa away, whereas the intended meaning is the prohibition of Musa from denying the Resurrection, or commanding him to affirm it. I say: there are two aspects to this.
One: turning the disbeliever away from belief in it is a cause of denial, so He mentioned the cause to indicate the effect.
The second: the turning away of the disbeliever results from the laxity of the man in religion and softness of his resolve, so He mentioned the effect to indicate the cause, as in their saying, "I shall not see you here," meaning, "Do not let me see you," and that being present in his presence is the cause of seeing him; so mentioning the effect is evidence of the cause, as if it were said: "Be firm of resolve and strong of purpose, so that it does not appear from you to one who disbelieves in the Resurrection that he may hope to turn you away from what you are upon." ﴿So you will perish﴾ may be in the accusative by way of the prohibition, or it may be in the nominative, i.e., "then you perish." Yahya read ﴿fa-tirdā﴾ with a kasra on the taʾ.

﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ This is a question whose content is alerting; He gathered the self (nafs) for what is brought upon it, though Allah, the Exalted, had known from eternity what it is; He only asked him in order to show him the greatness of what He, Mighty and Majestic, would create in the dry wood by turning it into a living, writhing serpent, and so that the vast difference between what is turned from and what it is turned into would become firmly fixed in his self, and to alert him to His overwhelming power. ("Ma") is an interrogative subject, ("tilka") is its predicate, and ﴿bi-yaminika﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, like His saying ﴿and this is my husband, an old man﴾ [Hud: 72], and the operating element is the demonstrative. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that ("tilka") be a relative pronoun whose relative clause is ﴿bi-yaminika﴾; Ibn ʿAtiyya mentioned no other.
