It is also said: it comes from "the ark ghammed" (was covered over), or from "the sea ghammed" (covered him). The apparent meaning is that it comes from "ghamma" in the sense of killing, when We took you from Egypt to Madyan.

Al-Futun is a verbal noun, or the plural of fitan or fitna, with the feminine ending dropped, like huju and budur from hujza and budra. The sense is: ﴿We tested you with trials﴾ (fatannaka), meaning various kinds of trials. Fitna means affliction and whatever is hard for a person. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: "We delivered you from one trial after another." He was born in a year when children were being killed, his mother cast him into the river, Pharaoh intended to kill him, he killed a Copt, he hired himself out for ten years, he lost the way, and his flock scattered on a dark night. End of quotation. These trials were those by which He tested him and delivered him, until he became fit for prophethood and was preserved for it. The years he spent in Madyan were ten. Wahb said: twenty-eight years, of which was the bride-price for his daughter. Between Egypt and Madyan there were eight stages. There is an elision in the speech; the supposed form is: ﴿We tested you with trials﴾, and then you went out fearful to ﴿the people of Madyan﴾, and remained there for years. When he went to Madyan he was twelve years old. He stayed ten years tending Shu'ayb's flock, then eighteen years after he married Shu'ayb's daughter, and children were born to him in that time. So he completed forty years, and that is the period at the end of which it is God's custom to send prophets.

﴿Then you came﴾ to the place where I met with you, spoke to you and made you a prophet. ﴿At an appointed time﴾, that is, a time set by Me, which you neither preceded nor lagged behind. It is said: at a measure of time in which prophets are inspired, which is forty years. The poet said:

He attained the caliphate, or it came to him at its appointed time, as Moses came to his Lord at an appointed time.

﴿And I chose you for Myself﴾: that is, I made you the object of favour and the place of bounty and kindness, I purified you with graces, and I selected you for My love. It is said: "Fulan made Fulan a favourite," meaning he took him as a favourite. It is a form derived from ṣun', which is kindness to a person so intense that it becomes attributed to him, so one says: "This is so-and-so's favour." Al-Zamakhshari said: This is an image of what He granted him in the rank of nearness, honour, and speech. His state is depicted by the state of one whom kings see as possessing all the qualities and distinctions fitting him to be nearest to them and most intimate in station. So they favour him with honour and preference and choose him for themselves. End of quotation.

The meaning of ﴿for Myself﴾ is: for My commands, for establishing My proofs and conveying My message. Therefore your movements and stillnesses are for Me, not for yourself, nor for anyone other than you.

[p. 242] [p. 243]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 25–41 (part 1 of 2):

(p-238) He said: "My Lord, expand my breast for me, and ease my task for me, and loosen a knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech, and appoint for me a minister from my family, Harun, my brother. Strengthen my back through him, and make him a partner in my affair, that we may glorify You much and remember You much. Indeed You are ever Seeing of us." He said: "You have been granted your request, O Musa. And We had already bestowed favour upon you another time, when We inspired to your mother what is inspired: 'Cast him into the chest, then cast it into the river, and let the river deposit him on the bank, and an enemy to Me and an enemy to him will take him.' And I cast upon you love from Me, and that you be raised under My eye. When your sister walked and said, 'Shall I direct you to one who will take charge of him?' So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve. And you killed a soul, but We delivered you from distress and tested you with a severe testing. And you stayed for years among the people of Madyan, then you came here by decree, O Musa. And I have chosen you for Myself."

(p-239) When He commanded him to go to Pharaoh, he knew that he had been charged with a great matter, requiring him to bear what only one of steady heart and broad breast can bear. So he asked his Lord and desired that He expand his breast, so that he could endure the hardships that would come upon him, which would constrict the breast; and that He ease his affair, for he was to be the Caliph of God on His earth, together with what accompanies that of undertaking great calamities. He knew what Pharaoh had of tyranny, rebellion and domination.

Ibn Juraij said: its meaning is, "Widen my breast so that I may retain from You what You entrust of Your revelation." Al-Karmani said: "Widen my heart and make it pliable to understand Your address, to deliver Your message, and to undertake what You have charged me with of its burdens." The "knot" (al-'uqdah) is a metaphor for a heaviness that was in his tongue by nature.

Mujahid said: it was from the ember that he put into his mouth, and Asiya had had God place love for him in her heart, and she asked Pharaoh not to slaughter him. While she was once dandling him, Pharaoh took him onto his lap and seized a lock of his beard. It was said: he slapped him. It was said: he struck him with a staff that was in his hand. Pharaoh became angry and summoned the executioner. She said: "He is only a child who does not distinguish between the ruby and the ember." So he brought [them] or intended to extend his hand to the ruby, but Jibril, peace be upon him, turned his hand to the ember, and he took it and put it in his mouth, and his tongue was burnt. End of quote. The burning of the fire and its effect on his tongue and not on his hand is evidence against the view of those who hold to "nature" (al-tabi'ah).

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: there was a lisp (ratta) in his tongue. It was also said: the knot arose after the intimate conversation, so that he would not speak to anyone after it. Qutrub said: there was in him a stammering (muskah) from speech. Ibn 'Isa said: the knot is like the tamtamah and the fa'fa'ah (speech impediments).

Musa's request for the untying of the knot was to the extent that his speech could be understood. It was said: some of it remained, for his saying: "My brother Harun is more eloquent in tongue than I" [al-Qasas: 34], and His saying: "and he can hardly make himself clear" [al-Zukhruf: 52]. It was said: it was removed by His saying "You have been granted your request, O Musa," and this is the view of al-Hasan. It was said: this is weak, because he did not say "and untie the knot," but said "a knot," so when He untied a knot, God had granted him his request. It was said regarding His saying "and he can hardly make himself clear" [al-Zukhruf: 52] that its meaning is that he does not bring clear explanation and proof; and Pharaoh said this only as deception, although he addressed him and his people, and they understood him. So how can the negation of clarity, or approximating it, be possible?

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask about His saying "Expand my breast for me and ease my affair for me": what is its benefit, when the speech stands without it? I say: He first made the speech vague, saying "expand for me" and "ease for me," so it was known that there was something expanded and something eased. Then he clarified and removed the vagueness by mentioning both, so this was more emphatic in asking for the expansion and easing of his breast, and [he commanded him] to say: "Expand my breast and ease my affair," in clear explanation, since it is a repetition of one meaning by way of both the general and the detailed. He also said: As for the indefiniteness of "knot" and the absence of "untie a knot" with "of my tongue," [it means] he asked for the untying of part of it, intending that he be understood well, and did not ask for complete eloquence; and "of my tongue" is an attribute of "knot," as if it were said: "a knot of the knots of my tongue." End of quote. It appears that "of my tongue" is connected to "untie," because the position of an attribute is for "knot," and so said al-Hawfi. Abu al-Baqa' permitted both views.

The "wazir" is the helper who bears the burdens of affairs, i.e., their weight; the king's wazir bears his burdens and expenses for him. It was also said: it is from "wizr," which is a refuge to which a person resorts. The poet said:

"Among the ravenous beasts, beyond him is a refuge; and among people, the worst of them is one beyond whom there is no refuge."

"How many a company were safe, whom no beast harmed; and we do not see a human who was not harmed by a human."

So the king takes refuge in his opinion and resorts to him in his affairs. Al-Asma'i said: it is from "mu'azarah," which is aid and support, and the regular form would be "azir"; likewise al-Zamakhshari said: the regular form would be "azir," and the hamzah was changed to a waw. The reason for changing it is that "fa'il" came in the sense of "mufa'il" in a valid manner, like 'ashir, jalis, qa'id, khalil, sadiq, nadim. So when it was changed in "akhi," it was changed in it too, and assigning a thing to its counterpart is not rare. [This is] in view of "yu'azir" and its kin and of "mu'azarah." End of quote. There is no need to claim the hamzah was changed to waw, because we have a clear derivation, which is "wizr." As for its change in "yu'azir," it is due to the damma before the waw, and that too is a non-obligatory substitution.

They also permitted that "waziran" with "li" be the two objects of "aj'al," with "Harun" as an apposition or a conjunctive explanation; and that "wazir" and "Harun" be its two objects, with the second placed first out of concern for the matter of the wizarah, and "akhi" as an apposition to "Harun" in these two cases.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If it is taken as another conjunctive explanation, it is permissible and good. End of quote. Yet conjunctive explanation is remote here, because usually in an explanation the first term is less well known than the second, whereas here the matter is the reverse.

They also permitted that "waziran min ahli" be the two objects, with "li" like His saying "and there is none comparable to Him" [al-Ikhlas: 4], meaning that the meaning is completed by it. "Harun" is as previously stated. They also permitted that "Harun" be in the accusative by a deleted verb, i.e., "join Harun to me," but this is not needed, because the sentence is complete without this deleted element.

al-Hasan, Zayd ibn 'Ali and Ibn 'Amir read "ashdud" with a fatha on the hamzah and "wa-ushrikhu" with a damma, as a jussive imperfect verb in answer to the imperative, and "wa-ushrikhu" is conjoined to it. The author of al-Lawami' said, from al-Hasan, that he read "ushaddidu bihi" as the imperfect of "shaddada," for intensity and repetition, i.e., whenever a matter saddened me, I strengthened "my back through him." The majority read "ashdud" and "wa-ashrikhu" in the sense of supplication for the strengthening of the back and the making of Harun a partner in prophethood. In the reading of Ibn 'Amir the imperative does not mean prophethood, but rather his management and assistance, because it is not for Musa to make anyone a partner in prophethood. In the codex of 'Abd Allah it reads "akhi washdud."

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible, for one who reads it in the imperative form, to make "akhi" nominative as the subject, with "ashdud bihi" as its predicate, and to pause at "Harun." End of quote. This is contrary to the apparent sense, so it is not to be resorted to without need. Harun was four years older than Musa. Musa made what he desired and asked for of blessings a cause that entails worship and striving in God's command, and mutual support and cooperation in worship is a stimulus to desire and increase in good.

"That we may glorify You" — "nunazzihaka": we declare You free of what is not befitting to You. "And remember You" — by supplication and praise of You. Glorification is mentioned first because it is His transcendence in His essence and attributes and His freedom from deficiencies, and its locus is the heart; remembrance and praise of God through attributes of perfection have the tongue as their locus, so what has the heart as its locus is placed before what has the tongue as its locus. "Much" (kathiran) is an attribute of a deleted verbal noun, or an accusative of circumstance, i.e., we glorify You with glorification in a state of their abundance, according to what Sibawayh held. "Indeed You are ever Seeing of us" — knowing our conditions.

"Su'l" (request) is a noun in the sense of the object requested, like "khubz" (bread) and "akl" (food) in the sense of what is baked and eaten. The meaning: you have been given your request and what you asked for of expansion of the breast, ease of the affair, untying of the knot, and making your brother a minister; and this is among the favours upon him.

Then He reminded him of His having previously bestowed favour upon him, by way of making him stand firm, so that his striving would grow and his insight strengthen. "Marratan" means "a favour," and "ukhra" is the feminine of "akhar" in the sense of "ghayr" (other): a favour other than this favour. "Ukhra" here is not in the sense of "akhirah" (last), which would be opposed to "the first." Some thought this, saying: He called it "ukhra" but it is first, because it is "ukhra" in mention; and "al-ukhra" is a homonymous word: the feminine of "al-akhar" with a fatha on the kha', and the feminine of "al-akhar" in the sense of its last, and this has the sense of lateness. The meaning is that I protected you while you were a suckling infant, so how would I not protect you when I have qualified you for the message? In "marratan ukhra" there is a generality that is explained by "when We inspired to your mother." Al-Jumhur said: it was an inspiration of inspiration (ilham), like His saying "And your Lord inspired the bee" [al-Nahl: 68]. It was said: it was an inspiration of information, either by showing this in a dream, or by sending an angel to her not in the manner of prophethood, as Mary was sent to. This is the apparent meaning, because of the apparent sense of "he will be taken by an enemy to Me and an enemy to him," and the apparent sense of the verse in al-Qasas: "We will return him to you and make him one of the messengers" [al-Qasas: 7]. What al-Zamakhshari began with, "from the one who returns his hand," is remote, whether it is on the tongue of a prophet of that time, like His saying "And when I inspired the disciples" [al-Ma'idah: 111]; for it is not reported that he was in the time of Pharaoh, and in the time of the disciples there were Zakariya and Yahya. In His saying "what is inspired" there is vagueness and generality, like His saying "when there covered the lote-tree that which covered" [al-Najm: 16], and "then there covered them of the sea that which covered them" [Ta-Ha: 78], and in it is awe-inspiring magnitude. It is explained here by His saying "Cast him into the chest."

Al-Zamakhshari said:
(p-241) "An" is the explanatory particle, because inspiration has the meaning of speech. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "An" in His saying "an uqdhifihi" is an apposition to "ma," meaning that "an" is verbal (masdariyyah), and for that reason it has a place in the grammatical structure. Both views are permissible. The apparent sense is that "the chest" was of wood. It was said: of papyrus from the tree of the believer of Pharaoh's family; she sealed its gaps, spread in it a mat (nith') — it was said: carded cotton — sealed its mouth, plastered it, pitched it, and cast it into the "yamm," which is the name for the sweet sea. It was said: it is the name for the Nile specifically. The first is correct, as in His saying "So We drowned them in the yamm" [al-A'raf: 136], and they were not drowned in the Nile.

The apparent sense is that the pronoun in "fa-uqdhifihi fi al-yamm" refers to Musa, and likewise the two pronouns after it, since he is the one spoken of, not the chest; the chest was mentioned only as a container and incidental detail. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the first pronoun in "uqdhifihi" refers to Musa, and in the second it refers to "the chest," though it could refer to Musa. Al-Zamakhshari said: All the pronouns refer to Musa; their referring partly to him and partly to the chest involves a blemish, because of the discord in arrangement it leads to. If you ask: the thing cast into the sea is the chest, and likewise the thing cast onto the bank? I say: what harm is there if you say that the one cast and the one cast onto the bank is Musa within the chest, so that the pronouns do not scatter and the arrangement does not become discordant for you, the arrangement which is the mother of the inimitability of the Qur'an, and the rule on which the challenge was made; observing it is the most important duty of the exegete. End of quote.

Someone might say: when a pronoun can refer either to the nearer or the more distant antecedent, referring it to the nearer one is preferred. The grammarians have stated this explicitly, so on this view the pronoun in ﴿فَلْيُلْقِهِ﴾ ("let it cast him") in ﴿فاقْذِفِيهِ في اليَمِّ فَلْيُلْقِهِ اليَمُّ﴾ should refer to the nearer noun, the ark (al-tabut). The answer is that when one of the two is the topic being discussed and the other is a secondary element, the pronoun is better referred to the topic, and nearness is not taken into account. For this reason we have refuted Abu Muhammad Ibn Hazm (d. 456 AH) in his claim that the pronoun in ﴿فَإنَّهُ رِجْسٌ﴾ [Al-An'am: 145] refers to swine (khinzir), because it is the nearest noun mentioned. On his view the fat, cartilage, bone and skin of swine would thereby be forbidden. Our answer is that the topic is the meat of swine, not the swine itself.

﴿فَلْيُلْقِهِ﴾ is an imperative in form, but its meaning is a statement of fact. It is cast in the form of a command for emphasis, since a command is the most decisive and binding of verbs. From this comes the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Stand up, and I will pray for you." He put a statement into the form of a command for emphasis. Because the verb takes the form of a command, its answer is likewise in that form, namely ﴿يَأْخُذْهُ﴾ ("let him take him").

Al-Zamakhshari said: Since it was the will and decree of God that the flow of the river's water should not fail to bring him to the shore and deposit him there, He followed the paths of metaphor. He treated the river as though it had discernment, commanded it to obey and carry out the command, and so it was said: ﴿let the river throw him onto the shore﴾. End of quotation. Al-Tirmidhi said: He expressed it in the form of a command because of His prior knowledge that the thing reported would come to pass as He had reported it, so it is as though the sea were commanded and obeying the command. Al-Farra' said: ﴿Cast him into the river﴾ is a command, and it carries the sense of a conditional: "Cast him, and the river will throw him up." The apparent meaning is that the sea did throw him onto the shore, and she picked him up from it.

It is related that Pharaoh was drinking at a place on the Nile when he saw the ark. He ordered it brought to him, and his wife was with him. They opened it and saw him. His wife took pity on him and asked for him, to adopt him as a son, and he permitted her to do so. It is also related that the ark came on the water to the watering-place where the maidservants of Pharaoh's wife drew water. They took the ark, brought it to her, opened it, and informed Pharaoh. The enemy of God and of Moses is Pharaoh. His mother was informed of this by way of inspiration, and that is why she said to his sister ﴿Follow him up﴾ [Al-Qasas: 11], although she did not know where he had come to rest.

﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾. It is said this was the love of Asiya and of Pharaoh. Pharaoh had come to love him intensely, so that he could not restrain himself from being patient away from him. Ibn 'Abbas said: God loved him and made him beloved to His creation. 'Atiyya said: a sheen of beauty was placed upon him, so that whoever saw him could hardly bear to be apart from him. Qatada said: there was a comeliness in his eyes, so that no one who saw him failed to love him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The strongest of the views is that it means acceptance. Al-Zamakhshari said: (minni, "from Me") must either be connected to ﴿alqaytu﴾ ("I cast"), in which case the meaning is "I loved you," and whoever God loves, hearts love; or it must be connected to a deleted element that is an adjective of "love," meaning: a love that is pure, or one that proceeds from Me. I have placed it in hearts and sown it there, and therefore Pharaoh and everyone who looked upon you loved you.

The majority of readers recited ﴿wa-litusna'a﴾ ("and that you might be raised") with a kasra on the lam of purpose (lam kay) and a damma on the taa', with the verb in the subjunctive. The sense is: "so that you might be reared and well treated, and I would watch over and observe you, as a man watches a thing with his eyes when he takes care of it." Qatada said something close to this. Al-Nahhas said: one says "sana'tu al-faras" ("I treated the horse well") when one treats it kindly. It is coordinated with a deleted cause, meaning: "so that he might be gentle with you" and "that you might be raised." Or it is connected to a later verb whose supposed form is "I did that." Al-Hasan and Abu Nahik read it with a fatha on the taa'. Tha'lab said: its meaning is "so that your movement and conduct would be under My eye." Shayba and Abu Ja'far, in one narration, read it with sukun on the lam and the 'ayn and a damma on the taa' as an imperative verb. From Abu Ja'far also it is so, except that he read the lam with a kasra.

﴿When your sister walked﴾. It is said her name was Maryam. The reason was that Asiya offered him for suckling, but he would not accept any woman. So she began to call out about him in the city, and he was taken around and presented to the wet-nurses, but he refused them. His mother remained in grief after he had been cast into the river. So she told his sister to search the city in case she might learn of his news. She saw him during her wandering and said: "I will guide you to someone who will nurse him for you, and they will be sincere in their care for him." They seized her and said: "Do you know this child?" She said: "No, but I know of the people of this house, their eagerness to draw near to the queen and their striving in her service and her pleasure." They left her and asked her to find a nurse, so she brought Moses' mother. When she brought him near, he took her breast, and Asiya was delighted. She said to her: "Stay with us in the palace." She said: "I would not leave my house and my child, but he may stay with me." Asiya said: "Yes." So she treated the people of that house with the utmost kindness, and the Children of Israel took pride in this suckling and in their kinship with the queen. When his suckling was complete, Asiya sent word to her: "Bring my son to me on such-and-such a day." She ordered her servants and those with her to meet him with gifts, presents and clothing. He reached her in that state, in the best condition and the most beautiful youth. She was delighted with him and entered with him to Pharaoh so that he might see him and bestow him as a gift. Pharaoh was pleased with him and brought him near. Then Moses seized Pharaoh's beard, and what happened to him was mentioned in the discussion of the knot (in his tongue).

Regarding the element governing ﴿idh﴾ ("when"), Ibn 'Atiyya said it is a deleted verb whose supposed form is "and We bestowed favour when." Al-Zamakhshari said the governing element of ﴿idh tamshi﴾ is ﴿alqaytu﴾ ("I cast") or ﴿tusna'a﴾ ("be raised"). It may also be a substitute (badal) for ﴿idh awhayna﴾ ("when We inspired"). If you ask: how is substitution valid when the two times are different and far apart? I answer: just as it is valid, even though the time has widened and its two ends are distant, for a man to say to you: "I met so-and-so in such-and-such a year," and you reply: "I also met him at that time." Perhaps he met him at its beginning and you at its end. End of quotation. This is not as he stated, because a year admits of breadth, so that if their meeting occurs within it, that is possible. But these two ends are each narrow and not expansive, since each is specified by what is attached to it. It is not possible for the second to occur at the end where the first occurred, because the first is not wide enough to contain both the inspiration and the walking of the sister. The time of the inspiration does not include parts in which the walking occurred, unlike the year. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿idh﴾ is connected to ﴿tusna'a﴾, and you may also put ﴿idh﴾ in the accusative by a deleted verb whose supposed form is "and remember."

The majority read ﴿kay taqarra﴾ ("that she might be comforted") with a fatha on the taa' and the qaf. A group read it with a kasra on the qaf. It has already been stated that both are dialectal forms in ﴿wa-qarri 'aynan﴾ [Maryam: 26]. Jinah ibn Hubaysh read it with a damma on the taa' and a fatha on the qaf, in the passive form.

﴿You killed a soul﴾ [Al-Qasas: 19] refers to the Egyptian (Qibti) whom the Israelite called on him for help against, and he killed him when he was twelve years old. He was distressed because of the killing, fearing God's punishment and Pharaoh's retaliation. God forgave him when he asked forgiveness and said: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾ [Al-Qasas: 16]. He rescued him from Pharaoh when he migrated with him to Madyan. Ghamm ("distress") is what weighs upon the heart because of fear or the loss of an aim. In the dialect of Quraysh, ghamm means killing. It is also said: it comes from "the ark ghammed" (was covered over), or from "the sea ghammed" (covered him). The apparent meaning is that it comes from "ghamma" in the sense of killing, when We took you from Egypt to Madyan.

Al-Futun is a verbal noun, or the plural of fitan or fitna, with the feminine ending dropped, like huju and budur from hujza and budra. The sense is: ﴿We tested you with trials﴾ (fatannaka), meaning various kinds of trials. Fitna means affliction and whatever is hard for a person. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: "We delivered you from one trial after another." He was born in a year when children were being killed, his mother cast him into the river, Pharaoh intended to kill him, he killed a Copt, he hired himself out for ten years, he lost the way, and his flock scattered on a dark night. End of quotation. These trials were those by which He tested him and delivered him, until he became fit for prophethood and was preserved for it. The years he spent in Madyan were ten. Wahb said: twenty-eight years, of which was the bride-price for his daughter. Between Egypt and Madyan there were eight stages. There is an elision in the speech; the supposed form is: ﴿We tested you with trials﴾, and then you went out fearful to ﴿the people of Madyan﴾, and remained there for years. When he went to Madyan he was twelve years old. He stayed ten years tending Shu'ayb's flock, then eighteen years after he married Shu'ayb's daughter, and children were born to him in that time. So he completed forty years, and that is the period at the end of which it is God's custom to send prophets.

﴿Then you came﴾ to the place where I met with you, spoke to you and made you a prophet. ﴿At an appointed time﴾, that is, a time set by Me, which you neither preceded nor lagged behind. It is said: at a measure of time in which prophets are inspired, which is forty years. The poet said:

He attained the caliphate, or it came to him at its appointed time, as Moses came to his Lord at an appointed time.

﴿And I chose you for Myself﴾: that is, I made you the object of favour and the place of bounty and kindness, I purified you with graces, and I selected you for My love. It is said: "Fulan made Fulan a favourite," meaning he took him as a favourite. It is a form derived from ṣun', which is kindness to a person so intense that it becomes attributed to him, so one says: "This is so-and-so's favour." Al-Zamakhshari said: This is an image of what He granted him in the rank of nearness, honour, and speech. His state is depicted by the state of one whom kings see as possessing all the qualities and distinctions fitting him to be nearest to them and most intimate in station. So they favour him with honour and preference and choose him for themselves. End of quotation.

The meaning of ﴿for Myself﴾ is: for My commands, for establishing My proofs and conveying My message. Therefore your movements and stillnesses are for Me, not for yourself, nor for anyone other than you.

[p. 242] [p. 243]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 25–41 (part 1 of 2):

(p-238) He said: "My Lord, expand my breast for me, and ease my task for me, and loosen a knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech, and appoint for me a minister from my family, Harun, my brother. Strengthen my back through him, and make him a partner in my affair, that we may glorify You much and remember You much. Indeed You are ever Seeing of us." He said: "You have been granted your request, O Musa. And We had already bestowed favour upon you another time, when We inspired to your mother what is inspired: 'Cast him into the chest, then cast it into the river, and let the river deposit him on the bank, and an enemy to Me and an enemy to him will take him.' And I cast upon you love from Me, and that you be raised under My eye. When your sister walked and said, 'Shall I direct you to one who will take charge of him?' So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve. And you killed a soul, but We delivered you from distress and tested you with a severe testing. And you stayed for years among the people of Madyan, then you came here by decree, O Musa. And I have chosen you for Myself."

(p-239) When He commanded him to go to Pharaoh, he knew that he had been charged with a great matter, requiring him to bear what only one of steady heart and broad breast can bear. So he asked his Lord and desired that He expand his breast, so that he could endure the hardships that would come upon him, which would constrict the breast; and that He ease his affair, for he was to be the Caliph of God on His earth, together with what accompanies that of undertaking great calamities. He knew what Pharaoh had of tyranny, rebellion and domination.

Ibn Juraij said: its meaning is, "Widen my breast so that I may retain from You what You entrust of Your revelation." Al-Karmani said: "Widen my heart and make it pliable to understand Your address, to deliver Your message, and to undertake what You have charged me with of its burdens." The "knot" (al-'uqdah) is a metaphor for a heaviness that was in his tongue by nature.

Mujahid said: it was from the ember that he put into his mouth, and Asiya had had God place love for him in her heart, and she asked Pharaoh not to slaughter him. While she was once dandling him, Pharaoh took him onto his lap and seized a lock of his beard. It was said: he slapped him. It was said: he struck him with a staff that was in his hand. Pharaoh became angry and summoned the executioner. She said: "He is only a child who does not distinguish between the ruby and the ember." So he brought [them] or intended to extend his hand to the ruby, but Jibril, peace be upon him, turned his hand to the ember, and he took it and put it in his mouth, and his tongue was burnt. End of quote. The burning of the fire and its effect on his tongue and not on his hand is evidence against the view of those who hold to "nature" (al-tabi'ah).

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: there was a lisp (ratta) in his tongue. It was also said: the knot arose after the intimate conversation, so that he would not speak to anyone after it. Qutrub said: there was in him a stammering (muskah) from speech. Ibn 'Isa said: the knot is like the tamtamah and the fa'fa'ah (speech impediments).

Musa's request for the untying of the knot was to the extent that his speech could be understood. It was said: some of it remained, for his saying: "My brother Harun is more eloquent in tongue than I" [al-Qasas: 34], and His saying: "and he can hardly make himself clear" [al-Zukhruf: 52]. It was said: it was removed by His saying "You have been granted your request, O Musa," and this is the view of al-Hasan. It was said: this is weak, because he did not say "and untie the knot," but said "a knot," so when He untied a knot, God had granted him his request. It was said regarding His saying "and he can hardly make himself clear" [al-Zukhruf: 52] that its meaning is that he does not bring clear explanation and proof; and Pharaoh said this only as deception, although he addressed him and his people, and they understood him. So how can the negation of clarity, or approximating it, be possible?

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask about His saying "Expand my breast for me and ease my affair for me": what is its benefit, when the speech stands without it? I say: He first made the speech vague, saying "expand for me" and "ease for me," so it was known that there was something expanded and something eased. Then he clarified and removed the vagueness by mentioning both, so this was more emphatic in asking for the expansion and easing of his breast, and [he commanded him] to say: "Expand my breast and ease my affair," in clear explanation, since it is a repetition of one meaning by way of both the general and the detailed. He also said: As for the indefiniteness of "knot" and the absence of "untie a knot" with "of my tongue," [it means] he asked for the untying of part of it, intending that he be understood well, and did not ask for complete eloquence; and "of my tongue" is an attribute of "knot," as if it were said: "a knot of the knots of my tongue." End of quote. It appears that "of my tongue" is connected to "untie," because the position of an attribute is for "knot," and so said al-Hawfi. Abu al-Baqa' permitted both views.

The "wazir" is the helper who bears the burdens of affairs, i.e., their weight; the king's wazir bears his burdens and expenses for him. It was also said: it is from "wizr," which is a refuge to which a person resorts. The poet said:

"Among the ravenous beasts, beyond him is a refuge; and among people, the worst of them is one beyond whom there is no refuge."

"How many a company were safe, whom no beast harmed; and we do not see a human who was not harmed by a human."

So the king takes refuge in his opinion and resorts to him in his affairs. Al-Asma'i said: it is from "mu'azarah," which is aid and support, and the regular form would be "azir"; likewise al-Zamakhshari said: the regular form would be "azir," and the hamzah was changed to a waw. The reason for changing it is that "fa'il" came in the sense of "mufa'il" in a valid manner, like 'ashir, jalis, qa'id, khalil, sadiq, nadim. So when it was changed in "akhi," it was changed in it too, and assigning a thing to its counterpart is not rare. [This is] in view of "yu'azir" and its kin and of "mu'azarah." End of quote. There is no need to claim the hamzah was changed to waw, because we have a clear derivation, which is "wizr." As for its change in "yu'azir," it is due to the damma before the waw, and that too is a non-obligatory substitution.

They also permitted that "waziran" with "li" be the two objects of "aj'al," with "Harun" as an apposition or a conjunctive explanation; and that "wazir" and "Harun" be its two objects, with the second placed first out of concern for the matter of the wizarah, and "akhi" as an apposition to "Harun" in these two cases.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If it is taken as another conjunctive explanation, it is permissible and good. End of quote. Yet conjunctive explanation is remote here, because usually in an explanation the first term is less well known than the second, whereas here the matter is the reverse.

They also permitted that "waziran min ahli" be the two objects, with "li" like His saying "and there is none comparable to Him" [al-Ikhlas: 4], meaning that the meaning is completed by it. "Harun" is as previously stated. They also permitted that "Harun" be in the accusative by a deleted verb, i.e., "join Harun to me," but this is not needed, because the sentence is complete without this deleted element.

al-Hasan, Zayd ibn 'Ali and Ibn 'Amir read "ashdud" with a fatha on the hamzah and "wa-ushrikhu" with a damma, as a jussive imperfect verb in answer to the imperative, and "wa-ushrikhu" is conjoined to it. The author of al-Lawami' said, from al-Hasan, that he read "ushaddidu bihi" as the imperfect of "shaddada," for intensity and repetition, i.e., whenever a matter saddened me, I strengthened "my back through him." The majority read "ashdud" and "wa-ashrikhu" in the sense of supplication for the strengthening of the back and the making of Harun a partner in prophethood. In the reading of Ibn 'Amir the imperative does not mean prophethood, but rather his management and assistance, because it is not for Musa to make anyone a partner in prophethood. In the codex of 'Abd Allah it reads "akhi washdud."

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible, for one who reads it in the imperative form, to make "akhi" nominative as the subject, with "ashdud bihi" as its predicate, and to pause at "Harun." End of quote. This is contrary to the apparent sense, so it is not to be resorted to without need. Harun was four years older than Musa. Musa made what he desired and asked for of blessings a cause that entails worship and striving in God's command, and mutual support and cooperation in worship is a stimulus to desire and increase in good.

"That we may glorify You" — "nunazzihaka": we declare You free of what is not befitting to You. "And remember You" — by supplication and praise of You. Glorification is mentioned first because it is His transcendence in His essence and attributes and His freedom from deficiencies, and its locus is the heart; remembrance and praise of God through attributes of perfection have the tongue as their locus, so what has the heart as its locus is placed before what has the tongue as its locus. "Much" (kathiran) is an attribute of a deleted verbal noun, or an accusative of circumstance, i.e., we glorify You with glorification in a state of their abundance, according to what Sibawayh held. "Indeed You are ever Seeing of us" — knowing our conditions.

"Su'l" (request) is a noun in the sense of the object requested, like "khubz" (bread) and "akl" (food) in the sense of what is baked and eaten. The meaning: you have been given your request and what you asked for of expansion of the breast, ease of the affair, untying of the knot, and making your brother a minister; and this is among the favours upon him.

Then He reminded him of His having previously bestowed favour upon him, by way of making him stand firm, so that his striving would grow and his insight strengthen. "Marratan" means "a favour," and "ukhra" is the feminine of "akhar" in the sense of "ghayr" (other): a favour other than this favour. "Ukhra" here is not in the sense of "akhirah" (last), which would be opposed to "the first." Some thought this, saying: He called it "ukhra" but it is first, because it is "ukhra" in mention; and "al-ukhra" is a homonymous word: the feminine of "al-akhar" with a fatha on the kha', and the feminine of "al-akhar" in the sense of its last, and this has the sense of lateness. The meaning is that I protected you while you were a suckling infant, so how would I not protect you when I have qualified you for the message? In "marratan ukhra" there is a generality that is explained by "when We inspired to your mother." Al-Jumhur said: it was an inspiration of inspiration (ilham), like His saying "And your Lord inspired the bee" [al-Nahl: 68]. It was said: it was an inspiration of information, either by showing this in a dream, or by sending an angel to her not in the manner of prophethood, as Mary was sent to. This is the apparent meaning, because of the apparent sense of "he will be taken by an enemy to Me and an enemy to him," and the apparent sense of the verse in al-Qasas: "We will return him to you and make him one of the messengers" [al-Qasas: 7]. What al-Zamakhshari began with, "from the one who returns his hand," is remote, whether it is on the tongue of a prophet of that time, like His saying "And when I inspired the disciples" [al-Ma'idah: 111]; for it is not reported that he was in the time of Pharaoh, and in the time of the disciples there were Zakariya and Yahya. In His saying "what is inspired" there is vagueness and generality, like His saying "when there covered the lote-tree that which covered" [al-Najm: 16], and "then there covered them of the sea that which covered them" [Ta-Ha: 78], and in it is awe-inspiring magnitude. It is explained here by His saying "Cast him into the chest."

Al-Zamakhshari said:
(p-241) "An" is the explanatory particle, because inspiration has the meaning of speech. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "An" in His saying "an uqdhifihi" is an apposition to "ma," meaning that "an" is verbal (masdariyyah), and for that reason it has a place in the grammatical structure. Both views are permissible. The apparent sense is that "the chest" was of wood. It was said: of papyrus from the tree of the believer of Pharaoh's family; she sealed its gaps, spread in it a mat (nith') — it was said: carded cotton — sealed its mouth, plastered it, pitched it, and cast it into the "yamm," which is the name for the sweet sea. It was said: it is the name for the Nile specifically. The first is correct, as in His saying "So We drowned them in the yamm" [al-A'raf: 136], and they were not drowned in the Nile.

The apparent sense is that the pronoun in "fa-uqdhifihi fi al-yamm" refers to Musa, and likewise the two pronouns after it, since he is the one spoken of, not the chest; the chest was mentioned only as a container and incidental detail. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the first pronoun in "uqdhifihi" refers to Musa, and in the second it refers to "the chest," though it could refer to Musa. Al-Zamakhshari said: All the pronouns refer to Musa; their referring partly to him and partly to the chest involves a blemish, because of the discord in arrangement it leads to. If you ask: the thing cast into the sea is the chest, and likewise the thing cast onto the bank? I say: what harm is there if you say that the one cast and the one cast onto the bank is Musa within the chest, so that the pronouns do not scatter and the arrangement does not become discordant for you, the arrangement which is the mother of the inimitability of the Qur'an, and the rule on which the challenge was made; observing it is the most important duty of the exegete. End of quote.

Someone might say: when a pronoun can refer either to the nearer or the more distant antecedent, referring it to the nearer one is preferred. The grammarians have stated this explicitly, so on this view the pronoun in ﴿فَلْيُلْقِهِ﴾ ("let it cast him") in ﴿فاقْذِفِيهِ في اليَمِّ فَلْيُلْقِهِ اليَمُّ﴾ should refer to the nearer noun, the ark (al-tabut). The answer is that when one of the two is the topic being discussed and the other is a secondary element, the pronoun is better referred to the topic, and nearness is not taken into account. For this reason we have refuted Abu Muhammad Ibn Hazm (d. 456 AH) in his claim that the pronoun in ﴿فَإنَّهُ رِجْسٌ﴾ [Al-An'am: 145] refers to swine (khinzir), because it is the nearest noun mentioned. On his view the fat, cartilage, bone and skin of swine would thereby be forbidden. Our answer is that the topic is the meat of swine, not the swine itself.

﴿فَلْيُلْقِهِ﴾ is an imperative in form, but its meaning is a statement of fact. It is cast in the form of a command for emphasis, since a command is the most decisive and binding of verbs. From this comes the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Stand up, and I will pray for you." He put a statement into the form of a command for emphasis. Because the verb takes the form of a command, its answer is likewise in that form, namely ﴿يَأْخُذْهُ﴾ ("let him take him").

Al-Zamakhshari said: Since it was the will and decree of God that the flow of the river's water should not fail to bring him to the shore and deposit him there, He followed the paths of metaphor. He treated the river as though it had discernment, commanded it to obey and carry out the command, and so it was said: ﴿let the river throw him onto the shore﴾. End of quotation. Al-Tirmidhi said: He expressed it in the form of a command because of His prior knowledge that the thing reported would come to pass as He had reported it, so it is as though the sea were commanded and obeying the command. Al-Farra' said: ﴿Cast him into the river﴾ is a command, and it carries the sense of a conditional: "Cast him, and the river will throw him up." The apparent meaning is that the sea did throw him onto the shore, and she picked him up from it.

It is related that Pharaoh was drinking at a place on the Nile when he saw the ark. He ordered it brought to him, and his wife was with him. They opened it and saw him. His wife took pity on him and asked for him, to adopt him as a son, and he permitted her to do so. It is also related that the ark came on the water to the watering-place where the maidservants of Pharaoh's wife drew water. They took the ark, brought it to her, opened it, and informed Pharaoh. The enemy of God and of Moses is Pharaoh. His mother was informed of this by way of inspiration, and that is why she said to his sister ﴿Follow him up﴾ [Al-Qasas: 11], although she did not know where he had come to rest.

﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾. It is said this was the love of Asiya and of Pharaoh. Pharaoh had come to love him intensely, so that he could not restrain himself from being patient away from him. Ibn 'Abbas said: God loved him and made him beloved to His creation. 'Atiyya said: a sheen of beauty was placed upon him, so that whoever saw him could hardly bear to be apart from him. Qatada said: there was a comeliness in his eyes, so that no one who saw him failed to love him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The strongest of the views is that it means acceptance. Al-Zamakhshari said: (minni, "from Me") must either be connected to ﴿alqaytu﴾ ("I cast"), in which case the meaning is "I loved you," and whoever God loves, hearts love; or it must be connected to a deleted element that is an adjective of "love," meaning: a love that is pure, or one that proceeds from Me. I have placed it in hearts and sown it there, and therefore Pharaoh and everyone who looked upon you loved you.

The majority of readers recited ﴿wa-litusna'a﴾ ("and that you might be raised") with a kasra on the lam of purpose (lam kay) and a damma on the taa', with the verb in the subjunctive. The sense is: "so that you might be reared and well treated, and I would watch over and observe you, as a man watches a thing with his eyes when he takes care of it." Qatada said something close to this. Al-Nahhas said: one says "sana'tu al-faras" ("I treated the horse well") when one treats it kindly. It is coordinated with a deleted cause, meaning: "so that he might be gentle with you" and "that you might be raised." Or it is connected to a later verb whose supposed form is "I did that." Al-Hasan and Abu Nahik read it with a fatha on the taa'. Tha'lab said: its meaning is "so that your movement and conduct would be under My eye." Shayba and Abu Ja'far, in one narration, read it with sukun on the lam and the 'ayn and a damma on the taa' as an imperative verb. From Abu Ja'far also it is so, except that he read the lam with a kasra.

﴿When your sister walked﴾. It is said her name was Maryam. The reason was that Asiya offered him for suckling, but he would not accept any woman. So she began to call out about him in the city, and he was taken around and presented to the wet-nurses, but he refused them. His mother remained in grief after he had been cast into the river. So she told his sister to search the city in case she might learn of his news. She saw him during her wandering and said: "I will guide you to someone who will nurse him for you, and they will be sincere in their care for him." They seized her and said: "Do you know this child?" She said: "No, but I know of the people of this house, their eagerness to draw near to the queen and their striving in her service and her pleasure." They left her and asked her to find a nurse, so she brought Moses' mother. When she brought him near, he took her breast, and Asiya was delighted. She said to her: "Stay with us in the palace." She said: "I would not leave my house and my child, but he may stay with me." Asiya said: "Yes." So she treated the people of that house with the utmost kindness, and the Children of Israel took pride in this suckling and in their kinship with the queen. When his suckling was complete, Asiya sent word to her: "Bring my son to me on such-and-such a day." She ordered her servants and those with her to meet him with gifts, presents and clothing. He reached her in that state, in the best condition and the most beautiful youth. She was delighted with him and entered with him to Pharaoh so that he might see him and bestow him as a gift. Pharaoh was pleased with him and brought him near. Then Moses seized Pharaoh's beard, and what happened to him was mentioned in the discussion of the knot (in his tongue).

Regarding the element governing ﴿idh﴾ ("when"), Ibn 'Atiyya said it is a deleted verb whose supposed form is "and We bestowed favour when." Al-Zamakhshari said the governing element of ﴿idh tamshi﴾ is ﴿alqaytu﴾ ("I cast") or ﴿tusna'a﴾ ("be raised"). It may also be a substitute (badal) for ﴿idh awhayna﴾ ("when We inspired"). If you ask: how is substitution valid when the two times are different and far apart? I answer: just as it is valid, even though the time has widened and its two ends are distant, for a man to say to you: "I met so-and-so in such-and-such a year," and you reply: "I also met him at that time." Perhaps he met him at its beginning and you at its end. End of quotation. This is not as he stated, because a year admits of breadth, so that if their meeting occurs within it, that is possible. But these two ends are each narrow and not expansive, since each is specified by what is attached to it. It is not possible for the second to occur at the end where the first occurred, because the first is not wide enough to contain both the inspiration and the walking of the sister. The time of the inspiration does not include parts in which the walking occurred, unlike the year. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿idh﴾ is connected to ﴿tusna'a﴾, and you may also put ﴿idh﴾ in the accusative by a deleted verb whose supposed form is "and remember."

The majority read ﴿kay taqarra﴾ ("that she might be comforted") with a fatha on the taa' and the qaf. A group read it with a kasra on the qaf. It has already been stated that both are dialectal forms in ﴿wa-qarri 'aynan﴾ [Maryam: 26]. Jinah ibn Hubaysh read it with a damma on the taa' and a fatha on the qaf, in the passive form.

﴿You killed a soul﴾ [Al-Qasas: 19] refers to the Egyptian (Qibti) whom the Israelite called on him for help against, and he killed him when he was twelve years old. He was distressed because of the killing, fearing God's punishment and Pharaoh's retaliation. God forgave him when he asked forgiveness and said: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾ [Al-Qasas: 16]. He rescued him from Pharaoh when he migrated with him to Madyan. Ghamm ("distress") is what weighs upon the heart because of fear or the loss of an aim. In the dialect of Quraysh, ghamm means killing. It is also said: it comes from "the ark ghammed" (was covered over), or from "the sea ghammed" (covered him). The apparent meaning is that it comes from "ghamma" in the sense of killing, when We took you from Egypt to Madyan.

Al-Futun is a verbal noun, or the plural of fitan or fitna, with the feminine ending dropped, like huju and budur from hujza and budra. The sense is: ﴿We tested you with trials﴾ (fatannaka), meaning various kinds of trials. Fitna means affliction and whatever is hard for a person. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: "We delivered you from one trial after another." He was born in a year when children were being killed, his mother cast him into the river, Pharaoh intended to kill him, he killed a Copt, he hired himself out for ten years, he lost the way, and his flock scattered on a dark night. End of quotation. These trials were those by which He tested him and delivered him, until he became fit for prophethood and was preserved for it. The years he spent in Madyan were ten. Wahb said: twenty-eight years, of which was the bride-price for his daughter. Between Egypt and Madyan there were eight stages. There is an elision in the speech; the supposed form is: ﴿We tested you with trials﴾, and then you went out fearful to ﴿the people of Madyan﴾, and remained there for years. When he went to Madyan he was twelve years old. He stayed ten years tending Shu'ayb's flock, then eighteen years after he married Shu'ayb's daughter, and children were born to him in that time. So he completed forty years, and that is the period at the end of which it is God's custom to send prophets.

﴿Then you came﴾ to the place where I met with you, spoke to you and made you a prophet. ﴿At an appointed time﴾, that is, a time set by Me, which you neither preceded nor lagged behind. It is said: at a measure of time in which prophets are inspired, which is forty years. The poet said:

He attained the caliphate, or it came to him at its appointed time, as Moses came to his Lord at an appointed time.

﴿And I chose you for Myself﴾: that is, I made you the object of favour and the place of bounty and kindness, I purified you with graces, and I selected you for My love. It is said: "Fulan made Fulan a favourite," meaning he took him as a favourite. It is a form derived from ṣun', which is kindness to a person so intense that it becomes attributed to him, so one says: "This is so-and-so's favour." Al-Zamakhshari said: This is an image of what He granted him in the rank of nearness, honour, and speech. His state is depicted by the state of one whom kings see as possessing all the qualities and distinctions fitting him to be nearest to them and most intimate in station. So they favour him with honour and preference and choose him for themselves. End of quotation.

The meaning of ﴿for Myself﴾ is: for My commands, for establishing My proofs and conveying My message. Therefore your movements and stillnesses are for Me, not for yourself, nor for anyone other than you.

[p. 242] [p. 243]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 25–41 (part 1 of 2):

(p-238) He said: "My Lord, expand my breast for me, and ease my task for me, and loosen a knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech, and appoint for me a minister from my family, Harun, my brother. Strengthen my back through him, and make him a partner in my affair, that we may glorify You much and remember You much. Indeed You are ever Seeing of us." He said: "You have been granted your request, O Musa. And We had already bestowed favour upon you another time, when We inspired to your mother what is inspired: 'Cast him into the chest, then cast it into the river, and let the river deposit him on the bank, and an enemy to Me and an enemy to him will take him.' And I cast upon you love from Me, and that you be raised under My eye. When your sister walked and said, 'Shall I direct you to one who will take charge of him?' So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve. And you killed a soul, but We delivered you from distress and tested you with a severe testing. And you stayed for years among the people of Madyan, then you came here by decree, O Musa. And I have chosen you for Myself."

(p-239) When He commanded him to go to Pharaoh, he knew that he had been charged with a great matter, requiring him to bear what only one of steady heart and broad breast can bear. So he asked his Lord and desired that He expand his breast, so that he could endure the hardships that would come upon him, which would constrict the breast; and that He ease his affair, for he was to be the Caliph of God on His earth, together with what accompanies that of undertaking great calamities. He knew what Pharaoh had of tyranny, rebellion and domination.

Ibn Juraij said: its meaning is, "Widen my breast so that I may retain from You what You entrust of Your revelation." Al-Karmani said: "Widen my heart and make it pliable to understand Your address, to deliver Your message, and to undertake what You have charged me with of its burdens." The "knot" (al-'uqdah) is a metaphor for a heaviness that was in his tongue by nature.

Mujahid said: it was from the ember that he put into his mouth, and Asiya had had God place love for him in her heart, and she asked Pharaoh not to slaughter him. While she was once dandling him, Pharaoh took him onto his lap and seized a lock of his beard. It was said: he slapped him. It was said: he struck him with a staff that was in his hand. Pharaoh became angry and summoned the executioner. She said: "He is only a child who does not distinguish between the ruby and the ember." So he brought [them] or intended to extend his hand to the ruby, but Jibril, peace be upon him, turned his hand to the ember, and he took it and put it in his mouth, and his tongue was burnt. End of quote. The burning of the fire and its effect on his tongue and not on his hand is evidence against the view of those who hold to "nature" (al-tabi'ah).

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: there was a lisp (ratta) in his tongue. It was also said: the knot arose after the intimate conversation, so that he would not speak to anyone after it. Qutrub said: there was in him a stammering (muskah) from speech. Ibn 'Isa said: the knot is like the tamtamah and the fa'fa'ah (speech impediments).

Musa's request for the untying of the knot was to the extent that his speech could be understood. It was said: some of it remained, for his saying: "My brother Harun is more eloquent in tongue than I" [al-Qasas: 34], and His saying: "and he can hardly make himself clear" [al-Zukhruf: 52]. It was said: it was removed by His saying "You have been granted your request, O Musa," and this is the view of al-Hasan. It was said: this is weak, because he did not say "and untie the knot," but said "a knot," so when He untied a knot, God had granted him his request. It was said regarding His saying "and he can hardly make himself clear" [al-Zukhruf: 52] that its meaning is that he does not bring clear explanation and proof; and Pharaoh said this only as deception, although he addressed him and his people, and they understood him. So how can the negation of clarity, or approximating it, be possible?

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask about His saying "Expand my breast for me and ease my affair for me": what is its benefit, when the speech stands without it? I say: He first made the speech vague, saying "expand for me" and "ease for me," so it was known that there was something expanded and something eased. Then he clarified and removed the vagueness by mentioning both, so this was more emphatic in asking for the expansion and easing of his breast, and [he commanded him] to say: "Expand my breast and ease my affair," in clear explanation, since it is a repetition of one meaning by way of both the general and the detailed. He also said: As for the indefiniteness of "knot" and the absence of "untie a knot" with "of my tongue," [it means] he asked for the untying of part of it, intending that he be understood well, and did not ask for complete eloquence; and "of my tongue" is an attribute of "knot," as if it were said: "a knot of the knots of my tongue." End of quote. It appears that "of my tongue" is connected to "untie," because the position of an attribute is for "knot," and so said al-Hawfi. Abu al-Baqa' permitted both views.

The "wazir" is the helper who bears the burdens of affairs, i.e., their weight; the king's wazir bears his burdens and expenses for him. It was also said: it is from "wizr," which is a refuge to which a person resorts. The poet said:

"Among the ravenous beasts, beyond him is a refuge; and among people, the worst of them is one beyond whom there is no refuge."

"How many a company were safe, whom no beast harmed; and we do not see a human who was not harmed by a human."

So the king takes refuge in his opinion and resorts to him in his affairs. Al-Asma'i said: it is from "mu'azarah," which is aid and support, and the regular form would be "azir"; likewise al-Zamakhshari said: the regular form would be "azir," and the hamzah was changed to a waw. The reason for changing it is that "fa'il" came in the sense of "mufa'il" in a valid manner, like 'ashir, jalis, qa'id, khalil, sadiq, nadim. So when it was changed in "akhi," it was changed in it too, and assigning a thing to its counterpart is not rare. [This is] in view of "yu'azir" and its kin and of "mu'azarah." End of quote. There is no need to claim the hamzah was changed to waw, because we have a clear derivation, which is "wizr." As for its change in "yu'azir," it is due to the damma before the waw, and that too is a non-obligatory substitution.

They also permitted that "waziran" with "li" be the two objects of "aj'al," with "Harun" as an apposition or a conjunctive explanation; and that "wazir" and "Harun" be its two objects, with the second placed first out of concern for the matter of the wizarah, and "akhi" as an apposition to "Harun" in these two cases.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If it is taken as another conjunctive explanation, it is permissible and good. End of quote. Yet conjunctive explanation is remote here, because usually in an explanation the first term is less well known than the second, whereas here the matter is the reverse.

They also permitted that "waziran min ahli" be the two objects, with "li" like His saying "and there is none comparable to Him" [al-Ikhlas: 4], meaning that the meaning is completed by it. "Harun" is as previously stated. They also permitted that "Harun" be in the accusative by a deleted verb, i.e., "join Harun to me," but this is not needed, because the sentence is complete without this deleted element.

al-Hasan, Zayd ibn 'Ali and Ibn 'Amir read "ashdud" with a fatha on the hamzah and "wa-ushrikhu" with a damma, as a jussive imperfect verb in answer to the imperative, and "wa-ushrikhu" is conjoined to it. The author of al-Lawami' said, from al-Hasan, that he read "ushaddidu bihi" as the imperfect of "shaddada," for intensity and repetition, i.e., whenever a matter saddened me, I strengthened "my back through him." The majority read "ashdud" and "wa-ashrikhu" in the sense of supplication for the strengthening of the back and the making of Harun a partner in prophethood. In the reading of Ibn 'Amir the imperative does not mean prophethood, but rather his management and assistance, because it is not for Musa to make anyone a partner in prophethood. In the codex of 'Abd Allah it reads "akhi washdud."

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible, for one who reads it in the imperative form, to make "akhi" nominative as the subject, with "ashdud bihi" as its predicate, and to pause at "Harun." End of quote. This is contrary to the apparent sense, so it is not to be resorted to without need. Harun was four years older than Musa. Musa made what he desired and asked for of blessings a cause that entails worship and striving in God's command, and mutual support and cooperation in worship is a stimulus to desire and increase in good.

"That we may glorify You" — "nunazzihaka": we declare You free of what is not befitting to You. "And remember You" — by supplication and praise of You. Glorification is mentioned first because it is His transcendence in His essence and attributes and His freedom from deficiencies, and its locus is the heart; remembrance and praise of God through attributes of perfection have the tongue as their locus, so what has the heart as its locus is placed before what has the tongue as its locus. "Much" (kathiran) is an attribute of a deleted verbal noun, or an accusative of circumstance, i.e., we glorify You with glorification in a state of their abundance, according to what Sibawayh held. "Indeed You are ever Seeing of us" — knowing our conditions.

"Su'l" (request) is a noun in the sense of the object requested, like "khubz" (bread) and "akl" (food) in the sense of what is baked and eaten. The meaning: you have been given your request and what you asked for of expansion of the breast, ease of the affair, untying of the knot, and making your brother a minister; and this is among the favours upon him.

Then He reminded him of His having previously bestowed favour upon him, by way of making him stand firm, so that his striving would grow and his insight strengthen. "Marratan" means "a favour," and "ukhra" is the feminine of "akhar" in the sense of "ghayr" (other): a favour other than this favour. "Ukhra" here is not in the sense of "akhirah" (last), which would be opposed to "the first." Some thought this, saying: He called it "ukhra" but it is first, because it is "ukhra" in mention; and "al-ukhra" is a homonymous word: the feminine of "al-akhar" with a fatha on the kha', and the feminine of "al-akhar" in the sense of its last, and this has the sense of lateness. The meaning is that I protected you while you were a suckling infant, so how would I not protect you when I have qualified you for the message? In "marratan ukhra" there is a generality that is explained by "when We inspired to your mother." Al-Jumhur said: it was an inspiration of inspiration (ilham), like His saying "And your Lord inspired the bee" [al-Nahl: 68]. It was said: it was an inspiration of information, either by showing this in a dream, or by sending an angel to her not in the manner of prophethood, as Mary was sent to. This is the apparent meaning, because of the apparent sense of "he will be taken by an enemy to Me and an enemy to him," and the apparent sense of the verse in al-Qasas: "We will return him to you and make him one of the messengers" [al-Qasas: 7]. What al-Zamakhshari began with, "from the one who returns his hand," is remote, whether it is on the tongue of a prophet of that time, like His saying "And when I inspired the disciples" [al-Ma'idah: 111]; for it is not reported that he was in the time of Pharaoh, and in the time of the disciples there were Zakariya and Yahya. In His saying "what is inspired" there is vagueness and generality, like His saying "when there covered the lote-tree that which covered" [al-Najm: 16], and "then there covered them of the sea that which covered them" [Ta-Ha: 78], and in it is awe-inspiring magnitude. It is explained here by His saying "Cast him into the chest."

Al-Zamakhshari said:
(p-241) "An" is the explanatory particle, because inspiration has the meaning of speech. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "An" in His saying "an uqdhifihi" is an apposition to "ma," meaning that "an" is verbal (masdariyyah), and for that reason it has a place in the grammatical structure. Both views are permissible. The apparent sense is that "the chest" was of wood. It was said: of papyrus from the tree of the believer of Pharaoh's family; she sealed its gaps, spread in it a mat (nith') — it was said: carded cotton — sealed its mouth, plastered it, pitched it, and cast it into the "yamm," which is the name for the sweet sea. It was said: it is the name for the Nile specifically. The first is correct, as in His saying "So We drowned them in the yamm" [al-A'raf: 136], and they were not drowned in the Nile.

The apparent sense is that the pronoun in "fa-uqdhifihi fi al-yamm" refers to Musa, and likewise the two pronouns after it, since he is the one spoken of, not the chest; the chest was mentioned only as a container and incidental detail. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the first pronoun in "uqdhifihi" refers to Musa, and in the second it refers to "the chest," though it could refer to Musa. Al-Zamakhshari said: All the pronouns refer to Musa; their referring partly to him and partly to the chest involves a blemish, because of the discord in arrangement it leads to. If you ask: the thing cast into the sea is the chest, and likewise the thing cast onto the bank? I say: what harm is there if you say that the one cast and the one cast onto the bank is Musa within the chest, so that the pronouns do not scatter and the arrangement does not become discordant for you, the arrangement which is the mother of the inimitability of the Qur'an, and the rule on which the challenge was made; observing it is the most important duty of the exegete. End of quote.

Someone might say: when a pronoun can refer either to the nearer or the more distant antecedent, referring it to the nearer one is preferred. The grammarians have stated this explicitly, so on this view the pronoun in ﴿فَلْيُلْقِهِ﴾ ("let it cast him") in ﴿فاقْذِفِيهِ في اليَمِّ فَلْيُلْقِهِ اليَمُّ﴾ should refer to the nearer noun, the ark (al-tabut). The answer is that when one of the two is the topic being discussed and the other is a secondary element, the pronoun is better referred to the topic, and nearness is not taken into account. For this reason we have refuted Abu Muhammad Ibn Hazm (d. 456 AH) in his claim that the pronoun in ﴿فَإنَّهُ رِجْسٌ﴾ [Al-An'am: 145] refers to swine (khinzir), because it is the nearest noun mentioned. On his view the fat, cartilage, bone and skin of swine would thereby be forbidden. Our answer is that the topic is the meat of swine, not the swine itself.

﴿فَلْيُلْقِهِ﴾ is an imperative in form, but its meaning is a statement of fact. It is cast in the form of a command for emphasis, since a command is the most decisive and binding of verbs. From this comes the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Stand up, and I will pray for you." He put a statement into the form of a command for emphasis. Because the verb takes the form of a command, its answer is likewise in that form, namely ﴿يَأْخُذْهُ﴾ ("let him take him").

Al-Zamakhshari said: Since it was the will and decree of God that the flow of the river's water should not fail to bring him to the shore and deposit him there, He followed the paths of metaphor. He treated the river as though it had discernment, commanded it to obey and carry out the command, and so it was said: ﴿let the river throw him onto the shore﴾. End of quotation. Al-Tirmidhi said: He expressed it in the form of a command because of His prior knowledge that the thing reported would come to pass as He had reported it, so it is as though the sea were commanded and obeying the command. Al-Farra' said: ﴿Cast him into the river﴾ is a command, and it carries the sense of a conditional: "Cast him, and the river will throw him up." The apparent meaning is that the sea did throw him onto the shore, and she picked him up from it.

It is related that Pharaoh was drinking at a place on the Nile when he saw the ark. He ordered it brought to him, and his wife was with him. They opened it and saw him. His wife took pity on him and asked for him, to adopt him as a son, and he permitted her to do so. It is also related that the ark came on the water to the watering-place where the maidservants of Pharaoh's wife drew water. They took the ark, brought it to her, opened it, and informed Pharaoh. The enemy of God and of Moses is Pharaoh. His mother was informed of this by way of inspiration, and that is why she said to his sister ﴿Follow him up﴾ [Al-Qasas: 11], although she did not know where he had come to rest.

﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾. It is said this was the love of Asiya and of Pharaoh. Pharaoh had come to love him intensely, so that he could not restrain himself from being patient away from him. Ibn 'Abbas said: God loved him and made him beloved to His creation. 'Atiyya said: a sheen of beauty was placed upon him, so that whoever saw him could hardly bear to be apart from him. Qatada said: there was a comeliness in his eyes, so that no one who saw him failed to love him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The strongest of the views is that it means acceptance. Al-Zamakhshari said: (minni, "from Me") must either be connected to ﴿alqaytu﴾ ("I cast"), in which case the meaning is "I loved you," and whoever God loves, hearts love; or it must be connected to a deleted element that is an adjective of "love," meaning: a love that is pure, or one that proceeds from Me. I have placed it in hearts and sown it there, and therefore Pharaoh and everyone who looked upon you loved you.

The majority of readers recited ﴿wa-litusna'a﴾ ("and that you might be raised") with a kasra on the lam of purpose (lam kay) and a damma on the taa', with the verb in the subjunctive. The sense is: "so that you might be reared and well treated, and I would watch over and observe you, as a man watches a thing with his eyes when he takes care of it." Qatada said something close to this. Al-Nahhas said: one says "sana'tu al-faras" ("I treated the horse well") when one treats it kindly. It is coordinated with a deleted cause, meaning: "so that he might be gentle with you" and "that you might be raised." Or it is connected to a later verb whose supposed form is "I did that." Al-Hasan and Abu Nahik read it with a fatha on the taa'. Tha'lab said: its meaning is "so that your movement and conduct would be under My eye." Shayba and Abu Ja'far, in one narration, read it with sukun on the lam and the 'ayn and a damma on the taa' as an imperative verb. From Abu Ja'far also it is so, except that he read the lam with a kasra.

﴿When your sister walked﴾. It is said her name was Maryam. The reason was that Asiya offered him for suckling, but he would not accept any woman. So she began to call out about him in the city, and he was taken around and presented to the wet-nurses, but he refused them. His mother remained in grief after he had been cast into the river. So she told his sister to search the city in case she might learn of his news. She saw him during her wandering and said: "I will guide you to someone who will nurse him for you, and they will be sincere in their care for him." They seized her and said: "Do you know this child?" She said: "No, but I know of the people of this house, their eagerness to draw near to the queen and their striving in her service and her pleasure." They left her and asked her to find a nurse, so she brought Moses' mother. When she brought him near, he took her breast, and Asiya was delighted. She said to her: "Stay with us in the palace." She said: "I would not leave my house and my child, but he may stay with me." Asiya said: "Yes." So she treated the people of that house with the utmost kindness, and the Children of Israel took pride in this suckling and in their kinship with the queen. When his suckling was complete, Asiya sent word to her: "Bring my son to me on such-and-such a day." She ordered her servants and those with her to meet him with gifts, presents and clothing. He reached her in that state, in the best condition and the most beautiful youth. She was delighted with him and entered with him to Pharaoh so that he might see him and bestow him as a gift. Pharaoh was pleased with him and brought him near. Then Moses seized Pharaoh's beard, and what happened to him was mentioned in the discussion of the knot (in his tongue).

Regarding the element governing ﴿idh﴾ ("when"), Ibn 'Atiyya said it is a deleted verb whose supposed form is "and We bestowed favour when." Al-Zamakhshari said the governing element of ﴿idh tamshi﴾ is ﴿alqaytu﴾ ("I cast") or ﴿tusna'a﴾ ("be raised"). It may also be a substitute (badal) for ﴿idh awhayna﴾ ("when We inspired"). If you ask: how is substitution valid when the two times are different and far apart? I answer: just as it is valid, even though the time has widened and its two ends are distant, for a man to say to you: "I met so-and-so in such-and-such a year," and you reply: "I also met him at that time." Perhaps he met him at its beginning and you at its end. End of quotation. This is not as he stated, because a year admits of breadth, so that if their meeting occurs within it, that is possible. But these two ends are each narrow and not expansive, since each is specified by what is attached to it. It is not possible for the second to occur at the end where the first occurred, because the first is not wide enough to contain both the inspiration and the walking of the sister. The time of the inspiration does not include parts in which the walking occurred, unlike the year. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿idh﴾ is connected to ﴿tusna'a﴾, and you may also put ﴿idh﴾ in the accusative by a deleted verb whose supposed form is "and remember."

The majority read ﴿kay taqarra﴾ ("that she might be comforted") with a fatha on the taa' and the qaf. A group read it with a kasra on the qaf. It has already been stated that both are dialectal forms in ﴿wa-qarri 'aynan﴾ [Maryam: 26]. Jinah ibn Hubaysh read it with a damma on the taa' and a fatha on the qaf, in the passive form.

﴿You killed a soul﴾ [Al-Qasas: 19] refers to the Egyptian (Qibti) whom the Israelite called on him for help against, and he killed him when he was twelve years old. He was distressed because of the killing, fearing God's punishment and Pharaoh's retaliation. God forgave him when he asked forgiveness and said: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾ [Al-Qasas: 16]. He rescued him from Pharaoh when he migrated with him to Madyan. Ghamm ("distress") is what weighs upon the heart because of fear or the loss of an aim. In the dialect of Quraysh, ghamm means killing. It is also said: it comes from "the ark ghammed" (was covered over), or from "the sea ghammed" (covered him). The apparent meaning is that it comes from "ghamma" in the sense of killing, when We took you from Egypt to Madyan.

Al-Futun is a verbal noun, or the plural of fitan or fitna, with the feminine ending dropped, like huju and budur from hujza and budra. The sense is: ﴿We tested you with trials﴾ (fatannaka), meaning various kinds of trials. Fitna means affliction and whatever is hard for a person. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: "We delivered you from one trial after another." He was born in a year when children were being killed, his mother cast him into the river, Pharaoh intended to kill him, he killed a Copt, he hired himself out for ten years, he lost the way, and his flock scattered on a dark night. End of quotation. These trials were those by which He tested him and delivered him, until he became fit for prophethood and was preserved for it. The years he spent in Madyan were ten. Wahb said: twenty-eight years, of which was the bride-price for his daughter. Between Egypt and Madyan there were eight stages. There is an elision in the speech; the supposed form is: ﴿We tested you with trials﴾, and then you went out fearful to ﴿the people of Madyan﴾, and remained there for years. When he went to Madyan he was twelve years old. He stayed ten years tending Shu'ayb's flock, then eighteen years after he married Shu'ayb's daughter, and children were born to him in that time. So he completed forty years, and that is the period at the end of which it is God's custom to send prophets.
