He said: ﴿Then who is your Lord, O Musa?﴾ He addressed the two of them together, but singled out Musa for the call. Ibn Atiyya said: because he was the one who had the great station of the message and the noble signs. Al-Zamakhshari said: because he is the root of prophethood, and Harun is his minister and follower. It is possible that his wickedness and violence led him to seek the speech of Musa rather than the speech of his brother, because of what is known of Harun's eloquence and the lisp in Musa's tongue, and this is shown by His words: ﴿Am I not better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly make himself clear?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 52]. End quote.

Musa, peace be upon him, took independent charge of answering Pharaoh, in that he singled him out with both the question and the call. Then he informed him of the attributes of Allah the Exalted by the attribute in which Pharaoh has no share, nor any figurative sense. Al-Zamakhshari said: How excellent is this answer, how concise, how comprehensive, and how clear, for one who applies his mind and looks with an eye of fairness and seeks the truth. End quote.

The meaning is: He gave every thing its creation and its form suited to what is fitting for it in perfection. He did not make the creation of man like the creation of beasts, nor the creation of beasts like the creation of man, but He created every thing and measured it with due measure.

The poet said:
"For Him in every thing is a creation, and so Allah does what He wills."

This is the view of Mujahid, Ata and Muqatil. Al-Dahhak said: "His creation" refers to the benefit attached to it, suited to it. ﴿Then guided﴾, i.e., He made easy for every thing its benefits and its conveniences. So He gave the eye the form that suits sight, and the ear the shape that suits hearing, and likewise the nose, the hand, the foot and the tongue; each of them suits the benefit attached to it, without being a substitute for it. Al-Qushayri said: "creation" here means the created thing, because seizing, walking, seeing and speaking are created meanings which Allah deposited in the limbs. On this view the first object of "gave" is ﴿every thing﴾ and the second is "its creation." The same is the view of Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi: the meaning is ﴿He gave every thing﴾ its counterpart of its own kind, i.e., every male animal its female counterpart in form. So He did not pair any of them with other than its own kind; then He guided it to its mating, its food, its drink and its dwelling. It is related from Ibn Abbas that He guided it to its mate, to union with it and to mating. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: ﴿He gave every thing﴾ its goodness, and guided it to what would make it right.

It has also been said: ﴿every thing﴾ is the second object of "gave," and "its creation" is the first object, i.e., He gave His creatures ﴿every thing﴾ they need and from which they derive benefit. Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] and some companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Nahik, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-A'mash, al-Hasan, Nusayr from al-Kisa'i, Ibn Nuh from Qutaybah, and Salam read ﴿khalqahu﴾ with a fatha on the lam, as a past-tense verb in the position of a description of "every thing" or of "a thing," and the second object of "gave" is omitted by restriction, i.e., ﴿every thing that He created﴾ He did not leave without His gift and bounty. ﴿Then guided﴾, i.e., he knew how to benefit from what was given and how to reach it. It has also been said that the object is omitted by abbreviation, because the meaning shows it, i.e., ﴿He gave every thing its creation﴾ what it needs. Ibn Atiyya estimated it as its perfection or its benefit.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verse 42–50 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and do not slacken in remembering Me.﴾ ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has indeed transgressed.﴾ ﴿Speak to him gently, that perhaps he may take heed or fear.﴾ ﴿They said: Our Lord, we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress.﴾ ﴿He said: Fear not; indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing.﴾ ﴿So go to him and say: We are two messengers of your Lord, so send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them. We have indeed come to you with a sign from your Lord, and peace is upon whoever follows the guidance.﴾ ﴿It has indeed been revealed to us that the punishment is upon whoever denies and turns away.﴾ ﴿He said: Who then is your Lord, O Musa?﴾ ﴿He said: Our Lord is He who gave every thing its creation, then guided it.﴾ ﴿He said: What then is the state of the former generations?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 51] ﴿He said: Their knowledge is with my Lord, in a Book. My Lord neither errs nor forgets.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52]

(p. 244 [sic: 245])

God, exalted is He, commanded him to go to Pharaoh. When he (Musa) called upon his Lord and asked for things, among them that He make his brother Harun a partner with him, God mentioned that He had granted him his request, and this included making his brother a partner. So here He commands him and his brother to go. The words ﴿Akhūka﴾ (your brother) [Yusuf: 69] are in apposition (ma'tuf) to the pronoun concealed in ﴿Idhhab anta wa-akhūka﴾ in Surat al-Ma'ida. As for the view of some grammarians that "wa-Rabbuka" (and your Lord) is nominative by an implied verb, meaning "and let your Lord go," that question is discussed here.

It is related that God revealed to Harun, while he was in Egypt, that he should go out to meet Musa. It was also said that he heard of his coming. It was also said that he was inspired with this. The word ﴿bi-āyātī﴾ (with My signs) is in plural form. It was said that these are the staff, the hand, and the knot in his tongue. It was also said: the hand and the staff. The plural may be used for the dual, and these two are the ones mentioned earlier; for this reason, when he said ﴿fa-'ti bi-āya﴾ (then bring a sign), he threw the staff and drew out the hand, and said: "These are two proofs" (burhanān). It was also said: the staff included the signs of its transformation into a serpent, first being small, then it grew until it became a great serpent, and then Musa put his hand into its mouth and it did not harm him. It was also said: it refers to whatever miracle and revelation he was given.

﴿Wa-lā tanīyā﴾ means: do not weaken and do not fall short. It was said: do not forget Me, and I will not cease to be in remembrance of you wherever you turn. It is also permissible that "dhikr" (remembrance) here means conveying the message, since dhikr applies to all acts of worship, and conveying the message is among the greatest and most important of them, so it was fitting that it be called dhikr. Ibn Wathhab recited ﴿wa-lā tinīyā﴾ with a kasra on the ta' to match the vowel of the nun. In the codex of Abdullah it reads ﴿wa-lā tahinā﴾, meaning: do not soften, from the saying "hayyin layyin" (gentle, easy). When He omitted who is to go in the first command, He specified it in this second command. So: ﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾, that is, with the message. He who holds that they were first commanded to go to the people and then to Pharaoh is far from the truth; the command to go was repeated because the object differed. He pointed out the reason for going to him with the message from Him in His words ﴿innahu ṭagā﴾ (for he has transgressed) [Ta-Ha: 24], meaning he exceeded the limit in corruption and claimed lordship and divinity apart from God.

The gentle speech is like what is in al-Nazi'at: ﴿Would you like to purify yourself, and that I guide you to your Lord so that you fear Him?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18]. This is among the subtle expressions, for it presented the matter in the form of a question, consultation, and offering, because of the great success it contains. It was also said: He promised him a youth that would never age, and a kingdom that would not be taken from him except by death, and that the pleasure of food, drink, and marriage would remain for him until his death. It was also said: do not confront him with what he dislikes, and be gentle in speech, because of his right to have raised Musa. It was also said: they addressed him by his kunya, for he had four kunyas: Abu Murrah, Abu Mus'ab, Abu al-Walid, and Abu al-Abbas. It was also said: the gentle speech is "There is no god but God, alone, with no partner," and its gentleness is its lightness on the tongue. Al-Hasan said: it is their saying, "Indeed for you there is a Lord, indeed for you there is a return, and indeed before you are a Garden and a Fire. So believe in God and He will admit you to the Garden and protect you from the punishment of the Fire." It was also said: God commanded them to put promises before threats, as the poet said:

*Advance with the promise before the threat,*
*so that its ignorant ones may restrain the tribes.*

It was also said: when Musa and Harun, peace be upon them, presented what they presented to him, he consulted Asiya, and she said: "It is not fitting for anyone to reject this." Then he consulted Haman, who would not decide any matter without his opinion, and Haman said to him: "I thought you were a man of intellect! You would be a master, and become a slave; a lord, and become one who is lorded over!" So he refused to accept what Musa had offered him. The expression of hope (al-tarajji) on their part, since its occurrence from God is impossible: that is, go in accordance with your hope and desire, and proceed as one who hopes and expects that his work will bear fruit and his effort will not be in vain. The benefit of sending them, although God knows he will not believe, is to establish the proof against him and remove any excuse (p. 246), as God said: ﴿And had We destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said...﴾ [Ta-Ha: 134], and so on.

It was also said: the gentle speech is what God related here, namely ﴿fa-'tiyāhu fa-qūlā innā rasūlā rabbika﴾ up to His words ﴿wa-al-salāmu ʿalā man ittaba'a al-hudā﴾. Abu Mu'adh said: ﴿qawlan layyinan﴾. Al-Farra' said: "la'alla" here means "kay" (in order that): "in order that he may take heed or fear," just as you say, "Work, so that you may take your reward," meaning "in order that you take your reward." It was also said: "la'alla" here is interrogative, meaning "will he take heed or fear?" The correct view is that it retains its meaning of hope (tarajji), and this is with respect to humans. The words ﴿la'allahu yatadhakkaru aw yakhsha﴾ indicate that he was not doubting God. It was also said: "yatadhakkaru" means: recall his state when the Nile was held back; he went to its bank, moved far away, fell down prostrate to God, hoping that He would not disgrace him. Then he rode, and the Nile began following the hoofprints of his horse. So he hoped he would recall God's forbearance and generosity and beware of God's punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, "yatadhakkaru" (he may recall) and reflect, so that he would exercise fairness toward himself and submit to the truth, ﴿aw yakhsha﴾ (or fear) that the matter is as they describe, and that his denial would drag him to ruin.

*Faraṭa* means: it preceded and advanced; from it comes *al-fāriṭ*, the one who goes ahead of those coming to water. A *farasun farṭun* is a horse that outruns the rest. End. The poet said:

*They hastened us, though they were of our companions,*
*as the forerunner of the water-seekers precedes.*

In the hadith: "I am your *faraṭ* at the Pool," meaning: your one who goes before you and outpaces you. The meaning is: we fear that punishment will be hastened upon us and that he will rush at us with it. Yahya, Abu Nawfal, and Ibn Muhaysin in one transmission recited ﴿an yufraṭa﴾ in the passive, meaning: he be forestalled in punishment and be hastened with it. It is also possible that it is from *ifrāṭ* (excess) and exceeding the limit in punishment: they feared that some driver might push him to hasten the punishment, whether from a devil, or from his tyranny and arrogance and his claim to lordship, or from his love of leadership, or from his Coptic people who were rebellious, about whom God said: ﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said﴾ [al-A'raf: 109], ﴿And the chiefs of his people said﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 33].

A group, and al-Za'faranī from Ibn Muhaysin, read: (yufrida) with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ra', from *ifrāṭ* in harm: ﴿aw an yaṭghā﴾ (or that he transgress) in overstepping to the point of saying about you what is not fitting, out of insolence toward you and hardness of his heart. In mentioning it in this unrestricted and allusive way is a door of good manners and avoidance of uttering great things.

*Al-ma'iyya* (being with) here means with help and support: "I hear your speech and see your actions." Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿asma'u﴾ means "I hear his answer to you," and ﴿wa-arā﴾ "I see what he does to you." These two are an expression for knowledge.

﴿Fa-'tiyāhu﴾: He repeated the command to come. ﴿Fa-qūlā innā rasūlā rabbika﴾: they addressed him with the words "your Lord," belittling him and informing him that he is one who is lorded over and owned, since he himself claimed lordship. They were commanded to call him to send the Children of Israel with them and to free them from the humiliation of serving the Copts, who tormented them by imposing hard labor, digging, building, carrying stones, and forced service in everything, along with killing the boys and keeping the women for service. Calling him to faith is mentioned in other verses, so the content of what Pharaoh was called to was faith and the sending of the Children of Israel.

* *

Then they mentioned what would show the truth of their being sent to him, and said: ﴿We have come to you with a sign from your Lord.﴾ Their words ﴿from your Lord﴾ are also repeated, as an emphasis that he is one who is nurtured and subdued. The sign to which they referred was the staff and the hand. Since the two of them shared in the mission, it is correct to attribute the coming with the sign to both of them, even though it came from only one of them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿We have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾ runs on from the first sentence, ﴿We are two messengers of your Lord﴾, in the manner of an explanation and elaboration, because a claim to being a messenger is not established except by its proof, which is the coming with a sign. He used the singular "a sign" and did not use the dual, though they had two signs, because the purpose in this place is to establish the claim by its evidence. It is as if he said: "We have come to you with a miracle, a proof and an argument for what we have claimed of being messengers." Likewise: ﴿Indeed I have come to you with clear evidence from your Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 105]; ﴿So bring a sign, if you are of the truthful﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 154]; ﴿Even if I brought you something clear?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 30]. End quote.

It has also been said: the sign is the hand. And it has been said: the staff. The meaning is: with a sign that testifies for us that we are the two messengers of your Lord.

Apparently, His words ﴿And peace be upon him who follows guidance﴾ are a closing remark to the speech. So "peace" here means a greeting: they turned away from him with it, following the custom of saying farewell at the end of speech. So they gave peace to those who follow guidance, and in this there is a rebuke to him. People have used this verse in this sense in their address and conversation.

It has also been said that it is connected by insertion with His words ﴿We have indeed been revealed to that the punishment is upon him who denies and turns away﴾, so it would then be a report of the safety of the guided from the punishment.

It has also been said that (upon) means (for), i.e., safety is for ﴿him who follows guidance﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The peace of the angels, who are the guardians of Paradise, is upon the guided, and the rebuke of the guardians of the Fire and the punishment is upon the deniers. End quote. This is a strange interpretation.

It may be said: "peace" here means safety from punishment, as evidenced by His words ﴿We have indeed been revealed to that the punishment is upon him who denies and turns away﴾. The verb ﴿has been revealed﴾ is in the passive because its agent is not named, and the one who revealed is not mentioned, because Pharaoh had a hasty temper, and it might have happened that he would say about the Revealer what is not fitting. The meaning is: upon him who denied the prophets and turned away from faith. Ibn Abbas said: this is the most hopeful verse in the Qur'an, because the believer does not deny and turn away, so no part of the punishment reaches him.

In the speech there is an omission. Its estimated form is: they came to Pharaoh and said to him what Allah had commanded them to convey. He said: ﴿Then who is your Lord, O Musa?﴾ He addressed the two of them together, but singled out Musa for the call. Ibn Atiyya said: because he was the one who had the great station of the message and the noble signs. Al-Zamakhshari said: because he is the root of prophethood, and Harun is his minister and follower. It is possible that his wickedness and violence led him to seek the speech of Musa rather than the speech of his brother, because of what is known of Harun's eloquence and the lisp in Musa's tongue, and this is shown by His words: ﴿Am I not better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly make himself clear?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 52]. End quote.

Musa, peace be upon him, took independent charge of answering Pharaoh, in that he singled him out with both the question and the call. Then he informed him of the attributes of Allah the Exalted by the attribute in which Pharaoh has no share, nor any figurative sense. Al-Zamakhshari said: How excellent is this answer, how concise, how comprehensive, and how clear, for one who applies his mind and looks with an eye of fairness and seeks the truth. End quote.

The meaning is: He gave every thing its creation and its form suited to what is fitting for it in perfection. He did not make the creation of man like the creation of beasts, nor the creation of beasts like the creation of man, but He created every thing and measured it with due measure.

The poet said:
"For Him in every thing is a creation, and so Allah does what He wills."

This is the view of Mujahid, Ata and Muqatil. Al-Dahhak said: "His creation" refers to the benefit attached to it, suited to it. ﴿Then guided﴾, i.e., He made easy for every thing its benefits and its conveniences. So He gave the eye the form that suits sight, and the ear the shape that suits hearing, and likewise the nose, the hand, the foot and the tongue; each of them suits the benefit attached to it, without being a substitute for it. Al-Qushayri said: "creation" here means the created thing, because seizing, walking, seeing and speaking are created meanings which Allah deposited in the limbs. On this view the first object of "gave" is ﴿every thing﴾ and the second is "its creation." The same is the view of Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi: the meaning is ﴿He gave every thing﴾ its counterpart of its own kind, i.e., every male animal its female counterpart in form. So He did not pair any of them with other than its own kind; then He guided it to its mating, its food, its drink and its dwelling. It is related from Ibn Abbas that He guided it to its mate, to union with it and to mating. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: ﴿He gave every thing﴾ its goodness, and guided it to what would make it right.

It has also been said: ﴿every thing﴾ is the second object of "gave," and "its creation" is the first object, i.e., He gave His creatures ﴿every thing﴾ they need and from which they derive benefit. Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] and some companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Nahik, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-A'mash, al-Hasan, Nusayr from al-Kisa'i, Ibn Nuh from Qutaybah, and Salam read ﴿khalqahu﴾ with a fatha on the lam, as a past-tense verb in the position of a description of "every thing" or of "a thing," and the second object of "gave" is omitted by restriction, i.e., ﴿every thing that He created﴾ He did not leave without His gift and bounty. ﴿Then guided﴾, i.e., he knew how to benefit from what was given and how to reach it. It has also been said that the object is omitted by abbreviation, because the meaning shows it, i.e., ﴿He gave every thing its creation﴾ what it needs. Ibn Atiyya estimated it as its perfection or its benefit.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 51–52:

﴿He said: "What then is the state of the former generations?"﴾ When Musa answered him with a reply that silenced him, and Pharaoh could not counter it, he moved on to another question, namely: what is the state of those generations that perished? This was a way of evading the acknowledgment of what Musa had said and of his answer to it, through deflection and sophistry. It was said that he asked him about their news and their stories, in order to test whether the two of them were prophets or were among the storytellers (qussas) who had studied the accounts of past nations. He, peace be upon him, did not yet have knowledge of the Torah, since it was revealed to him only after the destruction of Pharaoh, so he said: ﴿Its knowledge is with my Lord﴾. It was also said: his purpose in asking about them was: why did you worship idols and not worship God, if the truth is what you describe? It was also said: his purpose was: what is their state, that they are not resurrected, not called to account, and not recompensed? So he replied: ﴿Its knowledge is with my Lord﴾, meaning that this is a question about the unseen, which God has kept to Himself, and none knows it but Him.

Al-Naqqash said: He only asked when he heard the admonition of the believer of Pharaoh's family: ﴿O my people, I fear for you a day like the day of the factions﴾ [Ghafir: 30] and so on, and so he referred the knowledge of that to God, because the Torah had not yet been revealed to him.

It was also said: when he said ﴿We have indeed been revealed that the punishment is upon him who denies and turns away﴾ [Ta-Ha: 48], Pharaoh said: ﴿What then is the state of the former generations?﴾, for they denied and yet they were not punished.

It was also said: when he [Musa] established the matter of the origin and the decisive proof for affirming the Creator, Pharaoh said: if what you mention is in utmost clarity, then what is the state of the former generations, who forgot it and abandoned it? For if the proof were clear, the past generations would necessarily not have been heedless of it. Thus he opposed the transmitted proof. It is also possible that Pharaoh disputed with him over God's comprehensive knowledge of everything and His distinct knowledge of every known thing, so he obstinately said: what do you say about the bygone generations, their vast numbers, and the wide dispersal of their counts? How did He encompass them with all their parts and essences? So he replied that every existent is encompassed by His knowledge and is recorded with Him ﴿in a Book﴾, and that error and forgetfulness are not applicable to Him as they are applicable to you, O worthless servant and feeble human. That is: ﴿He does not err﴾ as you err, ﴿nor forget﴾ as you forget, O claimant to lordship, by ignorance and audacity. This is what al-Zamakhshari said.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in (ilmuha) is to ﴿the former generations﴾, meaning: it is written with my Lord in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), of which it is not possible that He errs regarding anything or forgets it. It is said: "dalaltu al-shay'" when one misses it in its place; and "dalaltuhu" is a second form, meaning one did not find it, as in your saying: "dalaltu al-tariq" and "al-manzil" (I lost the way and the dwelling). One does not say "adlaltuhu" except when it is lost from you, like an animal when it escapes and the like; this was said by al-Farra'. Al-Zajjaj said: "dalaltuhu udhillu-hu" when you place it somewhere and do not know where it is, and "adlaltuhu" (the two forms). Here "al-Kitab" is the Preserved Tablet. It was also said: ﴿in a Book﴾ means what the angels have written of the affairs of mankind. It was also said: the pronoun in ﴿ilmuha﴾ refers to the Resurrection, because he had asked him about the resurrection of the nations. Al-Suddi said: ﴿does not err﴾ means does not become heedless. Ibn Isa said: ﴿does not err﴾ means nothing escapes Him; the Arabs say "dalla manzilahu" without an alif, and in regard to animals "adalla ba'irahu" with an alif. It was also said: the implied sense is ﴿My Lord does not err﴾ in the Book ﴿nor forget﴾ what is in it; this was said by Muqatil. Al-Qaffal said: ﴿does not err﴾ from knowledge of things, so He encompasses all that is known; ﴿nor forget﴾ points to the permanence of that knowledge forever in its state, unchanging. Al-Hasan said: He does not err regarding the time of resurrection, nor forget it.

Mujahid said: the meaning of the two clauses is one, and it indicates that nothing arises in His knowledge that would alter it. Ibn Jarir said: He does not err in disposing, so that He would believe something wrong to be right; and when He knows it, He does not forget it. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: God's knowledge is an attribute subsisting in Him, and it cannot be present in the Book, for that is not conceivable; so the meaning is that the persistence of those known things in His knowledge is like the persistence of what is written in the Book. The aim is to affirm that their secrets are known to Him, and that none of them vanishes. This is reinforced by His saying ﴿My Lord does not err nor forget﴾. Or the meaning is that He has recorded those rulings in a Book with Him, which becomes manifest to the angels, adding to their evidence that He knows all known things, exalted above inattention and heedlessness. End. There is some abridgment in it.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Jahdari, Hammad ibn Salamah, Ibn Muhaysin and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read ﴿لا يُضِلُّ﴾ with a dammah on the ya' (lā yuḍillu), meaning: God does not cause that Book to go astray so that it is lost, nor does He forget what He has recorded in it. Al-Sulami read ﴿لا يُضَلُّ رَبِّي ولا يُنْسى﴾ (lā yuḍallu rabbī wa-lā yunsā) in the passive voice. The apparent reading is that the two clauses are a new sentence (isti'naf) and an informing about Him, Exalted, of the negation of these two attributes. It was also said: they are in the position of a qualifier for ﴿in a Book﴾, with the returning pronoun to the qualified noun omitted, meaning: my Lord does not err in it nor forget it. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿nor forget﴾ refers to God. It was also said: it may refer to (Book), meaning: it leaves nothing out; forgetting here is a metaphor, as in His saying ﴿except that He has counted them﴾ [al-Kahf: 49], where counting is attributed to it on account of the restriction within it. From Ibn 'Abbas: He does not leave him who disbelieved in Him until He takes vengeance upon him, and He does not leave him who affirmed His oneness until He recompenses him.

So he replied: ﴿Its knowledge is with my Lord﴾, meaning that this is a question about the unseen, which God has kept to Himself, and none knows it but Him.

Al-Naqqash said: He only asked when he heard the admonition of the believer of Pharaoh's family: ﴿O my people, I fear for you a day like the day of the factions﴾ [Ghafir: 30] and so on, and so he referred the knowledge of that to God, because the Torah had not yet been revealed to him.

It was also said: when he said ﴿We have indeed been revealed that the punishment is upon him who denies and turns away﴾ [Ta-Ha: 48], Pharaoh said: ﴿What then is the state of the former generations?﴾, for they denied and yet they were not punished.

It was also said: when he [Musa] established the matter of the origin and the decisive proof for affirming the Creator, Pharaoh said: if what you mention is in utmost clarity, then what is the state of the former generations, who forgot it and abandoned it? For if the proof were clear, the past generations would necessarily not have been heedless of it. Thus he opposed the transmitted proof. It is also possible that Pharaoh disputed with him over God's comprehensive knowledge of everything and His distinct knowledge of every known thing, so he obstinately said: what do you say about the bygone generations, their vast numbers, and the wide dispersal of their counts? How did He encompass them with all their parts and essences? So he replied that every existent is encompassed by His knowledge and is recorded with Him ﴿in a Book﴾, and that error and forgetfulness are not applicable to Him as they are applicable to you, O worthless servant and feeble human. That is: ﴿He does not err﴾ as you err, ﴿nor forget﴾ as you forget, O claimant to lordship, by ignorance and audacity. This is what al-Zamakhshari said.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in (ilmuha) is to ﴿the former generations﴾, meaning: it is written with my Lord in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), of which it is not possible that He errs regarding anything or forgets it. It is said: "dalaltu al-shay'" when one misses it in its place; and "dalaltuhu" is a second form, meaning one did not find it, as in your saying: "dalaltu al-tariq" and "al-manzil" (I lost the way and the dwelling). One does not say "adlaltuhu" except when it is lost from you, like an animal when it escapes and the like; this was said by al-Farra'. Al-Zajjaj said: "dalaltuhu udhillu-hu" when you place it somewhere and do not know where it is, and "adlaltuhu" (the two forms). Here "al-Kitab" is the Preserved Tablet. It was also said: ﴿in a Book﴾ means what the angels have written of the affairs of mankind. It was also said: the pronoun in ﴿ilmuha﴾ refers to the Resurrection, because he had asked him about the resurrection of the nations. Al-Suddi said: ﴿does not err﴾ means does not become heedless. Ibn Isa said: ﴿does not err﴾ means nothing escapes Him; the Arabs say "dalla manzilahu" without an alif, and in regard to animals "adalla ba'irahu" with an alif. It was also said: the implied sense is ﴿My Lord does not err﴾ in the Book ﴿nor forget﴾ what is in it; this was said by Muqatil. Al-Qaffal said: ﴿does not err﴾ from knowledge of things, so He encompasses all that is known; ﴿nor forget﴾ points to the permanence of that knowledge forever in its state, unchanging. Al-Hasan said: He does not err regarding the time of resurrection, nor forget it.

Mujahid said: the meaning of the two clauses is one, and it indicates that nothing arises in His knowledge that would alter it. Ibn Jarir said: He does not err in disposing, so that He would believe something wrong to be right; and when He knows it, He does not forget it. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: God's knowledge is an attribute subsisting in Him, and it cannot be present in the Book, for that is not conceivable; so the meaning is that the persistence of those known things in His knowledge is like the persistence of what is written in the Book. The aim is to affirm that their secrets are known to Him, and that none of them vanishes. This is reinforced by His saying ﴿My Lord does not err nor forget﴾. Or the meaning is that He has recorded those rulings in a Book with Him, which becomes manifest to the angels, adding to their evidence that He knows all known things, exalted above inattention and heedlessness. End. There is some abridgment in it.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Jahdari, Hammad ibn Salamah, Ibn Muhaysin and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read ﴿لا يُضِلُّ﴾ with a dammah on the ya' (lā yuḍillu), meaning: God does not cause that Book to go astray so that it is lost, nor does He forget what He has recorded in it. Al-Sulami read ﴿لا يُضَلُّ رَبِّي ولا يُنْسى﴾ (lā yuḍallu rabbī wa-lā yunsā) in the passive voice. The apparent reading is that the two clauses are a new sentence (isti'naf) and an informing about Him, Exalted, of the negation of these two attributes. It was also said: they are in the position of a qualifier for ﴿in a Book﴾, with the returning pronoun to the qualified noun omitted, meaning: my Lord does not err in it nor forget it. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿nor forget﴾ refers to God. It was also said: it may refer to (Book), meaning: it leaves nothing out; forgetting here is a metaphor, as in His saying ﴿except that He has counted them﴾ [al-Kahf: 49], where counting is attributed to it on account of the restriction within it. From Ibn 'Abbas: He does not leave him who disbelieved in Him until He takes vengeance upon him, and He does not leave him who affirmed His oneness until He recompenses him.

(p-250) When Musa had pointed to the proof of the Lord's lordship, and his speech was complete at His saying, ﴿and He does not forget﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52], Allah mentioned what He used to draw attention to His power and His oneness. He informed about Himself that He is the One who made such-and-such. We have taken the view that this is the speech of Allah, due to His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ (p-251) and His saying ﴿eat and graze your livestock﴾ and His saying ﴿We certainly showed him﴾. So His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ and ﴿We showed him﴾ is an iltifat (a shift of grammatical person, here from the third-person pronoun in ja'ala and salaka to the first-person plural pronoun of one who magnifies himself). An iltifat does not occur from speakers who are different. Even more remote is the view of those who said that alladhi is an adjective (na't) of the word (Rabbi), so that it would be in the nominative position, or in the accusative position as praise (madh). Al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari said both of these, because then the speech would be Musa's, and the iltifat in His saying (so We brought forth) and ﴿We showed him﴾ would not be possible.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that (so We brought forth) is part of Musa's speech, relating from Allah the Exalted, with the implied phrase "He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: so We brought forth." It is also possible that Musa's speech was complete at His saying ﴿and sent down from the sky water﴾, and then Allah joined Musa's speech with His informing Muhammad (ﷺ). The address in ﴿for you﴾ is intended for all of creation, drawing their attention to these signs.

Al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿mahdan﴾ with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the ha'. The rest of the seven read mihadan, and likewise in al-Zukhruf. Al-Mufaddal said: they are two verbal nouns (masdar), mahda mahdan and mihadan. Abu 'Ubayd said: mihad is a noun (ism), and mahd is the verb, meaning the verbal noun. Another said: mahd is singular and mihad is its plural. The meaning of this is that He made it for them, so that they can move about upon it in all their conditions and benefits, and He laid out for you roads within it for your purposes, so that your interests are not hindered. The pronoun in ﴿by it﴾ refers to the water, that is, by its means.

﴿pairs﴾, that is, kinds. This iltifat in (akhrajna) is like it in His saying ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sent down water from the sky, so We brought forth﴾ [Fatir: 27], ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow﴾ [An-Naml: 60], and ﴿And it is He who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth by it the vegetation of every thing﴾ [Al-An'am: 99]. In this iltifat there is also a specification that We alone have the power to do the like of this, and it does not fall under the power of anyone. The better view is that ﴿diverse﴾ (shatta) is in the accusative position as an adjective (na't) of ﴿pairs﴾, because it is that which is being spoken of.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that it is an adjective of the vegetation (nabat). Nabat is a verbal noun used as the name of that which grows, just as it is called nabt, so the singular and plural are alike in it. He means that they are ﴿diverse﴾, differing in benefit, taste, colour, scent and form; some are suitable for people and some for animals.

They said: From His blessing, the Mighty and Majestic, is that the sustenance of the servants is obtained only through the work of livestock, and Allah has made their fodder from what exceeds their needs and what they cannot eat. ﴿Eat and graze your livestock﴾ is a command of permission (amr ibaha) governed by an omitted circumstantial state (hal), meaning: ﴿so We brought forth﴾ speaking [to you], that is, permitting you to benefit from them, allowing you to eat some of them and feed some of them. Here ﴿and graze﴾ is transitive. Ra'a (to graze) can be intransitive and transitive; you say: the animal grazed (ra'at al-dabbatu ra'yan), and its owner pastured it (ra'aha sahibuha ri'ayatan), when he drove it out, sent it out to pasture and let it rest. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

By His saying ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, He pointed to the preceding signs: the making of the earth as a cradle, the laying of its roads, the sending down of water, and the bringing forth of vegetation. They said: ﴿al-nuha﴾ is the plural of nuha, which is intellect, named so because it restrains (yanha) from ugly deeds. Abu 'Ali permitted that it be a verbal noun, like al-huda (guidance). The pronoun in ﴿from it﴾ refers to the earth, and He meant the creation of their origin, Adam. It was also said: an angel goes to the soil of the place where the one to be created will be buried, and scatters it over the sperm-drop, so that he is created from both dust and sperm-drop together. This was said by 'Ata al-Khurasani. It was also said: it refers to the foods that grow out of the earth, from which the humours are generated from which man is formed; this is then a metaphor of a metaphor. ﴿And into it We return you﴾, that is, by burial in it or by being torn apart upon it. ﴿And from it We bring you forth again﴾ by resurrection, ﴿another time﴾, once more: He gathers their scattered parts and returns them as they were, living. His saying ﴿another time﴾ means another bringing-forth, because the meaning of His saying ﴿from it We created you﴾ is "We brought you forth."

﴿And We certainly showed him all Our signs﴾. This is an informing from Allah the Exalted to Muhammad (ﷺ), and this indicates that His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ is indeed an address to him (peace be upon him). ﴿We showed him Our signs﴾: the ones meant are those taken from the visual sense of seeing (ra'a al-basariyya), and for this reason it takes two objects by the transitivity-causing hamza. ﴿Our signs﴾ is not general, since He did not show him all the signs; rather the meaning is the signs of Ours that he saw, and so the idafa (construct) conveys what the definite article conveys of familiarity (al-'ahd). He saw the staff, the hand, the blotting out, and other things he saw; the emphasis (p-252) is then in relation to these known signs. It was also said: the meaning is signs in their entirety, and He attributed the signs to Himself as a mark of honour, as if He had said "signs for Us." It was also said: Musa had shown him His signs and enumerated for him what other prophets had been given of their signs and miracles, and he is a truthful prophet, with no difference between what he reports and what he shows. ﴿So he denied and refused﴾ all of them, and ﴿refused﴾ to accept any of them. End. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, and it is remote, because informing about a thing is not called seeing except by a distant figurative usage.

It was also said: ﴿We showed him﴾ here is from seeing of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb), not seeing of the eye, because at that time he had been shown only the staff and the white hand, meaning: ﴿We certainly made him know Our signs, all of them﴾. These are the nine signs. It was said: it is permissible that by the signs He meant the signs of His oneness which He displayed to us in the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and then it would be from seeing of the eye. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ubayy said: it implies the acquisition (kasb) of Pharaoh, and this is what reward and punishment depend upon. The object of ﴿denied﴾ is omitted; the apparent meaning is that it is the signs. It is possible that the intended meaning is: ﴿he denied﴾ Musa and ﴿refused﴾ to accept what he brought him of his message.

It was said: It is also permissible that he meant: he denied that they were signs of Allah, and said: they are sorcery. For this reason he said: ﴿Have you come to us to expel us from our land by your sorcery, O Musa?﴾ This view is weakened by His saying ﴿You know well that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as insights﴾ [Al-Isra: 102], and His saying ﴿and they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [An-Naml: 14]. So it appears that he denied out of his wrongdoing, not that it was confused for him whether they were signs of sorcery. In his saying ﴿Have you come to us to expel us﴾ there is weakness, which is evident from him, and much agitation regarding what Musa brought, since he knew that he was upon the truth and that he would inevitably overcome him in his kingdom. He mentioned the cause of the coming, which is the expulsion of them, and he cast this into the ears of his people so that they would become intensely hostile towards him, since expulsion from one's homeland is among the things that are very hard. Allah made it equal to killing in His saying ﴿Kill yourselves or leave your homes﴾ [An-Nisa: 66]. His saying ﴿by your sorcery﴾ is an excuse and bewilderment, because it is not hidden from him that a sorcerer cannot expel a king like himself from his land and overcome him in his kingdom by sorcery. He presented this as a doubt casting aspersion on prophethood, and that a miracle is distinguished from sorcery only by the miracle being something whose opposition is impossible. Therefore he said: ﴿So we will surely bring you sorcery like it﴾. This indicates that Musa's affair (peace be upon him) had grown strong, and his protection among the Children of Israel had increased, and his matter had come to be in the hearts of the people, since this is the speech of one who needs proof, not of one who proclaims his own affair. Their land is the land of Egypt. He addressed him with ﴿your sorcery﴾ because the conversation was with him, and the staff and the hand had appeared from his direction. ﴿So we will surely bring you﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, which gave people the impression that what Musa brought was of the kind of sorcery, and that with him there was someone who could match him in that. So he sought to set an appointment for a contest in sorcery. The apparent meaning is that ﴿an appointment﴾ here is a time: that is, appoint for us a time of gathering. For this reason he answered with His saying ﴿He said: Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. The meaning of ﴿we will not fail it﴾ is that we will not break that time in gathering there. Some took it to be a known place, and its source is His saying ﴿your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾.

Al-Qushayri said: The more apparent view is that it is a verbal noun, and for this reason he said ﴿we will not fail it﴾, that is, that appointment; and failing (al-ikhlaf) is to promise something and not fulfil it. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you take it to be a time, in view of His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾, which corresponds to it, then two things would be necessary for you: that you make the time the thing that is failed, and that the governing verb (nasib) of ﴿a place﴾ would be obstructed for you. And if you take it as a place corresponding to His saying ﴿a place equal﴾, it would also be necessary for you that the failing falls upon the place, and that it not correspond to His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. The reading of al-Hasan does not correspond to it at all in place, because he read ﴿the Day of Adornment﴾ in the accusative, so it remains that it be taken as a verbal noun meaning a promise, and that an omitted genitive construction be assumed, that is, "the place of an appointment," and that the pronoun in ﴿we will not fail it﴾ and ﴿a place﴾ be taken as a substitute (badal) for the omitted place. If you say: How do you make it correspond to His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾, when you must take it as a time, and the question is about a place, not a time? I say: It corresponds in meaning even if it does not correspond in wording, because they must gather on the Day of Adornment in a particular place known for their gathering in it on that day, so by mentioning the time the place is known.

As for the reading of al-Hasan, the appointment in it is only a verbal noun, and the meaning is the fulfilment of your promise on the Day of Adornment, and this also corresponds (p-253) in terms of meaning. It is also permissible that an omitted genitive construction be assumed, and the meaning would be: make between us and between you a promise which we will not fail. If you say: On what is ﴿a place﴾ in the accusative? I say: On the verbal noun, or on a verb indicated by the verbal noun. If you say: How does the answer correspond to it? I say: As for the reading of al-Hasan, it is clear; as for the reading of the majority, it is according to the assumption "your promise is the promise of the Day of Adornment."

It is permissible, according to the reading of al-Hasan, that ﴿your appointment﴾ be the subject (mubtada') with the meaning of a time, and ﴿in the forenoon﴾ (duha) be its predicate, with the intention of definiteness in it, since it had been described before the action by His saying ﴿we will not fail it﴾, and it is a relative clause, and the verbal noun, when it is described before it acts, may not act in their view. And the saying "and (duha) is its predicate with the intention of definiteness in it" is because it is the forenoon of that very day. Although it is the forenoon of that very day, it is not with the intention of definiteness; rather it is indefinite, even if it is from a particular day, because it is not replaced from the definite article (alif-lam) as in sihr (sorcery), nor is it defined by annexation. If you say: "I came on Friday at dawn (bukran)," we do not claim that bukran is definite, even though we know that it is from a particular day.

Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read ﴿لا نُخْلِفْهُ﴾ (*lā nukhlifhu*, "we shall not fail it") with the *fa'* in jussive (*jazm*, the mood marking that ends a verb with a sukun), taking it as the answer to the imperative. The majority (*al-jumhūr*) read it with *raf'* (nominative), as a qualifier (*ṣifah*) of *mawʿidan* (a promise/appointment).

Al-Ḥawfī said: ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ (*mawʿidan*) is the object of ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾ (*ijʿal*, "appoint"), and ﴿مَكانًا﴾ (*makānan*, "a place") is an adverbial of place (*ẓarf*), whose governing element is ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾. Abu ʿAli said: ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ is the first object of ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾ and ﴿مَكانًا﴾ is the second object. He prohibited ﴿مَكانًا﴾ from being governed by ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ because the latter has already been qualified.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: These nouns that function as verbs (*al-asmāʾ al-ʿāmilah ʿamal al-fiʿl*), when they are qualified, or when something is conjoined to them, or when they are predicated about, or diminutivized, or pluralized, and become fully nominal in this way, do not govern, and nothing that belongs to them may be attached to them. The adverbs (*ẓurūf*) may be treated more loosely, so something may be attached to them after what we have mentioned, as in the words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿يُنادَوْنَ لَمَقْتُ اللَّهِ أكْبَرُ مِن مَقْتِكم أنْفُسَكم إذْ تُدْعَوْنَ إلى الإيمانِ﴾ [Ghafir: 10] ("They will be called: Surely God's hatred is greater than your hatred of yourselves, when you were called to faith"). Here ﴿إذْ﴾ (*idh*, "when") is attached to ﴿لَمَقْتُ﴾ (*lamaqtu*, "hatred"), and he has been predicated about. This is permitted only with adverbs. A group prohibited ﴿مَكانًا﴾ from being in the accusative as the second object of ﴿لُنُخْلِفُهُ﴾, but a group of grammarians permitted it, its rationale being that it is an extension (*ittisāʿ*) in the sense of "to fail the promise." End of quote.

His phrase "when they are qualified" is not agreed upon for every element that functions as a verb. Consider the active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*) without *al-*: if it is qualified before it governs, there is disagreement. The Basrans prohibit it, the Kufans permit it. Likewise, if it is diminutivized, there is disagreement over its governing. As for pluralization, there is no known disagreement about its governing. As for the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) when pluralized, there is disagreement about whether it may govern. As for his exception of the adverbs from the governed elements, others hold that this is prohibited absolutely for the verbal noun, and that ﴿إذْ﴾ governs a verb implied by what precedes it, meaning: "their hatred of you when you are called."

﴿ولا أنْتَ﴾ (*wa-lā anta*, "nor you") is conjoined to the implicit pronoun in ﴿نُخْلِفُهُ﴾, which is emphasized by the word "we" (*naḥnu*).

Ibn ʿAmir, Ḥamzah, ʿAsim, Yaʿqub, al-Ḥasan, Qatadah, Ṭalḥah, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Abi Laylā, Abu Ḥatim and Ibn Jarir read ﴿سُوًى﴾ (*suwan*) with *ḍammah* on the *sīn*, with tanwin in connected speech. The rest of the seven read it with *kasrah* on the *sīn*, with tanwin in connected speech. Al-Ḥasan also read ﴿سُوى﴾ with *ḍammah* on the *sīn* without tanwin in both states, treating connected speech as pause (*ajrā al-waṣl majrā al-waqf*), not because it is prevented from taking tanwin (*ṣarf*), since a *fiʿl* form among the adjectives is inflected, like *ḥaṭum* and *labad*. ʿIsa read *siwā* with *kasrah* on the *sīn*, without tanwin in both states, also treating connected speech as pause.

The meaning of ﴿سُوًى﴾ is "just and equitable." Abu ʿAli said: It is as though he said, "His nearness to you is his nearness to us." Others said: He meant that our position in it is equal, so that this encompasses the Qur'an, and that ranks in it are one in the pursuit of truth, so that leadership (*riʾāsah*) does not obstruct you in it, and only proof is intended. From Mujahid: it derives from *istiwāʾ* (equality), because the distance from the middle to the two extremes is equal, without disparity. This is the meaning of what preceded from Abu ʿAli's words: "His nearness to you is his nearness to us."

Al-Akhfash said: ﴿سُوًى﴾ is *maqṣūr* (short-vowelled, without the final alif extended) if you read its *sīn* with *kasrah* or *ḍammah*, and *mamdūd* (extended) if you read it with *fatḥah*. There are three dialects, and in all of them it carries the meaning of ﴿غَيْرِ﴾ (*ghayr*, "other than") [Ṭaha: 22] and the meaning of "just," and "middle between the two parties." The poet said:

*And indeed our father was a settler among his people, equitable between the Qays of Ghaylan and the Fizr.*

He said: You say "I passed by a man *siwāka*, *suwāka*, *sawāka*," meaning "other than you," and it applies to all. The highest of these dialects is the *kasrah*, as al-Naḥḥas said.

A group said: The meaning of ﴿مَكانًا سُوًى﴾ (*makānan suwan*, "a place level") is a level place from the earth, that is, without rough ground, without mountain, without hill, and without a depression in the earth, such that the gaze of anyone would not be obstructed, so that they would not see the place of Musa and the magicians and what issues from them. He said this confident of the magicians' victory over Musa; then when they witnessed his victory over them, they would return from what they had believed in.

A group said: Its meaning is "a place other than this place of ours." This is not right, because ﴿سِوًى﴾ when it means ﴿غَيْرِ﴾ is used only in construct form (*muḍāfah*) in wording and is not separated from the construct.

Al-Ḥasan, al-Aʿmash, ʿAsim in one narration, Abu Ḥaywah, Ibn Abi ʿAblah, Qatadah, al-Jaḥdari, Hubayrah and al-Zaʿfarani read ﴿يَوْمَ الزِّينَةِ﴾ (*yawma al-zīnah*, "the day of adornment") with *fatḥah* on the *mīm*. The derivation of this reading has been mentioned in al-Zamakhshari's words. It is narrated that ﴿يَوْمَ الزِّينَةِ﴾ was a festival (*ʿīd*) for them and a day of gathering (*yawman mashhūdan*), and it coincided with ʿAshura, and it was a Saturday. It is said: It is the day of the breaking of the canal that remains until today. It is said: It is the day of Nowruz, which was the beginning of their year. It is said: It is Saturday, for it is a day of rest and ease. It is said: It is a market day for them. It is said: It is ʿAshura.

Ibn Masʿud, al-Jaḥdari, Abu ʿImran al-Jawni, Abu Nahik, and ʿAmr ibn Fa'id read ﴿وأنْ تُحْشَرَ﴾ (*wa-an tuḥsar*, "and that they be gathered") with the second-person *tā'* (addressing), meaning "O Pharaoh." It is narrated from them also with *yā'* in the third person. ﴿النّاسُ﴾ (*al-nās*, "the people") is in the accusative in both readings.

The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: "And that the gatherer gathers the people in the forenoon," so the subject is omitted because it is known. This omission of the subject in such a construction is not permitted according to the Basrans. Others said: ﴿وأنْ يُحْشَرَ﴾ refers to the people. He said: It is also permitted that the pronoun of Pharaoh be in it, mentioned with third-person wording, either according to the custom by which kings are addressed, or because he addressed the people with ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ﴾ (*mawʿiduku-m*, "your appointment"), and made ﴿يُحْشَرَ﴾ refer to Pharaoh. It is also permitted that ﴿وأنْ يُحْشَرَ﴾ be in the nominative position as conjoined to ﴿يَوْمُ الزِّينَةِ﴾, or in the genitive position as conjoined to ﴿الزِّينَةِ﴾.

﴿ضُحًى﴾ (*ḍuḥan*, "in the forenoon") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarf*), and it is the rising of the day. It may be feminine or masculine. The *ḍuḥāʾ* with *fatḥah* on the *ḍād* is *mamdūd* (extended) and masculine; it is at the highest rise of the day. Musa appointed this day for them only so that the exaltation of God's word, the manifestation of His religion, the humiliation of the unbeliever, and the destruction of falsehood would occur in full view of the witnesses. In al-Majma' al-Ghāṣṣ: so that the desire of whoever desires to follow the truth may grow, that the edge of the falsifiers and their partisans may be blunted, and that the report of this clear matter may spread in every desert and settlement, and be disseminated among all the dwellers of tents and cities.

The apparent view is that His words ﴿قالَ مَوْعِدُكم يَوْمُ الزِّينَةِ﴾ (*qāla mawʿiduku-m yawmu al-zīnah*, "He said: Your appointment is the day of adornment") are the words of Musa, peace be upon him, because it is a reply to Pharaoh's words ﴿فاجْعَلْ بَيْنَنا وبَيْنَكَ مَوْعِدًا﴾ ("Appoint between us and you an appointment"), and because specifying the day is fitting only for the one who is in the right, whose hand is known to be strong, not for the falsifier who is known to have nothing but deception. Also, His words ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ﴾ are addressed to all. He who held that it is the words of Pharaoh is far from the truth.

(p-250) When Musa had pointed to the proof of the Lord's lordship, and his speech was complete at His saying, ﴿and He does not forget﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52], Allah mentioned what He used to draw attention to His power and His oneness. He informed about Himself that He is the One who made such-and-such. We have taken the view that this is the speech of Allah, due to His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ (p-251) and His saying ﴿eat and graze your livestock﴾ and His saying ﴿We certainly showed him﴾. So His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ and ﴿We showed him﴾ is an iltifat (a shift of grammatical person, here from the third-person pronoun in ja'ala and salaka to the first-person plural pronoun of one who magnifies himself). An iltifat does not occur from speakers who are different. Even more remote is the view of those who said that alladhi is an adjective (na't) of the word (Rabbi), so that it would be in the nominative position, or in the accusative position as praise (madh). Al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari said both of these, because then the speech would be Musa's, and the iltifat in His saying (so We brought forth) and ﴿We showed him﴾ would not be possible.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that (so We brought forth) is part of Musa's speech, relating from Allah the Exalted, with the implied phrase "He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: so We brought forth." It is also possible that Musa's speech was complete at His saying ﴿and sent down from the sky water﴾, and then Allah joined Musa's speech with His informing Muhammad (ﷺ). The address in ﴿for you﴾ is intended for all of creation, drawing their attention to these signs.

Al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿mahdan﴾ with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the ha'. The rest of the seven read mihadan, and likewise in al-Zukhruf. Al-Mufaddal said: they are two verbal nouns (masdar), mahda mahdan and mihadan. Abu 'Ubayd said: mihad is a noun (ism), and mahd is the verb, meaning the verbal noun. Another said: mahd is singular and mihad is its plural. The meaning of this is that He made it for them, so that they can move about upon it in all their conditions and benefits, and He laid out for you roads within it for your purposes, so that your interests are not hindered. The pronoun in ﴿by it﴾ refers to the water, that is, by its means.

﴿pairs﴾, that is, kinds. This iltifat in (akhrajna) is like it in His saying ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sent down water from the sky, so We brought forth﴾ [Fatir: 27], ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow﴾ [An-Naml: 60], and ﴿And it is He who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth by it the vegetation of every thing﴾ [Al-An'am: 99]. In this iltifat there is also a specification that We alone have the power to do the like of this, and it does not fall under the power of anyone. The better view is that ﴿diverse﴾ (shatta) is in the accusative position as an adjective (na't) of ﴿pairs﴾, because it is that which is being spoken of.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that it is an adjective of the vegetation (nabat). Nabat is a verbal noun used as the name of that which grows, just as it is called nabt, so the singular and plural are alike in it. He means that they are ﴿diverse﴾, differing in benefit, taste, colour, scent and form; some are suitable for people and some for animals.

They said: From His blessing, the Mighty and Majestic, is that the sustenance of the servants is obtained only through the work of livestock, and Allah has made their fodder from what exceeds their needs and what they cannot eat. ﴿Eat and graze your livestock﴾ is a command of permission (amr ibaha) governed by an omitted circumstantial state (hal), meaning: ﴿so We brought forth﴾ speaking [to you], that is, permitting you to benefit from them, allowing you to eat some of them and feed some of them. Here ﴿and graze﴾ is transitive. Ra'a (to graze) can be intransitive and transitive; you say: the animal grazed (ra'at al-dabbatu ra'yan), and its owner pastured it (ra'aha sahibuha ri'ayatan), when he drove it out, sent it out to pasture and let it rest. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

By His saying ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, He pointed to the preceding signs: the making of the earth as a cradle, the laying of its roads, the sending down of water, and the bringing forth of vegetation. They said: ﴿al-nuha﴾ is the plural of nuha, which is intellect, named so because it restrains (yanha) from ugly deeds. Abu 'Ali permitted that it be a verbal noun, like al-huda (guidance). The pronoun in ﴿from it﴾ refers to the earth, and He meant the creation of their origin, Adam. It was also said: an angel goes to the soil of the place where the one to be created will be buried, and scatters it over the sperm-drop, so that he is created from both dust and sperm-drop together. This was said by 'Ata al-Khurasani. It was also said: it refers to the foods that grow out of the earth, from which the humours are generated from which man is formed; this is then a metaphor of a metaphor. ﴿And into it We return you﴾, that is, by burial in it or by being torn apart upon it. ﴿And from it We bring you forth again﴾ by resurrection, ﴿another time﴾, once more: He gathers their scattered parts and returns them as they were, living. His saying ﴿another time﴾ means another bringing-forth, because the meaning of His saying ﴿from it We created you﴾ is "We brought you forth."

﴿And We certainly showed him all Our signs﴾. This is an informing from Allah the Exalted to Muhammad (ﷺ), and this indicates that His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ is indeed an address to him (peace be upon him). ﴿We showed him Our signs﴾: the ones meant are those taken from the visual sense of seeing (ra'a al-basariyya), and for this reason it takes two objects by the transitivity-causing hamza. ﴿Our signs﴾ is not general, since He did not show him all the signs; rather the meaning is the signs of Ours that he saw, and so the idafa (construct) conveys what the definite article conveys of familiarity (al-'ahd). He saw the staff, the hand, the blotting out, and other things he saw; the emphasis (p-252) is then in relation to these known signs. It was also said: the meaning is signs in their entirety, and He attributed the signs to Himself as a mark of honour, as if He had said "signs for Us." It was also said: Musa had shown him His signs and enumerated for him what other prophets had been given of their signs and miracles, and he is a truthful prophet, with no difference between what he reports and what he shows. ﴿So he denied and refused﴾ all of them, and ﴿refused﴾ to accept any of them. End. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, and it is remote, because informing about a thing is not called seeing except by a distant figurative usage.

It was also said: ﴿We showed him﴾ here is from seeing of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb), not seeing of the eye, because at that time he had been shown only the staff and the white hand, meaning: ﴿We certainly made him know Our signs, all of them﴾. These are the nine signs. It was said: it is permissible that by the signs He meant the signs of His oneness which He displayed to us in the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and then it would be from seeing of the eye. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ubayy said: it implies the acquisition (kasb) of Pharaoh, and this is what reward and punishment depend upon. The object of ﴿denied﴾ is omitted; the apparent meaning is that it is the signs. It is possible that the intended meaning is: ﴿he denied﴾ Musa and ﴿refused﴾ to accept what he brought him of his message.

It was said: It is also permissible that he meant: he denied that they were signs of Allah, and said: they are sorcery. For this reason he said: ﴿Have you come to us to expel us from our land by your sorcery, O Musa?﴾ This view is weakened by His saying ﴿You know well that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as insights﴾ [Al-Isra: 102], and His saying ﴿and they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [An-Naml: 14]. So it appears that he denied out of his wrongdoing, not that it was confused for him whether they were signs of sorcery. In his saying ﴿Have you come to us to expel us﴾ there is weakness, which is evident from him, and much agitation regarding what Musa brought, since he knew that he was upon the truth and that he would inevitably overcome him in his kingdom. He mentioned the cause of the coming, which is the expulsion of them, and he cast this into the ears of his people so that they would become intensely hostile towards him, since expulsion from one's homeland is among the things that are very hard. Allah made it equal to killing in His saying ﴿Kill yourselves or leave your homes﴾ [An-Nisa: 66]. His saying ﴿by your sorcery﴾ is an excuse and bewilderment, because it is not hidden from him that a sorcerer cannot expel a king like himself from his land and overcome him in his kingdom by sorcery. He presented this as a doubt casting aspersion on prophethood, and that a miracle is distinguished from sorcery only by the miracle being something whose opposition is impossible. Therefore he said: ﴿So we will surely bring you sorcery like it﴾. This indicates that Musa's affair (peace be upon him) had grown strong, and his protection among the Children of Israel had increased, and his matter had come to be in the hearts of the people, since this is the speech of one who needs proof, not of one who proclaims his own affair. Their land is the land of Egypt. He addressed him with ﴿your sorcery﴾ because the conversation was with him, and the staff and the hand had appeared from his direction. ﴿So we will surely bring you﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, which gave people the impression that what Musa brought was of the kind of sorcery, and that with him there was someone who could match him in that. So he sought to set an appointment for a contest in sorcery. The apparent meaning is that ﴿an appointment﴾ here is a time: that is, appoint for us a time of gathering. For this reason he answered with His saying ﴿He said: Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. The meaning of ﴿we will not fail it﴾ is that we will not break that time in gathering there. Some took it to be a known place, and its source is His saying ﴿your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾.

Al-Qushayri said: The more apparent view is that it is a verbal noun, and for this reason he said ﴿we will not fail it﴾, that is, that appointment; and failing (al-ikhlaf) is to promise something and not fulfil it. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you take it to be a time, in view of His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾, which corresponds to it, then two things would be necessary for you: that you make the time the thing that is failed, and that the governing verb (nasib) of ﴿a place﴾ would be obstructed for you. And if you take it as a place corresponding to His saying ﴿a place equal﴾, it would also be necessary for you that the failing falls upon the place, and that it not correspond to His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. The reading of al-Hasan does not correspond to it at all in place, because he read ﴿the Day of Adornment﴾ in the accusative, so it remains that it be taken as a verbal noun meaning a promise, and that an omitted genitive construction be assumed, that is, "the place of an appointment," and that the pronoun in ﴿we will not fail it﴾ and ﴿a place﴾ be taken as a substitute (badal) for the omitted place. If you say: How do you make it correspond to His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾, when you must take it as a time, and the question is about a place, not a time? I say: It corresponds in meaning even if it does not correspond in wording, because they must gather on the Day of Adornment in a particular place known for their gathering in it on that day, so by mentioning the time the place is known.

As for the reading of al-Hasan, the appointment in it is only a verbal noun, and the meaning is the fulfilment of your promise on the Day of Adornment, and this also corresponds (p-253) in terms of meaning. It is also permissible that an omitted genitive construction be assumed, and the meaning would be: make between us and between you a promise which we will not fail. If you say: On what is ﴿a place﴾ in the accusative? I say: On the verbal noun, or on a verb indicated by the verbal noun. If you say: How does the answer correspond to it? I say: As for the reading of al-Hasan, it is clear; as for the reading of the majority, it is according to the assumption "your promise is the promise of the Day of Adornment."

It is permissible, according to the reading of al-Hasan, that ﴿your appointment﴾ be the subject (mubtada') with the meaning of a time, and ﴿in the forenoon﴾ (duha) be its predicate, with the intention of definiteness in it, since it had been described before the action by His saying ﴿we will not fail it﴾, and it is a relative clause, and the verbal noun, when it is described before it acts, may not act in their view. And the saying "and (duha) is its predicate with the intention of definiteness in it" is because it is the forenoon of that very day. Although it is the forenoon of that very day, it is not with the intention of definiteness; rather it is indefinite, even if it is from a particular day, because it is not replaced from the definite article (alif-lam) as in sihr (sorcery), nor is it defined by annexation. If you say: "I came on Friday at dawn (bukran)," we do not claim that bukran is definite, even though we know that it is from a particular day.

Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read ﴿لا نُخْلِفْهُ﴾ (*lā nukhlifhu*, "we shall not fail it") with the *fa'* in jussive (*jazm*, the mood marking that ends a verb with a sukun), taking it as the answer to the imperative. The majority (*al-jumhūr*) read it with *raf'* (nominative), as a qualifier (*ṣifah*) of *mawʿidan* (a promise/appointment).

Al-Ḥawfī said: ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ (*mawʿidan*) is the object of ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾ (*ijʿal*, "appoint"), and ﴿مَكانًا﴾ (*makānan*, "a place") is an adverbial of place (*ẓarf*), whose governing element is ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾. Abu ʿAli said: ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ is the first object of ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾ and ﴿مَكانًا﴾ is the second object. He prohibited ﴿مَكانًا﴾ from being governed by ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ because the latter has already been qualified.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: These nouns that function as verbs (*al-asmāʾ al-ʿāmilah ʿamal al-fiʿl*), when they are qualified, or when something is conjoined to them, or when they are predicated about, or diminutivized, or pluralized, and become fully nominal in this way, do not govern, and nothing that belongs to them may be attached to them. The adverbs (*ẓurūf*) may be treated more loosely, so something may be attached to them after what we have mentioned, as in the words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿يُنادَوْنَ لَمَقْتُ اللَّهِ أكْبَرُ مِن مَقْتِكم أنْفُسَكم إذْ تُدْعَوْنَ إلى الإيمانِ﴾ [Ghafir: 10] ("They will be called: Surely God's hatred is greater than your hatred of yourselves, when you were called to faith"). Here ﴿إذْ﴾ (*idh*, "when") is attached to ﴿لَمَقْتُ﴾ (*lamaqtu*, "hatred"), and he has been predicated about. This is permitted only with adverbs. A group prohibited ﴿مَكانًا﴾ from being in the accusative as the second object of ﴿لُنُخْلِفُهُ﴾, but a group of grammarians permitted it, its rationale being that it is an extension (*ittisāʿ*) in the sense of "to fail the promise." End of quote.

His phrase "when they are qualified" is not agreed upon for every element that functions as a verb. Consider the active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*) without *al-*: if it is qualified before it governs, there is disagreement. The Basrans prohibit it, the Kufans permit it. Likewise, if it is diminutivized, there is disagreement over its governing. As for pluralization, there is no known disagreement about its governing. As for the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) when pluralized, there is disagreement about whether it may govern. As for his exception of the adverbs from the governed elements, others hold that this is prohibited absolutely for the verbal noun, and that ﴿إذْ﴾ governs a verb implied by what precedes it, meaning: "their hatred of you when you are called."

﴿ولا أنْتَ﴾ (*wa-lā anta*, "nor you") is conjoined to the implicit pronoun in ﴿نُخْلِفُهُ﴾, which is emphasized by the word "we" (*naḥnu*).

Ibn ʿAmir, Ḥamzah, ʿAsim, Yaʿqub, al-Ḥasan, Qatadah, Ṭalḥah, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Abi Laylā, Abu Ḥatim and Ibn Jarir read ﴿سُوًى﴾ (*suwan*) with *ḍammah* on the *sīn*, with tanwin in connected speech. The rest of the seven read it with *kasrah* on the *sīn*, with tanwin in connected speech. Al-Ḥasan also read ﴿سُوى﴾ with *ḍammah* on the *sīn* without tanwin in both states, treating connected speech as pause (*ajrā al-waṣl majrā al-waqf*), not because it is prevented from taking tanwin (*ṣarf*), since a *fiʿl* form among the adjectives is inflected, like *ḥaṭum* and *labad*. ʿIsa read *siwā* with *kasrah* on the *sīn*, without tanwin in both states, also treating connected speech as pause.

The meaning of ﴿سُوًى﴾ is "just and equitable." Abu ʿAli said: It is as though he said, "His nearness to you is his nearness to us." Others said: He meant that our position in it is equal, so that this encompasses the Qur'an, and that ranks in it are one in the pursuit of truth, so that leadership (*riʾāsah*) does not obstruct you in it, and only proof is intended. From Mujahid: it derives from *istiwāʾ* (equality), because the distance from the middle to the two extremes is equal, without disparity. This is the meaning of what preceded from Abu ʿAli's words: "His nearness to you is his nearness to us."

Al-Akhfash said: ﴿سُوًى﴾ is *maqṣūr* (short-vowelled, without the final alif extended) if you read its *sīn* with *kasrah* or *ḍammah*, and *mamdūd* (extended) if you read it with *fatḥah*. There are three dialects, and in all of them it carries the meaning of ﴿غَيْرِ﴾ (*ghayr*, "other than") [Ṭaha: 22] and the meaning of "just," and "middle between the two parties." The poet said:

*And indeed our father was a settler among his people, equitable between the Qays of Ghaylan and the Fizr.*

He said: You say "I passed by a man *siwāka*, *suwāka*, *sawāka*," meaning "other than you," and it applies to all. The highest of these dialects is the *kasrah*, as al-Naḥḥas said.

A group said: The meaning of ﴿مَكانًا سُوًى﴾ (*makānan suwan*, "a place level") is a level place from the earth, that is, without rough ground, without mountain, without hill, and without a depression in the earth, such that the gaze of anyone would not be obstructed, so that they would not see the place of Musa and the magicians and what issues from them. He said this confident of the magicians' victory over Musa; then when they witnessed his victory over them, they would return from what they had believed in.

A group said: Its meaning is "a place other than this place of ours." This is not right, because ﴿سِوًى﴾ when it means ﴿غَيْرِ﴾ is used only in construct form (*muḍāfah*) in wording and is not separated from the construct.

Al-Ḥasan, al-Aʿmash, ʿAsim in one narration, Abu Ḥaywah, Ibn Abi ʿAblah, Qatadah, al-Jaḥdari, Hubayrah and al-Zaʿfarani read ﴿يَوْمَ الزِّينَةِ﴾ (*yawma al-zīnah*, "the day of adornment") with *fatḥah* on the *mīm*. The derivation of this reading has been mentioned in al-Zamakhshari's words. It is narrated that ﴿يَوْمَ الزِّينَةِ﴾ was a festival (*ʿīd*) for them and a day of gathering (*yawman mashhūdan*), and it coincided with ʿAshura, and it was a Saturday. It is said: It is the day of the breaking of the canal that remains until today. It is said: It is the day of Nowruz, which was the beginning of their year. It is said: It is Saturday, for it is a day of rest and ease. It is said: It is a market day for them. It is said: It is ʿAshura.

Ibn Masʿud, al-Jaḥdari, Abu ʿImran al-Jawni, Abu Nahik, and ʿAmr ibn Fa'id read ﴿وأنْ تُحْشَرَ﴾ (*wa-an tuḥsar*, "and that they be gathered") with the second-person *tā'* (addressing), meaning "O Pharaoh." It is narrated from them also with *yā'* in the third person. ﴿النّاسُ﴾ (*al-nās*, "the people") is in the accusative in both readings.

The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: "And that the gatherer gathers the people in the forenoon," so the subject is omitted because it is known. This omission of the subject in such a construction is not permitted according to the Basrans. Others said: ﴿وأنْ يُحْشَرَ﴾ refers to the people. He said: It is also permitted that the pronoun of Pharaoh be in it, mentioned with third-person wording, either according to the custom by which kings are addressed, or because he addressed the people with ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ﴾ (*mawʿiduku-m*, "your appointment"), and made ﴿يُحْشَرَ﴾ refer to Pharaoh. It is also permitted that ﴿وأنْ يُحْشَرَ﴾ be in the nominative position as conjoined to ﴿يَوْمُ الزِّينَةِ﴾, or in the genitive position as conjoined to ﴿الزِّينَةِ﴾.

﴿ضُحًى﴾ (*ḍuḥan*, "in the forenoon") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarf*), and it is the rising of the day. It may be feminine or masculine. The *ḍuḥāʾ* with *fatḥah* on the *ḍād* is *mamdūd* (extended) and masculine; it is at the highest rise of the day. Musa appointed this day for them only so that the exaltation of God's word, the manifestation of His religion, the humiliation of the unbeliever, and the destruction of falsehood would occur in full view of the witnesses. In al-Majma' al-Ghāṣṣ: so that the desire of whoever desires to follow the truth may grow, that the edge of the falsifiers and their partisans may be blunted, and that the report of this clear matter may spread in every desert and settlement, and be disseminated among all the dwellers of tents and cities.

The apparent view is that His words ﴿قالَ مَوْعِدُكم يَوْمُ الزِّينَةِ﴾ (*qāla mawʿiduku-m yawmu al-zīnah*, "He said: Your appointment is the day of adornment") are the words of Musa, peace be upon him, because it is a reply to Pharaoh's words ﴿فاجْعَلْ بَيْنَنا وبَيْنَكَ مَوْعِدًا﴾ ("Appoint between us and you an appointment"), and because specifying the day is fitting only for the one who is in the right, whose hand is known to be strong, not for the falsifier who is known to have nothing but deception. Also, His words ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ﴾ are addressed to all. He who held that it is the words of Pharaoh is far from the truth.

(p-250) When Musa had pointed to the proof of the Lord's lordship, and his speech was complete at His saying, ﴿and He does not forget﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52], Allah mentioned what He used to draw attention to His power and His oneness. He informed about Himself that He is the One who made such-and-such. We have taken the view that this is the speech of Allah, due to His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ (p-251) and His saying ﴿eat and graze your livestock﴾ and His saying ﴿We certainly showed him﴾. So His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ and ﴿We showed him﴾ is an iltifat (a shift of grammatical person, here from the third-person pronoun in ja'ala and salaka to the first-person plural pronoun of one who magnifies himself). An iltifat does not occur from speakers who are different. Even more remote is the view of those who said that alladhi is an adjective (na't) of the word (Rabbi), so that it would be in the nominative position, or in the accusative position as praise (madh). Al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari said both of these, because then the speech would be Musa's, and the iltifat in His saying (so We brought forth) and ﴿We showed him﴾ would not be possible.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that (so We brought forth) is part of Musa's speech, relating from Allah the Exalted, with the implied phrase "He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: so We brought forth." It is also possible that Musa's speech was complete at His saying ﴿and sent down from the sky water﴾, and then Allah joined Musa's speech with His informing Muhammad (ﷺ). The address in ﴿for you﴾ is intended for all of creation, drawing their attention to these signs.

Al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿mahdan﴾ with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the ha'. The rest of the seven read mihadan, and likewise in al-Zukhruf. Al-Mufaddal said: they are two verbal nouns (masdar), mahda mahdan and mihadan. Abu 'Ubayd said: mihad is a noun (ism), and mahd is the verb, meaning the verbal noun. Another said: mahd is singular and mihad is its plural. The meaning of this is that He made it for them, so that they can move about upon it in all their conditions and benefits, and He laid out for you roads within it for your purposes, so that your interests are not hindered. The pronoun in ﴿by it﴾ refers to the water, that is, by its means.

﴿pairs﴾, that is, kinds.
