This iltifat in (akhrajna) is like it in His saying ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sent down water from the sky, so We brought forth﴾ [Fatir: 27], ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow﴾ [An-Naml: 60], and ﴿And it is He who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth by it the vegetation of every thing﴾ [Al-An'am: 99]. In this iltifat there is also a specification that We alone have the power to do the like of this, and it does not fall under the power of anyone. The better view is that ﴿diverse﴾ (shatta) is in the accusative position as an adjective (na't) of ﴿pairs﴾, because it is that which is being spoken of.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that it is an adjective of the vegetation (nabat). Nabat is a verbal noun used as the name of that which grows, just as it is called nabt, so the singular and plural are alike in it. He means that they are ﴿diverse﴾, differing in benefit, taste, colour, scent and form; some are suitable for people and some for animals.

They said: From His blessing, the Mighty and Majestic, is that the sustenance of the servants is obtained only through the work of livestock, and Allah has made their fodder from what exceeds their needs and what they cannot eat. ﴿Eat and graze your livestock﴾ is a command of permission (amr ibaha) governed by an omitted circumstantial state (hal), meaning: ﴿so We brought forth﴾ speaking [to you], that is, permitting you to benefit from them, allowing you to eat some of them and feed some of them. Here ﴿and graze﴾ is transitive. Ra'a (to graze) can be intransitive and transitive; you say: the animal grazed (ra'at al-dabbatu ra'yan), and its owner pastured it (ra'aha sahibuha ri'ayatan), when he drove it out, sent it out to pasture and let it rest. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

By His saying ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, He pointed to the preceding signs: the making of the earth as a cradle, the laying of its roads, the sending down of water, and the bringing forth of vegetation. They said: ﴿al-nuha﴾ is the plural of nuha, which is intellect, named so because it restrains (yanha) from ugly deeds. Abu 'Ali permitted that it be a verbal noun, like al-huda (guidance). The pronoun in ﴿from it﴾ refers to the earth, and He meant the creation of their origin, Adam. It was also said: an angel goes to the soil of the place where the one to be created will be buried, and scatters it over the sperm-drop, so that he is created from both dust and sperm-drop together. This was said by 'Ata al-Khurasani. It was also said: it refers to the foods that grow out of the earth, from which the humours are generated from which man is formed; this is then a metaphor of a metaphor. ﴿And into it We return you﴾, that is, by burial in it or by being torn apart upon it. ﴿And from it We bring you forth again﴾ by resurrection, ﴿another time﴾, once more: He gathers their scattered parts and returns them as they were, living. His saying ﴿another time﴾ means another bringing-forth, because the meaning of His saying ﴿from it We created you﴾ is "We brought you forth."

﴿And We certainly showed him all Our signs﴾. This is an informing from Allah the Exalted to Muhammad (ﷺ), and this indicates that His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ is indeed an address to him (peace be upon him). ﴿We showed him Our signs﴾: the ones meant are those taken from the visual sense of seeing (ra'a al-basariyya), and for this reason it takes two objects by the transitivity-causing hamza. ﴿Our signs﴾ is not general, since He did not show him all the signs; rather the meaning is the signs of Ours that he saw, and so the idafa (construct) conveys what the definite article conveys of familiarity (al-'ahd). He saw the staff, the hand, the blotting out, and other things he saw; the emphasis (p-252) is then in relation to these known signs. It was also said: the meaning is signs in their entirety, and He attributed the signs to Himself as a mark of honour, as if He had said "signs for Us." It was also said: Musa had shown him His signs and enumerated for him what other prophets had been given of their signs and miracles, and he is a truthful prophet, with no difference between what he reports and what he shows. ﴿So he denied and refused﴾ all of them, and ﴿refused﴾ to accept any of them. End. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, and it is remote, because informing about a thing is not called seeing except by a distant figurative usage.

It was also said: ﴿We showed him﴾ here is from seeing of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb), not seeing of the eye, because at that time he had been shown only the staff and the white hand, meaning: ﴿We certainly made him know Our signs, all of them﴾. These are the nine signs. It was said: it is permissible that by the signs He meant the signs of His oneness which He displayed to us in the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and then it would be from seeing of the eye. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ubayy said: it implies the acquisition (kasb) of Pharaoh, and this is what reward and punishment depend upon. The object of ﴿denied﴾ is omitted; the apparent meaning is that it is the signs. It is possible that the intended meaning is: ﴿he denied﴾ Musa and ﴿refused﴾ to accept what he brought him of his message.

It was said: It is also permissible that he meant: he denied that they were signs of Allah, and said: they are sorcery. For this reason he said: ﴿Have you come to us to expel us from our land by your sorcery, O Musa?﴾ This view is weakened by His saying ﴿You know well that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as insights﴾ [Al-Isra: 102], and His saying ﴿and they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [An-Naml: 14]. So it appears that he denied out of his wrongdoing, not that it was confused for him whether they were signs of sorcery. In his saying ﴿Have you come to us to expel us﴾ there is weakness, which is evident from him, and much agitation regarding what Musa brought, since he knew that he was upon the truth and that he would inevitably overcome him in his kingdom. He mentioned the cause of the coming, which is the expulsion of them, and he cast this into the ears of his people so that they would become intensely hostile towards him, since expulsion from one's homeland is among the things that are very hard. Allah made it equal to killing in His saying ﴿Kill yourselves or leave your homes﴾ [An-Nisa: 66]. His saying ﴿by your sorcery﴾ is an excuse and bewilderment, because it is not hidden from him that a sorcerer cannot expel a king like himself from his land and overcome him in his kingdom by sorcery. He presented this as a doubt casting aspersion on prophethood, and that a miracle is distinguished from sorcery only by the miracle being something whose opposition is impossible. Therefore he said: ﴿So we will surely bring you sorcery like it﴾. This indicates that Musa's affair (peace be upon him) had grown strong, and his protection among the Children of Israel had increased, and his matter had come to be in the hearts of the people, since this is the speech of one who needs proof, not of one who proclaims his own affair. Their land is the land of Egypt. He addressed him with ﴿your sorcery﴾ because the conversation was with him, and the staff and the hand had appeared from his direction. ﴿So we will surely bring you﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, which gave people the impression that what Musa brought was of the kind of sorcery, and that with him there was someone who could match him in that. So he sought to set an appointment for a contest in sorcery. The apparent meaning is that ﴿an appointment﴾ here is a time: that is, appoint for us a time of gathering. For this reason he answered with His saying ﴿He said: Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. The meaning of ﴿we will not fail it﴾ is that we will not break that time in gathering there. Some took it to be a known place, and its source is His saying ﴿your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾.

Al-Qushayri said: The more apparent view is that it is a verbal noun, and for this reason he said ﴿we will not fail it﴾, that is, that appointment; and failing (al-ikhlaf) is to promise something and not fulfil it. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you take it to be a time, in view of His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾, which corresponds to it, then two things would be necessary for you: that you make the time the thing that is failed, and that the governing verb (nasib) of ﴿a place﴾ would be obstructed for you. And if you take it as a place corresponding to His saying ﴿a place equal﴾, it would also be necessary for you that the failing falls upon the place, and that it not correspond to His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. The reading of al-Hasan does not correspond to it at all in place, because he read ﴿the Day of Adornment﴾ in the accusative, so it remains that it be taken as a verbal noun meaning a promise, and that an omitted genitive construction be assumed, that is, "the place of an appointment," and that the pronoun in ﴿we will not fail it﴾ and ﴿a place﴾ be taken as a substitute (badal) for the omitted place. If you say: How do you make it correspond to His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾, when you must take it as a time, and the question is about a place, not a time? I say: It corresponds in meaning even if it does not correspond in wording, because they must gather on the Day of Adornment in a particular place known for their gathering in it on that day, so by mentioning the time the place is known.

As for the reading of al-Hasan, the appointment in it is only a verbal noun, and the meaning is the fulfilment of your promise on the Day of Adornment, and this also corresponds (p-253) in terms of meaning. It is also permissible that an omitted genitive construction be assumed, and the meaning would be: make between us and between you a promise which we will not fail. If you say: On what is ﴿a place﴾ in the accusative? I say: On the verbal noun, or on a verb indicated by the verbal noun. If you say: How does the answer correspond to it? I say: As for the reading of al-Hasan, it is clear; as for the reading of the majority, it is according to the assumption "your promise is the promise of the Day of Adornment."

It is permissible, according to the reading of al-Hasan, that ﴿your appointment﴾ be the subject (mubtada') with the meaning of a time, and ﴿in the forenoon﴾ (duha) be its predicate, with the intention of definiteness in it, since it had been described before the action by His saying ﴿we will not fail it﴾, and it is a relative clause, and the verbal noun, when it is described before it acts, may not act in their view. And the saying "and (duha) is its predicate with the intention of definiteness in it" is because it is the forenoon of that very day. Although it is the forenoon of that very day, it is not with the intention of definiteness; rather it is indefinite, even if it is from a particular day, because it is not replaced from the definite article (alif-lam) as in sihr (sorcery), nor is it defined by annexation. If you say: "I came on Friday at dawn (bukran)," we do not claim that bukran is definite, even though we know that it is from a particular day.

Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read ﴿لا نُخْلِفْهُ﴾ (*lā nukhlifhu*, "we shall not fail it") with the *fa'* in jussive (*jazm*, the mood marking that ends a verb with a sukun), taking it as the answer to the imperative. The majority (*al-jumhūr*) read it with *raf'* (nominative), as a qualifier (*ṣifah*) of *mawʿidan* (a promise/appointment).

Al-Ḥawfī said: ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ (*mawʿidan*) is the object of ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾ (*ijʿal*, "appoint"), and ﴿مَكانًا﴾ (*makānan*, "a place") is an adverbial of place (*ẓarf*), whose governing element is ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾. Abu ʿAli said: ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ is the first object of ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾ and ﴿مَكانًا﴾ is the second object. He prohibited ﴿مَكانًا﴾ from being governed by ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ because the latter has already been qualified.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: These nouns that function as verbs (*al-asmāʾ al-ʿāmilah ʿamal al-fiʿl*), when they are qualified, or when something is conjoined to them, or when they are predicated about, or diminutivized, or pluralized, and become fully nominal in this way, do not govern, and nothing that belongs to them may be attached to them. The adverbs (*ẓurūf*) may be treated more loosely, so something may be attached to them after what we have mentioned, as in the words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿يُنادَوْنَ لَمَقْتُ اللَّهِ أكْبَرُ مِن مَقْتِكم أنْفُسَكم إذْ تُدْعَوْنَ إلى الإيمانِ﴾ [Ghafir: 10] ("They will be called: Surely God's hatred is greater than your hatred of yourselves, when you were called to faith"). Here ﴿إذْ﴾ (*idh*, "when") is attached to ﴿لَمَقْتُ﴾ (*lamaqtu*, "hatred"), and he has been predicated about. This is permitted only with adverbs. A group prohibited ﴿مَكانًا﴾ from being in the accusative as the second object of ﴿لُنُخْلِفُهُ﴾, but a group of grammarians permitted it, its rationale being that it is an extension (*ittisāʿ*) in the sense of "to fail the promise." End of quote.

His phrase "when they are qualified" is not agreed upon for every element that functions as a verb. Consider the active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*) without *al-*: if it is qualified before it governs, there is disagreement. The Basrans prohibit it, the Kufans permit it. Likewise, if it is diminutivized, there is disagreement over its governing. As for pluralization, there is no known disagreement about its governing. As for the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) when pluralized, there is disagreement about whether it may govern. As for his exception of the adverbs from the governed elements, others hold that this is prohibited absolutely for the verbal noun, and that ﴿إذْ﴾ governs a verb implied by what precedes it, meaning: "their hatred of you when you are called."

﴿ولا أنْتَ﴾ (*wa-lā anta*, "nor you") is conjoined to the implicit pronoun in ﴿نُخْلِفُهُ﴾, which is emphasized by the word "we" (*naḥnu*).

Ibn ʿAmir, Ḥamzah, ʿAsim, Yaʿqub, al-Ḥasan, Qatadah, Ṭalḥah, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Abi Laylā, Abu Ḥatim and Ibn Jarir read ﴿سُوًى﴾ (*suwan*) with *ḍammah* on the *sīn*, with tanwin in connected speech. The rest of the seven read it with *kasrah* on the *sīn*, with tanwin in connected speech. Al-Ḥasan also read ﴿سُوى﴾ with *ḍammah* on the *sīn* without tanwin in both states, treating connected speech as pause (*ajrā al-waṣl majrā al-waqf*), not because it is prevented from taking tanwin (*ṣarf*), since a *fiʿl* form among the adjectives is inflected, like *ḥaṭum* and *labad*. ʿIsa read *siwā* with *kasrah* on the *sīn*, without tanwin in both states, also treating connected speech as pause.

The meaning of ﴿سُوًى﴾ is "just and equitable." Abu ʿAli said: It is as though he said, "His nearness to you is his nearness to us." Others said: He meant that our position in it is equal, so that this encompasses the Qur'an, and that ranks in it are one in the pursuit of truth, so that leadership (*riʾāsah*) does not obstruct you in it, and only proof is intended. From Mujahid: it derives from *istiwāʾ* (equality), because the distance from the middle to the two extremes is equal, without disparity. This is the meaning of what preceded from Abu ʿAli's words: "His nearness to you is his nearness to us."

Al-Akhfash said: ﴿سُوًى﴾ is *maqṣūr* (short-vowelled, without the final alif extended) if you read its *sīn* with *kasrah* or *ḍammah*, and *mamdūd* (extended) if you read it with *fatḥah*. There are three dialects, and in all of them it carries the meaning of ﴿غَيْرِ﴾ (*ghayr*, "other than") [Ṭaha: 22] and the meaning of "just," and "middle between the two parties." The poet said:

*And indeed our father was a settler among his people, equitable between the Qays of Ghaylan and the Fizr.*

He said: You say "I passed by a man *siwāka*, *suwāka*, *sawāka*," meaning "other than you," and it applies to all. The highest of these dialects is the *kasrah*, as al-Naḥḥas said.

A group said: The meaning of ﴿مَكانًا سُوًى﴾ (*makānan suwan*, "a place level") is a level place from the earth, that is, without rough ground, without mountain, without hill, and without a depression in the earth, such that the gaze of anyone would not be obstructed, so that they would not see the place of Musa and the magicians and what issues from them. He said this confident of the magicians' victory over Musa; then when they witnessed his victory over them, they would return from what they had believed in.

A group said: Its meaning is "a place other than this place of ours." This is not right, because ﴿سِوًى﴾ when it means ﴿غَيْرِ﴾ is used only in construct form (*muḍāfah*) in wording and is not separated from the construct.

Al-Ḥasan, al-Aʿmash, ʿAsim in one narration, Abu Ḥaywah, Ibn Abi ʿAblah, Qatadah, al-Jaḥdari, Hubayrah and al-Zaʿfarani read ﴿يَوْمَ الزِّينَةِ﴾ (*yawma al-zīnah*, "the day of adornment") with *fatḥah* on the *mīm*. The derivation of this reading has been mentioned in al-Zamakhshari's words. It is narrated that ﴿يَوْمَ الزِّينَةِ﴾ was a festival (*ʿīd*) for them and a day of gathering (*yawman mashhūdan*), and it coincided with ʿAshura, and it was a Saturday. It is said: It is the day of the breaking of the canal that remains until today. It is said: It is the day of Nowruz, which was the beginning of their year. It is said: It is Saturday, for it is a day of rest and ease. It is said: It is a market day for them. It is said: It is ʿAshura.

Ibn Masʿud, al-Jaḥdari, Abu ʿImran al-Jawni, Abu Nahik, and ʿAmr ibn Fa'id read ﴿وأنْ تُحْشَرَ﴾ (*wa-an tuḥsar*, "and that they be gathered") with the second-person *tā'* (addressing), meaning "O Pharaoh." It is narrated from them also with *yā'* in the third person. ﴿النّاسُ﴾ (*al-nās*, "the people") is in the accusative in both readings.

The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: "And that the gatherer gathers the people in the forenoon," so the subject is omitted because it is known. This omission of the subject in such a construction is not permitted according to the Basrans. Others said: ﴿وأنْ يُحْشَرَ﴾ refers to the people. He said: It is also permitted that the pronoun of Pharaoh be in it, mentioned with third-person wording, either according to the custom by which kings are addressed, or because he addressed the people with ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ﴾ (*mawʿiduku-m*, "your appointment"), and made ﴿يُحْشَرَ﴾ refer to Pharaoh. It is also permitted that ﴿وأنْ يُحْشَرَ﴾ be in the nominative position as conjoined to ﴿يَوْمُ الزِّينَةِ﴾, or in the genitive position as conjoined to ﴿الزِّينَةِ﴾.

﴿ضُحًى﴾ (*ḍuḥan*, "in the forenoon") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarf*), and it is the rising of the day. It may be feminine or masculine. The *ḍuḥāʾ* with *fatḥah* on the *ḍād* is *mamdūd* (extended) and masculine; it is at the highest rise of the day. Musa appointed this day for them only so that the exaltation of God's word, the manifestation of His religion, the humiliation of the unbeliever, and the destruction of falsehood would occur in full view of the witnesses. In al-Majma' al-Ghāṣṣ: so that the desire of whoever desires to follow the truth may grow, that the edge of the falsifiers and their partisans may be blunted, and that the report of this clear matter may spread in every desert and settlement, and be disseminated among all the dwellers of tents and cities.

The apparent view is that His words ﴿قالَ مَوْعِدُكم يَوْمُ الزِّينَةِ﴾ (*qāla mawʿiduku-m yawmu al-zīnah*, "He said: Your appointment is the day of adornment") are the words of Musa, peace be upon him, because it is a reply to Pharaoh's words ﴿فاجْعَلْ بَيْنَنا وبَيْنَكَ مَوْعِدًا﴾ ("Appoint between us and you an appointment"), and because specifying the day is fitting only for the one who is in the right, whose hand is known to be strong, not for the falsifier who is known to have nothing but deception. Also, His words ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ﴾ are addressed to all. He who held that it is the words of Pharaoh is far from the truth.

(p-250) When Musa had pointed to the proof of the Lord's lordship, and his speech was complete at His saying, ﴿and He does not forget﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52], Allah mentioned what He used to draw attention to His power and His oneness. He informed about Himself that He is the One who made such-and-such. We have taken the view that this is the speech of Allah, due to His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ (p-251) and His saying ﴿eat and graze your livestock﴾ and His saying ﴿We certainly showed him﴾. So His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ and ﴿We showed him﴾ is an iltifat (a shift of grammatical person, here from the third-person pronoun in ja'ala and salaka to the first-person plural pronoun of one who magnifies himself). An iltifat does not occur from speakers who are different. Even more remote is the view of those who said that alladhi is an adjective (na't) of the word (Rabbi), so that it would be in the nominative position, or in the accusative position as praise (madh). Al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari said both of these, because then the speech would be Musa's, and the iltifat in His saying (so We brought forth) and ﴿We showed him﴾ would not be possible.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that (so We brought forth) is part of Musa's speech, relating from Allah the Exalted, with the implied phrase "He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: so We brought forth." It is also possible that Musa's speech was complete at His saying ﴿and sent down from the sky water﴾, and then Allah joined Musa's speech with His informing Muhammad (ﷺ). The address in ﴿for you﴾ is intended for all of creation, drawing their attention to these signs.

Al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿mahdan﴾ with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the ha'. The rest of the seven read mihadan, and likewise in al-Zukhruf. Al-Mufaddal said: they are two verbal nouns (masdar), mahda mahdan and mihadan. Abu 'Ubayd said: mihad is a noun (ism), and mahd is the verb, meaning the verbal noun. Another said: mahd is singular and mihad is its plural. The meaning of this is that He made it for them, so that they can move about upon it in all their conditions and benefits, and He laid out for you roads within it for your purposes, so that your interests are not hindered. The pronoun in ﴿by it﴾ refers to the water, that is, by its means.

﴿pairs﴾, that is, kinds. This iltifat in (akhrajna) is like it in His saying ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sent down water from the sky, so We brought forth﴾ [Fatir: 27], ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow﴾ [An-Naml: 60], and ﴿And it is He who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth by it the vegetation of every thing﴾ [Al-An'am: 99]. In this iltifat there is also a specification that We alone have the power to do the like of this, and it does not fall under the power of anyone. The better view is that ﴿diverse﴾ (shatta) is in the accusative position as an adjective (na't) of ﴿pairs﴾, because it is that which is being spoken of.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that it is an adjective of the vegetation (nabat). Nabat is a verbal noun used as the name of that which grows, just as it is called nabt, so the singular and plural are alike in it. He means that they are ﴿diverse﴾, differing in benefit, taste, colour, scent and form; some are suitable for people and some for animals.

They said: From His blessing, the Mighty and Majestic, is that the sustenance of the servants is obtained only through the work of livestock, and Allah has made their fodder from what exceeds their needs and what they cannot eat. ﴿Eat and graze your livestock﴾ is a command of permission (amr ibaha) governed by an omitted circumstantial state (hal), meaning: ﴿so We brought forth﴾ speaking [to you], that is, permitting you to benefit from them, allowing you to eat some of them and feed some of them. Here ﴿and graze﴾ is transitive. Ra'a (to graze) can be intransitive and transitive; you say: the animal grazed (ra'at al-dabbatu ra'yan), and its owner pastured it (ra'aha sahibuha ri'ayatan), when he drove it out, sent it out to pasture and let it rest. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

By His saying ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, He pointed to the preceding signs: the making of the earth as a cradle, the laying of its roads, the sending down of water, and the bringing forth of vegetation. They said: ﴿al-nuha﴾ is the plural of nuha, which is intellect, named so because it restrains (yanha) from ugly deeds. Abu 'Ali permitted that it be a verbal noun, like al-huda (guidance). The pronoun in ﴿from it﴾ refers to the earth, and He meant the creation of their origin, Adam. It was also said: an angel goes to the soil of the place where the one to be created will be buried, and scatters it over the sperm-drop, so that he is created from both dust and sperm-drop together. This was said by 'Ata al-Khurasani. It was also said: it refers to the foods that grow out of the earth, from which the humours are generated from which man is formed; this is then a metaphor of a metaphor. ﴿And into it We return you﴾, that is, by burial in it or by being torn apart upon it. ﴿And from it We bring you forth again﴾ by resurrection, ﴿another time﴾, once more: He gathers their scattered parts and returns them as they were, living. His saying ﴿another time﴾ means another bringing-forth, because the meaning of His saying ﴿from it We created you﴾ is "We brought you forth."

﴿And We certainly showed him all Our signs﴾. This is an informing from Allah the Exalted to Muhammad (ﷺ), and this indicates that His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ is indeed an address to him (peace be upon him). ﴿We showed him Our signs﴾: the ones meant are those taken from the visual sense of seeing (ra'a al-basariyya), and for this reason it takes two objects by the transitivity-causing hamza. ﴿Our signs﴾ is not general, since He did not show him all the signs; rather the meaning is the signs of Ours that he saw, and so the idafa (construct) conveys what the definite article conveys of familiarity (al-'ahd). He saw the staff, the hand, the blotting out, and other things he saw; the emphasis (p-252) is then in relation to these known signs. It was also said: the meaning is signs in their entirety, and He attributed the signs to Himself as a mark of honour, as if He had said "signs for Us." It was also said: Musa had shown him His signs and enumerated for him what other prophets had been given of their signs and miracles, and he is a truthful prophet, with no difference between what he reports and what he shows. ﴿So he denied and refused﴾ all of them, and ﴿refused﴾ to accept any of them. End. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, and it is remote, because informing about a thing is not called seeing except by a distant figurative usage.

It was also said: ﴿We showed him﴾ here is from seeing of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb), not seeing of the eye, because at that time he had been shown only the staff and the white hand, meaning: ﴿We certainly made him know Our signs, all of them﴾. These are the nine signs. It was said: it is permissible that by the signs He meant the signs of His oneness which He displayed to us in the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and then it would be from seeing of the eye. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ubayy said: it implies the acquisition (kasb) of Pharaoh, and this is what reward and punishment depend upon. The object of ﴿denied﴾ is omitted; the apparent meaning is that it is the signs. It is possible that the intended meaning is: ﴿he denied﴾ Musa and ﴿refused﴾ to accept what he brought him of his message.

It was said: It is also permissible that he meant: he denied that they were signs of Allah, and said: they are sorcery. For this reason he said: ﴿Have you come to us to expel us from our land by your sorcery, O Musa?﴾ This view is weakened by His saying ﴿You know well that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as insights﴾ [Al-Isra: 102], and His saying ﴿and they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [An-Naml: 14]. So it appears that he denied out of his wrongdoing, not that it was confused for him whether they were signs of sorcery. In his saying ﴿Have you come to us to expel us﴾ there is weakness, which is evident from him, and much agitation regarding what Musa brought, since he knew that he was upon the truth and that he would inevitably overcome him in his kingdom. He mentioned the cause of the coming, which is the expulsion of them, and he cast this into the ears of his people so that they would become intensely hostile towards him, since expulsion from one's homeland is among the things that are very hard. Allah made it equal to killing in His saying ﴿Kill yourselves or leave your homes﴾ [An-Nisa: 66]. His saying ﴿by your sorcery﴾ is an excuse and bewilderment, because it is not hidden from him that a sorcerer cannot expel a king like himself from his land and overcome him in his kingdom by sorcery. He presented this as a doubt casting aspersion on prophethood, and that a miracle is distinguished from sorcery only by the miracle being something whose opposition is impossible. Therefore he said: ﴿So we will surely bring you sorcery like it﴾. This indicates that Musa's affair (peace be upon him) had grown strong, and his protection among the Children of Israel had increased, and his matter had come to be in the hearts of the people, since this is the speech of one who needs proof, not of one who proclaims his own affair. Their land is the land of Egypt. He addressed him with ﴿your sorcery﴾ because the conversation was with him, and the staff and the hand had appeared from his direction. ﴿So we will surely bring you﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, which gave people the impression that what Musa brought was of the kind of sorcery, and that with him there was someone who could match him in that. So he sought to set an appointment for a contest in sorcery. The apparent meaning is that ﴿an appointment﴾ here is a time: that is, appoint for us a time of gathering. For this reason he answered with His saying ﴿He said: Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. The meaning of ﴿we will not fail it﴾ is that we will not break that time in gathering there. Some took it to be a known place, and its source is His saying ﴿your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾.

Al-Qushayri said: The more apparent view is that it is a verbal noun, and for this reason he said ﴿we will not fail it﴾, that is, that appointment; and failing (al-ikhlaf) is to promise something and not fulfil it. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you take it to be a time, in view of His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾, which corresponds to it, then two things would be necessary for you: that you make the time the thing that is failed, and that the governing verb (nasib) of ﴿a place﴾ would be obstructed for you. And if you take it as a place corresponding to His saying ﴿a place equal﴾, it would also be necessary for you that the failing falls upon the place, and that it not correspond to His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. The reading of al-Hasan does not correspond to it at all in place, because he read ﴿the Day of Adornment﴾ in the accusative, so it remains that it be taken as a verbal noun meaning a promise, and that an omitted genitive construction be assumed, that is, "the place of an appointment," and that the pronoun in ﴿we will not fail it﴾ and ﴿a place﴾ be taken as a substitute (badal) for the omitted place. If you say: How do you make it correspond to His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾, when you must take it as a time, and the question is about a place, not a time? I say: It corresponds in meaning even if it does not correspond in wording, because they must gather on the Day of Adornment in a particular place known for their gathering in it on that day, so by mentioning the time the place is known.

As for the reading of al-Hasan, the appointment in it is only a verbal noun, and the meaning is the fulfilment of your promise on the Day of Adornment, and this also corresponds (p-253) in terms of meaning. It is also permissible that an omitted genitive construction be assumed, and the meaning would be: make between us and between you a promise which we will not fail. If you say: On what is ﴿a place﴾ in the accusative? I say: On the verbal noun, or on a verb indicated by the verbal noun. If you say: How does the answer correspond to it? I say: As for the reading of al-Hasan, it is clear; as for the reading of the majority, it is according to the assumption "your promise is the promise of the Day of Adornment."

It is permissible, according to the reading of al-Hasan, that ﴿your appointment﴾ be the subject (mubtada') with the meaning of a time, and ﴿in the forenoon﴾ (duha) be its predicate, with the intention of definiteness in it, since it had been described before the action by His saying ﴿we will not fail it﴾, and it is a relative clause, and the verbal noun, when it is described before it acts, may not act in their view. And the saying "and (duha) is its predicate with the intention of definiteness in it" is because it is the forenoon of that very day. Although it is the forenoon of that very day, it is not with the intention of definiteness; rather it is indefinite, even if it is from a particular day, because it is not replaced from the definite article (alif-lam) as in sihr (sorcery), nor is it defined by annexation. If you say: "I came on Friday at dawn (bukran)," we do not claim that bukran is definite, even though we know that it is from a particular day.

Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read ﴿لا نُخْلِفْهُ﴾ (*lā nukhlifhu*, "we shall not fail it") with the *fa'* in jussive (*jazm*, the mood marking that ends a verb with a sukun), taking it as the answer to the imperative. The majority (*al-jumhūr*) read it with *raf'* (nominative), as a qualifier (*ṣifah*) of *mawʿidan* (a promise/appointment).

Al-Ḥawfī said: ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ (*mawʿidan*) is the object of ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾ (*ijʿal*, "appoint"), and ﴿مَكانًا﴾ (*makānan*, "a place") is an adverbial of place (*ẓarf*), whose governing element is ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾. Abu ʿAli said: ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ is the first object of ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾ and ﴿مَكانًا﴾ is the second object. He prohibited ﴿مَكانًا﴾ from being governed by ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ because the latter has already been qualified.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: These nouns that function as verbs (*al-asmāʾ al-ʿāmilah ʿamal al-fiʿl*), when they are qualified, or when something is conjoined to them, or when they are predicated about, or diminutivized, or pluralized, and become fully nominal in this way, do not govern, and nothing that belongs to them may be attached to them. The adverbs (*ẓurūf*) may be treated more loosely, so something may be attached to them after what we have mentioned, as in the words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿يُنادَوْنَ لَمَقْتُ اللَّهِ أكْبَرُ مِن مَقْتِكم أنْفُسَكم إذْ تُدْعَوْنَ إلى الإيمانِ﴾ [Ghafir: 10] ("They will be called: Surely God's hatred is greater than your hatred of yourselves, when you were called to faith"). Here ﴿إذْ﴾ (*idh*, "when") is attached to ﴿لَمَقْتُ﴾ (*lamaqtu*, "hatred"), and he has been predicated about. This is permitted only with adverbs. A group prohibited ﴿مَكانًا﴾ from being in the accusative as the second object of ﴿لُنُخْلِفُهُ﴾, but a group of grammarians permitted it, its rationale being that it is an extension (*ittisāʿ*) in the sense of "to fail the promise." End of quote.

His phrase "when they are qualified" is not agreed upon for every element that functions as a verb. Consider the active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*) without *al-*: if it is qualified before it governs, there is disagreement. The Basrans prohibit it, the Kufans permit it. Likewise, if it is diminutivized, there is disagreement over its governing. As for pluralization, there is no known disagreement about its governing. As for the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) when pluralized, there is disagreement about whether it may govern. As for his exception of the adverbs from the governed elements, others hold that this is prohibited absolutely for the verbal noun, and that ﴿إذْ﴾ governs a verb implied by what precedes it, meaning: "their hatred of you when you are called."

﴿ولا أنْتَ﴾ (*wa-lā anta*, "nor you") is conjoined to the implicit pronoun in ﴿نُخْلِفُهُ﴾, which is emphasized by the word "we" (*naḥnu*).

Ibn ʿAmir, Ḥamzah, ʿAsim, Yaʿqub, al-Ḥasan, Qatadah, Ṭalḥah, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Abi Laylā, Abu Ḥatim and Ibn Jarir read ﴿سُوًى﴾ (*suwan*) with *ḍammah* on the *sīn*, with tanwin in connected speech. The rest of the seven read it with *kasrah* on the *sīn*, with tanwin in connected speech. Al-Ḥasan also read ﴿سُوى﴾ with *ḍammah* on the *sīn* without tanwin in both states, treating connected speech as pause (*ajrā al-waṣl majrā al-waqf*), not because it is prevented from taking tanwin (*ṣarf*), since a *fiʿl* form among the adjectives is inflected, like *ḥaṭum* and *labad*. ʿIsa read *siwā* with *kasrah* on the *sīn*, without tanwin in both states, also treating connected speech as pause.

The meaning of ﴿سُوًى﴾ is "just and equitable." Abu ʿAli said: It is as though he said, "His nearness to you is his nearness to us." Others said: He meant that our position in it is equal, so that this encompasses the Qur'an, and that ranks in it are one in the pursuit of truth, so that leadership (*riʾāsah*) does not obstruct you in it, and only proof is intended. From Mujahid: it derives from *istiwāʾ* (equality), because the distance from the middle to the two extremes is equal, without disparity. This is the meaning of what preceded from Abu ʿAli's words: "His nearness to you is his nearness to us."

Al-Akhfash said: ﴿سُوًى﴾ is *maqṣūr* (short-vowelled, without the final alif extended) if you read its *sīn* with *kasrah* or *ḍammah*, and *mamdūd* (extended) if you read it with *fatḥah*. There are three dialects, and in all of them it carries the meaning of ﴿غَيْرِ﴾ (*ghayr*, "other than") [Ṭaha: 22] and the meaning of "just," and "middle between the two parties." The poet said:

*And indeed our father was a settler among his people, equitable between the Qays of Ghaylan and the Fizr.*

He said: You say "I passed by a man *siwāka*, *suwāka*, *sawāka*," meaning "other than you," and it applies to all. The highest of these dialects is the *kasrah*, as al-Naḥḥas said.

A group said: The meaning of ﴿مَكانًا سُوًى﴾ (*makānan suwan*, "a place level") is a level place from the earth, that is, without rough ground, without mountain, without hill, and without a depression in the earth, such that the gaze of anyone would not be obstructed, so that they would not see the place of Musa and the magicians and what issues from them. He said this confident of the magicians' victory over Musa; then when they witnessed his victory over them, they would return from what they had believed in.

A group said: Its meaning is "a place other than this place of ours." This is not right, because ﴿سِوًى﴾ when it means ﴿غَيْرِ﴾ is used only in construct form (*muḍāfah*) in wording and is not separated from the construct.

Al-Ḥasan, al-Aʿmash, ʿAsim in one narration, Abu Ḥaywah, Ibn Abi ʿAblah, Qatadah, al-Jaḥdari, Hubayrah and al-Zaʿfarani read ﴿يَوْمَ الزِّينَةِ﴾ (*yawma al-zīnah*, "the day of adornment") with *fatḥah* on the *mīm*. The derivation of this reading has been mentioned in al-Zamakhshari's words. It is narrated that ﴿يَوْمَ الزِّينَةِ﴾ was a festival (*ʿīd*) for them and a day of gathering (*yawman mashhūdan*), and it coincided with ʿAshura, and it was a Saturday. It is said: It is the day of the breaking of the canal that remains until today. It is said: It is the day of Nowruz, which was the beginning of their year. It is said: It is Saturday, for it is a day of rest and ease. It is said: It is a market day for them. It is said: It is ʿAshura.

Ibn Masʿud, al-Jaḥdari, Abu ʿImran al-Jawni, Abu Nahik, and ʿAmr ibn Fa'id read ﴿وأنْ تُحْشَرَ﴾ (*wa-an tuḥsar*, "and that they be gathered") with the second-person *tā'* (addressing), meaning "O Pharaoh." It is narrated from them also with *yā'* in the third person. ﴿النّاسُ﴾ (*al-nās*, "the people") is in the accusative in both readings.

The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: "And that the gatherer gathers the people in the forenoon," so the subject is omitted because it is known. This omission of the subject in such a construction is not permitted according to the Basrans. Others said: ﴿وأنْ يُحْشَرَ﴾ refers to the people. He said: It is also permitted that the pronoun of Pharaoh be in it, mentioned with third-person wording, either according to the custom by which kings are addressed, or because he addressed the people with ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ﴾ (*mawʿiduku-m*, "your appointment"), and made ﴿يُحْشَرَ﴾ refer to Pharaoh. It is also permitted that ﴿وأنْ يُحْشَرَ﴾ be in the nominative position as conjoined to ﴿يَوْمُ الزِّينَةِ﴾, or in the genitive position as conjoined to ﴿الزِّينَةِ﴾.

﴿ضُحًى﴾ (*ḍuḥan*, "in the forenoon") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarf*), and it is the rising of the day. It may be feminine or masculine. The *ḍuḥāʾ* with *fatḥah* on the *ḍād* is *mamdūd* (extended) and masculine; it is at the highest rise of the day. Musa appointed this day for them only so that the exaltation of God's word, the manifestation of His religion, the humiliation of the unbeliever, and the destruction of falsehood would occur in full view of the witnesses. In al-Majma' al-Ghāṣṣ: so that the desire of whoever desires to follow the truth may grow, that the edge of the falsifiers and their partisans may be blunted, and that the report of this clear matter may spread in every desert and settlement, and be disseminated among all the dwellers of tents and cities.

The apparent view is that His words ﴿قالَ مَوْعِدُكم يَوْمُ الزِّينَةِ﴾ (*qāla mawʿiduku-m yawmu al-zīnah*, "He said: Your appointment is the day of adornment") are the words of Musa, peace be upon him, because it is a reply to Pharaoh's words ﴿فاجْعَلْ بَيْنَنا وبَيْنَكَ مَوْعِدًا﴾ ("Appoint between us and you an appointment"), and because specifying the day is fitting only for the one who is in the right, whose hand is known to be strong, not for the falsifier who is known to have nothing but deception. Also, His words ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ﴾ are addressed to all. He who held that it is the words of Pharaoh is far from the truth.

(p-250) When Musa had pointed to the proof of the Lord's lordship, and his speech was complete at His saying, ﴿and He does not forget﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52], Allah mentioned what He used to draw attention to His power and His oneness. He informed about Himself that He is the One who made such-and-such. We have taken the view that this is the speech of Allah, due to His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ (p-251) and His saying ﴿eat and graze your livestock﴾ and His saying ﴿We certainly showed him﴾. So His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ and ﴿We showed him﴾ is an iltifat (a shift of grammatical person, here from the third-person pronoun in ja'ala and salaka to the first-person plural pronoun of one who magnifies himself). An iltifat does not occur from speakers who are different. Even more remote is the view of those who said that alladhi is an adjective (na't) of the word (Rabbi), so that it would be in the nominative position, or in the accusative position as praise (madh). Al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari said both of these, because then the speech would be Musa's, and the iltifat in His saying (so We brought forth) and ﴿We showed him﴾ would not be possible.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that (so We brought forth) is part of Musa's speech, relating from Allah the Exalted, with the implied phrase "He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: so We brought forth." It is also possible that Musa's speech was complete at His saying ﴿and sent down from the sky water﴾, and then Allah joined Musa's speech with His informing Muhammad (ﷺ). The address in ﴿for you﴾ is intended for all of creation, drawing their attention to these signs.

Al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿mahdan﴾ with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the ha'. The rest of the seven read mihadan, and likewise in al-Zukhruf. Al-Mufaddal said: they are two verbal nouns (masdar), mahda mahdan and mihadan. Abu 'Ubayd said: mihad is a noun (ism), and mahd is the verb, meaning the verbal noun. Another said: mahd is singular and mihad is its plural. The meaning of this is that He made it for them, so that they can move about upon it in all their conditions and benefits, and He laid out for you roads within it for your purposes, so that your interests are not hindered. The pronoun in ﴿by it﴾ refers to the water, that is, by its means.

﴿pairs﴾, that is, kinds. This iltifat in (akhrajna) is like it in His saying ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sent down water from the sky, so We brought forth﴾ [Fatir: 27], ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow﴾ [An-Naml: 60], and ﴿And it is He who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth by it the vegetation of every thing﴾ [Al-An'am: 99]. In this iltifat there is also a specification that We alone have the power to do the like of this, and it does not fall under the power of anyone. The better view is that ﴿diverse﴾ (shatta) is in the accusative position as an adjective (na't) of ﴿pairs﴾, because it is that which is being spoken of.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that it is an adjective of the vegetation (nabat). Nabat is a verbal noun used as the name of that which grows, just as it is called nabt, so the singular and plural are alike in it. He means that they are ﴿diverse﴾, differing in benefit, taste, colour, scent and form; some are suitable for people and some for animals.

They said: From His blessing, the Mighty and Majestic, is that the sustenance of the servants is obtained only through the work of livestock, and Allah has made their fodder from what exceeds their needs and what they cannot eat. ﴿Eat and graze your livestock﴾ is a command of permission (amr ibaha) governed by an omitted circumstantial state (hal), meaning: ﴿so We brought forth﴾ speaking [to you], that is, permitting you to benefit from them, allowing you to eat some of them and feed some of them. Here ﴿and graze﴾ is transitive. Ra'a (to graze) can be intransitive and transitive; you say: the animal grazed (ra'at al-dabbatu ra'yan), and its owner pastured it (ra'aha sahibuha ri'ayatan), when he drove it out, sent it out to pasture and let it rest. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

By His saying ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, He pointed to the preceding signs: the making of the earth as a cradle, the laying of its roads, the sending down of water, and the bringing forth of vegetation. They said: ﴿al-nuha﴾ is the plural of nuha, which is intellect, named so because it restrains (yanha) from ugly deeds. Abu 'Ali permitted that it be a verbal noun, like al-huda (guidance). The pronoun in ﴿from it﴾ refers to the earth, and He meant the creation of their origin, Adam. It was also said: an angel goes to the soil of the place where the one to be created will be buried, and scatters it over the sperm-drop, so that he is created from both dust and sperm-drop together. This was said by 'Ata al-Khurasani. It was also said: it refers to the foods that grow out of the earth, from which the humours are generated from which man is formed; this is then a metaphor of a metaphor. ﴿And into it We return you﴾, that is, by burial in it or by being torn apart upon it. ﴿And from it We bring you forth again﴾ by resurrection, ﴿another time﴾, once more: He gathers their scattered parts and returns them as they were, living. His saying ﴿another time﴾ means another bringing-forth, because the meaning of His saying ﴿from it We created you﴾ is "We brought you forth."

﴿And We certainly showed him all Our signs﴾. This is an informing from Allah the Exalted to Muhammad (ﷺ), and this indicates that His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ is indeed an address to him (peace be upon him). ﴿We showed him Our signs﴾: the ones meant are those taken from the visual sense of seeing (ra'a al-basariyya), and for this reason it takes two objects by the transitivity-causing hamza. ﴿Our signs﴾ is not general, since He did not show him all the signs; rather the meaning is the signs of Ours that he saw, and so the idafa (construct) conveys what the definite article conveys of familiarity (al-'ahd). He saw the staff, the hand, the blotting out, and other things he saw; the emphasis (p-252) is then in relation to these known signs. It was also said: the meaning is signs in their entirety, and He attributed the signs to Himself as a mark of honour, as if He had said "signs for Us." It was also said: Musa had shown him His signs and enumerated for him what other prophets had been given of their signs and miracles, and he is a truthful prophet, with no difference between what he reports and what he shows. ﴿So he denied and refused﴾ all of them, and ﴿refused﴾ to accept any of them. End. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, and it is remote, because informing about a thing is not called seeing except by a distant figurative usage.

It was also said: ﴿We showed him﴾ here is from seeing of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb), not seeing of the eye, because at that time he had been shown only the staff and the white hand, meaning: ﴿We certainly made him know Our signs, all of them﴾. These are the nine signs. It was said: it is permissible that by the signs He meant the signs of His oneness which He displayed to us in the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and then it would be from seeing of the eye. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ubayy said: it implies the acquisition (kasb) of Pharaoh, and this is what reward and punishment depend upon. The object of ﴿denied﴾ is omitted; the apparent meaning is that it is the signs. It is possible that the intended meaning is: ﴿he denied﴾ Musa and ﴿refused﴾ to accept what he brought him of his message.

It was said: It is also permissible that he meant: he denied that they were signs of Allah, and said: they are sorcery. For this reason he said: ﴿Have you come to us to expel us from our land by your sorcery, O Musa?﴾ This view is weakened by His saying ﴿You know well that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as insights﴾ [Al-Isra: 102], and His saying ﴿and they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [An-Naml: 14]. So it appears that he denied out of his wrongdoing, not that it was confused for him whether they were signs of sorcery. In his saying ﴿Have you come to us to expel us﴾ there is weakness, which is evident from him, and much agitation regarding what Musa brought, since he knew that he was upon the truth and that he would inevitably overcome him in his kingdom. He mentioned the cause of the coming, which is the expulsion of them, and he cast this into the ears of his people so that they would become intensely hostile towards him, since expulsion from one's homeland is among the things that are very hard. Allah made it equal to killing in His saying ﴿Kill yourselves or leave your homes﴾ [An-Nisa: 66]. His saying ﴿by your sorcery﴾ is an excuse and bewilderment, because it is not hidden from him that a sorcerer cannot expel a king like himself from his land and overcome him in his kingdom by sorcery. He presented this as a doubt casting aspersion on prophethood, and that a miracle is distinguished from sorcery only by the miracle being something whose opposition is impossible. Therefore he said: ﴿So we will surely bring you sorcery like it﴾. This indicates that Musa's affair (peace be upon him) had grown strong, and his protection among the Children of Israel had increased, and his matter had come to be in the hearts of the people, since this is the speech of one who needs proof, not of one who proclaims his own affair. Their land is the land of Egypt. He addressed him with ﴿your sorcery﴾ because the conversation was with him, and the staff and the hand had appeared from his direction. ﴿So we will surely bring you﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, which gave people the impression that what Musa brought was of the kind of sorcery, and that with him there was someone who could match him in that. So he sought to set an appointment for a contest in sorcery. The apparent meaning is that ﴿an appointment﴾ here is a time: that is, appoint for us a time of gathering. For this reason he answered with His saying ﴿He said: Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. The meaning of ﴿we will not fail it﴾ is that we will not break that time in gathering there. Some took it to be a known place, and its source is His saying ﴿your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾.

Al-Qushayri said: The more apparent view is that it is a verbal noun, and for this reason he said ﴿we will not fail it﴾, that is, that appointment; and failing (al-ikhlaf) is to promise something and not fulfil it. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you take it to be a time, in view of His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾, which corresponds to it, then two things would be necessary for you: that you make the time the thing that is failed, and that the governing verb (nasib) of ﴿a place﴾ would be obstructed for you. And if you take it as a place corresponding to His saying ﴿a place equal﴾, it would also be necessary for you that the failing falls upon the place, and that it not correspond to His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. The reading of al-Hasan does not correspond to it at all in place, because he read ﴿the Day of Adornment﴾ in the accusative, so it remains that it be taken as a verbal noun meaning a promise, and that an omitted genitive construction be assumed, that is, "the place of an appointment," and that the pronoun in ﴿we will not fail it﴾ and ﴿a place﴾ be taken as a substitute (badal) for the omitted place. If you say: How do you make it correspond to His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾, when you must take it as a time, and the question is about a place, not a time? I say: It corresponds in meaning even if it does not correspond in wording, because they must gather on the Day of Adornment in a particular place known for their gathering in it on that day, so by mentioning the time the place is known.

As for the reading of al-Hasan, the appointment in it is only a verbal noun, and the meaning is the fulfilment of your promise on the Day of Adornment, and this also corresponds (p-253) in terms of meaning. It is also permissible that an omitted genitive construction be assumed, and the meaning would be: make between us and between you a promise which we will not fail. If you say: On what is ﴿a place﴾ in the accusative? I say: On the verbal noun, or on a verb indicated by the verbal noun. If you say: How does the answer correspond to it? I say: As for the reading of al-Hasan, it is clear; as for the reading of the majority, it is according to the assumption "your promise is the promise of the Day of Adornment."

It is permissible, according to the reading of al-Hasan, that ﴿your appointment﴾ be the subject (mubtada') with the meaning of a time, and ﴿in the forenoon﴾ (duha) be its predicate, with the intention of definiteness in it, since it had been described before the action by His saying ﴿we will not fail it﴾, and it is a relative clause, and the verbal noun, when it is described before it acts, may not act in their view. And the saying "and (duha) is its predicate with the intention of definiteness in it" is because it is the forenoon of that very day. Although it is the forenoon of that very day, it is not with the intention of definiteness; rather it is indefinite, even if it is from a particular day, because it is not replaced from the definite article (alif-lam) as in sihr (sorcery), nor is it defined by annexation. If you say: "I came on Friday at dawn (bukran)," we do not claim that bukran is definite, even though we know that it is from a particular day.

Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read ﴿لا نُخْلِفْهُ﴾ (*lā nukhlifhu*, "we shall not fail it") with the *fa'* in jussive (*jazm*, the mood marking that ends a verb with a sukun), taking it as the answer to the imperative. The majority (*al-jumhūr*) read it with *raf'* (nominative), as a qualifier (*ṣifah*) of *mawʿidan* (a promise/appointment).

Al-Ḥawfī said: ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ (*mawʿidan*) is the object of ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾ (*ijʿal*, "appoint"), and ﴿مَكانًا﴾ (*makānan*, "a place") is an adverbial of place (*ẓarf*), whose governing element is ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾. Abu ʿAli said: ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ is the first object of ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾ and ﴿مَكانًا﴾ is the second object. He prohibited ﴿مَكانًا﴾ from being governed by ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ because the latter has already been qualified.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: These nouns that function as verbs (*al-asmāʾ al-ʿāmilah ʿamal al-fiʿl*), when they are qualified, or when something is conjoined to them, or when they are predicated about, or diminutivized, or pluralized, and become fully nominal in this way, do not govern, and nothing that belongs to them may be attached to them. The adverbs (*ẓurūf*) may be treated more loosely, so something may be attached to them after what we have mentioned, as in the words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿يُنادَوْنَ لَمَقْتُ اللَّهِ أكْبَرُ مِن مَقْتِكم أنْفُسَكم إذْ تُدْعَوْنَ إلى الإيمانِ﴾ [Ghafir: 10] ("They will be called: Surely God's hatred is greater than your hatred of yourselves, when you were called to faith"). Here ﴿إذْ﴾ (*idh*, "when") is attached to ﴿لَمَقْتُ﴾ (*lamaqtu*, "hatred"), and he has been predicated about. This is permitted only with adverbs. A group prohibited ﴿مَكانًا﴾ from being in the accusative as the second object of ﴿لُنُخْلِفُهُ﴾, but a group of grammarians permitted it, its rationale being that it is an extension (*ittisāʿ*) in the sense of "to fail the promise." End of quote.

His phrase "when they are qualified" is not agreed upon for every element that functions as a verb. Consider the active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*) without *al-*: if it is qualified before it governs, there is disagreement. The Basrans prohibit it, the Kufans permit it. Likewise, if it is diminutivized, there is disagreement over its governing. As for pluralization, there is no known disagreement about its governing. As for the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) when pluralized, there is disagreement about whether it may govern. As for his exception of the adverbs from the governed elements, others hold that this is prohibited absolutely for the verbal noun, and that ﴿إذْ﴾ governs a verb implied by what precedes it, meaning: "their hatred of you when you are called."

﴿ولا أنْتَ﴾ (*wa-lā anta*, "nor you") is conjoined to the implicit pronoun in ﴿نُخْلِفُهُ﴾, which is emphasized by the word "we" (*naḥnu*).

Ibn ʿAmir, Ḥamzah, ʿAsim, Yaʿqub, al-Ḥasan, Qatadah, Ṭalḥah, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Abi Laylā, Abu Ḥatim and Ibn Jarir read ﴿سُوًى﴾ (*suwan*) with *ḍammah* on the *sīn*, with tanwin in connected speech. The rest of the seven read it with *kasrah* on the *sīn*, with tanwin in connected speech. Al-Ḥasan also read ﴿سُوى﴾ with *ḍammah* on the *sīn* without tanwin in both states, treating connected speech as pause (*ajrā al-waṣl majrā al-waqf*), not because it is prevented from taking tanwin (*ṣarf*), since a *fiʿl* form among the adjectives is inflected, like *ḥaṭum* and *labad*. ʿIsa read *siwā* with *kasrah* on the *sīn*, without tanwin in both states, also treating connected speech as pause.

The meaning of ﴿سُوًى﴾ is "just and equitable." Abu ʿAli said: It is as though he said, "His nearness to you is his nearness to us." Others said: He meant that our position in it is equal, so that this encompasses the Qur'an, and that ranks in it are one in the pursuit of truth, so that leadership (*riʾāsah*) does not obstruct you in it, and only proof is intended. From Mujahid: it derives from *istiwāʾ* (equality), because the distance from the middle to the two extremes is equal, without disparity. This is the meaning of what preceded from Abu ʿAli's words: "His nearness to you is his nearness to us."

Al-Akhfash said: ﴿سُوًى﴾ is *maqṣūr* (short-vowelled, without the final alif extended) if you read its *sīn* with *kasrah* or *ḍammah*, and *mamdūd* (extended) if you read it with *fatḥah*. There are three dialects, and in all of them it carries the meaning of ﴿غَيْرِ﴾ (*ghayr*, "other than") [Ṭaha: 22] and the meaning of "just," and "middle between the two parties." The poet said:

*And indeed our father was a settler among his people, equitable between the Qays of Ghaylan and the Fizr.*

He said: You say "I passed by a man *siwāka*, *suwāka*, *sawāka*," meaning "other than you," and it applies to all. The highest of these dialects is the *kasrah*, as al-Naḥḥas said.

A group said: The meaning of ﴿مَكانًا سُوًى﴾ (*makānan suwan*, "a place level") is a level place from the earth, that is, without rough ground, without mountain, without hill, and without a depression in the earth, such that the gaze of anyone would not be obstructed, so that they would not see the place of Musa and the magicians and what issues from them. He said this confident of the magicians' victory over Musa; then when they witnessed his victory over them, they would return from what they had believed in.

A group said: Its meaning is "a place other than this place of ours." This is not right, because ﴿سِوًى﴾ when it means ﴿غَيْرِ﴾ is used only in construct form (*muḍāfah*) in wording and is not separated from the construct.

Al-Ḥasan, al-Aʿmash, ʿAsim in one narration, Abu Ḥaywah, Ibn Abi ʿAblah, Qatadah, al-Jaḥdari, Hubayrah and al-Zaʿfarani read ﴿يَوْمَ الزِّينَةِ﴾ (*yawma al-zīnah*, "the day of adornment") with *fatḥah* on the *mīm*. The derivation of this reading has been mentioned in al-Zamakhshari's words. It is narrated that ﴿يَوْمَ الزِّينَةِ﴾ was a festival (*ʿīd*) for them and a day of gathering (*yawman mashhūdan*), and it coincided with ʿAshura, and it was a Saturday. It is said: It is the day of the breaking of the canal that remains until today. It is said: It is the day of Nowruz, which was the beginning of their year. It is said: It is Saturday, for it is a day of rest and ease. It is said: It is a market day for them. It is said: It is ʿAshura.

Ibn Masʿud, al-Jaḥdari, Abu ʿImran al-Jawni, Abu Nahik, and ʿAmr ibn Fa'id read ﴿وأنْ تُحْشَرَ﴾ (*wa-an tuḥsar*, "and that they be gathered") with the second-person *tā'* (addressing), meaning "O Pharaoh." It is narrated from them also with *yā'* in the third person. ﴿النّاسُ﴾ (*al-nās*, "the people") is in the accusative in both readings.

The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: "And that the gatherer gathers the people in the forenoon," so the subject is omitted because it is known. This omission of the subject in such a construction is not permitted according to the Basrans. Others said: ﴿وأنْ يُحْشَرَ﴾ refers to the people. He said: It is also permitted that the pronoun of Pharaoh be in it, mentioned with third-person wording, either according to the custom by which kings are addressed, or because he addressed the people with ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ﴾ (*mawʿiduku-m*, "your appointment"), and made ﴿يُحْشَرَ﴾ refer to Pharaoh. It is also permitted that ﴿وأنْ يُحْشَرَ﴾ be in the nominative position as conjoined to ﴿يَوْمُ الزِّينَةِ﴾, or in the genitive position as conjoined to ﴿الزِّينَةِ﴾.

﴿ضُحًى﴾ (*ḍuḥan*, "in the forenoon") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarf*), and it is the rising of the day. It may be feminine or masculine. The *ḍuḥāʾ* with *fatḥah* on the *ḍād* is *mamdūd* (extended) and masculine; it is at the highest rise of the day. Musa appointed this day for them only so that the exaltation of God's word, the manifestation of His religion, the humiliation of the unbeliever, and the destruction of falsehood would occur in full view of the witnesses. In al-Majma' al-Ghāṣṣ: so that the desire of whoever desires to follow the truth may grow, that the edge of the falsifiers and their partisans may be blunted, and that the report of this clear matter may spread in every desert and settlement, and be disseminated among all the dwellers of tents and cities.

The apparent view is that His words ﴿قالَ مَوْعِدُكم يَوْمُ الزِّينَةِ﴾ (*qāla mawʿiduku-m yawmu al-zīnah*, "He said: Your appointment is the day of adornment") are the words of Musa, peace be upon him, because it is a reply to Pharaoh's words ﴿فاجْعَلْ بَيْنَنا وبَيْنَكَ مَوْعِدًا﴾ ("Appoint between us and you an appointment"), and because specifying the day is fitting only for the one who is in the right, whose hand is known to be strong, not for the falsifier who is known to have nothing but deception. Also, His words ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ﴾ are addressed to all. He who held that it is the words of Pharaoh is far from the truth.

(p-250) When Musa had pointed to the proof of the Lord's lordship, and his speech was complete at His saying, ﴿and He does not forget﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52], Allah mentioned what He used to draw attention to His power and His oneness. He informed about Himself that He is the One who made such-and-such. We have taken the view that this is the speech of Allah, due to His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ (p-251) and His saying ﴿eat and graze your livestock﴾ and His saying ﴿We certainly showed him﴾. So His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ and ﴿We showed him﴾ is an iltifat (a shift of grammatical person, here from the third-person pronoun in ja'ala and salaka to the first-person plural pronoun of one who magnifies himself). An iltifat does not occur from speakers who are different. Even more remote is the view of those who said that alladhi is an adjective (na't) of the word (Rabbi), so that it would be in the nominative position, or in the accusative position as praise (madh). Al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari said both of these, because then the speech would be Musa's, and the iltifat in His saying (so We brought forth) and ﴿We showed him﴾ would not be possible.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that (so We brought forth) is part of Musa's speech, relating from Allah the Exalted, with the implied phrase "He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: so We brought forth." It is also possible that Musa's speech was complete at His saying ﴿and sent down from the sky water﴾, and then Allah joined Musa's speech with His informing Muhammad (ﷺ). The address in ﴿for you﴾ is intended for all of creation, drawing their attention to these signs.

Al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿mahdan﴾ with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the ha'. The rest of the seven read mihadan, and likewise in al-Zukhruf. Al-Mufaddal said: they are two verbal nouns (masdar), mahda mahdan and mihadan. Abu 'Ubayd said: mihad is a noun (ism), and mahd is the verb, meaning the verbal noun. Another said: mahd is singular and mihad is its plural. The meaning of this is that He made it for them, so that they can move about upon it in all their conditions and benefits, and He laid out for you roads within it for your purposes, so that your interests are not hindered. The pronoun in ﴿by it﴾ refers to the water, that is, by its means.

﴿pairs﴾, that is, kinds. This iltifat in (akhrajna) is like it in His saying ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sent down water from the sky, so We brought forth﴾ [Fatir: 27], ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow﴾ [An-Naml: 60], and ﴿And it is He who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth by it the vegetation of every thing﴾ [Al-An'am: 99]. In this iltifat there is also a specification that We alone have the power to do the like of this, and it does not fall under the power of anyone. The better view is that ﴿diverse﴾ (shatta) is in the accusative position as an adjective (na't) of ﴿pairs﴾, because it is that which is being spoken of.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that it is an adjective of the vegetation (nabat). Nabat is a verbal noun used as the name of that which grows, just as it is called nabt, so the singular and plural are alike in it. He means that they are ﴿diverse﴾, differing in benefit, taste, colour, scent and form; some are suitable for people and some for animals.

They said: From His blessing, the Mighty and Majestic, is that the sustenance of the servants is obtained only through the work of livestock, and Allah has made their fodder from what exceeds their needs and what they cannot eat. ﴿Eat and graze your livestock﴾ is a command of permission (amr ibaha) governed by an omitted circumstantial state (hal), meaning: ﴿so We brought forth﴾ speaking [to you], that is, permitting you to benefit from them, allowing you to eat some of them and feed some of them. Here ﴿and graze﴾ is transitive. Ra'a (to graze) can be intransitive and transitive; you say: the animal grazed (ra'at al-dabbatu ra'yan), and its owner pastured it (ra'aha sahibuha ri'ayatan), when he drove it out, sent it out to pasture and let it rest. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

By His saying ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, He pointed to the preceding signs: the making of the earth as a cradle, the laying of its roads, the sending down of water, and the bringing forth of vegetation. They said: ﴿al-nuha﴾ is the plural of nuha, which is intellect, named so because it restrains (yanha) from ugly deeds. Abu 'Ali permitted that it be a verbal noun, like al-huda (guidance). The pronoun in ﴿from it﴾ refers to the earth, and He meant the creation of their origin, Adam. It was also said: an angel goes to the soil of the place where the one to be created will be buried, and scatters it over the sperm-drop, so that he is created from both dust and sperm-drop together. This was said by 'Ata al-Khurasani. It was also said: it refers to the foods that grow out of the earth, from which the humours are generated from which man is formed; this is then a metaphor of a metaphor. ﴿And into it We return you﴾, that is, by burial in it or by being torn apart upon it. ﴿And from it We bring you forth again﴾ by resurrection, ﴿another time﴾, once more: He gathers their scattered parts and returns them as they were, living. His saying ﴿another time﴾ means another bringing-forth, because the meaning of His saying ﴿from it We created you﴾ is "We brought you forth."

﴿And We certainly showed him all Our signs﴾. This is an informing from Allah the Exalted to Muhammad (ﷺ), and this indicates that His saying ﴿so We brought forth﴾ is indeed an address to him (peace be upon him). ﴿We showed him Our signs﴾: the ones meant are those taken from the visual sense of seeing (ra'a al-basariyya), and for this reason it takes two objects by the transitivity-causing hamza. ﴿Our signs﴾ is not general, since He did not show him all the signs; rather the meaning is the signs of Ours that he saw, and so the idafa (construct) conveys what the definite article conveys of familiarity (al-'ahd). He saw the staff, the hand, the blotting out, and other things he saw; the emphasis (p-252) is then in relation to these known signs. It was also said: the meaning is signs in their entirety, and He attributed the signs to Himself as a mark of honour, as if He had said "signs for Us." It was also said: Musa had shown him His signs and enumerated for him what other prophets had been given of their signs and miracles, and he is a truthful prophet, with no difference between what he reports and what he shows. ﴿So he denied and refused﴾ all of them, and ﴿refused﴾ to accept any of them. End. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, and it is remote, because informing about a thing is not called seeing except by a distant figurative usage.

It was also said: ﴿We showed him﴾ here is from seeing of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb), not seeing of the eye, because at that time he had been shown only the staff and the white hand, meaning: ﴿We certainly made him know Our signs, all of them﴾. These are the nine signs. It was said: it is permissible that by the signs He meant the signs of His oneness which He displayed to us in the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and then it would be from seeing of the eye. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ubayy said: it implies the acquisition (kasb) of Pharaoh, and this is what reward and punishment depend upon. The object of ﴿denied﴾ is omitted; the apparent meaning is that it is the signs. It is possible that the intended meaning is: ﴿he denied﴾ Musa and ﴿refused﴾ to accept what he brought him of his message.

It was said: It is also permissible that he meant: he denied that they were signs of Allah, and said: they are sorcery. For this reason he said: ﴿Have you come to us to expel us from our land by your sorcery, O Musa?﴾ This view is weakened by His saying ﴿You know well that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as insights﴾ [Al-Isra: 102], and His saying ﴿and they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [An-Naml: 14]. So it appears that he denied out of his wrongdoing, not that it was confused for him whether they were signs of sorcery. In his saying ﴿Have you come to us to expel us﴾ there is weakness, which is evident from him, and much agitation regarding what Musa brought, since he knew that he was upon the truth and that he would inevitably overcome him in his kingdom. He mentioned the cause of the coming, which is the expulsion of them, and he cast this into the ears of his people so that they would become intensely hostile towards him, since expulsion from one's homeland is among the things that are very hard. Allah made it equal to killing in His saying ﴿Kill yourselves or leave your homes﴾ [An-Nisa: 66]. His saying ﴿by your sorcery﴾ is an excuse and bewilderment, because it is not hidden from him that a sorcerer cannot expel a king like himself from his land and overcome him in his kingdom by sorcery. He presented this as a doubt casting aspersion on prophethood, and that a miracle is distinguished from sorcery only by the miracle being something whose opposition is impossible. Therefore he said: ﴿So we will surely bring you sorcery like it﴾. This indicates that Musa's affair (peace be upon him) had grown strong, and his protection among the Children of Israel had increased, and his matter had come to be in the hearts of the people, since this is the speech of one who needs proof, not of one who proclaims his own affair. Their land is the land of Egypt. He addressed him with ﴿your sorcery﴾ because the conversation was with him, and the staff and the hand had appeared from his direction. ﴿So we will surely bring you﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, which gave people the impression that what Musa brought was of the kind of sorcery, and that with him there was someone who could match him in that. So he sought to set an appointment for a contest in sorcery. The apparent meaning is that ﴿an appointment﴾ here is a time: that is, appoint for us a time of gathering. For this reason he answered with His saying ﴿He said: Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. The meaning of ﴿we will not fail it﴾ is that we will not break that time in gathering there. Some took it to be a known place, and its source is His saying ﴿your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾.

Al-Qushayri said: The more apparent view is that it is a verbal noun, and for this reason he said ﴿we will not fail it﴾, that is, that appointment; and failing (al-ikhlaf) is to promise something and not fulfil it. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you take it to be a time, in view of His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾, which corresponds to it, then two things would be necessary for you: that you make the time the thing that is failed, and that the governing verb (nasib) of ﴿a place﴾ would be obstructed for you. And if you take it as a place corresponding to His saying ﴿a place equal﴾, it would also be necessary for you that the failing falls upon the place, and that it not correspond to His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. The reading of al-Hasan does not correspond to it at all in place, because he read ﴿the Day of Adornment﴾ in the accusative, so it remains that it be taken as a verbal noun meaning a promise, and that an omitted genitive construction be assumed, that is, "the place of an appointment," and that the pronoun in ﴿we will not fail it﴾ and ﴿a place﴾ be taken as a substitute (badal) for the omitted place. If you say: How do you make it correspond to His saying ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾, when you must take it as a time, and the question is about a place, not a time? I say: It corresponds in meaning even if it does not correspond in wording, because they must gather on the Day of Adornment in a particular place known for their gathering in it on that day, so by mentioning the time the place is known.

As for the reading of al-Hasan, the appointment in it is only a verbal noun, and the meaning is the fulfilment of your promise on the Day of Adornment, and this also corresponds (p-253) in terms of meaning. It is also permissible that an omitted genitive construction be assumed, and the meaning would be: make between us and between you a promise which we will not fail. If you say: On what is ﴿a place﴾ in the accusative? I say: On the verbal noun, or on a verb indicated by the verbal noun. If you say: How does the answer correspond to it? I say: As for the reading of al-Hasan, it is clear; as for the reading of the majority, it is according to the assumption "your promise is the promise of the Day of Adornment."

It is permissible, according to the reading of al-Hasan, that ﴿your appointment﴾ be the subject (mubtada') with the meaning of a time, and ﴿in the forenoon﴾ (duha) be its predicate, with the intention of definiteness in it, since it had been described before the action by His saying ﴿we will not fail it﴾, and it is a relative clause, and the verbal noun, when it is described before it acts, may not act in their view. And the saying "and (duha) is its predicate with the intention of definiteness in it" is because it is the forenoon of that very day. Although it is the forenoon of that very day, it is not with the intention of definiteness; rather it is indefinite, even if it is from a particular day, because it is not replaced from the definite article (alif-lam) as in sihr (sorcery), nor is it defined by annexation. If you say: "I came on Friday at dawn (bukran)," we do not claim that bukran is definite, even though we know that it is from a particular day.

Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read ﴿لا نُخْلِفْهُ﴾ (*lā nukhlifhu*, "we shall not fail it") with the *fa'* in jussive (*jazm*, the mood marking that ends a verb with a sukun), taking it as the answer to the imperative. The majority (*al-jumhūr*) read it with *raf'* (nominative), as a qualifier (*ṣifah*) of *mawʿidan* (a promise/appointment).

Al-Ḥawfī said: ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ (*mawʿidan*) is the object of ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾ (*ijʿal*, "appoint"), and ﴿مَكانًا﴾ (*makānan*, "a place") is an adverbial of place (*ẓarf*), whose governing element is ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾. Abu ʿAli said: ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ is the first object of ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾ and ﴿مَكانًا﴾ is the second object. He prohibited ﴿مَكانًا﴾ from being governed by ﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ because the latter has already been qualified.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: These nouns that function as verbs (*al-asmāʾ al-ʿāmilah ʿamal al-fiʿl*), when they are qualified, or when something is conjoined to them, or when they are predicated about, or diminutivized, or pluralized, and become fully nominal in this way, do not govern, and nothing that belongs to them may be attached to them.
