Musa was also delayed for the sake of the fawasil, as in His saying ﴿لَكَانَ لِزَامًا وَأَجَلٌ مُسَمًّى﴾ ([Ta-Ha: 129]), and ﴿أَزْوَاجًا مِنْ نَبَاتٍ﴾ ([Ta-Ha: 53]), where shatta is an attribute of the word azwajan ([Ta-Ha: 53]). There is no difference between "Zayd and Amr stood" and "Amr and Zayd stood," since the particle waw does not require an order. Moreover, it is possible that the two statements came from two speakers: one group uttered their saying, "Lord of Musa and Harun," and another group uttered, "Lord of Harun and Musa." Since they shared in the meaning, it is valid to attribute each of the two statements to all of them. It was also said that Harun was mentioned first here because he was older than Musa. And it was said: because Pharaoh had raised Musa, so they began with Harun, so that Pharaoh's deception that he had raised Musa would be removed, for he would say, "I raised him." They said, "Lord of Harun and Musa," and did not suffice with their saying "Lord of the worlds," for the explicit statement that they believed in the Lord of these two, whereas previously he had claimed that he was the Lord of the worlds.

The difference in the reading of ﴿آمنتم﴾ (amantum, "you believed") has already been discussed, as well as ﴿لَأُقَطِّعَنَّ﴾ (la-uqatti'anna, "I will surely cut off") and ﴿ثُمَّ لَأُصَلِّبَنَّكُمْ﴾ (thumma la-usallibannakum, "then I will surely crucify you") in al-A'raf ([al-A'raf: 124]), and the explanation of the parallel of this verse appears there. There it is ﴿آمنتم له﴾ (amantum lahu, "you believed in him"), and here it is "lahu" as well. Amana takes the preposition bi when it refers to God, and li for others in most cases, as in ﴿فَمَا آمَنَ لِمُوسَى﴾ ([Yunus: 83]), ﴿لَنْ نُؤْمِنَ لَكَ﴾ ([al-Baqarah: 55]), ﴿وَمَا أَنْتَ بِمُؤْمِنٍ لَنَا﴾ ([Yusuf: 17]), and ﴿فَآمَنَ لَهُ لُوطٌ﴾ ([al-Ankabut: 26]). The pronoun in "bihi" may refer to Musa, or it may refer to the Lord. By cutting off and crucifying on the trunks, he intended to make an example of them. Since the trunk is a place of rest for the one crucified and encloses him in the manner of a container enclosing its contents, the verb was given the object by means of fi, which indicates a container. It was also said that fi here means ʿala ("upon"). And it was said: Pharaoh gouged out the wood and crucified them inside it, so it became a true container for them, so that they would die inside it of hunger and thirst. Among the instances of sallaba being followed by fi is the poet's verse:

They crucified al-ʿAbdi in the trunk of a palm tree,
So Shaybān never sneezed except with a severed nose.

Pharaoh was the first to crucify, and Pharaoh swore to this, which is his own act and the act of others, namely ﴿وَلَتَعْلَمُنَّ أَيُّنَا﴾ (wa-la-ta'lamunna ayyuna, "and you will surely know which of us"), that is, which of me and whoever you believed in. It was also said: "which of me and of Musa," and he said this in mockery, because Musa was not one of those to be punished. Al-Zamakhshari went to this view, saying: "The evidence is His saying: ﴿آمنتم له﴾, and the lam with belief in the Book of God is for other than God, as in His saying ﴿يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وَيُؤْمِنُ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ([al-Tawbah: 61])." In it there is a display of his power and dominance, and of what he was accustomed to and used to, namely the torture of people with various kinds of punishment, and a belittling of Musa, peace be upon him, with weakening and mockery of him. End of quotation. This is also the view of al-Tabari, who said: "He means himself and Musa, peace be upon him." The first view is more suitable to Pharaoh's bragging. ﴿وَلَتَعْلَمُنَّ﴾ here is mu'allaq (suspended), and ﴿أَيُّنَا أَشَدُّ﴾ (ayyuna ashaddu, "which of us is more severe") is an interrogative clause consisting of a subject and predicate, in a position of accusative for His saying ﴿وَلَتَعْلَمُنَّ﴾, serving in place of the two objects, or in the position of a single object if ﴿وَلَتَعْلَمُنَّ﴾ is transitive in the manner of ʿarafa. It is also permissible, according to the view of Sibawayh, that ﴿أيُّنا﴾ be the object of ﴿وَلَتَعْلَمُنَّ﴾, with ashaddu being the predicate of an omitted subject, and ayyuna being a relative pronoun whose clause follows it, the implied sense being: "and you will surely know who is ﴿more severe in punishment and more lasting﴾."

﴿So Pharaoh turned away﴾, meaning either that he turned away from accepting the truth, or that he took charge of the matter himself, or that he went back to his household to prepare his schemes, or that he withdrew in the manner of those who have made an appointment, each of whom turns his back on the other when they part. These are the opinions. ﴿Then he gathered his scheming﴾, meaning the people of his scheming, who were the magicians. They were a band whom God had not created to be more skilled in magic. ﴿Then he came﴾ to the appointed time that they had agreed upon. Moses also came with those among the Children of Israel who were with him. Moses said to them, ﴿Woe to you! Do not invent a lie against God, lest He destroy you with a punishment; and whoever invents has failed﴾. The explanation of "woe" (wayl) was given earlier in Surat al-Baqarah. He addressed them with the address of one who warns, and urged them to speak the truth when they saw it, and not to confront them with falsehood. It is reported from Wahb that when he said to the magicians, "Woe to you," they said, "This is not the speech of a magician."

﴿Lest He destroy you﴾ means lest He ruin you and root you out. In this there is an indication of the gravity of fabrication, and that it results in the ruin of total destruction. Then he mentioned that the one who fabricates will not attain his aim, and his pursuit will not succeed: ﴿whoever has invented﴾ a lie against God.

When the magicians heard this statement from him, it alarmed them and the awe of him settled in their souls. ﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves﴾, meaning they pulled at it in different directions, and disputing implies disagreement.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, al-A'mash, Talhah and Ibn Jarir recited ﴿yusihtakum﴾ with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the ḥā', from the quadriliteral form asḥata. The rest of the seven readers, Ruways, and Ibn 'Abbas recited it with a fatḥa on both, from the triliteral saḥata.

Their secret conferring was out of fear of Pharaoh, lest he discern weakness in them, because they were not resolved to overcome Moses; rather it was a supposition on the part of some of them. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that their secret conferring was: "If Moses overcomes us, we will follow him." It is reported from Qatadah: "If he is a magician, we will overcome him; and if he is from heaven, then he has a command."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The apparent meaning is that they consulted in secret and pulled at the edges of speech among themselves, and then ﴿they said, 'Indeed these two are magicians'﴾. Their secret conferring was in fabricating this speech and falsifying it, out of fear of being overcome by the two of them, and to discourage the people from following them." End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyyah related something close to this view from a group, who said: "Their private conferring was only with the verse that follows, ﴿Indeed these two are magicians﴾." But the more evident view is that that was said openly, and if their conferring had been that, there would have been no disputing among them.

Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, Shaybah, al-A'mash, Talhah, Humayd, Ayyub, Khalaf in his choice, Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Hatim, Ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, the two brothers (al-Akhawan) and the two companions (al-Sahibani) among the seven recited ﴿inna﴾ with a doubled nūn, ﴿hadhani﴾ with an alif and a light nūn, and ﴿la-sahiran﴾.

The early grammarians disagreed about the explanation of this reading. They said that it stands for an elided pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and the sense is "indeed it is: these two are magicians." The predicate of inna is the sentence "these two are magicians," and the lām in ﴿la-sahiran﴾ enters upon the predicate of the subject (khabar al-mubtada', the predicate of the nominal sentence). This view was criticized on the grounds that omitting this pronoun occurs only in poetry, and that the entry of the lām upon the predicate is anomalous.

Al-Zajjaj said: the lām did not enter upon the predicate; rather the sense is "for them both are magicians," so the lām entered upon the elided subject. His teacher Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad and the judge Isma'il ibn Ishaq ibn Hammad ibn Zayd approved this view. It was also said that ha is a pronoun of the story and is not elided, and on this view it would have been appropriate for it to be written joined in the script, so it would have been written ﴿inh-dhani la-sahiran﴾. This was criticized because it contradicts the orthography of the Mushaf.

It was also said that inna means "yes," and this is attested in the language; so the verse is read accordingly, and ﴿hadhani la-sahiran﴾ is a subject and predicate, and the lām in ﴿la-sahiran﴾ under these two estimations in this explanation follows the former explanation. To this view went al-Mubarrad, Isma'il ibn Ishaq, and Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash the Younger. What we prefer in explaining this reading is that it comes in the dialect of some Arabs who always write the dual with an alif. This is the dialect of Kinanah, reported by Abu al-Khattab, and of Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, Khath'am, Zubayd and the people of that region, reported from al-Kisa'i, and of Banu al-'Anbar, Banu al-Hujaym, Murad and 'Udhrah. Abu Zayd said: "I heard from the Arabs one who changes every yā' whose preceding letter is open into an alif."

Abu Bahriyyah, Abu Haywah, al-Zuhri, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, Ibn Sa'dan, Hafs and Ibn Kathir recited ﴿in﴾ with a light nūn, ﴿hadha﴾ with an alif, and Ibn Kathir doubled the nūn of ﴿hadhani﴾. The explanation of this reading is clear: ﴿in﴾ is the light form of the heavy one, ﴿hadhani﴾ is the subject, and ﴿la-sahiran﴾ is the predicate, and the lām serves to distinguish the negative in from the light form of the heavy in, according to the view of the Basrans, while the Kufans maintain that in is negative and the lām means "except."

A group recited ﴿in dhani la-sahiran﴾, and its explanation is like that of the reading preceding it. ʿĀ'ishah, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, al-Jahdari, al-A'mash, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn 'Ubayd and Abu 'Amr recited ﴿inna hadhayni﴾ with a doubled nūn in inna and with a yā' in hadhayni instead of the alif. The grammar of this is clear, since it follows the familiar pattern of the dual, as in His saying ﴿So these are two proofs﴾ [al-Qasas: 32] and ﴿one of my two daughters, these two﴾ [al-Qasas: 27], with the alif in the nominative and the yā' in the accusative and genitive. Al-Zajjaj said: "I do not permit the reading of Abu 'Amr, because it contradicts the Mushaf." Abu 'Ubayd said: "I saw it in the imam copy, the Mushaf of 'Uthman, written hadhani without an alif, and so I saw the nominative of the dual in that Mushaf written without the alif. When they wrote the accusative and genitive, they wrote it with a yā' and did not drop it." A group, including 'Ā'ishah and Abu 'Amr, said: "This is something in which the scribe made a mistake, and it was corrected to the correct form."

ʿAbd Allah recited ﴿in dhani illa sahiran﴾; this was reported by Ibn Khalawayh, and al-Zamakhshari attributed it to Ubayy. Ibn Mas'ud said: "anna hadhani sahiran," with a fatḥa on anna and without a lām, as an apposition (badal) of ﴿al-najwa﴾ [the secret conferring]. End of quotation. Some recited ﴿ma hadha illa sahiran﴾.

Their saying ﴿they want to drive you out of your land by their magic﴾ followed the saying of Pharaoh: ﴿Have you come to us to drive us out of our land by your magic?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 57]. They also attributed magic to Aaron, since he was a partner with him in the prophethood and followed his way. They attached the judgment to intention, though they had no knowledge of it, as a belittling of them both and a lowering of their status. Yet from the matter of the hand and the staff there had appeared to them what indicated the truth of the two of them, and they knew that no magician has the power to produce the like of that. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿they said﴾ refers to the magicians, who addressed one another. It was also said that they addressed Pharaoh with the address of honour. ﴿Al-muthla﴾ [the best] is the feminine of al-amthal, meaning the most excellent and finest. It was also said that the way (ṭarīqah) is an expression for the conduct, the realm and the state in which they stood, and that by it are meant the people of intellect, age and wisdom. They related that the Arabs say, "So-and-so is the way of his people," meaning their chief. Something similar is reported from 'Ali, who said: "and the dispositions of the notables of the people are turned towards them both." It was also said that there is an elided word, meaning: ﴿and they would go with the people of your way﴾, and these are the Children of Israel, in accordance with Moses' saying ﴿Send with us the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 17]. They exaggerated in alienating people from the two by ascribing them to magic, and by nature one is repelled by magic and by the sight of the magician; then by the intention to drive them out of their land; then by changing their condition from the offices and ranks that are desired.

God related of them, regarding their following of Pharaoh, in His saying ﴿So he gathered his scheming﴾, their saying ﴿So gather your scheming﴾. It was also said that this is from Pharaoh's speech, but the apparent meaning is that it is from the magicians' speech, some to others. The majority recited ﴿fa-ajmi'u﴾ with a hamzah at the beginning and a kasra on the mīm, from the quadriliteral ajma'a, meaning: resolve, and make it a matter agreed upon, so that you do not disagree and none of you holds back, like an agreed question. Al-Zuhri, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub in one transmission, and Abu Hatim recited with the hamzah elided and a fatḥa on the mīm, in agreement with His saying ﴿Then Pharaoh turned away and gathered his scheming﴾. The discussion of jama'a and ajma'a was given earlier in Surat Yunus in the story of Noah, peace be upon him.

They summoned one another to come ﴿in a row (ṣaffan)﴾, because it is more awe-inspiring in the eyes of the onlookers, and more evident in deception. ﴿Ṣaffan﴾ is in the accusative either as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning arranged in rows, or as an object, since it is the place where they gather for their festival and their prayers. Shibl ibn 'Abbad and Ibn Kathir, in Shibl's transmission from him, recited ﴿thumma i'tū﴾ with a kasra on the mīm and the hamzah changed to a yā' for ease. Abu 'Ali said: "This is an error, and there is no justification for a kasra on the mīm of thumma." Sahib al-Lawami' said: "That is because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, just as the fatḥa is in the common reading, like this: ﴿and he has indeed succeeded today﴾." That is: whoever sought exaltation in his affair and strove in his striving has triumphed and prevailed, attaining his aim. They differed greatly about the number of magicians. The least that was said is that they were seventy-two magicians, each with a staff and ropes, and the most that was said is nine hundred thousand.

(p-257) ﴿They said, "O Moses, either you throw first, or we will be the first to throw"﴾. ﴿He said, "Rather, you throw." And behold, their ropes and staffs appeared to him, through their magic, as though they were moving﴾. ﴿So Moses felt a fear within himself﴾. ﴿We said, "Do not fear; indeed you are the superior"﴾. ﴿And throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow what they have made. What they have made is only the scheming of a magician, and the magician does not succeed wherever he comes﴾ [Ta-Ha: 65–69]. ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate, saying, "We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses"﴾. ﴿He said, "Have you believed in Him before I gave you permission? Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic. So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees, and you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting"﴾. ﴿They said, "We will never prefer you over what has come to us of clear proofs and over Him who created us. So decide what you will decide. You only decide regarding this worldly life"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 72]. ﴿Indeed, we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins and the magic you compelled us to do. And God is better and more lasting﴾ [Ta-Ha: 73]. ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live﴾ [Ta-Ha: 74]. ﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds, those will have the high ranks﴾ [Ta-Ha: 75]. ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever; and that is the reward of him who purifies himself﴾ [Ta-Ha: 76].

In the speech there is an omission, whose estimate is: so they came in rows to the place of the appointment, each of them having in his hand a staff and a rope. Moses came with his brother, and with him his staff, and they stood, and ﴿they said, "O Moses, either you throw"﴾, and they mentioned the throwing because they knew that Moses' sign was the throwing of the staff. It was said: they gave him the choice out of confidence on their part in victory over Moses, and they believed that no one could withstand them in magic. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This choice on their part is the use of good manners with him, humility towards him, lowering the wing, and an indication that they gave justice from themselves. God, mighty and majestic, had inspired them with this, and taught Moses, peace be upon him, to choose that they throw first, together with what this involves of meeting manners with manners, until they reveal what they have of the schemes of magic and exhaust their utmost methods and effort. When they had done so, God displayed His sovereignty and cast the truth upon falsehood, so it crushed it, and He gave the miracle power over magic, so it annihilated it, and it was a clear sign to the observers and a clear proof to those who take heed." End of quotation. This is embellishment and rhetoric. What follows it is constructed as a verbal noun (maṣdar): either it is in the nominative or in the accusative, and the meaning is that you choose one of the two matters. Al-Zamakhshari estimated the nominative: "the matter is your throwing or our throwing," making it the predicate of an elided subject (mubtada', the subject of the nominal sentence). He preferred that it be the subject, with an elided predicate whose estimate is "your throwing is first," and the words ﴿or we will be the first to throw﴾ indicate it, so the contrast is good in meaning, though in terms of the verbal structure the contrast is not present, since we estimated "your throwing is first," and the contrast with their being the first to throw is present, but it entails that their throwing would be first, so it is a contrast in meaning. In al-Zamakhshari's estimate, "the matter is your throwing," there is no contrast.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verse 60–71 (part 2 of 3):

Al-Zamakhshari estimated the accusative (in ﴿إما نلقي﴾ / ﴿أن تلقي﴾) as: "Choose one of the two matters." This is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of i'rab (grammatical analysis). The explanation of the i'rab is: (immā) "we choose" ﴿أن تُلْقِيَ﴾ (an tulqiya, "that you throw"). A structure similar to this has already been mentioned in al-A'raf.

﴿قال بل ألقوا﴾ ("He said: Nay, throw you"). The command to throw does not fall under the category of permitting magic or commanding it, because the purpose in this is to distinguish between their throwing and the miracle. This became the established way to uncover the doubt, since the command is joined with a condition, i.e., "Throw if you are truthful," based on His saying ﴿فأتوا بسورة مثله﴾ ("then bring a surah like it," Yunus: 38), then He said ﴿إن كنتم صادقين﴾ ("if you are truthful," Yunus: 38). In the speech there is an elision, its estimate being: "So they threw, and then..."

Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿فإذا حبالهم﴾ ("then suddenly their ropes"): the fa' is the answer to what has been elided, and its estimate is "So they threw"; and idha ("suddenly") in this is an adverb of place, and the governing element of it is "they threw." End of quote. So his saying: "The fa' is the answer to what has been elided, and its estimate is 'So they threw'" — this fa' is not a fa' of answer, because "fa-alqaw" (so they threw) is not answered; rather it is for coordination: it coordinated the clause of sudden surprise upon that elided item. And his saying: "and idha in this is an adverb of place" means that idha which indicates sudden surprise is an adverb of place (p-259), and this is the view of al-Mubarrad. The apparent sense of Sibawayh's words, and his saying "and the governing element of it is they threw," is not correct, because the fa' prevents governance, and because this idha is only governed by the predicate of the subject, which is ﴿حبالهم وعصيهم﴾ ("their ropes and their staves"), unless one makes it itself in the position of the predicate; because the predicate may be "is imagined," and idha and "is imagined" may be in the position of a circumstantial state (hal). This is similar to: "I went out, and suddenly the lion was crouching," and "crouching" (rabidan): if we raise "crouching," idha is the governing element, and the estimate is "So in the presence is the lion crouching," or "in the place." If we put it in the accusative, idha is a predicate; therefore you may suffice with it and what follows it as a complete utterance, as in "I went out, and suddenly the lion."

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is said of this idha that it is idha of sudden surprise, and the verification concerning it is that it is idha which is the one meaning time, which requires a governing element for it, and a clause is added to it; in some places it is specified that its governing element is a specific verb, namely the verb of sudden surprise, and the clause is purely inceptive. So the estimate of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿فإذا حبالهم وعصيهم﴾ is: "So Moses was suddenly surprised at the time of the imagining of their ropes and staves," and this is an illustration; the meaning is: upon his being surprised by their ropes and staves imagined to him as running. End of quote.

So his saying: "The verification concerning it, if it is the one meaning time" — this is the view of al-Riyashi that idha of sudden surprise is an adverb of time, and this is a weak view; and the view of the Kufans that it is a particle is also a weak view. His saying "requires a governing element for it" is correct. His saying "and a clause is added to it" is, according to our companions, not correct; because it is either the predicate of the subject or governed by the predicate of the subject, and if that is so, it is impossible for it to be added to a clause, because it is either part of a clause or governed by part of it, so the addition is not possible. His saying "in some places it is specified that its governing element is a specific verb, namely the verb of sudden surprise" — we have already explained its governing element. His saying "and the clause is purely inceptive" — this restriction is not correct, rather al-Akhfash explicitly stated in al-Awsat that a clause accompanied by qad may follow it while being verbal; you say: "I went out, and suddenly qad Zayd had struck 'Amr," and on this he built the issue of the verb being occupied (al-ishtighal): "I went out, and suddenly Zayd, 'Amr had struck him," with Zayd in the nominative or accusative. As for his saying "and the meaning is upon his being surprised by their ropes and staves imagined to him as running," this is the reverse of what was estimated; rather the meaning is upon the surprise of their ropes and staves upon him. So if you say: "I went out, and suddenly the beast," the meaning is that the beast surprised me and its presence fell upon me.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Isa read ʿusayyahum with a damma on the ʿayn wherever it occurs, and this is the original form; the kasra is an assimilation to the vowel of the ṣād, and the vowel of the ṣād is for the sake of the yā'. In the book al-Lawami', al-Hasan and ʿuṣyuhum with a damma on the ʿayn, a sukun on the ṣād, and a lightened yā', with the nominative; this too is a plural like the common reading, but on the pattern fuʿl. Al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, Ibn Isa, Abu Haywa, Qatada, al-Jahdari, Rawh, al-Walidan, and Ibn Dhakwan read tukhayyalu with a tā' (on top) in the passive voice, and in it is the pronoun of the ropes and staves, and ﴿أنها تسعى﴾ ("that they run") is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for that pronoun. Abu al-Sammak read takhayyalu with a fatha on the tā', meaning "they imagine," and in it too is the pronoun of what they mentioned, and ﴿أنها تسعى﴾ is also a substitute of inclusion for that pronoun, but it is a subject in terms of meaning. Ibn Atiyya said: it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). Abu al-Qasim ibn Habara al-Hudhali al-Andalusi said in his book al-Kamil, on the authority of Abu al-Sammak, that he read tukhayyalu with a tā' from above, damma, and a kasra on the yā', and the pronoun in it is the subject, and ﴿أنها تسعى﴾ is in the position of an accusative as object. Ibn Atiyya attributed this reading to al-Hasan and al-Thaqafi, meaning Isa. Whoever built tukhayyalu for the passive, then the one who imagined it to them is God, as a trial and testing. Al-Hasan ibn Ayman related from Abu Haywa "nukhayyilu" with a nun and a kasra on the yā', so the one who imagined it to them is God. The pronoun in "ilayhi" (to him) apparently refers to Moses, because of His saying earlier ﴿قال بل ألقوا﴾ and His saying afterward ﴿فأوجس في نفسه خيفة موسى﴾. It has been said it refers to Pharaoh. The apparent sense from the narratives is that the ropes and staves were moving and shifting in a movement resembling the movement of a living thing, and for this reason He mentioned "running," which is the description of an animal that walks. It is related that they placed mercury in the ropes and staves and threw them in the sun, so the mercury received the sun's heat and the staves and ropes moved with it. It was also said: they dug the ground and placed fire beneath it, and the staves and ropes were filled with mercury, so when the heat of the earth reached them they moved, and this was of the category of the mechanism (dakk). It was also said: they did not actually move, and that was from the magic of the eyes; God has clearly stated this when they said ﴿سحروا أعين الناس﴾ ("they bewitched the eyes of the people," al-A'raf: 116), so the observer was imagined to see them moving. The explanation of awjasa has already been given.

Al-Zamakhshari said: That was due to the natural human disposition, and it is hardly possible to be free of its like; this is the saying of al-Hasan. It was also said: his fear was for the people, that they would be tempted by the awe of what he saw before he threw his staff; this is the saying of Muqatil. Ijas is from the hajis, which passes through the mind and does not settle. And khifatan (fear) originally was khawfatan; the waw was changed to yā' because of the kasra before it. Ibn Atiyya said: it is possible that it was khawfatan with a fatha on the kha', the waw was changed to yā', and then the kha' was given a kasra for harmony.

﴿إنك أنت الأعلى﴾ ("Indeed you are the Most High") is an affirmation of his dominance and conquest, and an emphasis by resumption, by the word of emphasis, by repetition of the pronoun, by the definite article, and by the superlative form indicating preference. ﴿وألق ما في يمينك﴾ ("and throw what is in your right hand"): the construction did not come as "throw your staff" because of what the word "right hand" contains of the meaning of blessing and prosperity. Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying ﴿ما في يمينك﴾ rather than "your staff" is permissible to be a diminutive of it, meaning: do not concern yourself with the abundance of their ropes and staves, and throw the single small little stick that is in your right hand, for by God's power it will swallow them, despite its thinness and their multitude, and its smallness and their greatness. It is also permissible that it be an exaltation of it, meaning: do not be impressed by these large and numerous bodies, for in your right hand is something greater than them all, and these, despite their multitude, are the least and most insignificant before it, so throw it and it will swallow them by God's permission and annihilate them. End of quote. This is an exaggeration, and his discourse has no great benefit in that.

In His saying ﴿تلقف﴾ ("it will swallow") there is a construction according to the meaning of "what" rather than its wording, since "ma" was applied to the staff, and the staff is feminine; had it been construed according to the wording, it would have been with the yā'. The majority read ﴿تلقف﴾ with a fatha on the lām and a shadda on the qāf, jussive as an answer to the command. Ibn Amir read likewise, but with a damma on the fā' as a new sentence or as a circumstantial state of what is thrown. Abu Ja'far, Hafs, and ʿIsma from ʿAsim read ﴿تلقف﴾ with a sukun on the lām and the fā' and a lightened qāf; from Qunbul, he used to read tashdid of "talaqqaf" meaning yatalaqqaf.

The majority read ﴿كيد﴾ ("a trick") in the nominative, with "ma" as a relative pronoun meaning "that which," and the returning pronoun is elided; it is possible that "ma" is a verbal noun, meaning: "that you have made is a trick." The meaning of ﴿صنعوا﴾ ("they have made") here is "they forged and fabricated," like His saying ﴿تلقف ما يأفكون﴾ ("it swallows what they fabricate," al-Shu'ara: 45). Mujahid, Humayd, and Zayd ibn Ali read "kayda sihrin" in the accusative as object of "sana'u," with "ma" as a preparatory particle (muhayyi'a). Abu Bahriyya, al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, Khalaf in his choice, Ibn Isa al-Isbahani, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, Ibn Jarir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "sihrin" with a kasra on the sīn and a sukun on the ḥāʾ, meaning "possessor of magic," or "possessors of magic," or "they, because of their deep involvement in their magic, are as if they were magic itself," or "clearly magic," or "a clear trick," because it is magic and non-magic, as "the hundred is clear with a dirham" (i.e., the hundred is distinct by one dirham), and similar to it: "knowledge of jurisprudence" and "knowledge of grammar."

The majority read ﴿ساحر﴾ ("magician") as an active participle from "sahara." The singular "sahir" is used because the action of all of them is one type of magic, namely the ropes and staves, so it is as if it proceeded from one magician, since its kinds are not different. Al-Zamakhshari said: because the intention in this speech is the sense of genus, not the sense of number; had it been pluralized, it would have seemed that the intended meaning is number. Do you not see that His saying ﴿ولا يفلح الساحر﴾ ("and the magician does not prosper"), i.e., this genus, End of quote.

He used the definite in His saying ﴿ولا يفلح الساحر﴾ because it refers back to the indefinite ﴿ساحر﴾ before it, as in His saying ﴿كما أرسلنا إلى فرعون رسولا﴾ ("as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger," al-Muzzammil: 15) ﴿فعصى فرعون الرسول﴾ ("but Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger," al-Muzzammil: 16). Al-Zamakhshari said: it was made indefinite here, meaning first, because of the indefiniteness of the genitive (muḍāf) and not because of its indefiniteness in itself, as in the verse of al-Ajjaj:

*In the striving of a worldly (dunya) matter, which has long been stretched out*

And in the hadith of Umar, may God be pleased with him: "Neither in a worldly matter nor in a matter of the Hereafter," the intended meaning is the indefiniteness of the matter, as if he said: "They have made a magical trick, and in a worldly striving and a worldly and otherworldly matter." End of quote. The verse of al-Ajjaj, "in a worldly striving," is taken as a poetic necessity, since dunya is the feminine of adna (nearer), and its feminine is not used except with the definite article or with a genitive construction. As for the saying of Umar, it is possible that it is among the distortions of the narrators.

And the meaning of ﴿and he will not succeed﴾ is that he will not attain his aim, ﴿wherever he goes﴾, meaning wherever he turns and travels. One group said: its meaning is that the sorcerer is killed wherever he is found, and this is the punishment of one who has been deprived of success. One group read ﴿أينَ أتى﴾ (ayna ata, "wherever he came") and there are omitted clauses after this, the implied sense being: the fear that had arisen was removed, he threw what was in his right hand, it swallowed their ropes and staffs, then it turned back into a staff; they lost the ropes and staffs, and they knew that this was a miracle beyond human capacity. ﴿So the sorcerers were thrown down prostrate﴾. The construction ﴿فَأُلْقِيَ السَّحَرَةُ﴾ (fa-ulqiya al-saharatu, "so the sorcerers were cast down") came rather than "so they prostrated," as if a command came to them and startled them and seized them, and it was done to them in this way. This is an expression for the speed with which they were affected by that great marvel, so they could not restrain themselves from falling prostrate. In al-A'raf, Musa was mentioned first and Harun was delayed, for the sake of the fawasil (verse-endings, the rhyming pauses), and because Musa is the one to whom the staff is attributed, in which the miracle appeared. Musa was also delayed for the sake of the fawasil, as in His saying ﴿لَكَانَ لِزَامًا وَأَجَلٌ مُسَمًّى﴾ ([Ta-Ha: 129]), and ﴿أَزْوَاجًا مِنْ نَبَاتٍ﴾ ([Ta-Ha: 53]), where shatta is an attribute of the word azwajan ([Ta-Ha: 53]). There is no difference between "Zayd and Amr stood" and "Amr and Zayd stood," since the particle waw does not require an order. Moreover, it is possible that the two statements came from two speakers: one group uttered their saying, "Lord of Musa and Harun," and another group uttered, "Lord of Harun and Musa." Since they shared in the meaning, it is valid to attribute each of the two statements to all of them. It was also said that Harun was mentioned first here because he was older than Musa. And it was said: because Pharaoh had raised Musa, so they began with Harun, so that Pharaoh's deception that he had raised Musa would be removed, for he would say, "I raised him." They said, "Lord of Harun and Musa," and did not suffice with their saying "Lord of the worlds," for the explicit statement that they believed in the Lord of these two, whereas previously he had claimed that he was the Lord of the worlds.

The difference in the reading of ﴿آمنتم﴾ (amantum, "you believed") has already been discussed, as well as ﴿لَأُقَطِّعَنَّ﴾ (la-uqatti'anna, "I will surely cut off") and ﴿ثُمَّ لَأُصَلِّبَنَّكُمْ﴾ (thumma la-usallibannakum, "then I will surely crucify you") in al-A'raf ([al-A'raf: 124]), and the explanation of the parallel of this verse appears there. There it is ﴿آمنتم له﴾ (amantum lahu, "you believed in him"), and here it is "lahu" as well. Amana takes the preposition bi when it refers to God, and li for others in most cases, as in ﴿فَمَا آمَنَ لِمُوسَى﴾ ([Yunus: 83]), ﴿لَنْ نُؤْمِنَ لَكَ﴾ ([al-Baqarah: 55]), ﴿وَمَا أَنْتَ بِمُؤْمِنٍ لَنَا﴾ ([Yusuf: 17]), and ﴿فَآمَنَ لَهُ لُوطٌ﴾ ([al-Ankabut: 26]). The pronoun in "bihi" may refer to Musa, or it may refer to the Lord. By cutting off and crucifying on the trunks, he intended to make an example of them. Since the trunk is a place of rest for the one crucified and encloses him in the manner of a container enclosing its contents, the verb was given the object by means of fi, which indicates a container. It was also said that fi here means ʿala ("upon"). And it was said: Pharaoh gouged out the wood and crucified them inside it, so it became a true container for them, so that they would die inside it of hunger and thirst. Among the instances of sallaba being followed by fi is the poet's verse:

They crucified al-ʿAbdi in the trunk of a palm tree,
So Shaybān never sneezed except with a severed nose.

Pharaoh was the first to crucify, and Pharaoh swore to this, which is his own act and the act of others, namely ﴿وَلَتَعْلَمُنَّ أَيُّنَا﴾ (wa-la-ta'lamunna ayyuna, "and you will surely know which of us"), that is, which of me and whoever you believed in. It was also said: "which of me and of Musa," and he said this in mockery, because Musa was not one of those to be punished. Al-Zamakhshari went to this view, saying: "The evidence is His saying: ﴿آمنتم له﴾, and the lam with belief in the Book of God is for other than God, as in His saying ﴿يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وَيُؤْمِنُ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ([al-Tawbah: 61])." In it there is a display of his power and dominance, and of what he was accustomed to and used to, namely the torture of people with various kinds of punishment, and a belittling of Musa, peace be upon him, with weakening and mockery of him. End of quotation. This is also the view of al-Tabari, who said: "He means himself and Musa, peace be upon him." The first view is more suitable to Pharaoh's bragging. ﴿وَلَتَعْلَمُنَّ﴾ here is mu'allaq (suspended), and ﴿أَيُّنَا أَشَدُّ﴾ (ayyuna ashaddu, "which of us is more severe") is an interrogative clause consisting of a subject and predicate, in a position of accusative for His saying ﴿وَلَتَعْلَمُنَّ﴾, serving in place of the two objects, or in the position of a single object if ﴿وَلَتَعْلَمُنَّ﴾ is transitive in the manner of ʿarafa. It is also permissible, according to the view of Sibawayh, that ﴿أيُّنا﴾ be the object of ﴿وَلَتَعْلَمُنَّ﴾, with ashaddu being the predicate of an omitted subject, and ayyuna being a relative pronoun whose clause follows it, the implied sense being: "and you will surely know who is ﴿more severe in punishment and more lasting﴾."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 72–79 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They said: "We will never prefer you﴾, that is, we will never choose to follow you, to be of your party, or to be spared your punishment, ﴿over the clear signs that have come to us﴾, which are the miracle that came to us and whose truth we know. In this statement of theirs there is a belittling of him, a making light of what he threatened them with, and a lack of concern for his words. In attributing the coming (of the signs) to them, although the signs came to them and to others, (there is a reason): they were more knowledgeable about magic than others, and they knew that what Musa brought was not magic, so they had clear knowledge of what is miraculous, while others followed them in this. Also, they were the ones who benefited from them, so the signs were clear proofs in their case.

The waw in ﴿and He who created us﴾ is a conjunctive waw (waw al-ʿatf, the waw of coordination) over ﴿what has come to us﴾. That is: and over ﴿He who created us﴾. When the proof of God in the miracle became evident to them, they began with it, then ascended to the One capable of breaking the normal course of things, who is God, Exalted. They mentioned the attribute of originating creation, which is their saying ﴿He who created us﴾, to demonstrate the impotence of Pharaoh and the falsity of his claim to lordship and divinity, for he is powerless to drive away a fly, let alone to create one.

It has also been said: the waw is for an oath, and its response is omitted, and ﴿we will never prefer you﴾ cannot be the response, because a negation with (lan) is not answered with it except in rare poetry. And (ma) is a relative pronoun in the sense of "who/that," and its relative clause is ﴿you are a judge﴾, with the returning pronoun omitted; that is: what you are judging. It has been said: (ma) cannot be a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), because the maṣdariyya is joined to verbs, whereas this one is joined to a nominal sentence (mubtadaʾ and khabar). End of quotation.

But this is not agreed upon. Rather, some of the grammarians have held that the verbal-noun (ma) may be joined to a nominal sentence. ﴿This worldly life﴾ is in the accusative as an adverbial of time/place (ẓarf), and (ma) is a restrictive particle (kāffa muhayyiʾa, a particle that prepares the verb or sentence), though it may be a verbal-noun particle. That is: your judgment is only in this worldly life, not in the Hereafter; rather, in the Hereafter there is bliss for us and punishment for you.

The majority read ﴿you decree﴾ (taqḍī) in the active voice, addressed to Pharaoh. Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read (tuqḍā), in the passive voice, with ﴿this life﴾ in the nominative: the adverbial was used in the manner of a direct object, then the verb was made passive for it and it took it as its subject, just as you say: "The day of Friday was fasted" and "He had sixty years born to him." It is not stated in the Qur'an that he carried out his threat against them, nor that he cut off their hands and feet and crucified them. Rather, the apparent meaning is that God Exalted saved them from him, and this is indicated by His saying: ﴿You two and whoever follows you are the victors﴾ [al-Qasas: 35]. It has also been said that he carried out his threat against them and crucified them on trunks of palm trees, and that his compulsion of them to practise magic (was also a punishment). It was said: he compelled them to oppose Musa. It was also said: he used to take the children of the people and train them in this, and the magicians pointed to this, as reported by al-Hasan.

﴿And God is better and more lasting﴾ is a rejoinder to his saying ﴿Which of us has the sterner and more lasting punishment?﴾ [Taha: 71]. That is: God's reward and what He has prepared for whoever believes in Him are better and more lasting. It is narrated that they said to Pharaoh: "Show us Musa asleep," so he did, and they found his staff guarding him. They said: "This is not magic. The magician, when he sleeps, his magic ceases." But he refused except that they should oppose him. And from their saying ﴿Surely we shall have a reward?﴾ it appears that there was no compulsion.

﴿Indeed, whoever comes﴾ to ﴿who has purified himself﴾. It has been said that this is a report from them as an admonition to Pharaoh. It has also been said that it is a statement from God, not in the form of quoting them, to draw attention to the ugliness of what Pharaoh did and the goodness of what the magicians did, as an exhortation and warning. The "criminal" here means the disbeliever, because of the mention of his opposite: ﴿and whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾, and because of His saying ﴿in which he will neither die nor live﴾. That is: he will be punished with a punishment that ends in death, then he is not finished off so that he may rest; rather, his skin is restored and his punishment is renewed. So he does not live a good life, unlike the believer who enters the Fire, for they approach death and are not finished off. This is the difference between the believer and the disbeliever. In a hadith (they will die a death), and this is its meaning, because he does not die in the Hereafter. And ﴿purified himself﴾ (tazakkā) means cleansed himself from the filth of disbelief. It has been said: he said, "There is no god but God."

﴿And We had indeed revealed to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants, and strike for them a dry path through the sea, not fearing being overtaken nor being afraid"﴾. ﴿Then Pharaoh followed them with his hosts, and the sea covered them with what covered them﴾. ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them﴾. ﴿O Children of Israel, We had saved you from your enemy and made an appointment with you at the right side of the Mount, and sent down to you manna and quail﴾ [Taha: 80]. ﴿Eat of the good things We have provided for you, but do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you; and he upon whom My wrath descends has indeed fallen﴾ [Taha: 81]. ﴿And indeed I am most forgiving to whoever repents, believes, does righteousness, and then remains guided﴾ [Taha: 82].

This is a resumption of a report about some of the affairs of Musa, peace be upon him, and between it and the statement of the magicians mentioned earlier there is a span of time in which events happened to Musa and Pharaoh. That is because when the affair of the magicians ended, and Musa prevailed and his affair grew strong, Pharaoh promised him that he would send the Children of Israel with him. Musa remained faithful to his promise until Pharaoh betrayed him, broke his word, and informed him that he would not send them with him. Then God sent the signs mentioned in other passages, the locusts, the lice, and so on to the end. Whenever a sign came, Pharaoh promised to send the Children of Israel when the punishment was lifted; but when it lifted, he broke his word, until another sign came. When the signs were complete, God revealed to Musa, peace be upon him, that he should bring the Children of Israel out at night, travelling (sarīyan), and al-sura is travel by night.

It is possible that (an) is explanatory (mufassira), and that it is the (an) that puts the present tense into the subjunctive. ﴿My servants﴾ is an idafa of honour, like His saying ﴿and I breathed into him of My spirit﴾ [al-Hijr: 29]. The apparent view is that the revelation to him of this, and of striking the sea, took place in Egypt before the time when Pharaoh followed Musa and his people with his hosts. It has also been said that the command to strike came when Pharaoh was about to overtake him and the fear of the Children of Israel grew strong. It is related that Musa, peace be upon him, set out with the Children of Israel, who were six hundred thousand people, and travelled from Egypt, heading for the Sea of Qulzum (the Red Sea). News reached Pharaoh, so he gathered his hosts and mustered them, and set out in pursuit. Then God revealed to Musa that he should make for the sea, and the Children of Israel panicked, seeing that the enemy was behind them and the sea in front of them, while Musa trusted in God's handiwork. When Pharaoh saw them setting out toward the sea, he coveted them, for their destination was a place where the sandy tracks and wide roads end. It has been said: among Pharaoh's cavalry were seventy thousand dark-bay horses, and the proportion of other colours is accordingly. It has also been said that there were more than this. Then Musa, peace be upon him, struck the sea, and it split into twelve paths, wide roads between which stood walls of water, and this is indicated by ﴿so every division was like a huge mountain﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 63]. It has also been said: it was one single path, because of His saying ﴿strike for them a dry path through the sea﴾. End of quotation.

The "criminal" here means the disbeliever, because of the mention of his opposite: ﴿and whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾, and because of His saying ﴿in which he will neither die nor live﴾. That is: he will be punished with a punishment that ends in death, then he is not finished off so that he may rest; rather, his skin is restored and his punishment is renewed. So he does not live a good life, unlike the believer who enters the Fire, for they approach death and are not finished off. This is the difference between the believer and the disbeliever. In a hadith (they will die a death), and this is its meaning, because he does not die in the Hereafter. And ﴿purified himself﴾ (tazakkā) means cleansed himself from the filth of disbelief. It has been said: he said, "There is no god but God."

﴿And We had indeed revealed to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants, and strike for them a dry path through the sea, not fearing being overtaken nor being afraid"﴾. ﴿Then Pharaoh followed them with his hosts, and the sea covered them with what covered them﴾. ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them﴾. ﴿O Children of Israel, We had saved you from your enemy and made an appointment with you at the right side of the Mount, and sent down to you manna and quail﴾ [Taha: 80]. ﴿Eat of the good things We have provided for you, but do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you; and he upon whom My wrath descends has indeed fallen﴾ [Taha: 81]. ﴿And indeed I am most forgiving to whoever repents, believes, does righteousness, and then remains guided﴾ [Taha: 82].

This is a resumption of a report about some of the affairs of Musa, peace be upon him, and between it and the statement of the magicians mentioned earlier there is a span of time in which events happened to Musa and Pharaoh. That is because when the affair of the magicians ended, and Musa prevailed and his affair grew strong, Pharaoh promised him that he would send the Children of Israel with him. Musa remained faithful to his promise until Pharaoh betrayed him, broke his word, and informed him that he would not send them with him. Then God sent the signs mentioned in other passages, the locusts, the lice, and so on to the end. Whenever a sign came, Pharaoh promised to send the Children of Israel when the punishment was lifted; but when it lifted, he broke his word, until another sign came. When the signs were complete, God revealed to Musa, peace be upon him, that he should bring the Children of Israel out at night, travelling (sarīyan), and al-sura is travel by night.

It is possible that (an) is explanatory (mufassira), and that it is the (an) that puts the present tense into the subjunctive. ﴿My servants﴾ is an idafa of honour, like His saying ﴿and I breathed into him of My spirit﴾ [al-Hijr: 29]. News reached Pharaoh, so he gathered his hosts and mustered them, and set out in pursuit. Then God revealed to Musa that he should make for the sea, and the Children of Israel panicked, seeing that the enemy was behind them and the sea in front of them, while Musa trusted in God's handiwork. When Pharaoh saw them setting out toward the sea, he coveted them, for their destination was a place where the sandy tracks and wide roads end. It has been said: among Pharaoh's cavalry were seventy thousand dark-bay horses, and the proportion of other colours is accordingly. It has also been said that there were more than this. When the old woman grows angry, divorce her, and do not appease her or flatter her.

It has been said: (ma) cannot be a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), because the maṣdariyya is joined to verbs, whereas this one is joined to a nominal sentence (mubtadaʾ and khabar). It has also been said: the waw is for an oath, and its response is omitted, and ﴿we will never prefer you﴾ cannot be the response, because a negation with (lan) is not answered with it except in rare poetry. And (ma) is a relative pronoun in the sense of "who/that," and its relative clause is ﴿you are a judge﴾, with the returning pronoun omitted; that is: what you are judging. It has been said: (ma) cannot be a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), because the maṣdariyya is joined to verbs, whereas this one is joined to a nominal sentence (mubtadaʾ and khabar). It has been said: he said, "There is no god but God."

﴿And We had indeed revealed to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants, and strike for them a dry path through the sea, not fearing being overtaken nor being afraid"﴾. ﴿Then Pharaoh followed them with his hosts, and the sea covered them with what covered them﴾. ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them﴾. ﴿O Children of Israel, We had saved you from your enemy and made an appointment with you at the right side of the Mount, and sent down to you manna and quail﴾ [Taha: 80]. ﴿Eat of the good things We have provided for you, but do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you; and he upon whom My wrath descends has indeed fallen﴾ [Taha: 81]. ﴿And indeed I am most forgiving to whoever repents, believes, does righteousness, and then remains guided﴾ [Taha: 82].

Musa remained faithful to his promise until Pharaoh betrayed him, broke his word, and informed him that he would not send them with him. Then God sent the signs mentioned in other passages, the locusts, the lice, and so on to the end. Whenever a sign came, Pharaoh promised to send the Children of Israel when the punishment was lifted; but when it lifted, he broke his word, until another sign came. News reached Pharaoh, so he gathered his hosts and mustered them, and set out in pursuit. When Pharaoh saw them setting out toward the sea, he coveted them, for their destination was a place where the sandy tracks and wide roads end. It has been said: among Pharaoh's cavalry were seventy thousand dark-bay horses, and the proportion of other colours is accordingly. It has also been said that there were more than this. Then Musa, peace be upon him, struck the sea, and it split into twelve paths, wide roads between which stood walls of water, and this is indicated by ﴿so every division was like a huge mountain﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 63]. Al-Hasan read (yabsan) with a sukun on the ba. There is an ellipsis in this view, its estimate being: then Musa and his people were saved, and Pharaoh and his people drowned. Al-Zajjaj said: it has been read (wa-junūduhu, and his hosts) as a coordination on Pharaoh."

The judge (al-Qadi, i.e., al-Baydawi) cited this in support of his school of thought, saying: "If misguidance were from the creation of Allah, it would not be permissible to say, ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray﴾; rather, it would have to be said: 'Allah led them astray,' because Allah, exalted is He, censured him for it. It is narrated that they said to Pharaoh: "Show us Musa asleep," so he did, and they found his staff guarding him. They said: "This is not magic. The magician, when he sleeps, his magic ceases." But he refused except that they should oppose him. And from their saying ﴿Surely we shall have a reward?﴾ it appears that there was no compulsion.

It has also been said that it is a statement from God, not in the form of quoting them, to draw attention to the ugliness of what Pharaoh did and the goodness of what the magicians did, as an exhortation and warning. The "criminal" here means the disbeliever, because of the mention of his opposite: ﴿and whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾, and because of His saying ﴿in which he will neither die nor live﴾. That is: he will be punished with a punishment that ends in death, then he is not finished off so that he may rest; rather, his skin is restored and his punishment is renewed. So he does not live a good life, unlike the believer who enters the Fire, for they approach death and are not finished off. This is the difference between the believer and the disbeliever. In a hadith (they will die a death), and this is its meaning, because he does not die in the Hereafter. And ﴿purified himself﴾ (tazakkā) means cleansed himself from the filth of disbelief. It has been said: he said, "There is no god but God."

﴿And We had indeed revealed to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants, and strike for them a dry path through the sea, not fearing being overtaken nor being afraid"﴾. ﴿Then Pharaoh followed them with his hosts, and the sea covered them with what covered them﴾. ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them﴾. ﴿O Children of Israel, We had saved you from your enemy and made an appointment with you at the right side of the Mount, and sent down to you manna and quail﴾ [Taha: 80]. ﴿Eat of the good things We have provided for you, but do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you; and he upon whom My wrath descends has indeed fallen﴾ [Taha: 81]. ﴿And indeed I am most forgiving to whoever repents, believes, does righteousness, and then remains guided﴾ [Taha: 82].

Musa remained faithful to his promise until Pharaoh betrayed him, broke his word, and informed him that he would not send them with him. Then God sent the signs mentioned in other passages, the locusts, the lice, and so on to the end. Whenever a sign came, Pharaoh promised to send the Children of Israel when the punishment was lifted; but when it lifted, he broke his word, until another sign came. It has also been said that the command to strike came when Pharaoh was about to overtake him and the fear of the Children of Israel grew strong. It is related that Musa, peace be upon him, set out with the Children of Israel, who were six hundred thousand people, and travelled from Egypt, heading for the Sea of Qulzum (the Red Sea). News reached Pharaoh, so he gathered his hosts and mustered them, and set out in pursuit. Then God revealed to Musa that he should make for the sea, and the Children of Israel panicked, seeing that the enemy was behind them and the sea in front of them, while Musa trusted in God's handiwork. When Pharaoh saw them setting out toward the sea, he coveted them, for their destination was a place where the sandy tracks and wide roads end. It has been said: among Pharaoh's cavalry were seventy thousand dark-bay horses, and the proportion of other colours is accordingly. It has also been said that there were more than this. He described it by what it came to be, since at the moment of striking it had not yet become dry; rather, the east wind passed over it and dried it, as is narrated. Al-Hasan read (yabsan) with a sukun on the ba. This is clarified in another verse: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it split﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 63]. So the meaning is: strike the sea with your staff so that it splits for them and becomes a path. The verb thus takes (li, for them) to indicate the path, because the path was the result of the striking; it was made as if it were the thing struck.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿strike for them a path﴾ means make for them, from the expression "he struck for him a share in his property" and "he struck the brick," meaning he made it. End of quotation.

In a hadith: "Strike for me with you a share" (i.e., cast lots for me with you). Since he did not mention the thing struck literally, which is the sea, had he explicitly mentioned the thing struck literally the construction would have been "a path in it," and it would have referred back to the sea that was struck. The word (yabasan, dry) is a verbal noun described by the word "path." He described it by what it came to be, since at the moment of striking it had not yet become dry; rather, the east wind passed over it and dried it, as is narrated. It is said: "yabisa yubsan and yabasan" like "ʿudm and ʿadam" (both meaning lack). Because it is a verbal noun, the feminine was described by it; they say: "a dry ewe (shāt yabas)" and "a dry she-camel (nāqa yabas)" when her milk has dried up. Al-Hasan read (yabsan) with a sukun on the ba. The author of al-Lawami' said: it may be a verbal noun like the common reading, and with the sukun it may be the verbal noun, while with the fatha it is the noun (ism), like "nafḍ" (a shaking out). Al-Zamakhshari said: yabas must be either a lightened form of yabs, or an adjective of the pattern fuʿl, or the plural of yābis, like ṣāḥib and ṣaḥb. It was described by the singular as an emphasis, like his saying "and together, hungry (jiyaʿan)," which he made, because of the extreme hunger, like a group of hungry people. End of quotation.

Abu Haywa read (yābisan), as an active participle.

The majority read ﴿do not fear﴾ (lā takhāfu), which is a clause in the place of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿so strike﴾. It has been said it is in the place of an attribute of the path, with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning "you do not fear in it." Al-Aʿmash, Hamza, and Ibn Abi Layla read (lā takhaf) with the jussive, as an answer to the imperative, or as a new prohibition, as al-Zajjaj said. Abu Haywa, Talha, and al-Aʿmash read (darkan) with a sukun on the ra, while the majority read it with a fatha. Both (darak) and (darak) are nouns from the root of attaining, meaning: Pharaoh and his hosts will not overtake you and will not reach you. ﴿Nor fear﴾, you or your people, drowning. Its coordination with the majority reading ﴿do not fear﴾ is clear. As for the jussive reading, it is explained as: the alif was added for the sake of the ends of the verses, as a rhyme-letter, like His saying ﴿and they led us astray from the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67]; or that it is a new report, meaning: "and you do not fear"; or that it is jussive by the deletion of a presumed vowel, according to the dialect of one who says: "Has he not come to you?" This is a rare dialect. The poet said:

When the old woman grows angry, divorce her, and do not appease her or flatter her.

The majority read ﴿so he followed them﴾ (fa-atbaʿahum) with a sukun on the ta. Atbaʿa may mean the same as tabiʿa (to follow), and then it takes one object, as in His saying ﴿so the devil followed him﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 175]; and it may take two objects, as in His saying: "We made their descendants follow them," so the ta is then extra, meaning: his hosts; or the ta is for a circumstance, and the second object is omitted, meaning: his chiefs and his retainers. Abu ʿAmr, in one narration, and al-Hasan read (fa-ittabaʿahum) with a shadda on the ta, and likewise from al-Hasan in all places in the Qur'an except ﴿so a piercing flame followed him﴾ [al-Saffat: 10]. The ba in (bi-junūdihi, with his hosts) is in the place of a circumstance, as you say: "Zayd went out with his weapons," or the ba is for transitivity to a second object by a preposition, since "ittabaʿa" does not take an object directly except through one preposition.

The majority read ﴿the sea covered them with what covered them﴾ in the pattern of an unaugmented verb (faʿila). A group, among them al-Aʿmash, read (fa-ghashshāhum min al-yammi mā ghashshāhum) with doubling of the ʿayn, so the agent in the first reading is (mā, what), and in the second the agent is God, meaning: God covered them. Al-Zamakhshari said: or Pharaoh, because he is the one who plunged his hosts into ruin and caused their destruction. He said: ﴿what covered them﴾ is from the category of abbreviation and of the comprehensive phrases which, though few in words, carry many meanings, meaning: there covered them what none knows the reality of except God. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: ﴿what covered them﴾ is a vagueness more awful than any explicit statement of the extent, and it is like His saying ﴿when there covers the lote-tree what covers it﴾ [al-Najm: 16]. The apparent view is that the pronoun in ﴿covered them﴾ in both places refers to Pharaoh and his people. It has been said: the first refers to Pharaoh and his people, and the second to Musa and his people. There is an ellipsis in this view, its estimate being: then Musa and his people were saved, and Pharaoh and his people drowned. Al-Zajjaj said: it has been read (wa-junūduhu, and his hosts) as a coordination on Pharaoh."

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 20, verses 72–79 (part 2 of 2):

(p-265) ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray﴾, i.e., from the very first time until this final end, meaning misguidance in religion. It was also said: he led them astray into the sea, because they drowned in it. The judge (al-Qadi, i.e., al-Baydawi) cited this in support of his school of thought, saying: "If misguidance were from the creation of Allah, it would not be permissible to say, ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray﴾; rather, it would have to be said: 'Allah led them astray,' because Allah, exalted is He, censured him for it. How, then, could He be the creator of disbelief? For whoever censures another for doing something must necessarily have the one censured as the doer of that act; otherwise the one who censures would deserve the censure." End of quotation.

This is in line with the Mu'tazili methodology. ﴿And he did not guide﴾, i.e., he did not guide them to the religion; or he did not save them from drowning; or he himself was not guided, because (hada) may also come in the sense of (ihtada), to be guided.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 20, verses 80–82:

﴿O Children of Israel, We have delivered you from your enemy﴾. He, exalted is He, reminded them of the various kinds of His blessings, and He began with the removal of the harm they had been suffering: humiliation, the kharaj (land tax), and the slaughter of their sons. This removal is more deserving of being mentioned first before the worldly benefit, because removing harm is a greater favour than bestowing that benefit. Then He followed this with mention of the religious benefit, which is His saying, ﴿And We made an appointment with you at the right side of the Mount﴾, since He sent down to their prophet Musa (Moses) a Book containing the explanation of their religion and the detailing of their law. Then He mentions the worldly benefit, which is His saying, ﴿And We sent down upon you the manna and the quail﴾. The apparent meaning is that the address is to those who were saved along with Musa after the drowning of Fir'awn (Pharaoh). It has also been said that the address is to the contemporaries of the Messenger (ﷺ), as an interjection in the course of the story of Musa, rebuking them because their predecessors did not show patience in performing the thanks for the blessings of Allah. In that case there is an elided noun (mudaf, an omitted element of a genitive construction), meaning: "We saved your fathers from the torment of the people of Fir'awn."

He addressed all of them with ﴿wa'adnakum (We made an appointment with you)﴾, even though those promised were the seventy whom Musa, peace be upon him, chose to hear the speech of Allah. This is because the benefit of the hearing of those seventy returns to all of them, since their hearts are reassured and tranquil. The discussion of ﴿the right side of the Mount﴾ has already passed in Surah Maryam, and the discussion of ﴿We sent down upon you the manna and the quail﴾ [al-Baqarah: 57] has passed in Surah al-Baqarah. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Talhah read ﴿qad anjaytukum (We have delivered you)﴾ and ﴿wa'adtukum (We made an appointment with you)﴾ and ﴿razaqtukum (We provided for you)﴾ with the tā' of the pronoun (the first person singular). The rest of the seven readers read with the nūn of majesty (the plural "We"). Humayd read ﴿najjaynākum﴾ with a shaddah on the jīm, without an alif before it, and with the nūn of majesty. The disagreement of Abu 'Amr has passed, as has the disagreement concerning wā'ada (to make an appointment) in al-Baqarah.

Al-tayyibāt (the good things) here means the lawful and delicious, because it combines the two attributes. It was read ﴿al-Ayman (the right)﴾ in the genitive, and al-Zamakhshari said: "in the genitive by way of proximity (jiwar, case-agreement by adjacency), like 'the ruined lizard hole' (juḥr ḍabbin kharib)." End of quote. This is among the rare and anomalous usages, such that the reading should not be construed upon it. The correct view is that it is an attribute of al-Tur (the Mount) because of the blessing (yumn) in it. As for it being on the right of one who faces the mountain, that is another matter.

He forbade them from transgression (al-ṭughyān) regarding what He had provided for them. This means that they should exceed the limits of Allah concerning it, by denying it, or by being distracted by its pleasures and blessings from performing its thanks, or by spending it in acts of disobedience and withholding the rights that are obligatory upon them concerning it.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿wa lā taṭghū fīhi (and do not transgress therein)﴾ with a ḍammah on the ghayn. From Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿wa lā taṭghaw fīhi﴾ means: "Let not some of you wrong others, so that one takes it from his companion, meaning without right." From al-Dahhak and Muqatil: "Do not go beyond the limit of what is permitted." From al-Kalbi: "Do not disbelieve the blessing," that is, "Do not seek help with My blessing against My disobedience." Al-Jumhur (the majority) read ﴿fayaḥilla (so there will befall)﴾ with a kasrah on the ḥā', and ﴿wa man yaḥlil (and whoever incurs)﴾ with a kasrah on the lām, meaning "so it will be obligatory and will attach." Al-Kisa'i read with a ḍammah on the ḥā' and on the lām of yaḥlul, meaning "will descend," and this is the reading of Qatada, Abu Hayway, al-A'mash and Talhah. Ibn 'Utayba agreed with them on yaḥlul, so he used a ḍammah. In al-Iqna' (a work on readings) by Abu 'Ali al-Ahwazi there is the following text: "Ibn Ghazwan, from Talhah: lā yaḥillanna 'alaykum ghaḍabī (let not My anger befall you), with a lām and a shaddah on the nūn, with a fatḥah on the lām and a kasrah on the ḥā', meaning: do not expose yourselves to transgression therein, lest My anger befall you, in the manner of lā arayannaka here." In the book al-Lawami' (a work on readings): Qatada, 'Abdullah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar, Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, read fayuḥillu with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the ḥā', from al-iḥlāl (causing to befall). It is then transitive, from ḥalla bi-nafsihi (to descend by itself), and the agent in it is implied, omitted because of its being well-known and because of its being understood: "so your transgression will cause My anger to befall you." This is indicated by ﴿wa lā taṭghaw (and do not transgress)﴾, so that ﴿ghaḍabī (My anger)﴾ is in the accusative position as the object. It is also possible that the verb is ascribed to ﴿ghaḍabī﴾, so that it is in the nominative position as the subject of its verb, and its object has been omitted, there being evidence for it, which is "the punishment" or something similar. End of quote.

﴿Then he has fallen (fa-qad hawā)﴾. He used this as a metaphor for destruction. Its origin is that one falls from a mountain and perishes. It is said: "hawā al-rajul," meaning "he fell." It resembles one who falls into calamity after having been in safety from it, falling down. Or ﴿hawā (he has fallen)﴾ means into Jahannam (Hell), and into the wrath of Allah and the anger of Allah, meaning His punishments. For this reason it is described with "descending."

When He, exalted is He, warned against transgression concerning what He provided, and warned against the descent of His anger, He opened the door of hope for those who repent, and He used the form of intensification (ṣīghat al-mubālaghah), which is His saying: ﴿And indeed I am Most Forgiving to whoever repents﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "from shirk (polytheism)." ﴿And believes﴾, meaning affirms the oneness of Allah. ﴿And does righteousness﴾, meaning performs the obligations. ﴿Then is guided﴾, meaning adheres to guidance and persists in it until death upon Islam. It has been said: its meaning is that he does not doubt his faith. It has also been said: "then he remains upright." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The view that is strongest regarding the meaning of ﴿then is guided﴾ is that it means: then he preserves his beliefs from opposing the truth in anything, because guidance in this sense is other than faith and other than action." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Guidance is steadfastness and firmness upon the aforementioned guidance, which is repentance, faith and righteous action. A similar expression is: ﴿Indeed, those who say: 'Our Lord is Allah,' then remain steadfast﴾ [Fussilat: 30]. The word of delay (thumma) indicates a difference between the two stations, just as it indicates a difference between two times, as in 'Zayd came to me, then 'Umar.' I mean that the station of steadfastness upon the report is distinct from the station of the report itself, because it is higher and more excellent."

(p-266)
