This is indicated by ﴿wa lā taṭghaw (and do not transgress)﴾, so that ﴿ghaḍabī (My anger)﴾ is in the accusative position as the object. It is also possible that the verb is ascribed to ﴿ghaḍabī﴾, so that it is in the nominative position as the subject of its verb, and its object has been omitted, there being evidence for it, which is "the punishment" or something similar. End of quote.

﴿Then he has fallen (fa-qad hawā)﴾. He used this as a metaphor for destruction. Its origin is that one falls from a mountain and perishes. It is said: "hawā al-rajul," meaning "he fell." It resembles one who falls into calamity after having been in safety from it, falling down. Or ﴿hawā (he has fallen)﴾ means into Jahannam (Hell), and into the wrath of Allah and the anger of Allah, meaning His punishments. For this reason it is described with "descending."

When He, exalted is He, warned against transgression concerning what He provided, and warned against the descent of His anger, He opened the door of hope for those who repent, and He used the form of intensification (ṣīghat al-mubālaghah), which is His saying: ﴿And indeed I am Most Forgiving to whoever repents﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "from shirk (polytheism)." ﴿And believes﴾, meaning affirms the oneness of Allah. ﴿And does righteousness﴾, meaning performs the obligations. ﴿Then is guided﴾, meaning adheres to guidance and persists in it until death upon Islam. It has been said: its meaning is that he does not doubt his faith. It has also been said: "then he remains upright." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The view that is strongest regarding the meaning of ﴿then is guided﴾ is that it means: then he preserves his beliefs from opposing the truth in anything, because guidance in this sense is other than faith and other than action." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Guidance is steadfastness and firmness upon the aforementioned guidance, which is repentance, faith and righteous action. A similar expression is: ﴿Indeed, those who say: 'Our Lord is Allah,' then remain steadfast﴾ [Fussilat: 30]. The word of delay (thumma) indicates a difference between the two stations, just as it indicates a difference between two times, as in 'Zayd came to me, then 'Umar.' I mean that the station of steadfastness upon the report is distinct from the station of the report itself, because it is higher and more excellent."

(p-266)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 83–88:

﴿Why has your haste brought you away from your people, O Musa?﴾ ﴿He said: "They are right behind me, and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased."﴾ ﴿He said: "Indeed We have tested your people after you, and al-Samiri has led them astray."﴾ ﴿So Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved. He said: "O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise? Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you, so that you broke your appointment with me?"﴾ ﴿They said: "We did not break our appointment with you by our own will, but we were made to carry burdens of the ornaments of the people, and we cast them, and thus al-Samiri cast."﴾ ﴿Then he brought out for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound. They said: "This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot."﴾ ﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them any word, and possesses for them neither harm nor benefit?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 89].

When Musa, peace be upon him, set out with the Children of Israel towards the right side of the Mount (al-Tur), where the appointment was that Allah would speak to Musa with what contains the honour of this world and the next, he judged, by way of ijtihad (independent reasoning), that he should go ahead alone, hastening to the command of Allah, eager for nearness to Him and longing for His intimate conversation. He appointed Harun over the Children of Israel and said to them: "Proceed towards the side of the Mount." When Musa, peace be upon him, arrived and conversed with his Lord, He extended the term by ten (nights). At that point He made him aware of his hastening ahead of the people, so that Musa would inform Him that they were following on his trail, and thus the information about what they had done would reach him. (Ma) is interrogative, meaning: "What hastened you away from them?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: He had gone with the chiefs (al-nuqaba') to the Mount at the appointed time, then he went ahead of them, out of longing for the speech of his Lord and to fulfil what he had been promised, relying on his own ijtihad, and he thought that this was closer to the pleasure of Allah, and he forgot that He, Mighty and Majestic, determines His acts only in consideration of the requirements of wisdom and knowledge of the interests attached to every time. So by "the people" is meant the chiefs. End.

The apparent meaning is that His words, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿from your people﴾ refer to all the Children of Israel, as we have explained before, not only the seventy. Al-Zamakhshari said: The view of one who permits that "all his people" is meant, and that he had left them before the appointed time, is not a sound view, since His words ﴿They are right behind me﴾ reject it. End.

﴿And what has hastened you﴾ is a question about the cause of the haste, and he answered with His words ﴿They are right behind me, and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾, because His words ﴿And what has hastened you﴾ implied the lateness of his people in coming after him. So he answered, pointing to them because of their nearness to him, that they were right behind him coming to the appointment, as he had been instructed that they should come to the appointment. Then he mentioned the reason that moved him to haste, which is contained in His words ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾: his seeking the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted, by precedence in going to what his Lord had promised him. The meaning of ﴿to You﴾ is "to the place of Your promise", and ﴿that You may be pleased﴾ means "that Your pleasure may endure and continue", since He, the Exalted, was already pleased with him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: "﴿And what has hastened you﴾ is a question about the cause of the haste, so the answer that would fit it would be: 'I sought greater pleasure of Yours and longing for Your speech, and to fulfil Your promise.' But His words ﴿They are right behind me﴾, as you see, do not fit it." I say: What the Lord of Might addressed him with contained two things: one, the denial of haste in itself; the other, the question about the cause of what was disapproved and what prompted it. The more important of the two matters for Musa was to spread out an excuse and prepare the reason for what he was rebuked for. So he pleaded that only a slight advance had come from him, the like of which is not counted in custom nor given weight, and that between me and the one I preceded there is only a short distance, such as a delegation's head and leader would advance by. Then he followed it with the answer to the question about the cause, saying ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾. One may say: he was bewildered by what came upon him of awe at the rebuke of Allah, which distracted him from the fitting answer arranged according to the limits of speech. End. In this there is a lapse of courtesy towards the prophets, peace be upon them.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Mu'adh, on the authority of his father, read ﴿أُولائِي﴾ with a kasra on the ya'. Ibn Wathhab and Isa, in one narration, read ﴿أُولاءِ﴾ with qasr (short vowel). A group read ﴿أُولايَ﴾ with a fatha on the ya'. Isa, Ya'qub, Abd al-Warith on the authority of Abu 'Amr, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿إثْرِي﴾ with a kasra on the hamza and sukun on the tha'. Al-Kisa'i reported ﴿أُثْرِي﴾ with a damma on the hamza and sukun on the tha', and it is narrated from Isa. The majority read ﴿أولاءِ﴾ with the long vowel and hamza, and ﴿أثَرِي﴾ with a fatha on the hamza and tha'. The phrase ﴿عَلى أثَرِي﴾ may be a second predicate after a predicate, or in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

He said: ﴿Indeed We have tested your people after you, and al-Samiri has led them astray﴾, i.e., We tested them by what al-Samiri did, or We cast them into a trial, that is, an inclination towards desires and falling into discord. ﴿After you﴾ means after your departure from them. Al-Zamakhshari said: He meant by "the people" those who were tempted, whom he left with Harun, and they were six hundred thousand, of whom only twelve thousand were saved from worshipping the calf. If you say: the story states that they remained twenty nights after his departure, and they reckoned forty with its days, and said, "We have completed the term," and then the matter of the calf came after that, so how is this reconciled with His words, Exalted, to Musa at his arrival, ﴿Indeed We have tested your people after you﴾? I say: Allah, Exalted, has informed of the trial that was awaited in the wording of what already exists and is in its usual course, and al-Samiri contrived his absence and resolved to mislead them shortly after his departure, and began to arrange that, so the beginning of the trial was already existing. End.

The majority read ﴿وأضَلَّهُمْ﴾ as a past verb. Abu Mu'adh and a group read ﴿وأضَلُّهم﴾ with a damma on the lam, as a subject (mubtada'), with al-Samiri as its predicate, and he was the most astray of them, because he was astray himself and led others astray. It is said: Manja, who was the son of Musa's maternal aunt or his paternal cousin; or a great man of the Children of Israel from a tribe known as the Samaritans; or a non-Arab from Kirman, or from Bajarma; or from the Jews; or from the Copts, who believed in Musa and went out with him, and he was his neighbour; or one of the worshippers of cows who came to Egypt, and entered among the Children of Israel outwardly while in his heart was the worship of the cow. These are the views. The manner of the making of the calf will come in al-A'raf, and before that in al-Baqarah, so its repetition here is unnecessary.

(Ma) is interrogative, meaning: "What hastened you away from them?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: He had gone with the chiefs (al-nuqaba') to the Mount at the appointed time, then he went ahead of them, out of longing for the speech of his Lord and to fulfil what he had been promised, relying on his own ijtihad, and he thought that this was closer to the pleasure of Allah, and he forgot that He, Mighty and Majestic, determines His acts only in consideration of the requirements of wisdom and knowledge of the interests attached to every time. So by "the people" is meant the chiefs. End.

The apparent meaning is that His words, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿from your people﴾ refer to all the Children of Israel, as we have explained before, not only the seventy. Al-Zamakhshari said: The view of one who permits that "all his people" is meant, and that he had left them before the appointed time, is not a sound view, since His words ﴿They are right behind me﴾ reject it. End.

﴿And what has hastened you﴾ is a question about the cause of the haste, and he answered with His words ﴿They are right behind me, and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾, because His words ﴿And what has hastened you﴾ implied the lateness of his people in coming after him. So he answered, pointing to them because of their nearness to him, that they were right behind him coming to the appointment, as he had been instructed that they should come to the appointment. Then he mentioned the reason that moved him to haste, which is contained in His words ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾: his seeking the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted, by precedence in going to what his Lord had promised him. The meaning of ﴿to You﴾ is "to the place of Your promise", and ﴿that You may be pleased﴾ means "that Your pleasure may endure and continue", since He, the Exalted, was already pleased with him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: "﴿And what has hastened you﴾ is a question about the cause of the haste, so the answer that would fit it would be: 'I sought greater pleasure of Yours and longing for Your speech, and to fulfil Your promise.' But His words ﴿They are right behind me﴾, as you see, do not fit it." I say: What the Lord of Might addressed him with contained two things: one, the denial of haste in itself; the other, the question about the cause of what was disapproved and what prompted it. The more important of the two matters for Musa was to spread out an excuse and prepare the reason for what he was rebuked for. So he pleaded that only a slight advance had come from him, the like of which is not counted in custom nor given weight, and that between me and the one I preceded there is only a short distance, such as a delegation's head and leader would advance by. Then he followed it with the answer to the question about the cause, saying ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾. One may say: he was bewildered by what came upon him of awe at the rebuke of Allah, which distracted him from the fitting answer arranged according to the limits of speech. End. In this there is a lapse of courtesy towards the prophets, peace be upon them.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Mu'adh, on the authority of his father, read ﴿أُولائِي﴾ with a kasra on the ya'. Ibn Wathhab and Isa, in one narration, read ﴿أُولاءِ﴾ with qasr (short vowel). A group read ﴿أُولايَ﴾ with a fatha on the ya'. Isa, Ya'qub, Abd al-Warith on the authority of Abu 'Amr, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿إثْرِي﴾ with a kasra on the hamza and sukun on the tha'. Al-Kisa'i reported ﴿أُثْرِي﴾ with a damma on the hamza and sukun on the tha', and it is narrated from Isa. The majority read ﴿أولاءِ﴾ with the long vowel and hamza, and ﴿أثَرِي﴾ with a fatha on the hamza and tha'. The phrase ﴿عَلى أثَرِي﴾ may be a second predicate after a predicate, or in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

He said: ﴿Indeed We have tested your people after you, and al-Samiri has led them astray﴾, i.e., We tested them by what al-Samiri did, or We cast them into a trial, that is, an inclination towards desires and falling into discord. ﴿After you﴾ means after your departure from them. Al-Zamakhshari said: He meant by "the people" those who were tempted, whom he left with Harun, and they were six hundred thousand, of whom only twelve thousand were saved from worshipping the calf. If you say: the story states that they remained twenty nights after his departure, and they reckoned forty with its days, and said, "We have completed the term," and then the matter of the calf came after that, so how is this reconciled with His words, Exalted, to Musa at his arrival, ﴿Indeed We have tested your people after you﴾? I say: Allah, Exalted, has informed of the trial that was awaited in the wording of what already exists and is in its usual course, and al-Samiri contrived his absence and resolved to mislead them shortly after his departure, and began to arrange that, so the beginning of the trial was already existing. End.

The majority read ﴿وأضَلَّهُمْ﴾ as a past verb. Abu Mu'adh and a group read ﴿وأضَلُّهم﴾ with a damma on the lam, as a subject (mubtada'), with al-Samiri as its predicate, and he was the most astray of them, because he was astray himself and led others astray. As for al-Samiri, it is said his name was Musa ibn Zafar. It is said: Manja, who was the son of Musa's maternal aunt or his paternal cousin; or a great man of the Children of Israel from a tribe known as the Samaritans; or a non-Arab from Kirman, or from Bajarma; or from the Jews; or from the Copts, who believed in Musa and went out with him, and he was his neighbour; or one of the worshippers of cows who came to Egypt, and entered among the Children of Israel outwardly while in his heart was the worship of the cow. These are the views. The manner of the making of the calf will come in al-A'raf, and before that in al-Baqarah, so its repetition here is unnecessary.

﴿So Musa returned to his people﴾ [Ta-Ha: 86], after he had completed the forty (nights). ﴿Angry and grieving﴾ [Ta-Ha: 86] is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), and asaf is the most intense form of anger. It has also been said that the grief and anger were of different kinds: his anger was because he had the power to change their wrongdoing, and his asaf, which is grief, was because he knew it was a situation of punishment that he could not repel, and it was unavoidable. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: In the speech of the Arabs, asaf is anger when it comes from one who has power over those below him, and it is grief when it comes from the weaker toward the stronger. Consider this, for it is consistent. Then Musa, peace be upon him, began to rebuke them for leading them astray and for the good promise that he had made to them, namely reaching the right side of the mountain (al-Tur) and what would follow of conquests in the land, forgiveness for those who repent and believe, and other things that Allah promised to the people of His obedience.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Allah promised them, after the forty (nights) were completed, that He would give them the Torah, in which there is guidance and light, and there is no promise better or more beautiful than that.

Al-Hasan said: The good promise is Paradise. It has also been said: it is that He would let them hear His speech. The ʿahd (covenant, here meaning time) refers to his absence from them; it is said ṭāla ʿahdī bi-kadhā, meaning "my time has lengthened because of your absence." Their promise to him was that they would remain upon his command and upon the faith he had left them with, but they broke their promise by worshipping the calf. End of quotation.

﴿Promise﴾, waʿdan (ḥasanan), is in the accusative as a maṣdar (verbal noun). The second object of ﴿yaʿidukum﴾ is omitted, or the promise is used absolutely with the meaning of what is promised, in which case that is the second object. In His words ﴿Has the time seemed long to you?﴾ and to the end, there is a rebuke for excuses that they did not have and that would not be valid for them, namely that the time had been long until it appeared to them that there had been a breach in the promise and that the wrath of Allah was about to descend. None of that had happened, but they acted like those who did not reflect. The punishment was called ghaḍab (wrath) because it arises from wrath. If the word is taken to mean will (irada), then it is an attribute of the Essence; or if it means the manifestation of vengeance and punishment, then it is an attribute of action.

﴿My promise﴾, mawʿidī, is a maṣdar which may be construed with the agent as its genitive, meaning: "Did you find that I broke what I promised you?" This is from the Arabs' saying, "So-and-so broke the promise of so-and-so," when he found that a breach had occurred in it; al-Mufaddal said this. It may also be construed with the object as its genitive, and they had promised him that they would hold fast to the religion of Allah and the sunnah of Musa, peace be upon him, and would never oppose the command of Allah, but they broke their promise to him by worshipping the calf.

Al-Akhawan, al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, and Qaʿnab read bi-mulkinā with a ḍammah on the mīm. Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba, and Ibn Saʿdān read it with a fatḥah on the mīm, and the rest of the seven read it with a kasrah. ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, read bi-malakinā with a fatḥah on the mīm and the lām. Its real meaning is bi-sulṭāninā (by our authority). Thus al-mulk, al-mulk, and al-malk are like naqḍ and nuqḍ (variant forms of one word). Apparently these are dialects and the meaning is one, but Abū ʿAlī and others distinguished between their meanings. The meaning with the ḍammah is that we had no authority, so that we could break your promise by his authority; rather, we broke it by an opinion that led to what al-Samiri did, so the meaning is not that they had authority. This is like the saying of Dhū al-Rumma:

"None of them stumbles, though the wastelands have danced with them until their backs are bent."

That is, there is no stumble from them that would cause complaint. The fatḥah on the mīm is a maṣdar from malaka, and the meaning is: we did not do that because we possessed the right course or stood for it, but our own souls overcame us. The kasrah on the mīm is commonly used for what the hand holds, but it is also used for matters that a person resolves upon, and its meaning is like the one before it. In both of these readings, the maṣdar is in the genitive construction with the agent, and the object is implied: "(what) possesses us" is the right course.

Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, "we did not break your promise" by being in control of our affair; that is, if we had been in control of our affair, and left to our own judgment, we would not have broken it, but we were overcome by al-Samiri and his scheming.

Al-Akhawan, Abū ʿAmr, and Ibn Muḥaysin read ḥummilnā with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ and the mīm. Abū Rajāʾ read it with a ḍammah on the ḥāʾ and a kasrah on the mīm. The rest of the seven, Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba, Ḥumayd, and Yaʿqūb except Rawḥ read it the same way, except that they doubled the mīm. Awzār means loads. It was applied to what they had borrowed from Laqīṭ in the manner of adornment, calling it awzār because of its weight, or because they sinned in it, so it was named awzār when the awzār (sins) resulted from it. The people here are the Copts. It has been said that Musa commanded them to borrow, and it has been said that Allah commanded Musa to do so. It has been said that it is what the sea threw up from what had been on those who drowned. It has been said that the awzār which are sins are because they did not return them to their owners, and the meaning of their bearing sins and throwing them on their backs is like their coming to them bearing their burdens on their backs. It has been said that the meaning of ﴿so we threw them﴾ is that they threw the ornaments onto themselves and their children. It has been said ﴿so we threw it﴾ into the fire, that is, that ornament, and al-Samiri had advised them to do this, so a pit was dug, the fire was kindled in it, and each one who had something of that with him threw it into the fire, and al-Samiri threw what he had with him. The meaning of ﴿thus﴾ is: like our throwing it, ﴿al-Samiri cast﴾ [Ta-Ha: 87] what he had with him. The apparent meaning of these words is that al-Samiri did not make the calf.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Thus al-Samiri cast﴾ [Ta-Ha: 87] showed them that he would cast an ornament into his hand like what they had cast, but he only cast the dust that he had taken from the place where the hoof of Jibril's horse had stepped. His companion, Satan, inspired him that if it touched dead matter it would become living. So al-Samiri brought forth for them from the pit a calf that Allah had created from the ornaments that the fire had melted; it lowed like the lowing of calves. The meaning of His words ﴿We have indeed tried your people﴾ [Ta-Ha: 85] is the creation of the calf as a test; that is, we tested them by the creation of the calf, and al-Samiri led them into error and caused them to fall into it when he said to them ﴿This is your god and the god of Musa﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88]. End of quotation.

It has been said that the meaning of jasadan (a body) is a person. It has been said that it does not eat. What was said about ﴿it had a lowing﴾ [al-A'raf: 148] has already been discussed in al-Aʿraf. The pronoun in ﴿they said﴾ refers to the Children of Israel, meaning that they went astray when their elders said to their young, and ﴿this﴾ refers to the calf. It has been said that the pronoun in ﴿they said﴾ refers to al-Samiri, and it is expressed in the plural to magnify his crime. It has also been said that it refers to him and his followers.

Al-Aʿmash read fanasiya with a sukūn on the yāʾ. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿fanasiya﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88] refers to al-Samiri, meaning ﴿he forgot﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88] his Islam and his faith, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās; or ﴿he abandoned what he had been upon of the religion﴾, as said by Makhul, which is like Ibn ʿAbbās's view. Or ﴿he forgot﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88] that the calf ﴿does not return to them a word, nor does it possess for them any harm or benefit﴾. And ﴿he forgot﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88] the reasoning for the createdness of bodies and that God does not dwell in anything, nor does anything dwell in Him. According to these views, ﴿fanasiya﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88] is a report from Allah about al-Samiri. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to Musa, peace be upon him, meaning ﴿Musa forgot﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88] to mention to you that this is your god, or ﴿Musa forgot﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88] the way to his Lord. Both of these views are reported from Ibn ʿAbbās. Or ﴿Musa forgot﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88] his god with you and went his own way, as said by Qatada. According to these views, it is part of al-Samiri's speech.

Then Allah, exalted is He, showed the corruption of their belief, that divinity is not fitting for one who lacks these attributes, and He said: ﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them a word, and does not possess for them any harm or benefit?﴾ This is like the words of Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿Why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees?﴾ [Maryam: 42]. Here ru'ya (seeing) means ʿilm (knowledge), and for this reason it is followed by anna, the lightened form of the heavy one, as in ﴿Do they not see that it does not speak to them?﴾ [al-A'raf: 148], with the heavy anna. The majority read yarjiʿu with a ḍammah (nominative). Abū Ḥayawa read allā yarjiʿa with a fatḥah on the ʿayn (subjunctive), as Ibn Khālawayh said, and al-Kāmil agreed with him on this. Al-Zaʿfarānī, Ibn Ṣubayḥ, Abān, and al-Shāfiʿī Muḥammad ibn Idrīs al-Imām al-Muṭṭalibī agreed on the accusative of walā yamlik, making anna the one that governs the present tense, and the ru'ya then is from ibṣār (seeing with the eyes).

[p. 270]

﴿Aaron had already said to them, "O my people, you are only being tested by it, and your Lord is the Most Merciful. So follow me and obey my command."﴾ ﴿They said, "We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us."﴾ ﴿He said, "O Aaron, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray, ﴿from following me? Did you then disobey my command?"﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:92-93] ﴿He said, "O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or my head. I feared that you would say, 'You have caused a division among the Children of Israel, and you did not observe my word.'"﴾ [20:94] ﴿He said, "What is your business, O Samiri?"﴾ [20:95] ﴿He said, "I perceived what they did not perceive, so I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger and threw it away. Thus my soul enticed me."﴾ [20:96] ﴿He said, "Then go, for it is yours in this life to say, 'No touching.' And there is a appointed time for you that you will not fail to meet. Look at your god to which you remained devoted; we will surely burn it, then we will scatter it into the sea, scattering."﴾ [20:97] ﴿"Your God is only Allah, other than whom there is no god; He encompasses all things in knowledge."﴾ [20:98]

Aaron showed compassion for himself and for them, and offered them sincere advice. He made clear that what they had turned to regarding the matter of the calf was only a trial (fitna), since he had been commanded by God to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. He was also commanded by his brother Moses, peace be upon him, in the words of God, ﴿"Take my place among my people"﴾ [al-A'raf 7:142], and it was not possible for him to oppose the command of God and the command of his brother.

It is narrated that God revealed to Yusha' (Joshua): "I am going to destroy forty thousand of your people." He said, "My Lord, what of the righteous?" He said, "They did not become angry at My anger."

As for the genitive (al-mudaf ilayhi) that has been cut off from what precedes, "min qablu" (before), al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "before the Samiri said to them what he said," as though when their eyes first fell upon it, when it emerged from the pit, they were tempted by it and found it pleasing, before the Samiri spoke. Aaron, peace be upon him, hastened with his words, ﴿"You are only being tested by it, and your Lord is the Most Merciful."﴾

Ibn 'Atiyya said: God informed us that Aaron had said to them at the very beginning of the calf's appearance, "It is only a trial, a affliction and a deception from the Samiri. Your Lord is the Most Merciful, who possesses power, knowledge, creation and origination." ﴿"So follow me"﴾ to the Mount to which God, exalted is He, promised you, ﴿"and obey my command"﴾ in what I have mentioned to you. End of quotation.

The pronoun in "bihi" (by it) refers to the calf. Aaron first warned them against falsehood and the removal of doubt by saying ﴿"You are only being tested"﴾, then reminded them to know their Lord, and mentioned the attribute of mercy as an indication that whenever they repent, He accepts them, and as a reminder of His rescuing them from Pharaoh's time, when the calf did not exist. Then he commanded them to follow him, as an indication that he was a prophet who must be followed and whose command must be obeyed.

Al-Hasan, 'Isa and Abu 'Amr, in one narration, read "wa-anna Rabbakum" with an opened hamza, whereas the majority read it with a kasra. The verbal noun formed from it occupies the position of the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated form being "and the matter is ﴿'your Lord is the Most Merciful'﴾." Thus it is coordinated as a clause upon a clause. Abu Hatim estimated it as "wa-li-anna Rabbakum al-Rahman" (and because your Lord is the Most Merciful). A group read "anama" and "wa-anna Rabbakum" with both hamzas opened, and the explanation of this reading is according to the dialect of Sulaym, where they open "anna" after verbs of saying in all cases.

When Aaron admonished them and drew their attention to what was right for them, they followed the path of error and ﴿"said, 'We will not cease'"﴾ to worship it, remaining, staying constantly with it. They limited this to the return of Moses. In their saying this there is evidence that they did not return to reasoning, and that the Samiri had led them by imitation. It also shows that "lan" does not necessarily imply perpetuity, contrary to al-Zamakhshari. For if perpetuity were part of its meaning, the limitation by "hatta" (until) would not be permissible, since limitation occurs only where the matter is possibly open, and so the limitation removes that possibility.

[p. 271]

The plural of "qa'" is "aqw'" and "aqwa'" and "qi'an." Makki reported that in the language "qa'" means an exposed place. Some lexicographers said: "qa'" is a pool of standing water. "Al-Saffsaf" is the level, smooth ground; it is also said to be that in which there is no vegetation, and it is doubled like "al-sabsab." "Al-Amt" is a hill. "Al-Iwaj" is crookedness in the mountain passes, as Ibn al-A'rabi said. "Al-Hams" is a faint sound, as Abu 'Ubayda said. It is also said to be the treading of feet. The poet said:

*And they walk with us, whispering (hamisan).*

The lion is called "al-hamus" because of the faintness of its tread, and it is said "hams al-ta'am" for chewing food. "A'naa ya'nu" means to be humbled and submissive; and "a'naahu ghayruhu" means someone else humbled him. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

*A King over the throne of the heavens, Guardian; by His might the faces are humbled and prostrate.*

"Al-Hadm" is diminishment. The Arabs say, "I lowered my right for you," meaning I reduced it. From this is "hadim al-kashhayn," meaning slender of the flanks. In al-Sihah: a man who is "hadim" and "mutahaddim" is wronged; "tahdamahu" and "ihtadamahu" mean he wronged him. Al-Mutawakkil al-Laythi said:

*Indeed the humiliated and the base are a group whose master is the one wronged and oppressed.*

"'Ara ya'ra" means he had no covering over his skin to protect him. The poet said:

*And if the girls are clothed, they would be bare, so the eye turns away from the lean generous one.*

"Duha yadha": he came out into the sun. Amr ibn Abi Rabi'a said:

*She saw a man: when the sun confronted him, he was exposed to it; and in the evening he was present.*

"Al-Dank" is narrowness and hardship. One says "danuka 'ishatan," "yadnuku," "dankan" (a hard life), and a woman is "danak" when her flesh is abundant and her skin becomes so.

"Zahrat" with the ha vowelled or sukun, like "nahr" and "nahar," is what shines of blossom. A lamp is "zahir" when it has a glitter. "Al-anjum al-zahr" are shining stars. "Azhara al-shajar" means the tree's blossom appeared, and it is the flower.

Did you then disobey my command?"﴾ [20:92-93] ﴿He said, "O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or my head. I feared that you would say, 'You have caused a division among the Children of Israel, and you did not observe my word.'"﴾ [20:94] ﴿He said, "What is your business, O Samiri?"﴾ [20:95] ﴿He said, "I perceived what they did not perceive, so I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger and threw it away. Thus my soul enticed me."﴾ [20:96] ﴿He said, "Then go, for it is yours in this life to say, 'No touching.' And there is an appointed time for you that you will not fail to meet. Look at your god to which you remained devoted; we will surely burn it, then we will scatter it into the sea, scattering."﴾ [20:97] ﴿"Your God is only Allah, other than whom there is no god; He encompasses all things in knowledge."﴾ [20:98]

Before His words ﴿He said, "O Harun..."﴾ there is an omitted statement, whose sense is: "Musa returned and found them devoted to the worship of the calf. He said, 'O Harun...'" The calf had appeared on the thirty-sixth day, they worshipped it, and Musa came to them after the completion of the forty days. He reproached Harun for not following him when he saw that they had gone astray. The "la" (not) is extra, as it is in His words ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [al-A'raf: 12]. Ali ibn Isa said: "Here 'la' has entered because the meaning is: 'What called you to not follow me? What led you to not follow me, with those among the believers who were with you?'" ﴿Did you then disobey my command?﴾ refers to His words ﴿Take my place﴾ [al-A'raf: 142], and so on.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "'What prevented you from following me' means: in anger for the sake of God and in severe rebuke against disbelief and sins. 'Why did you not fight those who disbelieved with those who believed?' And 'What was the matter with you that you did not take up the matter as I would have taken it up, had I been present?' Or: 'What was the matter with you that you did not join me?'" In this there is an imposing upon the wording of what it cannot bear, and an excess. Since His words "follow me" do not mention their object, the apparent meaning is "that you should not follow me to Mount Sinai with the Children of Israel." Then Harun's excuse comes with His words ﴿I feared that you would say, "You have caused a division among the Children of Israel"﴾, since only the believers followed him, and the worshippers of the calf remained devoted to it, as they said: ﴿We will not cease to be devoted to it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 91]. It is also possible that the meaning is: "Follow me" means "move according to my course in reform and rectification," so his excuse comes that the matter had grown severe, and if he had strengthened himself against them they would have fought and disagreed, which would have been division among them. Rather, he had only been lenient to the extent of his effort.

Isa ibn Sulayman al-Hijazi read ﴿bi-lihyati﴾ with a fatha on the lam, and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. Musa, peace be upon him, was extremely angry for God and for His religion. When he saw that his people had worshipped a calf besides God, after witnessing the great signs, he could not restrain himself from turning to his brother, seizing him by the hair of his head—he had abundant hair—and by the hair of his face, pulling him toward himself. Then Harun presented his excuse: if he had set some of them against others, they would have dispersed and destroyed one another. So he waited for Musa so that he would be the one to rectify them, and he feared Musa's reproach for abandoning what he had charged him with and for failing to act on its requirements. The discussion of ﴿son of my mother﴾ [al-A'raf: 150] has already preceded, regarding its recitation, its grammatical analysis, and other matters. Abu Ja'far read ﴿wa-lam yurqib﴾ with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the qaf, the imperfect of arqaba.

When his brother had offered his excuse, he returned to addressing the one who had led them into misguidance, namely the Samiri. The discussion of "khatb" has already preceded in Surat Yusuf. Ibn Atiyya said: "﴿What is your affair?﴾ is like your saying 'What is your concern? What is your matter?' But the word 'khatb' implies reproach, because 'khatb' is used for what is disliked; it is as if he said: 'What is your ill-omen and your misfortune? What is this calamity that has come from you?'" End of quote.

This is not as he stated. Do you not see His words, when He said ﴿What is your business, O messengers?﴾ [al-Hijr: 57], which is the statement of Ibrahim to the angels of God? So this does not imply reproach or anything of what he mentioned. Al-Zamakhshari said: "'Khatb' is the verbal noun of 'khataba al-amr' when one seeks it. So when one says to someone doing something, 'What is your khatb?', its meaning is 'What is your seeking of it?'" End of quote. From this is the "khitbah" of marriage, which is the seeking of it. It was also said that it is derived from "khitab" (address), as if he said to him: "What led you to address the Children of Israel with what you addressed them, and to do with them what you did?" ﴿He said, "I perceived what they did not perceive"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 96]. Abu Ubayda said: "I knew what they did not know." Al-Zajjaj said: "'Basura bi-al-shay'' means he knew it, and 'absara' means he looked at it." It was also said: "Basara bihi and absarahu have the same meaning." Al-A'mash and Abu al-Sammak read ﴿basirtu﴾ with a kasra on the sad, and ﴿bima lam tabsaru﴾ with a fatha on the sad. Amr ibn Ubayd read ﴿busirtu﴾ with a damma on the ba' and a damma on the sad, and ﴿bima lam tubsiru﴾ with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the sad, both in the passive. The majority read ﴿basurtu﴾ with a damma on the sad, while Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bahriyya, al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Munadhir, Ibn Sa'dan and Qa'nab read ﴿tabsuru﴾ with the ta' of address, addressed to Musa and the Children of Israel. The rest of the seven read ﴿yabsuru﴾ with the ya' of the third person.

The majority read ﴿faqabadtu qabdatan﴾ with a dad in both, meaning: I took with my palm together with the fingers. Abdullah, Ubayy, Ibn al-Zubayr, Humayd and al-Hasan read it with a sad in both, which is taking with the tips of the fingers. Al-Hasan, in another narration from him, Qatada and Nasr ibn Asim read it with a damma on the qaf and the unpointed sad. Ibn Muhaysin assimilated the pointed dad into the ta' of the speaker, and kept the emphatic quality with the shaddah on the ta'.

The exegetes said that ﴿the messenger﴾ here is Jibril, peace be upon him. Its implied phrase is "from the trace of the horse of the messenger," and so Abdullah also read it. The "athar" is the dust beneath its hoof. ﴿So I threw it﴾ means I cast it upon the jewelry from which the calf was formed, and so there came from it what you saw. Most said: the Samiri saw Jibril on the day the sea was split. It is narrated from Ali that he saw him when Musa went to the mountain and Jibril came to him, and he saw him apart from the people.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: why did He call him 'the messenger' and not Jibril or Ruh al-Qudus?" I say: When the appointed time for going to the mountain arrived, God sent Jibril to Musa, riding Haizum, the horse of life, to take him away. The Samiri saw him and said, "Indeed this has a matter." So he took a handful of the dust of his footprint. When Musa asked him about his story, he said, "I took a handful from the trace of the horse of the one sent to you on the day the appointed time arrived." Perhaps he did not know that it was Jibril." End of quote. This is the view of Ali together with an addition.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: "There is no explicit statement in the Qur'an for what the exegetes have mentioned. Here there is another possibility: that by 'the messenger' is meant Musa, peace be upon him, and his trace is his way and his custom which he commanded. Rather, he had only been lenient to the extent of his effort.

The discussion of ﴿son of my mother﴾ [al-A'raf: 150] has already preceded, regarding its recitation, its grammatical analysis, and other matters. Abu Ja'far read ﴿wa-lam yurqib﴾ with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the qaf, the imperfect of arqaba.

And I had taken a handful from your trace, O messenger, meaning some of your religion, ﴿so I threw it﴾, meaning I cast it away. At that point Musa was informed of what punishment he would have in this world and the Hereafter. He intended only the wording of reporting about an absent party, as a man says to his chief while facing him, "What does the Amir say about such-and-such? Or what does the Amir command?" And calling him "messenger" despite his denial and disbelief is in accordance with the view of those whom God reports as saying ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, you are indeed a madman﴾ [al-Hijr: 6]. It was said: What they said is improbable, because Jibril is not known by the name "messenger," and no prior mention of him has occurred, so that the definite article in "al-rasul" would refer to something previously mentioned. Also, what they said requires an implied phrase, namely "from the trace of the hoof of the horse of the messenger," and implication departs from the original. Also, the Samiri's being singled out to see Jibril and to recognize him among the people is very unlikely. How did he know that the hoof of his horse would produce this strange, wondrous trace of giving life to inanimate matter and turning it into flesh and blood? How did Jibril come to visit a prophet while knowing his prophethood and being certain of it, yet attempt to mislead him? And how did a disbeliever come to know of dust of such a nature? One may answer: perhaps Musa witnessed something else resembling this, and for its sake he brought the miracles, so this would be a flaw in what they brought of extraordinary events. End of quote. This is what this speaker preferred over the view of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani.

And thus did my soul prompt me": that is, just as what happened occurred, my soul made it appealing to me, made it seem fitting that I should do it, and made it my course until I did it. He ordered the Children of Israel to shun him and his tribe, that they should not eat with him or marry him. Al-Zamakhshari said: He was punished in this world with a punishment than which nothing is more grievous or more desolate. And from it is the saying of Ru'bah:

"Until the Azd say, 'No touching.'"

End of quotation.

Thus Musa, peace be upon him, had two rising-up journeys.

And thus did my soul prompt me": that is, just as what happened occurred, my soul made it appealing to me, made it seem fitting that I should do it, and made it my course until I did it. Musa, peace be upon him, would not kill the Children of Israel except for a prescribed penalty (ḥadd) or by revelation (waḥy). So he punished him (the Samiri) by his own independent judgment (ijtihād, reasoned personal effort), by banishing him and removing him from among the people. He ordered the Children of Israel to shun him and his tribe, that they should not eat with him or marry him. He made it his (the Samiri's) condition, for the duration of his life, to say: ﴿No touching﴾, that is, no contact and no approach.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He was punished in this world with a punishment than which nothing is more grievous or more desolate. That is because he was forbidden from mixing with people in a total prohibition (p-275), and it was forbidden for them to meet him, speak with him, trade with him, face him, or engage in any of the dealings by which people live with one another. If he happened to touch anyone, man or woman, both the toucher and the one touched would be struck with fever, so people kept away from him and he kept away from them. He would cry out: ﴿No touching﴾. It is said that this remains among his people to this day. End of quotation.

The claim that fever seizes the one who touches and the one touched is the statement of Qatadah. The command to depart is literal. The particle fa (then) is used to indicate sequence, following the exchange and his expulsion without any temporal delay. He expressed "touching" as a metaphor for "mixing," because touching is the least of the means of association, so by mentioning the lesser he alerted to the greater. The meaning is: there shall be no mixing between you and the people. So he fled from people, clung to the wilderness, abandoned the desert and remained with the wild beasts until he became estranged, and whenever he saw anyone he would say: ﴿No touching﴾, that is, do not touch me and I will not touch you.

It was said: He was afflicted with a torment, and he was told ﴿No touching﴾ by the whisper (waswās), which is what the poet meant by his saying:

"So that became like the Samiri, when Musa said to him, 'No touching.'"

And from it is the saying of Ru'bah:

"Until the Azd say, 'No touching.'"

It was also said: Musa intended to kill him, but God prevented him from killing him because he was an old man. Some of our shaykhs said: Something like this has occurred in our own law, in the story of the three who were left behind, whom the Messenger, peace be upon him, commanded that no one should speak to them or mix with them, and that they should withdraw from their wives until God accepted their repentance.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read ﴿لا مِساسَ﴾ with a fatḥah on the sīn and a kasrah on the mīm of the second element... [note: the text reads: "بِفَتْحِ السِّينِ والمِيمِ المَكْسُورَةِ"], so the reading is: lā misās, with fatḥah on the sīn and kasrah on the mīm. Misās is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of māssa, like qitāl from qātala. It is negated by lā (the one used for the negation of the genus), and this negation is intended as a prohibition, meaning: do not touch me and I will not touch you.

Al-Ḥasan, Abū Ḥaywah, Ibn Abī ʿAbla and Quʿnab read it with a fatḥah on the mīm and a kasrah on the sīn. Ṣāḥib al-Lawāmiḥ (author of al-Lawāmiḥ) said: It is in the form of nizāl and niẓār, from the names of verbs (ism al-fiʿl, verbal nouns functioning as verbs), with the meanings "descend" and "look." These nouns of this pattern are definite (maʿārif), and only the negating lā, which governs indefinite nouns, enters upon them, as in lā māla laka (you have no wealth). But in it there is a negation of the action, so its estimation is: there shall not be from you any misās. I would not say misāsa, and its meaning is prohibition, that is, do not touch me. End of quotation. The apparent sense of this is that misās is a name of a verb.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿لا مِساسَ﴾ is on the pattern of fijār, and similar to it is their saying about gazelles:

"If they come to the water, there is no ʿubāb (cry of thirst); and if they miss it, there is no ibāb (seeking)."

These are proper names (aʿlām) for the act of touching, the cry, and the seeking. The ibāb is a single instance of abb, which is seeking. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: ﴿لا مِساسَ﴾ is a transferred form (maʿdūl) from the verbal noun, like fijār and similar, and Abu ʿUbayda and others compared it to nizāl, dirāk and similar. The comparison is sound in that they are all transferred forms, but it differs from them in that these were transferred from the imperative, whereas misās and fijār were transferred from the verbal noun. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Tamim is like the tribe of the Samiri, and his saying: Surely the Samiri does not desire misās."

End of quotation.

* *

The statements of al-Zamakhshari and Ibn ʿAṭiyya indicate that misās is a transferred form from the verbal noun which is the "touch" (massah), like fijār being transferred from the fajara (the wicked). ﴿وإنَّ لَكَ مَوْعِدًا﴾ means: and indeed for you is an appointment, that is, on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿لَنْ تُخْلَفَهُ﴾ with a damma on the tāʾ and a fatḥah on the lām, meaning: there shall be no failure in it; rather God will fulfil it for you in the Hereafter, for your polytheism and corruption, after He has punished you in this world. Al-Zamakhshari said: This is from akhlaftu al-mawʿid, when you find the appointment broken. Al-Aʿshā said:

"He stayed and shortened his night to provision himself, then went, and broke the appointment with Qutaylah."

Ibn Kathir, al-Aʿmash and Abu ʿAmr read it with a damma on the tāʾ and a kasrah on the lām, meaning: you will not be able to evade it or turn away from it, so that you would be removed from the appointed time of punishment.

Abu Nahik read: lan takhlufahu, with a fatḥah on the tāʾ and a damma on the lām, written thus with a dotted tāʾ above, from Abu Nahik according to the transmission of Ibn Khalawayh. In al-Lawāmiḥ it is: Abu Nahik, lan yakhlufahu, with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and a damma on the lām, from khalafahu yakhlufuhu, when one comes after him, that is: the appointment that is yours will not repel your saying that you will say afterwards: ﴿No touching﴾ in deed, so it is attributed to the appointment; or: the appointment will not differ from what has been decreed for you of punishment in the Hereafter. Sahl, meaning Abu Hatim, said: No school of thought is known for the reading of Abu Nahik. End of quotation.

Ibn Masʿud and al-Ḥasan, with a variant from him, read nakhlifahu with a nūn and a kasrah on the lām, meaning: We will not diminish from the time We promised you anything. Ibn Jinni said: He will not find it failing. Al-Zamakhshari said: God will not fail it, quoting His saying, Mighty and Majestic, as has passed in ﴿لِأَهَبَ لَكِ﴾ [Maryam 19:19], that I may grant you. End of quotation.

* *

Then Musa, peace be upon him, rebuked the Samiri for what he intended to do to the calf, which he had taken as a god, in terms of the outrage against it by altering its form. So he addressed him with the words: ﴿And look at your god﴾, and addressed him alone, since he was the head of misguidance, while he was looking on at their saying: ﴿We will not cease to be devoted to it﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:91]. And he swore: ﴿We will surely burn it﴾, which is the greatest corruption of its form, ﴿then we will surely scatter it into the sea﴾, so that its parts are dispersed and cannot be gathered. It appears that since the Samiri had taken a handful from the hoofprint of Jibrīl's horse while he was in the sea at the time Pharaoh advanced, and Pharaoh followed him into the sea, it was fitting that the calf which the Samiri had fashioned from the jewelry originally belonging to the Copts should be scattered. He cast the handful into it in the sea, so that this would be a warning that what had given it life returned to nothingness. It was cast in the place where the life had resided. And it is said that God cast the wealth of the Copts into the sea in such a way that it could not be benefited from, just as God cast the persons of its owners into the sea and drowned them in it.

Al-Jumhur and Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, in Ibn Yaʿmar's reading, read ﴿ظَلْتَ﴾ with a fatḥah on the ẓāʾ and a sukun on the lām. Ibn Masʿud, Qatadah, al-Aʿmash with a variant from him, Abu Ḥaywah, Ibn Abī ʿAbla and Ibn Yaʿmar with a variant from him likewise, except that they read the ẓāʾ with a kasrah; and from Ibn Yaʿmar a damma on it; and from Ubayy and al-Aʿmash: ẓalilta with two lāms, according to the original form. As for the deletion of the lām, Sibawayh mentioned it as an anomaly, meaning an anomaly of analogy and not an anomaly of usage, with the verb massat, whose original is massist, and aḥassat, whose original is aḥsist. Ibn al-Anbārī mentioned hammat, whose original is hamamt, and this only happens when the final letter of the verb is made quiescent, as in ẓallat, whose original is ẓalilt. Some of those we have known said that this is analogical in every verb doubled in its middle and last radical in the dialect of Banu Sulaym, where the final letter of the verb is made quiescent.

We have examined this question at length in our commentary on al-Tashīl, our own composition. As for the one who read the ẓāʾ with a kasrah, it is because he transferred the vowel of the lām to the ẓāʾ after removing its vowel in estimation, then deleted the lām. As for the one who read it with a damma, it is on the basis that in some dialects the verb came in the pattern with a damma on the middle radical in both, and the damma of the lām was transferred to the ẓāʾ, as was done in the case of the kasrah, as has been established.

* *

Al-Jumhur read ﴿لَنُحَرِّقَنَّهُ﴾ with shadda, the imperfect of ḥarraqa with shadda. Al-Ḥasan, Qatadah, Abu Jaʿfar, Abu Rajāʾ and al-Kalbi read it without shadda, from aḥraqa in the quadriliteral form. ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ḥumayd, Abu Jaʿfar in one narration, and ʿAmr ibn Fāʾid read with a fatḥah on the nūn, a sukun on the ḥāʾ, and a damma on the rāʾ. The apparent meaning is that ḥarraqa and aḥraqa both mean with fire. As for the third reading, its meaning is: "we will surely file it down with a file." It is said: ḥaraqa, yaḥruqu and yaḥriqu, with a damma and a kasrah on the rāʾ of the imperfect. Abu ʿAlī mentioned that the shadda may be intensive in ḥarraqa when it is filed with a file. In the codex of Ubayy and ʿAbdullāh: ﴿لَنَذْبَحَنَّهُ ثُمَّ لَنُحَرِّقَنَّهُ ثُمَّ لَنَنْسِفَنَّهُ﴾ — we will surely slaughter it, then we will surely burn it, then we will surely scatter it. This reading agrees with the one who narrated that it became flesh and blood with a living spirit, and burning with fire is consequent upon this. As for if it was an inanimate object fashioned from jewelry, then filing it down follows, not burning it, unless by it is meant melting it.

Al-Suddi said: Musa was commanded to slaughter the calf, so it was slaughtered and blood flowed from it, then it was burned and its ashes were scattered. It is said: its bones were filed with a file until they reached a state in which they could be scattered.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿لَنَنْسِفَنَّهُ﴾ with a kasrah on the sīn. A group among them, ʿĪsā, read it with a damma on the sīn. Ibn Miqsam read: lanunassifannahu, with a damma on the first nūn, a fatḥah on the second, and shadda on the sīn. The apparent meaning, and the statement of al-Jumhur, is that Musa hastened alone, so the matter of the calf occurred; then Musa came and did to the calf what he did; then after that he went out with the seventy, for the purpose of intercession for the sin of the Children of Israel and so that he might also inform them about the matter of the whispered communion. Thus Musa, peace be upon him, had two rising-up journeys.

(p-٢٧٧) Makki cited a view contrary to this: that Musa was with the seventy at the (divine) conversation, and that the affair of the calf occurred at that time. God informed Musa of it, so he concealed it from them and brought them until they heard the clamour of the Children of Israel around the calf, and then Musa made them aware of it. End of quotation. When he had finished refuting what the Samiri had done, he returned to explaining the true religion and said: ﴿Your God is only God﴾ [Ta-Ha: 98]. The majority of readers read (wasi'a), so that ʿilman is in the accusative as a tamyiz (a specifying accusative, a noun clarifying the sense of a verb or phrase), transferred from the subject. Its parallel was mentioned in al-An'am. Mujahid and Qatada read wassa'a, with the sin doubled. Al-Zamakhshari said: its basis is that wasi'a is transitive to one object, which is "everything" (kull shay'). As for ʿilman, its accusative is as a tamyiz, and in meaning it is the subject. When the verb is made heavier (doubled), it is transferred to be transitive to two objects, and so it puts both in the accusative as objects, because the specified noun is the subject in meaning. As you say: "Zayd feared ʿAmr", and "I made Zayd fear ʿAmr". Thus by the transfer, what was the subject becomes an object. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: (wasi'a) means the creation of things and their multiplicity by bringing them into being, so He encompassed them as existing things. End of quotation.

﴿Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has passed, and We have given you from Us a Reminder﴾. ﴿Whoever turns away from it, he will bear a burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿Abiding therein, and evil is their burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿The Day the Trumpet is blown, and We will gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed﴾. ﴿Whispering among themselves: "You remained only ten"﴾. ﴿We know best what they say, when the most exemplary of them in way says: "You remained only a day"﴾. ﴿And they ask you about the mountains; say: "My Lord will blow them away with a blast"﴾. ﴿And He will leave them a level plain﴾. ﴿You will not see therein any crookedness or unevenness﴾. ﴿That Day they will follow the summoner, with no deviation from him, and voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a whisper﴾.

Thus the demonstrative (dhalika) refers to the account of Musa, the Children of Israel and Pharaoh. That is, as We relate this wondrous account, We relate to you some of the news of the earlier nations. This contains mention of a great blessing, namely the informing of you about the news of past nations, so that you may be consoled by it and know that what the nations did to their messengers, and what the messengers endured from them, is the same. The apparent meaning is that the Reminder here is the Qur'an. He, exalted is He, bestowed a favour upon him by giving him the Reminder, which includes stories and reports, indicating through that miracles that were given to him. Muqatil said: "(dhikran)" means "clarification". Abu Sahl said: "honour and renown among people".

﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾: that is, from the Qur'an, by not believing in it and not following what is in it. The majority read (yahmilu), the present tense of ḥamala, lightly, in the active voice. A group, among them Dawud ibn Rufayʿ, read (yuḥammalu), with the mim doubled, in the passive voice, because he is burdened with that, not that he bears it willingly. (wizran) is the second object. (wizran) means a heavy, crushing weight, which its carrying exhausts, and it is the weight of punishment. Mujahid said: "sin". Al-Thawri said: "polytheism". The apparent meaning is that He expressed the punishment by the word "burden", because it is its cause. Therefore He said ﴿abiding therein﴾, that is, in the punishment and chastisement. He used the plural "abiding" (khalidin), and the pronoun in (lahum) is in agreement with the sense after agreement with its wording in (aʿrada) and in (fa-innahu yahmilu). The thing praised or condemned is omitted, that is, their burden. (lahum) is for clarification, as in ﴿Hayta laka﴾ [Yusuf: 23], not connected to (sa'a). (sa'a) here is the one that functions like (bi'sa), not the (sa'a) meaning "to sadden and worry", because that would corrupt the meaning.

"The day He blows" (yawma nunfakh) is a substitute for "the Day of Resurrection". The majority read (yunfakhu) in the passive voice, and (nahshuru) with the nun in the active voice, the nun of majesty. Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd read (nanfakhu) with the nun of majesty, like (nahshuru). He attributed the blowing to the one who commands it. The one who blows is Israfil, and out of honour for him He attributed what he undertakes to His own sanctified self. (al-Suwar) (the Trumpet) has been discussed in al-An'am. It was also read (yanfakhu) and (yahshuru) with the ya' in both, in the active voice. al-Hasan and Ibn ʿIyad, with a group, read ﴿fi al-Suwar﴾ on the pattern of (durar). Al-Hasan also read (yuhsharu) with the ya', in the passive voice, and (yahshuru) in the active voice, with the ya', that is, "and Allah gathers". The apparent meaning of "blue" (zurq) is the blueness of the eyes. Blue eyes were the most hated eye colour among the Arabs, because the Romans, who were their enemies, had blue eyes. For this reason they described the enemy as: "black-livered, reddish-moustached, blue-eyed". A poet said:

"I never feared that his death would be by the hand of a blue-eyed, lowered-eyed, Sabani horseman."

It is mentioned in another verse that they will be gathered with black faces, so the meaning is the disfiguring of the appearance, through the blackness of the face and the blueness of the eye. Also, the Arabs regard blueness as a bad omen. A poet said:

"Your eyes have grown dim, O son of Mukaʿbar! Surely every Dabbi is blue from baseness."

It was said: the meaning is "blind", because when the eye's light departs, its pupil turns blue. With this interpretation, the combination of His words "blue" (zurqan) in this verse and "blind" (ʿumyan) in the other verse is reconciled. It was said: the colours of their bodies turn blue, and this is extreme disfigurement, since they come like the colour of ash. In Arabic speech this colour is called blue. Skins do not turn blue except from enduring hardships and the drying of their moisture. It was said: (zurqan) means "thirsty", and severe thirst returns the blackness of the eye to whiteness. From this comes the saying "a blue spear-head", and his words:

"When they reached the water, blue with its crowd" —

that is, it turned white. The two verses were mentioned to Ibn ʿAbbas, and he said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: in one state they will be blue, and in another state they will be blind."

﴿Whispering (yatakhafatun)﴾: they speak secretly to one another out of the terror of the appearance and the intense distraction of their minds. The amount of time they remained has escaped them. ﴿You remained﴾: that is, in the abode of this world, or in the barzakh (intermediate state), or between the two blasts of the Trumpet. There are three opinions. Describing the time they spent there as short is because, compared with what they witness of hardships, the days they had in this world were days of joy, and days of joy are short. Or because of their departure from them and their passing. Whatever its duration, the thing that has gone is short in that it has ended. Or because they regard the Hereafter as long, and as everlasting and eternal, against which the life of this world is considered short. It is said: its people remained in it, in comparison with their remaining in the Hereafter. (idh) is governed by (aʿlam). (amthaluhum) means "the most upright of them". (ṭarīqatan) is in the accusative as a tamyiz.

﴿Except a day﴾ indicates the brevity of the period they remained. ﴿Except ten﴾ may mean ten nights or ten days, because when the masculine noun is omitted and its number kept, the feminine ta' may not be used. al-Kisai related from Abu al-Jarrah: "We fasted five from the month", and from this is what came in the hadith: "Then he followed it with six from Shawwal", meaning six days. The omission here is made good by the fact that this is the end of a verse, and by the fact that the first mention was the upper limit of the smallest number, which is ten. And he mentioned the most upright of them in way as the smallest number, which is one day. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿except a day﴾ shows that what is meant by their words ﴿ten﴾ is ten days.

* *

The third person pronoun in ﴿They ask you﴾ refers to the Quraysh who denied the Resurrection, or to the believers who asked about that, or to a man from Thaqif and a group from his people. There are three opinions. The second-person (ka) is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that the question did occur. The view of one who said there was no question is far-fetched; rather the meaning is that they would ask you ﴿about the mountains, then say﴾, so it implies the conditional, and therefore it is answered with the fa'. It is narrated that God sends a wind upon the mountains, which pounds them until they are like carded wool, then it continues upon them until it reduces them to dust scattered in the air. That is the (nasf), the blowing away. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿fa-yadharuha﴾ refers to the mountains, that is, after the blowing away they remain ﴿a level plain﴾, that is, flat, even ground. It was said: "He leaves their places of settlement and centres". It was said: it refers to the earth, though no mention of it has preceded, because the mountains indicate it.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: (ʿiwajan) means "a slope", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a trace like the thong of a sandal". From him also: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a valley", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a hill". From him also: "al-amt is elevation". Qatada said: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a fissure", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a mound". It was said: al-amt means cracks in the earth. It was said: a slight unevenness in a place in open country and mountain, and a flash in a place, as reported by al-Sulli. It was said: the amt in the verse is the ʿiwaj (crookedness) in the sky, facing the air, while the ʿiwaj in the earth is specific to the earth.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "They have distinguished between ʿiwaj and ʿawaj; they said: ʿiwaj with a kasra is used for meanings, and ʿawaj with a fatha is used for physical objects and the earth. How then is the form with kasra under the ʿayn valid for it?" I say: the choice of this word has a fine and striking effect in describing the earth as level and smooth and negating crookedness from it in the most emphatic way. That is because if you took a piece of land, levelled it, and went to great lengths in levelling it, by your own eye and the eyes of the keen-sighted among the farmers, and you all agreed that there remained no crookedness in it at all, then if you consulted an engineer about it and ordered him to test its evenness by the geometric measures, he would find crookedness in some place which cannot be perceived by the sense of sight, but only by geometric measurement. So God, mighty and majestic, negated that crookedness which is so subtle and fine as to escape perception, except by the measure known to the one who understands measurement and geometry. Since that crookedness is not perceived except by measurement and not by the senses, it is treated as an abstract meaning, so it is called ʿiwaj with a kasra. al-Amt is the slight protrusion. It is said: "He stretched his rope until there was no amt in it." End of quotation.

* *

(On that day) that is, the day on which God blows away the mountains, (they will follow) that is, the creatures will follow (the summoner) the summoner of God to the place of gathering, like His words: ﴿hastening toward the summoner﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]. He is Israfil, who stands on the rock of Jerusalem calling the people, and they come from every direction. He puts the trumpets to his mouth and says: "O decayed bones, torn skins, and scattered flesh, come forward to be presented before the Most Merciful." Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: "They will be gathered in darkness, the sky will have been folded up and the stars scattered. Then a caller will call out, and they will die a single death." ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: "(al-dāʿī) here is the Messenger (ﷺ), who used to call them to God. They will deviate from the path to the right and to the left, turning away from him with great deviation. So on that day following him will not benefit them." The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (lahu) refers to ﴿al-dāʿī﴾. He negated crookedness from him, that is, ﴿no crookedness﴾ is theirs in regard to him; rather they come towards him, following his voice without deviation. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, no one invited by him is made crooked; rather they go straight to him. End of quotation.

* *

It was said: ﴿no crookedness for him﴾ is in the place of a description of a suppressed noun, that is, following ﴿no crookedness for him﴾, so the pronoun in (lahu) refers to that omitted verbal noun. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it may be intended as a report, that is, there is no doubt about it, and its existence does not contradict its report. It may also be intended as: no one can escape from following it, and walking towards its voice. Al-khushu' is humility and lowliness, and in regard to voices it is a metaphor meaning concealment. The "hushing" (istisrar) is for the Most Merciful, that is, out of awe of the Most Merciful, whose power is evident. It was said: it is by omission of a modifier, that is, "and the people of voices were humbled." Al-hams is a low, hidden sound. It may be intended that the whispering is what is heard, their secret speech among themselves. It may also be intended as the sound of footsteps, and that the sounds of speech are silent.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿Except a whisper﴾": it is a faint sound (al-rikz al-khafi), and from it comes the term "unvoiced letters" (al-huruf al-mahmusa). It has also been said that it derives from the whispering of camels, which is the sound of their hooves when they walk; meaning that nothing is heard except the tread of feet and their movement toward the gathering place. End of quote.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and Ibn Jubayr that al-hams is the treading of feet, and al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj preferred this view. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the moving of the lips without uttering sound, and from Mujahid that it is quiet speech. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "﴿So they will not speak except in a whisper﴾." From Abu 'Ubayda: "al-sawt al-khafi" (the faint sound). "That Day" is a substitute for "That Day they will follow"; or the sense is "the Day when they will follow," and it is in the accusative governed by "will not benefit." "Man" is the object of "﴿will not benefit﴾," and "lahu" means "for his sake," as also in "﴿and whose words He approves﴾," meaning for his sake. "Man" may refer to the one for whom intercession is made, or it may be a substitute for "intercession," with an elided noun, meaning "except the intercession of one whom He has permitted." The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "﴿what is before them and what is behind them﴾" refers to the created beings gathered, who are the followers of the caller. It has been said that it refers to the angels, and it has been said that it refers to people in general, not restricted to the gathering and following. The explanation of this phrase has already been given in the Verse of the Throne in al-Baqara. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to "ma" (what): "﴿and they do not encompass it﴾ in knowledge," that is, of His knowledge. The apparent sense is that "the faces" is general, meaning the faces of all creatures, and "the faces" was specified because the signs of humiliation first appear on the faces. Talq ibn Habib said: the intended meaning is the prostration of people upon their faces and the seven limbs. If he related that this will occur on the Day of Resurrection, then the verse is a report about it, and the meaning is sound; but if he meant in this world, then that is not consistent with the verses before and after it. Al-Zamakhshari said: by "faces" is meant the faces of the disobedient, and that when they witness on the Day of Resurrection disappointment, wretchedness and evil reckoning, their faces become "humbled," that is, abased and submissive, like the faces of captives, the prisoners; and similar is "﴿So when they see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed﴾" [al-Mulk: 27] and "﴿And faces that Day will be gloomy﴾" [al-Qiyama: 24]. (p-٢٧٧) Makki cited a view contrary to this: that Musa was with the seventy at the (divine) conversation, and that the affair of the calf occurred at that time. God informed Musa of it, so he concealed it from them and brought them until they heard the clamour of the Children of Israel around the calf, and then Musa made them aware of it. End of quotation. When he had finished refuting what the Samiri had done, he returned to explaining the true religion and said: ﴿Your God is only God﴾ [Ta-Ha: 98]. The majority of readers read (wasi'a), so that ʿilman is in the accusative as a tamyiz (a specifying accusative, a noun clarifying the sense of a verb or phrase), transferred from the subject. When the verb is made heavier (doubled), it is transferred to be transitive to two objects, and so it puts both in the accusative as objects, because the specified noun is the subject in meaning. ﴿Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has passed, and We have given you from Us a Reminder﴾. ﴿Whoever turns away from it, he will bear a burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿Abiding therein, and evil is their burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿The Day the Trumpet is blown, and We will gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed﴾. ﴿Whispering among themselves: "You remained only ten"﴾. ﴿We know best what they say, when the most exemplary of them in way says: "You remained only a day"﴾. ﴿And they ask you about the mountains; say: "My Lord will blow them away with a blast"﴾. ﴿And He will leave them a level plain﴾. ﴿You will not see therein any crookedness or unevenness﴾. ﴿That Day they will follow the summoner, with no deviation from him, and voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a whisper﴾.

Thus the demonstrative (dhalika) refers to the account of Musa, the Children of Israel and Pharaoh. That is, as We relate this wondrous account, We relate to you some of the news of the earlier nations. This contains mention of a great blessing, namely the informing of you about the news of past nations, so that you may be consoled by it and know that what the nations did to their messengers, and what the messengers endured from them, is the same. The apparent meaning is that the Reminder here is the Qur'an. He, exalted is He, bestowed a favour upon him by giving him the Reminder, which includes stories and reports, indicating through that miracles that were given to him. Muqatil said: "(dhikran)" means "clarification". Abu Sahl said: "honour and renown among people".

﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾: that is, from the Qur'an, by not believing in it and not following what is in it. The majority read (yahmilu), the present tense of ḥamala, lightly, in the active voice. A group, among them Dawud ibn Rufayʿ, read (yuḥammalu), with the mim doubled, in the passive voice, because he is burdened with that, not that he bears it willingly. (wizran) is the second object. The apparent meaning is that He expressed the punishment by the word "burden", because it is its cause. Therefore He said ﴿abiding therein﴾, that is, in the punishment and chastisement. He used the plural "abiding" (khalidin), and the pronoun in (lahum) is in agreement with the sense after agreement with its wording in (aʿrada) and in (fa-innahu yahmilu). The thing praised or condemned is omitted, that is, their burden. (lahum) is for clarification, as in ﴿Hayta laka﴾ [Yusuf: 23], not connected to (sa'a). (sa'a) here is the one that functions like (bi'sa), not the (sa'a) meaning "to sadden and worry", because that would corrupt the meaning.

"The day He blows" (yawma nunfakh) is a substitute for "the Day of Resurrection". The majority read (yunfakhu) in the passive voice, and (nahshuru) with the nun in the active voice, the nun of majesty. Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd read (nanfakhu) with the nun of majesty, like (nahshuru). He attributed the blowing to the one who commands it. The one who blows is Israfil, and out of honour for him He attributed what he undertakes to His own sanctified self. (al-Suwar) (the Trumpet) has been discussed in al-An'am. Al-Hasan also read (yuhsharu) with the ya', in the passive voice, and (yahshuru) in the active voice, with the ya', that is, "and Allah gathers". The apparent meaning of "blue" (zurq) is the blueness of the eyes. Blue eyes were the most hated eye colour among the Arabs, because the Romans, who were their enemies, had blue eyes. For this reason they described the enemy as: "black-livered, reddish-moustached, blue-eyed". A poet said:

"I never feared that his death would be by the hand of a blue-eyed, lowered-eyed, Sabani horseman."

It is mentioned in another verse that they will be gathered with black faces, so the meaning is the disfiguring of the appearance, through the blackness of the face and the blueness of the eye. Also, the Arabs regard blueness as a bad omen. A poet said:

"Your eyes have grown dim, O son of Mukaʿbar! Surely every Dabbi is blue from baseness."

It was said: the meaning is "blind", because when the eye's light departs, its pupil turns blue. With this interpretation, the combination of His words "blue" (zurqan) in this verse and "blind" (ʿumyan) in the other verse is reconciled. It was said: the colours of their bodies turn blue, and this is extreme disfigurement, since they come like the colour of ash. In Arabic speech this colour is called blue. Skins do not turn blue except from enduring hardships and the drying of their moisture. It was said: (zurqan) means "thirsty", and severe thirst returns the blackness of the eye to whiteness. From this comes the saying "a blue spear-head", and his words:

"When they reached the water, blue with its crowd" —

that is, it turned white. The two verses were mentioned to Ibn ʿAbbas, and he said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: in one state they will be blue, and in another state they will be blind."

﴿Whispering (yatakhafatun)﴾: they speak secretly to one another out of the terror of the appearance and the intense distraction of their minds. The amount of time they remained has escaped them. ﴿You remained﴾: that is, in the abode of this world, or in the barzakh (intermediate state), or between the two blasts of the Trumpet. There are three opinions. Describing the time they spent there as short is because, compared with what they witness of hardships, the days they had in this world were days of joy, and days of joy are short. Or because of their departure from them and their passing. Whatever its duration, the thing that has gone is short in that it has ended. Or because they regard the Hereafter as long, and as everlasting and eternal, against which the life of this world is considered short. It is said: its people remained in it, in comparison with their remaining in the Hereafter. (idh) is governed by (aʿlam). (amthaluhum) means "the most upright of them". (ṭarīqatan) is in the accusative as a tamyiz.

﴿Except a day﴾ indicates the brevity of the period they remained. ﴿Except ten﴾ may mean ten nights or ten days, because when the masculine noun is omitted and its number kept, the feminine ta' may not be used. al-Kisai related from Abu al-Jarrah: "We fasted five from the month", and from this is what came in the hadith: "Then he followed it with six from Shawwal", meaning six days. The omission here is made good by the fact that this is the end of a verse, and by the fact that the first mention was the upper limit of the smallest number, which is ten. And he mentioned the most upright of them in way as the smallest number, which is one day. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿except a day﴾ shows that what is meant by their words ﴿ten﴾ is ten days.

* *

The third person pronoun in ﴿They ask you﴾ refers to the Quraysh who denied the Resurrection, or to the believers who asked about that, or to a man from Thaqif and a group from his people.
