The view of one who said there was no question is far-fetched; rather the meaning is that they would ask you ﴿about the mountains, then say﴾, so it implies the conditional, and therefore it is answered with the fa'. It is narrated that God sends a wind upon the mountains, which pounds them until they are like carded wool, then it continues upon them until it reduces them to dust scattered in the air. That is the (nasf), the blowing away. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿fa-yadharuha﴾ refers to the mountains, that is, after the blowing away they remain ﴿a level plain﴾, that is, flat, even ground. It was said: "He leaves their places of settlement and centres". It was said: it refers to the earth, though no mention of it has preceded, because the mountains indicate it.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: (ʿiwajan) means "a slope", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a trace like the thong of a sandal". From him also: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a valley", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a hill". From him also: "al-amt is elevation". Qatada said: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a fissure", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a mound". It was said: al-amt means cracks in the earth. It was said: a slight unevenness in a place in open country and mountain, and a flash in a place, as reported by al-Sulli. It was said: the amt in the verse is the ʿiwaj (crookedness) in the sky, facing the air, while the ʿiwaj in the earth is specific to the earth.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "They have distinguished between ʿiwaj and ʿawaj; they said: ʿiwaj with a kasra is used for meanings, and ʿawaj with a fatha is used for physical objects and the earth. How then is the form with kasra under the ʿayn valid for it?" I say: the choice of this word has a fine and striking effect in describing the earth as level and smooth and negating crookedness from it in the most emphatic way. That is because if you took a piece of land, levelled it, and went to great lengths in levelling it, by your own eye and the eyes of the keen-sighted among the farmers, and you all agreed that there remained no crookedness in it at all, then if you consulted an engineer about it and ordered him to test its evenness by the geometric measures, he would find crookedness in some place which cannot be perceived by the sense of sight, but only by geometric measurement. So God, mighty and majestic, negated that crookedness which is so subtle and fine as to escape perception, except by the measure known to the one who understands measurement and geometry. Since that crookedness is not perceived except by measurement and not by the senses, it is treated as an abstract meaning, so it is called ʿiwaj with a kasra. al-Amt is the slight protrusion. It is said: "He stretched his rope until there was no amt in it." End of quotation.

(On that day) that is, the day on which God blows away the mountains, (they will follow) that is, the creatures will follow (the summoner) the summoner of God to the place of gathering, like His words: ﴿hastening toward the summoner﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]. He is Israfil, who stands on the rock of Jerusalem calling the people, and they come from every direction. He puts the trumpets to his mouth and says: "O decayed bones, torn skins, and scattered flesh, come forward to be presented before the Most Merciful." Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: "They will be gathered in darkness, the sky will have been folded up and the stars scattered. Then a caller will call out, and they will die a single death." ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: "(al-dāʿī) here is the Messenger (ﷺ), who used to call them to God. They will deviate from the path to the right and to the left, turning away from him with great deviation. So on that day following him will not benefit them." The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (lahu) refers to ﴿al-dāʿī﴾. He negated crookedness from him, that is, ﴿no crookedness﴾ is theirs in regard to him; rather they come towards him, following his voice without deviation. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, no one invited by him is made crooked; rather they go straight to him. End of quotation.

It was said: ﴿no crookedness for him﴾ is in the place of a description of a suppressed noun, that is, following ﴿no crookedness for him﴾, so the pronoun in (lahu) refers to that omitted verbal noun. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it may be intended as a report, that is, there is no doubt about it, and its existence does not contradict its report. It may also be intended as: no one can escape from following it, and walking towards its voice. Al-khushu' is humility and lowliness, and in regard to voices it is a metaphor meaning concealment. The "hushing" (istisrar) is for the Most Merciful, that is, out of awe of the Most Merciful, whose power is evident. It was said: it is by omission of a modifier, that is, "and the people of voices were humbled." Al-hams is a low, hidden sound. It may be intended that the whispering is what is heard, their secret speech among themselves. It may also be intended as the sound of footsteps, and that the sounds of speech are silent.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿Except a whisper﴾": it is a faint sound (al-rikz al-khafi), and from it comes the term "unvoiced letters" (al-huruf al-mahmusa). It has also been said that it derives from the whispering of camels, which is the sound of their hooves when they walk; meaning that nothing is heard except the tread of feet and their movement toward the gathering place. End of quote.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿fa-yadharuha﴾ refers to the mountains, that is, after the blowing away they remain ﴿a level plain﴾, that is, flat, even ground. It was said: "He leaves their places of settlement and centres". It was said: it refers to the earth, though no mention of it has preceded, because the mountains indicate it.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: (ʿiwajan) means "a slope", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a trace like the thong of a sandal". From him also: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a valley", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a hill". From him also: "al-amt is elevation". Qatada said: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a fissure", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a mound". It was said: al-amt means cracks in the earth. It was said: a slight unevenness in a place in open country and mountain, and a flash in a place, as reported by al-Sulli. It was said: the amt in the verse is the ʿiwaj (crookedness) in the sky, facing the air, while the ʿiwaj in the earth is specific to the earth.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "They have distinguished between ʿiwaj and ʿawaj; they said: ʿiwaj with a kasra is used for meanings, and ʿawaj with a fatha is used for physical objects and the earth. How then is the form with kasra under the ʿayn valid for it?" I say: the choice of this word has a fine and striking effect in describing the earth as level and smooth and negating crookedness from it in the most emphatic way. That is because if you took a piece of land, levelled it, and went to great lengths in levelling it, by your own eye and the eyes of the keen-sighted among the farmers, and you all agreed that there remained no crookedness in it at all, then if you consulted an engineer about it and ordered him to test its evenness by the geometric measures, he would find crookedness in some place which cannot be perceived by the sense of sight, but only by geometric measurement. So God, mighty and majestic, negated that crookedness which is so subtle and fine as to escape perception, except by the measure known to the one who understands measurement and geometry. Since that crookedness is not perceived except by measurement and not by the senses, it is treated as an abstract meaning, so it is called ʿiwaj with a kasra. al-Amt is the slight protrusion. It is said: "He stretched his rope until there was no amt in it." End of quotation.

* *

(On that day) that is, the day on which God blows away the mountains, (they will follow) that is, the creatures will follow (the summoner) the summoner of God to the place of gathering, like His words: ﴿hastening toward the summoner﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]. He is Israfil, who stands on the rock of Jerusalem calling the people, and they come from every direction. He puts the trumpets to his mouth and says: "O decayed bones, torn skins, and scattered flesh, come forward to be presented before the Most Merciful." Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: "They will be gathered in darkness, the sky will have been folded up and the stars scattered. Then a caller will call out, and they will die a single death." ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: "(al-dāʿī) here is the Messenger (ﷺ), who used to call them to God. They will deviate from the path to the right and to the left, turning away from him with great deviation. So on that day following him will not benefit them." The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (lahu) refers to ﴿al-dāʿī﴾. He negated crookedness from him, that is, ﴿no crookedness﴾ is theirs in regard to him; rather they come towards him, following his voice without deviation. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, no one invited by him is made crooked; rather they go straight to him. End of quotation.

* *

It was said: ﴿no crookedness for him﴾ is in the place of a description of a suppressed noun, that is, following ﴿no crookedness for him﴾, so the pronoun in (lahu) refers to that omitted verbal noun. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it may be intended as a report, that is, there is no doubt about it, and its existence does not contradict its report. It may also be intended as: no one can escape from following it, and walking towards its voice. Al-khushu' is humility and lowliness, and in regard to voices it is a metaphor meaning concealment. The "hushing" (istisrar) is for the Most Merciful, that is, out of awe of the Most Merciful, whose power is evident. It was said: it is by omission of a modifier, that is, "and the people of voices were humbled." Al-hams is a low, hidden sound. It may be intended that the whispering is what is heard, their secret speech among themselves. It may also be intended as the sound of footsteps, and that the sounds of speech are silent.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿Except a whisper﴾": it is a faint sound (al-rikz al-khafi), and from it comes the term "unvoiced letters" (al-huruf al-mahmusa). It has also been said that it derives from the whispering of camels, which is the sound of their hooves when they walk; meaning that nothing is heard except the tread of feet and their movement toward the gathering place. End of quote.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and Ibn Jubayr that al-hams is the treading of feet, and al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj preferred this view. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the moving of the lips without uttering sound, and from Mujahid that it is quiet speech. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "﴿So they will not speak except in a whisper﴾." From Abu 'Ubayda: "al-sawt al-khafi" (the faint sound). "That Day" is a substitute for "That Day they will follow"; or the sense is "the Day when they will follow," and it is in the accusative governed by "will not benefit." "Man" is the object of "﴿will not benefit﴾," and "lahu" means "for his sake," as also in "﴿and whose words He approves﴾," meaning for his sake. "Man" may refer to the one for whom intercession is made, or it may be a substitute for "intercession," with an elided noun, meaning "except the intercession of one whom He has permitted." Or it may be an exceptive in the accusative on this reading, or a disjunctive exception, in which case it is accusative in the Hijazi dialect and nominative in the Tamim dialect. In all these interpretations "man" refers to the intercessor. The "word that is approved" is, according to Ibn 'Abbas, "There is no god but Allah."

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "﴿what is before them and what is behind them﴾" refers to the created beings gathered, who are the followers of the caller. It has been said that it refers to the angels, and it has been said that it refers to people in general, not restricted to the gathering and following. The explanation of this phrase has already been given in the Verse of the Throne in al-Baqara. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to "ma" (what): "﴿and they do not encompass it﴾ in knowledge," that is, of His knowledge. The apparent sense is that "the faces" is general, meaning the faces of all creatures, and "the faces" was specified because the signs of humiliation first appear on the faces. Talq ibn Habib said: the intended meaning is the prostration of people upon their faces and the seven limbs. If he related that this will occur on the Day of Resurrection, then the verse is a report about it, and the meaning is sound; but if he meant in this world, then that is not consistent with the verses before and after it. Al-Zamakhshari said: by "faces" is meant the faces of the disobedient, and that when they witness on the Day of Resurrection disappointment, wretchedness and evil reckoning, their faces become "humbled," that is, abased and submissive, like the faces of captives, the prisoners; and similar is "﴿So when they see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed﴾" [al-Mulk: 27] and "﴿And faces that Day will be gloomy﴾" [al-Qiyama: 24]. As for "al-Qayyum," its discussion has already been given in al-Baqara.

(p-٢٧٧) Makki cited a view contrary to this: that Musa was with the seventy at the (divine) conversation, and that the affair of the calf occurred at that time. God informed Musa of it, so he concealed it from them and brought them until they heard the clamour of the Children of Israel around the calf, and then Musa made them aware of it. End of quotation. When he had finished refuting what the Samiri had done, he returned to explaining the true religion and said: ﴿Your God is only God﴾ [Ta-Ha: 98]. The majority of readers read (wasi'a), so that ʿilman is in the accusative as a tamyiz (a specifying accusative, a noun clarifying the sense of a verb or phrase), transferred from the subject. Its parallel was mentioned in al-An'am. Mujahid and Qatada read wassa'a, with the sin doubled. Al-Zamakhshari said: its basis is that wasi'a is transitive to one object, which is "everything" (kull shay'). As for ʿilman, its accusative is as a tamyiz, and in meaning it is the subject. When the verb is made heavier (doubled), it is transferred to be transitive to two objects, and so it puts both in the accusative as objects, because the specified noun is the subject in meaning. As you say: "Zayd feared ʿAmr", and "I made Zayd fear ʿAmr". Thus by the transfer, what was the subject becomes an object. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: (wasi'a) means the creation of things and their multiplicity by bringing them into being, so He encompassed them as existing things. End of quotation.

﴿Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has passed, and We have given you from Us a Reminder﴾. ﴿Whoever turns away from it, he will bear a burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿Abiding therein, and evil is their burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿The Day the Trumpet is blown, and We will gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed﴾. ﴿Whispering among themselves: "You remained only ten"﴾. ﴿We know best what they say, when the most exemplary of them in way says: "You remained only a day"﴾. ﴿And they ask you about the mountains; say: "My Lord will blow them away with a blast"﴾. ﴿And He will leave them a level plain﴾. ﴿You will not see therein any crookedness or unevenness﴾. ﴿That Day they will follow the summoner, with no deviation from him, and voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a whisper﴾.

Thus the demonstrative (dhalika) refers to the account of Musa, the Children of Israel and Pharaoh. That is, as We relate this wondrous account, We relate to you some of the news of the earlier nations. This contains mention of a great blessing, namely the informing of you about the news of past nations, so that you may be consoled by it and know that what the nations did to their messengers, and what the messengers endured from them, is the same. The apparent meaning is that the Reminder here is the Qur'an. He, exalted is He, bestowed a favour upon him by giving him the Reminder, which includes stories and reports, indicating through that miracles that were given to him. Muqatil said: "(dhikran)" means "clarification". Abu Sahl said: "honour and renown among people".

﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾: that is, from the Qur'an, by not believing in it and not following what is in it. The majority read (yahmilu), the present tense of ḥamala, lightly, in the active voice. A group, among them Dawud ibn Rufayʿ, read (yuḥammalu), with the mim doubled, in the passive voice, because he is burdened with that, not that he bears it willingly. (wizran) is the second object. (wizran) means a heavy, crushing weight, which its carrying exhausts, and it is the weight of punishment. Mujahid said: "sin". Al-Thawri said: "polytheism". The apparent meaning is that He expressed the punishment by the word "burden", because it is its cause. Therefore He said ﴿abiding therein﴾, that is, in the punishment and chastisement. He used the plural "abiding" (khalidin), and the pronoun in (lahum) is in agreement with the sense after agreement with its wording in (aʿrada) and in (fa-innahu yahmilu). The thing praised or condemned is omitted, that is, their burden. (lahum) is for clarification, as in ﴿Hayta laka﴾ [Yusuf: 23], not connected to (sa'a). (sa'a) here is the one that functions like (bi'sa), not the (sa'a) meaning "to sadden and worry", because that would corrupt the meaning.

"The day He blows" (yawma nunfakh) is a substitute for "the Day of Resurrection". The majority read (yunfakhu) in the passive voice, and (nahshuru) with the nun in the active voice, the nun of majesty. Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd read (nanfakhu) with the nun of majesty, like (nahshuru). He attributed the blowing to the one who commands it. The one who blows is Israfil, and out of honour for him He attributed what he undertakes to His own sanctified self. (al-Suwar) (the Trumpet) has been discussed in al-An'am. It was also read (yanfakhu) and (yahshuru) with the ya' in both, in the active voice. al-Hasan and Ibn ʿIyad, with a group, read ﴿fi al-Suwar﴾ on the pattern of (durar). Al-Hasan also read (yuhsharu) with the ya', in the passive voice, and (yahshuru) in the active voice, with the ya', that is, "and Allah gathers". The apparent meaning of "blue" (zurq) is the blueness of the eyes. Blue eyes were the most hated eye colour among the Arabs, because the Romans, who were their enemies, had blue eyes. For this reason they described the enemy as: "black-livered, reddish-moustached, blue-eyed". A poet said:

"I never feared that his death would be by the hand of a blue-eyed, lowered-eyed, Sabani horseman."

It is mentioned in another verse that they will be gathered with black faces, so the meaning is the disfiguring of the appearance, through the blackness of the face and the blueness of the eye. Also, the Arabs regard blueness as a bad omen. A poet said:

"Your eyes have grown dim, O son of Mukaʿbar! Surely every Dabbi is blue from baseness."

It was said: the meaning is "blind", because when the eye's light departs, its pupil turns blue. With this interpretation, the combination of His words "blue" (zurqan) in this verse and "blind" (ʿumyan) in the other verse is reconciled. It was said: the colours of their bodies turn blue, and this is extreme disfigurement, since they come like the colour of ash. In Arabic speech this colour is called blue. Skins do not turn blue except from enduring hardships and the drying of their moisture. It was said: (zurqan) means "thirsty", and severe thirst returns the blackness of the eye to whiteness. From this comes the saying "a blue spear-head", and his words:

"When they reached the water, blue with its crowd" —

that is, it turned white. The two verses were mentioned to Ibn ʿAbbas, and he said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: in one state they will be blue, and in another state they will be blind."

﴿Whispering (yatakhafatun)﴾: they speak secretly to one another out of the terror of the appearance and the intense distraction of their minds. The amount of time they remained has escaped them. ﴿You remained﴾: that is, in the abode of this world, or in the barzakh (intermediate state), or between the two blasts of the Trumpet. There are three opinions. Describing the time they spent there as short is because, compared with what they witness of hardships, the days they had in this world were days of joy, and days of joy are short. Or because of their departure from them and their passing. Whatever its duration, the thing that has gone is short in that it has ended. Or because they regard the Hereafter as long, and as everlasting and eternal, against which the life of this world is considered short. It is said: its people remained in it, in comparison with their remaining in the Hereafter. (idh) is governed by (aʿlam). (amthaluhum) means "the most upright of them". (ṭarīqatan) is in the accusative as a tamyiz.

﴿Except a day﴾ indicates the brevity of the period they remained. ﴿Except ten﴾ may mean ten nights or ten days, because when the masculine noun is omitted and its number kept, the feminine ta' may not be used. al-Kisai related from Abu al-Jarrah: "We fasted five from the month", and from this is what came in the hadith: "Then he followed it with six from Shawwal", meaning six days. The omission here is made good by the fact that this is the end of a verse, and by the fact that the first mention was the upper limit of the smallest number, which is ten. And he mentioned the most upright of them in way as the smallest number, which is one day. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿except a day﴾ shows that what is meant by their words ﴿ten﴾ is ten days.

(wizran) means a heavy, crushing weight, which its carrying exhausts, and it is the weight of punishment. Mujahid said: "sin". Al-Thawri said: "polytheism". The apparent meaning is that He expressed the punishment by the word "burden", because it is its cause. Therefore He said ﴿abiding therein﴾, that is, in the punishment and chastisement. He used the plural "abiding" (khalidin), and the pronoun in (lahum) is in agreement with the sense after agreement with its wording in (aʿrada) and in (fa-innahu yahmilu). The thing praised or condemned is omitted, that is, their burden. (lahum) is for clarification, as in ﴿Hayta laka﴾ [Yusuf: 23], not connected to (sa'a). "The day He blows" (yawma nunfakh) is a substitute for "the Day of Resurrection". The majority read (yunfakhu) in the passive voice, and (nahshuru) with the nun in the active voice, the nun of majesty. Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd read (nanfakhu) with the nun of majesty, like (nahshuru). He attributed the blowing to the one who commands it. The one who blows is Israfil, and out of honour for him He attributed what he undertakes to His own sanctified self. (al-Suwar) (the Trumpet) has been discussed in al-An'am. It was also read (yanfakhu) and (yahshuru) with the ya' in both, in the active voice. al-Hasan and Ibn ʿIyad, with a group, read ﴿fi al-Suwar﴾ on the pattern of (durar). Al-Hasan also read (yuhsharu) with the ya', in the passive voice, and (yahshuru) in the active voice, with the ya', that is, "and Allah gathers". The apparent meaning of "blue" (zurq) is the blueness of the eyes. Blue eyes were the most hated eye colour among the Arabs, because the Romans, who were their enemies, had blue eyes. For this reason they described the enemy as: "black-livered, reddish-moustached, blue-eyed". A poet said:

"I never feared that his death would be by the hand of a blue-eyed, lowered-eyed, Sabani horseman."

It is mentioned in another verse that they will be gathered with black faces, so the meaning is the disfiguring of the appearance, through the blackness of the face and the blueness of the eye. Also, the Arabs regard blueness as a bad omen. A poet said:

"Your eyes have grown dim, O son of Mukaʿbar! Surely every Dabbi is blue from baseness."

It was said: the meaning is "blind", because when the eye's light departs, its pupil turns blue. With this interpretation, the combination of His words "blue" (zurqan) in this verse and "blind" (ʿumyan) in the other verse is reconciled. It was said: the colours of their bodies turn blue, and this is extreme disfigurement, since they come like the colour of ash. In Arabic speech this colour is called blue. "When they reached the water, blue with its crowd" —

that is, it turned white. The two verses were mentioned to Ibn ʿAbbas, and he said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: in one state they will be blue, and in another state they will be blind."

The amount of time they remained has escaped them. ﴿You remained﴾: that is, in the abode of this world, or in the barzakh (intermediate state), or between the two blasts of the Trumpet. There are three opinions. Describing the time they spent there as short is because, compared with what they witness of hardships, the days they had in this world were days of joy, and days of joy are short. Or because of their departure from them and their passing. Whatever its duration, the thing that has gone is short in that it has ended. Or because they regard the Hereafter as long, and as everlasting and eternal, against which the life of this world is considered short. (ṭarīqatan) is in the accusative as a tamyiz.

﴿Except a day﴾ indicates the brevity of the period they remained. ﴿Except ten﴾ may mean ten nights or ten days, because when the masculine noun is omitted and its number kept, the feminine ta' may not be used. al-Kisai related from Abu al-Jarrah: "We fasted five from the month", and from this is what came in the hadith: "Then he followed it with six from Shawwal", meaning six days. * *

The third person pronoun in ﴿They ask you﴾ refers to the Quraysh who denied the Resurrection, or to the believers who asked about that, or to a man from Thaqif and a group from his people. There are three opinions. The second-person (ka) is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that the question did occur. The view of one who said there was no question is far-fetched; rather the meaning is that they would ask you ﴿about the mountains, then say﴾, so it implies the conditional, and therefore it is answered with the fa'. It is narrated that God sends a wind upon the mountains, which pounds them until they are like carded wool, then it continues upon them until it reduces them to dust scattered in the air. That is the (nasf), the blowing away. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿fa-yadharuha﴾ refers to the mountains, that is, after the blowing away they remain ﴿a level plain﴾, that is, flat, even ground. It was said: "He leaves their places of settlement and centres". It was said: it refers to the earth, though no mention of it has preceded, because the mountains indicate it.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: (ʿiwajan) means "a slope", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a trace like the thong of a sandal". From him also: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a valley", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a hill". From him also: "al-amt is elevation". Qatada said: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a fissure", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a mound". It was said: al-amt means cracks in the earth. It was said: a slight unevenness in a place in open country and mountain, and a flash in a place, as reported by al-Sulli. It was said: the amt in the verse is the ʿiwaj (crookedness) in the sky, facing the air, while the ʿiwaj in the earth is specific to the earth.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "They have distinguished between ʿiwaj and ʿawaj; they said: ʿiwaj with a kasra is used for meanings, and ʿawaj with a fatha is used for physical objects and the earth. How then is the form with kasra under the ʿayn valid for it?" I say: the choice of this word has a fine and striking effect in describing the earth as level and smooth and negating crookedness from it in the most emphatic way. So God, mighty and majestic, negated that crookedness which is so subtle and fine as to escape perception, except by the measure known to the one who understands measurement and geometry. Since that crookedness is not perceived except by measurement and not by the senses, it is treated as an abstract meaning, so it is called ʿiwaj with a kasra. al-Amt is the slight protrusion. It is said: "He stretched his rope until there was no amt in it." End of quotation.

* *

(On that day) that is, the day on which God blows away the mountains, (they will follow) that is, the creatures will follow (the summoner) the summoner of God to the place of gathering, like His words: ﴿hastening toward the summoner﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]. He is Israfil, who stands on the rock of Jerusalem calling the people, and they come from every direction. He puts the trumpets to his mouth and says: "O decayed bones, torn skins, and scattered flesh, come forward to be presented before the Most Merciful." Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: "They will be gathered in darkness, the sky will have been folded up and the stars scattered. Then a caller will call out, and they will die a single death." ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: "(al-dāʿī) here is the Messenger (ﷺ), who used to call them to God. They will deviate from the path to the right and to the left, turning away from him with great deviation. So on that day following him will not benefit them." The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (lahu) refers to ﴿al-dāʿī﴾. He negated crookedness from him, that is, ﴿no crookedness﴾ is theirs in regard to him; rather they come towards him, following his voice without deviation. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, no one invited by him is made crooked; rather they go straight to him. End of quotation.

* *

It was said: ﴿no crookedness for him﴾ is in the place of a description of a suppressed noun, that is, following ﴿no crookedness for him﴾, so the pronoun in (lahu) refers to that omitted verbal noun. It may also be intended as: no one can escape from following it, and walking towards its voice. Al-khushu' is humility and lowliness, and in regard to voices it is a metaphor meaning concealment. The "hushing" (istisrar) is for the Most Merciful, that is, out of awe of the Most Merciful, whose power is evident. It was said: it is by omission of a modifier, that is, "and the people of voices were humbled." Al-hams is a low, hidden sound. It may be intended that the whispering is what is heard, their secret speech among themselves. It may also be intended as the sound of footsteps, and that the sounds of speech are silent.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿Except a whisper﴾": it is a faint sound (al-rikz al-khafi), and from it comes the term "unvoiced letters" (al-huruf al-mahmusa). End of quote.

This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "﴿So they will not speak except in a whisper﴾." From Abu 'Ubayda: "al-sawt al-khafi" (the faint sound). "That Day" is a substitute for "That Day they will follow"; or the sense is "the Day when they will follow," and it is in the accusative governed by "will not benefit." "Man" is the object of "﴿will not benefit﴾," and "lahu" means "for his sake," as also in "﴿and whose words He approves﴾," meaning for his sake. "Man" may refer to the one for whom intercession is made, or it may be a substitute for "intercession," with an elided noun, meaning "except the intercession of one whom He has permitted." Or it may be an exceptive in the accusative on this reading, or a disjunctive exception, in which case it is accusative in the Hijazi dialect and nominative in the Tamim dialect. In all these interpretations "man" refers to the intercessor. The "word that is approved" is, according to Ibn 'Abbas, "There is no god but Allah."

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "﴿what is before them and what is behind them﴾" refers to the created beings gathered, who are the followers of the caller. It has been said that it refers to the angels, and it has been said that it refers to people in general, not restricted to the gathering and following. The explanation of this phrase has already been given in the Verse of the Throne in al-Baqara. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to "ma" (what): "﴿and they do not encompass it﴾ in knowledge," that is, of His knowledge. The apparent sense is that "the faces" is general, meaning the faces of all creatures, and "the faces" was specified because the signs of humiliation first appear on the faces. Talq ibn Habib said: the intended meaning is the prostration of people upon their faces and the seven limbs. If he related that this will occur on the Day of Resurrection, then the verse is a report about it, and the meaning is sound; but if he meant in this world, then that is not consistent with the verses before and after it. Al-Zamakhshari said: by "faces" is meant the faces of the disobedient, and that when they witness on the Day of Resurrection disappointment, wretchedness and evil reckoning, their faces become "humbled," that is, abased and submissive, like the faces of captives, the prisoners; and similar is "﴿So when they see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed﴾" [al-Mulk: 27] and "﴿And faces that Day will be gloomy﴾" [al-Qiyama: 24]. As for "al-Qayyum," its discussion has already been given in al-Baqara.

(p-٢٧٧) Makki cited a view contrary to this: that Musa was with the seventy at the (divine) conversation, and that the affair of the calf occurred at that time. God informed Musa of it, so he concealed it from them and brought them until they heard the clamour of the Children of Israel around the calf, and then Musa made them aware of it. End of quotation. When he had finished refuting what the Samiri had done, he returned to explaining the true religion and said: ﴿Your God is only God﴾ [Ta-Ha: 98]. The majority of readers read (wasi'a), so that ʿilman is in the accusative as a tamyiz (a specifying accusative, a noun clarifying the sense of a verb or phrase), transferred from the subject. Its parallel was mentioned in al-An'am. Mujahid and Qatada read wassa'a, with the sin doubled. Al-Zamakhshari said: its basis is that wasi'a is transitive to one object, which is "everything" (kull shay'). As for ʿilman, its accusative is as a tamyiz, and in meaning it is the subject. When the verb is made heavier (doubled), it is transferred to be transitive to two objects, and so it puts both in the accusative as objects, because the specified noun is the subject in meaning. As you say: "Zayd feared ʿAmr", and "I made Zayd fear ʿAmr". Thus by the transfer, what was the subject becomes an object. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: (wasi'a) means the creation of things and their multiplicity by bringing them into being, so He encompassed them as existing things. End of quotation.

﴿Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has passed, and We have given you from Us a Reminder﴾. ﴿Whoever turns away from it, he will bear a burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿Abiding therein, and evil is their burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿The Day the Trumpet is blown, and We will gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed﴾. ﴿Whispering among themselves: "You remained only ten"﴾. ﴿We know best what they say, when the most exemplary of them in way says: "You remained only a day"﴾. ﴿And they ask you about the mountains; say: "My Lord will blow them away with a blast"﴾. ﴿And He will leave them a level plain﴾. ﴿You will not see therein any crookedness or unevenness﴾. ﴿That Day they will follow the summoner, with no deviation from him, and voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a whisper﴾.

That is, as We relate this wondrous account, We relate to you some of the news of the earlier nations. This contains mention of a great blessing, namely the informing of you about the news of past nations, so that you may be consoled by it and know that what the nations did to their messengers, and what the messengers endured from them, is the same. The apparent meaning is that the Reminder here is the Qur'an. He, exalted is He, bestowed a favour upon him by giving him the Reminder, which includes stories and reports, indicating through that miracles that were given to him. Muqatil said: "(dhikran)" means "clarification". Abu Sahl said: "honour and renown among people".

This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "﴿So they will not speak except in a whisper﴾." From Abu 'Ubayda: "al-sawt al-khafi" (the faint sound). "That Day" is a substitute for "That Day they will follow"; or the sense is "the Day when they will follow," and it is in the accusative governed by "will not benefit." "Man" is the object of "﴿will not benefit﴾," and "lahu" means "for his sake," as also in "﴿and whose words He approves﴾," meaning for his sake. "Man" may refer to the one for whom intercession is made, or it may be a substitute for "intercession," with an elided noun, meaning "except the intercession of one whom He has permitted." The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "﴿what is before them and what is behind them﴾" refers to the created beings gathered, who are the followers of the caller. It has been said that it refers to the angels, and it has been said that it refers to people in general, not restricted to the gathering and following. The explanation of this phrase has already been given in the Verse of the Throne in al-Baqara. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to "ma" (what): "﴿and they do not encompass it﴾ in knowledge," that is, of His knowledge. The apparent sense is that "the faces" is general, meaning the faces of all creatures, and "the faces" was specified because the signs of humiliation first appear on the faces. Talq ibn Habib said: the intended meaning is the prostration of people upon their faces and the seven limbs. If he related that this will occur on the Day of Resurrection, then the verse is a report about it, and the meaning is sound; but if he meant in this world, then that is not consistent with the verses before and after it. Al-Zamakhshari said: by "faces" is meant the faces of the disobedient, and that when they witness on the Day of Resurrection disappointment, wretchedness and evil reckoning, their faces become "humbled," that is, abased and submissive, like the faces of captives, the prisoners; and similar is "﴿So when they see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed﴾" [al-Mulk: 27] and "﴿And faces that Day will be gloomy﴾" [al-Qiyama: 24]. As for "al-Qayyum," its discussion has already been given in al-Baqara.

(p-٢٧٧) Makki cited a view contrary to this: that Musa was with the seventy at the (divine) conversation, and that the affair of the calf occurred at that time. God informed Musa of it, so he concealed it from them and brought them until they heard the clamour of the Children of Israel around the calf, and then Musa made them aware of it. End of quotation. When he had finished refuting what the Samiri had done, he returned to explaining the true religion and said: ﴿Your God is only God﴾ [Ta-Ha: 98]. The majority of readers read (wasi'a), so that ʿilman is in the accusative as a tamyiz (a specifying accusative, a noun clarifying the sense of a verb or phrase), transferred from the subject. When the verb is made heavier (doubled), it is transferred to be transitive to two objects, and so it puts both in the accusative as objects, because the specified noun is the subject in meaning. As you say: "Zayd feared ʿAmr", and "I made Zayd fear ʿAmr". Thus by the transfer, what was the subject becomes an object. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: (wasi'a) means the creation of things and their multiplicity by bringing them into being, so He encompassed them as existing things. End of quotation.

﴿Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has passed, and We have given you from Us a Reminder﴾. ﴿Whoever turns away from it, he will bear a burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿Abiding therein, and evil is their burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿The Day the Trumpet is blown, and We will gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed﴾. ﴿Whispering among themselves: "You remained only ten"﴾. ﴿We know best what they say, when the most exemplary of them in way says: "You remained only a day"﴾. ﴿And they ask you about the mountains; say: "My Lord will blow them away with a blast"﴾. ﴿And He will leave them a level plain﴾. ﴿You will not see therein any crookedness or unevenness﴾. ﴿That Day they will follow the summoner, with no deviation from him, and voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a whisper﴾.

Thus the demonstrative (dhalika) refers to the account of Musa, the Children of Israel and Pharaoh. That is, as We relate this wondrous account, We relate to you some of the news of the earlier nations. This contains mention of a great blessing, namely the informing of you about the news of past nations, so that you may be consoled by it and know that what the nations did to their messengers, and what the messengers endured from them, is the same. The apparent meaning is that the Reminder here is the Qur'an. He, exalted is He, bestowed a favour upon him by giving him the Reminder, which includes stories and reports, indicating through that miracles that were given to him. Muqatil said: "(dhikran)" means "clarification". Abu Sahl said: "honour and renown among people".

﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾: that is, from the Qur'an, by not believing in it and not following what is in it. The majority read (yahmilu), the present tense of ḥamala, lightly, in the active voice. A group, among them Dawud ibn Rufayʿ, read (yuḥammalu), with the mim doubled, in the passive voice, because he is burdened with that, not that he bears it willingly. (wizran) is the second object. (wizran) means a heavy, crushing weight, which its carrying exhausts, and it is the weight of punishment. Mujahid said: "sin". Al-Thawri said: "polytheism". The apparent meaning is that He expressed the punishment by the word "burden", because it is its cause. Therefore He said ﴿abiding therein﴾, that is, in the punishment and chastisement. He used the plural "abiding" (khalidin), and the pronoun in (lahum) is in agreement with the sense after agreement with its wording in (aʿrada) and in (fa-innahu yahmilu). The thing praised or condemned is omitted, that is, their burden. (lahum) is for clarification, as in ﴿Hayta laka﴾ [Yusuf: 23], not connected to (sa'a). (sa'a) here is the one that functions like (bi'sa), not the (sa'a) meaning "to sadden and worry", because that would corrupt the meaning.

"The day He blows" (yawma nunfakh) is a substitute for "the Day of Resurrection". The majority read (yunfakhu) in the passive voice, and (nahshuru) with the nun in the active voice, the nun of majesty. Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd read (nanfakhu) with the nun of majesty, like (nahshuru). He attributed the blowing to the one who commands it. The one who blows is Israfil, and out of honour for him He attributed what he undertakes to His own sanctified self. (al-Suwar) (the Trumpet) has been discussed in al-An'am. It was also read (yanfakhu) and (yahshuru) with the ya' in both, in the active voice. al-Hasan and Ibn ʿIyad, with a group, read ﴿fi al-Suwar﴾ on the pattern of (durar). Al-Hasan also read (yuhsharu) with the ya', in the passive voice, and (yahshuru) in the active voice, with the ya', that is, "and Allah gathers". The apparent meaning of "blue" (zurq) is the blueness of the eyes. Blue eyes were the most hated eye colour among the Arabs, because the Romans, who were their enemies, had blue eyes. For this reason they described the enemy as: "black-livered, reddish-moustached, blue-eyed". A poet said:

"I never feared that his death would be by the hand of a blue-eyed, lowered-eyed, Sabani horseman."

It is mentioned in another verse that they will be gathered with black faces, so the meaning is the disfiguring of the appearance, through the blackness of the face and the blueness of the eye. Also, the Arabs regard blueness as a bad omen. A poet said:

"Your eyes have grown dim, O son of Mukaʿbar! Surely every Dabbi is blue from baseness."

It was said: the meaning is "blind", because when the eye's light departs, its pupil turns blue. With this interpretation, the combination of His words "blue" (zurqan) in this verse and "blind" (ʿumyan) in the other verse is reconciled. It was said: the colours of their bodies turn blue, and this is extreme disfigurement, since they come like the colour of ash. In Arabic speech this colour is called blue. Skins do not turn blue except from enduring hardships and the drying of their moisture. It was said: (zurqan) means "thirsty", and severe thirst returns the blackness of the eye to whiteness. From this comes the saying "a blue spear-head", and his words:

"When they reached the water, blue with its crowd" —

that is, it turned white. The two verses were mentioned to Ibn ʿAbbas, and he said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: in one state they will be blue, and in another state they will be blind."

﴿Whispering (yatakhafatun)﴾: they speak secretly to one another out of the terror of the appearance and the intense distraction of their minds. The amount of time they remained has escaped them. ﴿You remained﴾: that is, in the abode of this world, or in the barzakh (intermediate state), or between the two blasts of the Trumpet. There are three opinions. Describing the time they spent there as short is because, compared with what they witness of hardships, the days they had in this world were days of joy, and days of joy are short. Or because of their departure from them and their passing. Whatever its duration, the thing that has gone is short in that it has ended. Or because they regard the Hereafter as long, and as everlasting and eternal, against which the life of this world is considered short. It is said: its people remained in it, in comparison with their remaining in the Hereafter. (idh) is governed by (aʿlam). (amthaluhum) means "the most upright of them". (ṭarīqatan) is in the accusative as a tamyiz.

﴿Except a day﴾ indicates the brevity of the period they remained. ﴿Except ten﴾ may mean ten nights or ten days, because when the masculine noun is omitted and its number kept, the feminine ta' may not be used. al-Kisai related from Abu al-Jarrah: "We fasted five from the month", and from this is what came in the hadith: "Then he followed it with six from Shawwal", meaning six days. The omission here is made good by the fact that this is the end of a verse, and by the fact that the first mention was the upper limit of the smallest number, which is ten. And he mentioned the most upright of them in way as the smallest number, which is one day. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿except a day﴾ shows that what is meant by their words ﴿ten﴾ is ten days.

The third person pronoun in ﴿They ask you﴾ refers to the Quraysh who denied the Resurrection, or to the believers who asked about that, or to a man from Thaqif and a group from his people. There are three opinions. The second-person (ka) is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that the question did occur. The view of one who said there was no question is far-fetched; rather the meaning is that they would ask you ﴿about the mountains, then say﴾, so it implies the conditional, and therefore it is answered with the fa'. It is narrated that God sends a wind upon the mountains, which pounds them until they are like carded wool, then it continues upon them until it reduces them to dust scattered in the air. That is the (nasf), the blowing away. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿fa-yadharuha﴾ refers to the mountains, that is, after the blowing away they remain ﴿a level plain﴾, that is, flat, even ground. It was said: "He leaves their places of settlement and centres". It was said: it refers to the earth, though no mention of it has preceded, because the mountains indicate it.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: (ʿiwajan) means "a slope", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a trace like the thong of a sandal". From him also: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a valley", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a hill". From him also: "al-amt is elevation". Qatada said: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a fissure", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a mound". It was said: al-amt means cracks in the earth. It was said: a slight unevenness in a place in open country and mountain, and a flash in a place, as reported by al-Sulli. It was said: the amt in the verse is the ʿiwaj (crookedness) in the sky, facing the air, while the ʿiwaj in the earth is specific to the earth.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "They have distinguished between ʿiwaj and ʿawaj; they said: ʿiwaj with a kasra is used for meanings, and ʿawaj with a fatha is used for physical objects and the earth. How then is the form with kasra under the ʿayn valid for it?" I say: the choice of this word has a fine and striking effect in describing the earth as level and smooth and negating crookedness from it in the most emphatic way. That is because if you took a piece of land, levelled it, and went to great lengths in levelling it, by your own eye and the eyes of the keen-sighted among the farmers, and you all agreed that there remained no crookedness in it at all, then if you consulted an engineer about it and ordered him to test its evenness by the geometric measures, he would find crookedness in some place which cannot be perceived by the sense of sight, but only by geometric measurement. So God, mighty and majestic, negated that crookedness which is so subtle and fine as to escape perception, except by the measure known to the one who understands measurement and geometry. Since that crookedness is not perceived except by measurement and not by the senses, it is treated as an abstract meaning, so it is called ʿiwaj with a kasra. al-Amt is the slight protrusion. It is said: "He stretched his rope until there was no amt in it." End of quotation.

He is Israfil, who stands on the rock of Jerusalem calling the people, and they come from every direction. He puts the trumpets to his mouth and says: "O decayed bones, torn skins, and scattered flesh, come forward to be presented before the Most Merciful." Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: "They will be gathered in darkness, the sky will have been folded up and the stars scattered. Then a caller will call out, and they will die a single death." ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: "(al-dāʿī) here is the Messenger (ﷺ), who used to call them to God. They will deviate from the path to the right and to the left, turning away from him with great deviation. So on that day following him will not benefit them." The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (lahu) refers to ﴿al-dāʿī﴾. He negated crookedness from him, that is, ﴿no crookedness﴾ is theirs in regard to him; rather they come towards him, following his voice without deviation. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, no one invited by him is made crooked; rather they go straight to him. End of quotation.

There are three opinions. The second-person (ka) is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that the question did occur. The view of one who said there was no question is far-fetched; rather the meaning is that they would ask you ﴿about the mountains, then say﴾, so it implies the conditional, and therefore it is answered with the fa'. It is narrated that God sends a wind upon the mountains, which pounds them until they are like carded wool, then it continues upon them until it reduces them to dust scattered in the air. That is the (nasf), the blowing away. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿fa-yadharuha﴾ refers to the mountains, that is, after the blowing away they remain ﴿a level plain﴾, that is, flat, even ground. It was said: "He leaves their places of settlement and centres". It was said: it refers to the earth, though no mention of it has preceded, because the mountains indicate it.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: (ʿiwajan) means "a slope", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a trace like the thong of a sandal". From him also: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a valley", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a hill". From him also: "al-amt is elevation". Qatada said: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a fissure", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a mound". It was said: al-amt means cracks in the earth. It was said: a slight unevenness in a place in open country and mountain, and a flash in a place, as reported by al-Sulli. It was said: the amt in the verse is the ʿiwaj (crookedness) in the sky, facing the air, while the ʿiwaj in the earth is specific to the earth.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "They have distinguished between ʿiwaj and ʿawaj; they said: ʿiwaj with a kasra is used for meanings, and ʿawaj with a fatha is used for physical objects and the earth. How then is the form with kasra under the ʿayn valid for it?" I say: the choice of this word has a fine and striking effect in describing the earth as level and smooth and negating crookedness from it in the most emphatic way. That is because if you took a piece of land, levelled it, and went to great lengths in levelling it, by your own eye and the eyes of the keen-sighted among the farmers, and you all agreed that there remained no crookedness in it at all, then if you consulted an engineer about it and ordered him to test its evenness by the geometric measures, he would find crookedness in some place which cannot be perceived by the sense of sight, but only by geometric measurement. So God, mighty and majestic, negated that crookedness which is so subtle and fine as to escape perception, except by the measure known to the one who understands measurement and geometry. Since that crookedness is not perceived except by measurement and not by the senses, it is treated as an abstract meaning, so it is called ʿiwaj with a kasra. al-Amt is the slight protrusion. It is said: "He stretched his rope until there was no amt in it." End of quotation.

* *

(On that day) that is, the day on which God blows away the mountains, (they will follow) that is, the creatures will follow (the summoner) the summoner of God to the place of gathering, like His words: ﴿hastening toward the summoner﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]. He is Israfil, who stands on the rock of Jerusalem calling the people, and they come from every direction. He puts the trumpets to his mouth and says: "O decayed bones, torn skins, and scattered flesh, come forward to be presented before the Most Merciful." Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: "They will be gathered in darkness, the sky will have been folded up and the stars scattered. Then a caller will call out, and they will die a single death." ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: "(al-dāʿī) here is the Messenger (ﷺ), who used to call them to God. They will deviate from the path to the right and to the left, turning away from him with great deviation. So on that day following him will not benefit them." The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (lahu) refers to ﴿al-dāʿī﴾. He negated crookedness from him, that is, ﴿no crookedness﴾ is theirs in regard to him; rather they come towards him, following his voice without deviation. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, no one invited by him is made crooked; rather they go straight to him. End of quotation.

* *

It was said: ﴿no crookedness for him﴾ is in the place of a description of a suppressed noun, that is, following ﴿no crookedness for him﴾, so the pronoun in (lahu) refers to that omitted verbal noun. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it may be intended as a report, that is, there is no doubt about it, and its existence does not contradict its report. It may also be intended as: no one can escape from following it, and walking towards its voice. Al-khushu' is humility and lowliness, and in regard to voices it is a metaphor meaning concealment. The "hushing" (istisrar) is for the Most Merciful, that is, out of awe of the Most Merciful, whose power is evident. It was said: it is by omission of a modifier, that is, "and the people of voices were humbled." Al-hams is a low, hidden sound. It may be intended that the whispering is what is heard, their secret speech among themselves. It may also be intended as the sound of footsteps, and that the sounds of speech are silent.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿Except a whisper﴾": it is a faint sound (al-rikz al-khafi), and from it comes the term "unvoiced letters" (al-huruf al-mahmusa). It has also been said that it derives from the whispering of camels, which is the sound of their hooves when they walk; meaning that nothing is heard except the tread of feet and their movement toward the gathering place. End of quote.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and Ibn Jubayr that al-hams is the treading of feet, and al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj preferred this view. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the moving of the lips without uttering sound, and from Mujahid that it is quiet speech. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "﴿So they will not speak except in a whisper﴾." From Abu 'Ubayda: "al-sawt al-khafi" (the faint sound). "That Day" is a substitute for "That Day they will follow"; or the sense is "the Day when they will follow," and it is in the accusative governed by "will not benefit." "Man" is the object of "﴿will not benefit﴾," and "lahu" means "for his sake," as also in "﴿and whose words He approves﴾," meaning for his sake. "Man" may refer to the one for whom intercession is made, or it may be a substitute for "intercession," with an elided noun, meaning "except the intercession of one whom He has permitted." Or it may be an exceptive in the accusative on this reading, or a disjunctive exception, in which case it is accusative in the Hijazi dialect and nominative in the Tamim dialect. In all these interpretations "man" refers to the intercessor. The "word that is approved" is, according to Ibn 'Abbas, "There is no god but Allah."

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "﴿what is before them and what is behind them﴾" refers to the created beings gathered, who are the followers of the caller. It has been said that it refers to the angels, and it has been said that it refers to people in general, not restricted to the gathering and following. The explanation of this phrase has already been given in the Verse of the Throne in al-Baqara. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to "ma" (what): "﴿and they do not encompass it﴾ in knowledge," that is, of His knowledge. The apparent sense is that "the faces" is general, meaning the faces of all creatures, and "the faces" was specified because the signs of humiliation first appear on the faces. Talq ibn Habib said: the intended meaning is the prostration of people upon their faces and the seven limbs. If he related that this will occur on the Day of Resurrection, then the verse is a report about it, and the meaning is sound; but if he meant in this world, then that is not consistent with the verses before and after it. Al-Zamakhshari said: by "faces" is meant the faces of the disobedient, and that when they witness on the Day of Resurrection disappointment, wretchedness and evil reckoning, their faces become "humbled," that is, abased and submissive, like the faces of captives, the prisoners; and similar is "﴿So when they see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed﴾" [al-Mulk: 27] and "﴿And faces that Day will be gloomy﴾" [al-Qiyama: 24]. As for "al-Qayyum," its discussion has already been given in al-Baqara.

(p-٢٧٧) Makki cited a view contrary to this: that Musa was with the seventy at the (divine) conversation, and that the affair of the calf occurred at that time. God informed Musa of it, so he concealed it from them and brought them until they heard the clamour of the Children of Israel around the calf, and then Musa made them aware of it. End of quotation. When he had finished refuting what the Samiri had done, he returned to explaining the true religion and said: ﴿Your God is only God﴾ [Ta-Ha: 98]. The majority of readers read (wasi'a), so that ʿilman is in the accusative as a tamyiz (a specifying accusative, a noun clarifying the sense of a verb or phrase), transferred from the subject. Its parallel was mentioned in al-An'am. Mujahid and Qatada read wassa'a, with the sin doubled. Al-Zamakhshari said: its basis is that wasi'a is transitive to one object, which is "everything" (kull shay'). As for ʿilman, its accusative is as a tamyiz, and in meaning it is the subject. When the verb is made heavier (doubled), it is transferred to be transitive to two objects, and so it puts both in the accusative as objects, because the specified noun is the subject in meaning. As you say: "Zayd feared ʿAmr", and "I made Zayd fear ʿAmr". Thus by the transfer, what was the subject becomes an object. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: (wasi'a) means the creation of things and their multiplicity by bringing them into being, so He encompassed them as existing things. End of quotation.

﴿Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has passed, and We have given you from Us a Reminder﴾. ﴿Whoever turns away from it, he will bear a burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿Abiding therein, and evil is their burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿The Day the Trumpet is blown, and We will gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed﴾. ﴿Whispering among themselves: "You remained only ten"﴾. ﴿We know best what they say, when the most exemplary of them in way says: "You remained only a day"﴾. ﴿And they ask you about the mountains; say: "My Lord will blow them away with a blast"﴾. ﴿And He will leave them a level plain﴾. ﴿You will not see therein any crookedness or unevenness﴾. ﴿That Day they will follow the summoner, with no deviation from him, and voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a whisper﴾.

Thus the demonstrative (dhalika) refers to the account of Musa, the Children of Israel and Pharaoh. That is, as We relate this wondrous account, We relate to you some of the news of the earlier nations. This contains mention of a great blessing, namely the informing of you about the news of past nations, so that you may be consoled by it and know that what the nations did to their messengers, and what the messengers endured from them, is the same. The apparent meaning is that the Reminder here is the Qur'an. He, exalted is He, bestowed a favour upon him by giving him the Reminder, which includes stories and reports, indicating through that miracles that were given to him. Muqatil said: "(dhikran)" means "clarification". Abu Sahl said: "honour and renown among people".

﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾: that is, from the Qur'an, by not believing in it and not following what is in it. The majority read (yahmilu), the present tense of ḥamala, lightly, in the active voice. A group, among them Dawud ibn Rufayʿ, read (yuḥammalu), with the mim doubled, in the passive voice, because he is burdened with that, not that he bears it willingly. (wizran) is the second object. (wizran) means a heavy, crushing weight, which its carrying exhausts, and it is the weight of punishment. Mujahid said: "sin". Al-Thawri said: "polytheism". The apparent meaning is that He expressed the punishment by the word "burden", because it is its cause. Therefore He said ﴿abiding therein﴾, that is, in the punishment and chastisement. He used the plural "abiding" (khalidin), and the pronoun in (lahum) is in agreement with the sense after agreement with its wording in (aʿrada) and in (fa-innahu yahmilu). The thing praised or condemned is omitted, that is, their burden. (lahum) is for clarification, as in ﴿Hayta laka﴾ [Yusuf: 23], not connected to (sa'a). (sa'a) here is the one that functions like (bi'sa), not the (sa'a) meaning "to sadden and worry", because that would corrupt the meaning.

"The day He blows" (yawma nunfakh) is a substitute for "the Day of Resurrection". The majority read (yunfakhu) in the passive voice, and (nahshuru) with the nun in the active voice, the nun of majesty. Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd read (nanfakhu) with the nun of majesty, like (nahshuru). He attributed the blowing to the one who commands it. The one who blows is Israfil, and out of honour for him He attributed what he undertakes to His own sanctified self. (al-Suwar) (the Trumpet) has been discussed in al-An'am. It was also read (yanfakhu) and (yahshuru) with the ya' in both, in the active voice. al-Hasan and Ibn ʿIyad, with a group, read ﴿fi al-Suwar﴾ on the pattern of (durar). Al-Hasan also read (yuhsharu) with the ya', in the passive voice, and (yahshuru) in the active voice, with the ya', that is, "and Allah gathers". The apparent meaning of "blue" (zurq) is the blueness of the eyes. Blue eyes were the most hated eye colour among the Arabs, because the Romans, who were their enemies, had blue eyes. For this reason they described the enemy as: "black-livered, reddish-moustached, blue-eyed". A poet said:

"I never feared that his death would be by the hand of a blue-eyed, lowered-eyed, Sabani horseman."

It is mentioned in another verse that they will be gathered with black faces, so the meaning is the disfiguring of the appearance, through the blackness of the face and the blueness of the eye. Also, the Arabs regard blueness as a bad omen. A poet said:

"Your eyes have grown dim, O son of Mukaʿbar! Surely every Dabbi is blue from baseness."

It was said: the meaning is "blind", because when the eye's light departs, its pupil turns blue. With this interpretation, the combination of His words "blue" (zurqan) in this verse and "blind" (ʿumyan) in the other verse is reconciled. It was said: the colours of their bodies turn blue, and this is extreme disfigurement, since they come like the colour of ash. In Arabic speech this colour is called blue. Skins do not turn blue except from enduring hardships and the drying of their moisture. It was said: (zurqan) means "thirsty", and severe thirst returns the blackness of the eye to whiteness. From this comes the saying "a blue spear-head", and his words:

"When they reached the water, blue with its crowd" —

that is, it turned white. The two verses were mentioned to Ibn ʿAbbas, and he said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: in one state they will be blue, and in another state they will be blind."

﴿Whispering (yatakhafatun)﴾: they speak secretly to one another out of the terror of the appearance and the intense distraction of their minds. The amount of time they remained has escaped them. ﴿You remained﴾: that is, in the abode of this world, or in the barzakh (intermediate state), or between the two blasts of the Trumpet. There are three opinions. Describing the time they spent there as short is because, compared with what they witness of hardships, the days they had in this world were days of joy, and days of joy are short. Or because of their departure from them and their passing. Whatever its duration, the thing that has gone is short in that it has ended. Or because they regard the Hereafter as long, and as everlasting and eternal, against which the life of this world is considered short. It is said: its people remained in it, in comparison with their remaining in the Hereafter. (idh) is governed by (aʿlam). (amthaluhum) means "the most upright of them". (ṭarīqatan) is in the accusative as a tamyiz.

﴿Except a day﴾ indicates the brevity of the period they remained. ﴿Except ten﴾ may mean ten nights or ten days, because when the masculine noun is omitted and its number kept, the feminine ta' may not be used. al-Kisai related from Abu al-Jarrah: "We fasted five from the month", and from this is what came in the hadith: "Then he followed it with six from Shawwal", meaning six days. The omission here is made good by the fact that this is the end of a verse, and by the fact that the first mention was the upper limit of the smallest number, which is ten. And he mentioned the most upright of them in way as the smallest number, which is one day. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿except a day﴾ shows that what is meant by their words ﴿ten﴾ is ten days.

﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾: that is, from the Qur'an, by not believing in it and not following what is in it. The majority read (yahmilu), the present tense of ḥamala, lightly, in the active voice. A group, among them Dawud ibn Rufayʿ, read (yuḥammalu), with the mim doubled, in the passive voice, because he is burdened with that, not that he bears it willingly. (wizran) is the second object. (wizran) means a heavy, crushing weight, which its carrying exhausts, and it is the weight of punishment. Mujahid said: "sin". Al-Thawri said: "polytheism". The apparent meaning is that He expressed the punishment by the word "burden", because it is its cause. Therefore He said ﴿abiding therein﴾, that is, in the punishment and chastisement. He used the plural "abiding" (khalidin), and the pronoun in (lahum) is in agreement with the sense after agreement with its wording in (aʿrada) and in (fa-innahu yahmilu). The thing praised or condemned is omitted, that is, their burden. (lahum) is for clarification, as in ﴿Hayta laka﴾ [Yusuf: 23], not connected to (sa'a). (sa'a) here is the one that functions like (bi'sa), not the (sa'a) meaning "to sadden and worry", because that would corrupt the meaning.

"The day He blows" (yawma nunfakh) is a substitute for "the Day of Resurrection". The majority read (yunfakhu) in the passive voice, and (nahshuru) with the nun in the active voice, the nun of majesty. Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd read (nanfakhu) with the nun of majesty, like (nahshuru). He attributed the blowing to the one who commands it. The one who blows is Israfil, and out of honour for him He attributed what he undertakes to His own sanctified self. (al-Suwar) (the Trumpet) has been discussed in al-An'am. It was also read (yanfakhu) and (yahshuru) with the ya' in both, in the active voice. al-Hasan and Ibn ʿIyad, with a group, read ﴿fi al-Suwar﴾ on the pattern of (durar). Al-Hasan also read (yuhsharu) with the ya', in the passive voice, and (yahshuru) in the active voice, with the ya', that is, "and Allah gathers". The apparent meaning of "blue" (zurq) is the blueness of the eyes. Blue eyes were the most hated eye colour among the Arabs, because the Romans, who were their enemies, had blue eyes. For this reason they described the enemy as: "black-livered, reddish-moustached, blue-eyed". A poet said:

"I never feared that his death would be by the hand of a blue-eyed, lowered-eyed, Sabani horseman."

It is mentioned in another verse that they will be gathered with black faces, so the meaning is the disfiguring of the appearance, through the blackness of the face and the blueness of the eye. Also, the Arabs regard blueness as a bad omen. A poet said:

"Your eyes have grown dim, O son of Mukaʿbar! Surely every Dabbi is blue from baseness."

It was said: the meaning is "blind", because when the eye's light departs, its pupil turns blue. With this interpretation, the combination of His words "blue" (zurqan) in this verse and "blind" (ʿumyan) in the other verse is reconciled. It was said: the colours of their bodies turn blue, and this is extreme disfigurement, since they come like the colour of ash. In Arabic speech this colour is called blue. Skins do not turn blue except from enduring hardships and the drying of their moisture. It was said: (zurqan) means "thirsty", and severe thirst returns the blackness of the eye to whiteness. that is, it turned white. The two verses were mentioned to Ibn ʿAbbas, and he said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: in one state they will be blue, and in another state they will be blind."

The amount of time they remained has escaped them. ﴿You remained﴾: that is, in the abode of this world, or in the barzakh (intermediate state), or between the two blasts of the Trumpet. There are three opinions. Describing the time they spent there as short is because, compared with what they witness of hardships, the days they had in this world were days of joy, and days of joy are short. Or because of their departure from them and their passing. Whatever its duration, the thing that has gone is short in that it has ended. Or because they regard the Hereafter as long, and as everlasting and eternal, against which the life of this world is considered short. It is said: its people remained in it, in comparison with their remaining in the Hereafter. (idh) is governed by (aʿlam). (amthaluhum) means "the most upright of them". (ṭarīqatan) is in the accusative as a tamyiz.

﴿Except a day﴾ indicates the brevity of the period they remained. ﴿Except ten﴾ may mean ten nights or ten days, because when the masculine noun is omitted and its number kept, the feminine ta' may not be used. al-Kisai related from Abu al-Jarrah: "We fasted five from the month", and from this is what came in the hadith: "Then he followed it with six from Shawwal", meaning six days. The omission here is made good by the fact that this is the end of a verse, and by the fact that the first mention was the upper limit of the smallest number, which is ten. And he mentioned the most upright of them in way as the smallest number, which is one day. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿except a day﴾ shows that what is meant by their words ﴿ten﴾ is ten days.

* *

The third person pronoun in ﴿They ask you﴾ refers to the Quraysh who denied the Resurrection, or to the believers who asked about that, or to a man from Thaqif and a group from his people. There are three opinions. The second-person (ka) is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that the question did occur. The view of one who said there was no question is far-fetched; rather the meaning is that they would ask you ﴿about the mountains, then say﴾, so it implies the conditional, and therefore it is answered with the fa'. It is narrated that God sends a wind upon the mountains, which pounds them until they are like carded wool, then it continues upon them until it reduces them to dust scattered in the air. That is the (nasf), the blowing away. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿fa-yadharuha﴾ refers to the mountains, that is, after the blowing away they remain ﴿a level plain﴾, that is, flat, even ground. It was said: "He leaves their places of settlement and centres". It was said: it refers to the earth, though no mention of it has preceded, because the mountains indicate it.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: (ʿiwajan) means "a slope", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a trace like the thong of a sandal". From him also: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a valley", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a hill". From him also: "al-amt is elevation". Qatada said: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a fissure", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a mound". It was said: al-amt means cracks in the earth. It was said: a slight unevenness in a place in open country and mountain, and a flash in a place, as reported by al-Sulli. It was said: the amt in the verse is the ʿiwaj (crookedness) in the sky, facing the air, while the ʿiwaj in the earth is specific to the earth.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "They have distinguished between ʿiwaj and ʿawaj; they said: ʿiwaj with a kasra is used for meanings, and ʿawaj with a fatha is used for physical objects and the earth. I say: the choice of this word has a fine and striking effect in describing the earth as level and smooth and negating crookedness from it in the most emphatic way. So God, mighty and majestic, negated that crookedness which is so subtle and fine as to escape perception, except by the measure known to the one who understands measurement and geometry. Since that crookedness is not perceived except by measurement and not by the senses, it is treated as an abstract meaning, so it is called ʿiwaj with a kasra. al-Amt is the slight protrusion. It is said: "He stretched his rope until there was no amt in it." End of quotation.

* *

(On that day) that is, the day on which God blows away the mountains, (they will follow) that is, the creatures will follow (the summoner) the summoner of God to the place of gathering, like His words: ﴿hastening toward the summoner﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]. He is Israfil, who stands on the rock of Jerusalem calling the people, and they come from every direction. He puts the trumpets to his mouth and says: "O decayed bones, torn skins, and scattered flesh, come forward to be presented before the Most Merciful." Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: "They will be gathered in darkness, the sky will have been folded up and the stars scattered. Then a caller will call out, and they will die a single death." ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: "(al-dāʿī) here is the Messenger (ﷺ), who used to call them to God. They will deviate from the path to the right and to the left, turning away from him with great deviation. So on that day following him will not benefit them." The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (lahu) refers to ﴿al-dāʿī﴾. He negated crookedness from him, that is, ﴿no crookedness﴾ is theirs in regard to him; rather they come towards him, following his voice without deviation. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, no one invited by him is made crooked; rather they go straight to him. End of quotation.

* *

It was said: ﴿no crookedness for him﴾ is in the place of a description of a suppressed noun, that is, following ﴿no crookedness for him﴾, so the pronoun in (lahu) refers to that omitted verbal noun. It may also be intended as: no one can escape from following it, and walking towards its voice. Al-khushu' is humility and lowliness, and in regard to voices it is a metaphor meaning concealment. The "hushing" (istisrar) is for the Most Merciful, that is, out of awe of the Most Merciful, whose power is evident. It was said: it is by omission of a modifier, that is, "and the people of voices were humbled." Al-hams is a low, hidden sound. It may be intended that the whispering is what is heard, their secret speech among themselves. It may also be intended as the sound of footsteps, and that the sounds of speech are silent.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿Except a whisper﴾": it is a faint sound (al-rikz al-khafi), and from it comes the term "unvoiced letters" (al-huruf al-mahmusa).
