End of quote.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and Ibn Jubayr that al-hams is the treading of feet, and al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj preferred this view. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the moving of the lips without uttering sound, and from Mujahid that it is quiet speech. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "﴿So they will not speak except in a whisper﴾." From Abu 'Ubayda: "al-sawt al-khafi" (the faint sound). "That Day" is a substitute for "That Day they will follow"; or the sense is "the Day when they will follow," and it is in the accusative governed by "will not benefit." "Man" is the object of "﴿will not benefit﴾," and "lahu" means "for his sake," as also in "﴿and whose words He approves﴾," meaning for his sake. "Man" may refer to the one for whom intercession is made, or it may be a substitute for "intercession," with an elided noun, meaning "except the intercession of one whom He has permitted." Or it may be an exceptive in the accusative on this reading, or a disjunctive exception, in which case it is accusative in the Hijazi dialect and nominative in the Tamim dialect. In all these interpretations "man" refers to the intercessor. The "word that is approved" is, according to Ibn 'Abbas, "There is no god but Allah."

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "﴿what is before them and what is behind them﴾" refers to the created beings gathered, who are the followers of the caller. It has been said that it refers to the angels, and it has been said that it refers to people in general, not restricted to the gathering and following. The explanation of this phrase has already been given in the Verse of the Throne in al-Baqara. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to "ma" (what): "﴿and they do not encompass it﴾ in knowledge," that is, of His knowledge. The apparent sense is that "the faces" is general, meaning the faces of all creatures, and "the faces" was specified because the signs of humiliation first appear on the faces. Talq ibn Habib said: the intended meaning is the prostration of people upon their faces and the seven limbs. If he related that this will occur on the Day of Resurrection, then the verse is a report about it, and the meaning is sound; but if he meant in this world, then that is not consistent with the verses before and after it. Al-Zamakhshari said: by "faces" is meant the faces of the disobedient, and that when they witness on the Day of Resurrection disappointment, wretchedness and evil reckoning, their faces become "humbled," that is, abased and submissive, like the faces of captives, the prisoners; and similar is "﴿So when they see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed﴾" [al-Mulk: 27] and "﴿And faces that Day will be gloomy﴾" [al-Qiyama: 24]. As for "al-Qayyum," its discussion has already been given in al-Baqara.

(p-٢٧٧) Makki cited a view contrary to this: that Musa was with the seventy at the (divine) conversation, and that the affair of the calf occurred at that time. God informed Musa of it, so he concealed it from them and brought them until they heard the clamour of the Children of Israel around the calf, and then Musa made them aware of it. End of quotation. When he had finished refuting what the Samiri had done, he returned to explaining the true religion and said: ﴿Your God is only God﴾ [Ta-Ha: 98]. The majority of readers read (wasi'a), so that ʿilman is in the accusative as a tamyiz (a specifying accusative, a noun clarifying the sense of a verb or phrase), transferred from the subject. Its parallel was mentioned in al-An'am. Mujahid and Qatada read wassa'a, with the sin doubled. Al-Zamakhshari said: its basis is that wasi'a is transitive to one object, which is "everything" (kull shay'). As for ʿilman, its accusative is as a tamyiz, and in meaning it is the subject. When the verb is made heavier (doubled), it is transferred to be transitive to two objects, and so it puts both in the accusative as objects, because the specified noun is the subject in meaning. As you say: "Zayd feared ʿAmr", and "I made Zayd fear ʿAmr". Thus by the transfer, what was the subject becomes an object. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: (wasi'a) means the creation of things and their multiplicity by bringing them into being, so He encompassed them as existing things. End of quotation.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and Ibn Jubayr that al-hams is the treading of feet, and al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj preferred this view. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the moving of the lips without uttering sound, and from Mujahid that it is quiet speech. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "﴿So they will not speak except in a whisper﴾." From Abu 'Ubayda: "al-sawt al-khafi" (the faint sound). "That Day" is a substitute for "That Day they will follow"; or the sense is "the Day when they will follow," and it is in the accusative governed by "will not benefit." "Man" is the object of "﴿will not benefit﴾," and "lahu" means "for his sake," as also in "﴿and whose words He approves﴾," meaning for his sake. "Man" may refer to the one for whom intercession is made, or it may be a substitute for "intercession," with an elided noun, meaning "except the intercession of one whom He has permitted." Or it may be an exceptive in the accusative on this reading, or a disjunctive exception, in which case it is accusative in the Hijazi dialect and nominative in the Tamim dialect. In all these interpretations "man" refers to the intercessor. The "word that is approved" is, according to Ibn 'Abbas, "There is no god but Allah."

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "﴿what is before them and what is behind them﴾" refers to the created beings gathered, who are the followers of the caller. It has been said that it refers to the angels, and it has been said that it refers to people in general, not restricted to the gathering and following. The explanation of this phrase has already been given in the Verse of the Throne in al-Baqara. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to "ma" (what): "﴿and they do not encompass it﴾ in knowledge," that is, of His knowledge. The apparent sense is that "the faces" is general, meaning the faces of all creatures, and "the faces" was specified because the signs of humiliation first appear on the faces. Talq ibn Habib said: the intended meaning is the prostration of people upon their faces and the seven limbs. If he related that this will occur on the Day of Resurrection, then the verse is a report about it, and the meaning is sound; but if he meant in this world, then that is not consistent with the verses before and after it. Al-Zamakhshari said: by "faces" is meant the faces of the disobedient, and that when they witness on the Day of Resurrection disappointment, wretchedness and evil reckoning, their faces become "humbled," that is, abased and submissive, like the faces of captives, the prisoners; and similar is "﴿So when they see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed﴾" [al-Mulk: 27] and "﴿And faces that Day will be gloomy﴾" [al-Qiyama: 24]. As for "al-Qayyum," its discussion has already been given in al-Baqara.

(p-٢٧٧) Makki cited a view contrary to this: that Musa was with the seventy at the (divine) conversation, and that the affair of the calf occurred at that time. God informed Musa of it, so he concealed it from them and brought them until they heard the clamour of the Children of Israel around the calf, and then Musa made them aware of it. End of quotation. When he had finished refuting what the Samiri had done, he returned to explaining the true religion and said: ﴿Your God is only God﴾ [Ta-Ha: 98]. The majority of readers read (wasi'a), so that ʿilman is in the accusative as a tamyiz (a specifying accusative, a noun clarifying the sense of a verb or phrase), transferred from the subject. Its parallel was mentioned in al-An'am. Mujahid and Qatada read wassa'a, with the sin doubled. Al-Zamakhshari said: its basis is that wasi'a is transitive to one object, which is "everything" (kull shay'). As for ʿilman, its accusative is as a tamyiz, and in meaning it is the subject. When the verb is made heavier (doubled), it is transferred to be transitive to two objects, and so it puts both in the accusative as objects, because the specified noun is the subject in meaning. As you say: "Zayd feared ʿAmr", and "I made Zayd fear ʿAmr". Thus by the transfer, what was the subject becomes an object. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: (wasi'a) means the creation of things and their multiplicity by bringing them into being, so He encompassed them as existing things. End of quotation.

﴿Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has passed, and We have given you from Us a Reminder﴾. ﴿Whoever turns away from it, he will bear a burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿Abiding therein, and evil is their burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿The Day the Trumpet is blown, and We will gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed﴾. ﴿Whispering among themselves: "You remained only ten"﴾. ﴿We know best what they say, when the most exemplary of them in way says: "You remained only a day"﴾. ﴿And they ask you about the mountains; say: "My Lord will blow them away with a blast"﴾. ﴿And He will leave them a level plain﴾. ﴿You will not see therein any crookedness or unevenness﴾. ﴿That Day they will follow the summoner, with no deviation from him, and voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a whisper﴾.

Thus the demonstrative (dhalika) refers to the account of Musa, the Children of Israel and Pharaoh. That is, as We relate this wondrous account, We relate to you some of the news of the earlier nations. This contains mention of a great blessing, namely the informing of you about the news of past nations, so that you may be consoled by it and know that what the nations did to their messengers, and what the messengers endured from them, is the same. The apparent meaning is that the Reminder here is the Qur'an. He, exalted is He, bestowed a favour upon him by giving him the Reminder, which includes stories and reports, indicating through that miracles that were given to him. Muqatil said: "(dhikran)" means "clarification". Abu Sahl said: "honour and renown among people".

﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾: that is, from the Qur'an, by not believing in it and not following what is in it. The majority read (yahmilu), the present tense of ḥamala, lightly, in the active voice. A group, among them Dawud ibn Rufayʿ, read (yuḥammalu), with the mim doubled, in the passive voice, because he is burdened with that, not that he bears it willingly. (wizran) is the second object. (wizran) means a heavy, crushing weight, which its carrying exhausts, and it is the weight of punishment. Mujahid said: "sin". Al-Thawri said: "polytheism". The apparent meaning is that He expressed the punishment by the word "burden", because it is its cause. Therefore He said ﴿abiding therein﴾, that is, in the punishment and chastisement. He used the plural "abiding" (khalidin), and the pronoun in (lahum) is in agreement with the sense after agreement with its wording in (aʿrada) and in (fa-innahu yahmilu). The thing praised or condemned is omitted, that is, their burden. (lahum) is for clarification, as in ﴿Hayta laka﴾ [Yusuf: 23], not connected to (sa'a). (sa'a) here is the one that functions like (bi'sa), not the (sa'a) meaning "to sadden and worry", because that would corrupt the meaning.

"The day He blows" (yawma nunfakh) is a substitute for "the Day of Resurrection". The majority read (yunfakhu) in the passive voice, and (nahshuru) with the nun in the active voice, the nun of majesty. Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd read (nanfakhu) with the nun of majesty, like (nahshuru). He attributed the blowing to the one who commands it. The one who blows is Israfil, and out of honour for him He attributed what he undertakes to His own sanctified self. (al-Suwar) (the Trumpet) has been discussed in al-An'am. It was also read (yanfakhu) and (yahshuru) with the ya' in both, in the active voice. al-Hasan and Ibn ʿIyad, with a group, read ﴿fi al-Suwar﴾ on the pattern of (durar). Al-Hasan also read (yuhsharu) with the ya', in the passive voice, and (yahshuru) in the active voice, with the ya', that is, "and Allah gathers". The apparent meaning of "blue" (zurq) is the blueness of the eyes. Blue eyes were the most hated eye colour among the Arabs, because the Romans, who were their enemies, had blue eyes. For this reason they described the enemy as: "black-livered, reddish-moustached, blue-eyed". A poet said:

"I never feared that his death would be by the hand of a blue-eyed, lowered-eyed, Sabani horseman."

It is mentioned in another verse that they will be gathered with black faces, so the meaning is the disfiguring of the appearance, through the blackness of the face and the blueness of the eye. Also, the Arabs regard blueness as a bad omen. A poet said:

"Your eyes have grown dim, O son of Mukaʿbar! Surely every Dabbi is blue from baseness."

It was said: the meaning is "blind", because when the eye's light departs, its pupil turns blue. With this interpretation, the combination of His words "blue" (zurqan) in this verse and "blind" (ʿumyan) in the other verse is reconciled. It was said: the colours of their bodies turn blue, and this is extreme disfigurement, since they come like the colour of ash. In Arabic speech this colour is called blue. Skins do not turn blue except from enduring hardships and the drying of their moisture. It was said: (zurqan) means "thirsty", and severe thirst returns the blackness of the eye to whiteness. From this comes the saying "a blue spear-head", and his words:

"When they reached the water, blue with its crowd" —

that is, it turned white. The two verses were mentioned to Ibn ʿAbbas, and he said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: in one state they will be blue, and in another state they will be blind."

﴿Whispering (yatakhafatun)﴾: they speak secretly to one another out of the terror of the appearance and the intense distraction of their minds. The amount of time they remained has escaped them. ﴿You remained﴾: that is, in the abode of this world, or in the barzakh (intermediate state), or between the two blasts of the Trumpet. There are three opinions. Describing the time they spent there as short is because, compared with what they witness of hardships, the days they had in this world were days of joy, and days of joy are short. Or because of their departure from them and their passing. Whatever its duration, the thing that has gone is short in that it has ended. Or because they regard the Hereafter as long, and as everlasting and eternal, against which the life of this world is considered short. It is said: its people remained in it, in comparison with their remaining in the Hereafter. (idh) is governed by (aʿlam). (amthaluhum) means "the most upright of them". (ṭarīqatan) is in the accusative as a tamyiz.

﴿Except a day﴾ indicates the brevity of the period they remained. ﴿Except ten﴾ may mean ten nights or ten days, because when the masculine noun is omitted and its number kept, the feminine ta' may not be used. al-Kisai related from Abu al-Jarrah: "We fasted five from the month", and from this is what came in the hadith: "Then he followed it with six from Shawwal", meaning six days. The omission here is made good by the fact that this is the end of a verse, and by the fact that the first mention was the upper limit of the smallest number, which is ten. And he mentioned the most upright of them in way as the smallest number, which is one day. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿except a day﴾ shows that what is meant by their words ﴿ten﴾ is ten days.

* *

The third person pronoun in ﴿They ask you﴾ refers to the Quraysh who denied the Resurrection, or to the believers who asked about that, or to a man from Thaqif and a group from his people. There are three opinions. The second-person (ka) is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that the question did occur. The view of one who said there was no question is far-fetched; rather the meaning is that they would ask you ﴿about the mountains, then say﴾, so it implies the conditional, and therefore it is answered with the fa'. It is narrated that God sends a wind upon the mountains, which pounds them until they are like carded wool, then it continues upon them until it reduces them to dust scattered in the air. That is the (nasf), the blowing away. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿fa-yadharuha﴾ refers to the mountains, that is, after the blowing away they remain ﴿a level plain﴾, that is, flat, even ground. It was said: "He leaves their places of settlement and centres". It was said: it refers to the earth, though no mention of it has preceded, because the mountains indicate it.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: (ʿiwajan) means "a slope", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a trace like the thong of a sandal". From him also: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a valley", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a hill". From him also: "al-amt is elevation". Qatada said: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ means "a fissure", ﴿nor unevenness﴾ means "a mound". It was said: al-amt means cracks in the earth. It was said: a slight unevenness in a place in open country and mountain, and a flash in a place, as reported by al-Sulli. It was said: the amt in the verse is the ʿiwaj (crookedness) in the sky, facing the air, while the ʿiwaj in the earth is specific to the earth.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "They have distinguished between ʿiwaj and ʿawaj; they said: ʿiwaj with a kasra is used for meanings, and ʿawaj with a fatha is used for physical objects and the earth. How then is the form with kasra under the ʿayn valid for it?" I say: the choice of this word has a fine and striking effect in describing the earth as level and smooth and negating crookedness from it in the most emphatic way. That is because if you took a piece of land, levelled it, and went to great lengths in levelling it, by your own eye and the eyes of the keen-sighted among the farmers, and you all agreed that there remained no crookedness in it at all, then if you consulted an engineer about it and ordered him to test its evenness by the geometric measures, he would find crookedness in some place which cannot be perceived by the sense of sight, but only by geometric measurement. So God, mighty and majestic, negated that crookedness which is so subtle and fine as to escape perception, except by the measure known to the one who understands measurement and geometry. Since that crookedness is not perceived except by measurement and not by the senses, it is treated as an abstract meaning, so it is called ʿiwaj with a kasra. al-Amt is the slight protrusion. It is said: "He stretched his rope until there was no amt in it." End of quotation.

* *

(On that day) that is, the day on which God blows away the mountains, (they will follow) that is, the creatures will follow (the summoner) the summoner of God to the place of gathering, like His words: ﴿hastening toward the summoner﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]. He is Israfil, who stands on the rock of Jerusalem calling the people, and they come from every direction. He puts the trumpets to his mouth and says: "O decayed bones, torn skins, and scattered flesh, come forward to be presented before the Most Merciful." Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: "They will be gathered in darkness, the sky will have been folded up and the stars scattered. Then a caller will call out, and they will die a single death." ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: "(al-dāʿī) here is the Messenger (ﷺ), who used to call them to God. They will deviate from the path to the right and to the left, turning away from him with great deviation. So on that day following him will not benefit them." The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (lahu) refers to ﴿al-dāʿī﴾. He negated crookedness from him, that is, ﴿no crookedness﴾ is theirs in regard to him; rather they come towards him, following his voice without deviation. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, no one invited by him is made crooked; rather they go straight to him. End of quotation.

* *

It was said: ﴿no crookedness for him﴾ is in the place of a description of a suppressed noun, that is, following ﴿no crookedness for him﴾, so the pronoun in (lahu) refers to that omitted verbal noun. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it may be intended as a report, that is, there is no doubt about it, and its existence does not contradict its report. It may also be intended as: no one can escape from following it, and walking towards its voice. Al-khushu' is humility and lowliness, and in regard to voices it is a metaphor meaning concealment. The "hushing" (istisrar) is for the Most Merciful, that is, out of awe of the Most Merciful, whose power is evident. It was said: it is by omission of a modifier, that is, "and the people of voices were humbled." Al-hams is a low, hidden sound. It may be intended that the whispering is what is heard, their secret speech among themselves. It may also be intended as the sound of footsteps, and that the sounds of speech are silent.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿Except a whisper﴾": it is a faint sound (al-rikz al-khafi), and from it comes the term "unvoiced letters" (al-huruf al-mahmusa). It has also been said that it derives from the whispering of camels, which is the sound of their hooves when they walk; meaning that nothing is heard except the tread of feet and their movement toward the gathering place. End of quote.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and Ibn Jubayr that al-hams is the treading of feet, and al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj preferred this view. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the moving of the lips without uttering sound, and from Mujahid that it is quiet speech. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "﴿So they will not speak except in a whisper﴾." From Abu 'Ubayda: "al-sawt al-khafi" (the faint sound). "That Day" is a substitute for "That Day they will follow"; or the sense is "the Day when they will follow," and it is in the accusative governed by "will not benefit." "Man" is the object of "﴿will not benefit﴾," and "lahu" means "for his sake," as also in "﴿and whose words He approves﴾," meaning for his sake. "Man" may refer to the one for whom intercession is made, or it may be a substitute for "intercession," with an elided noun, meaning "except the intercession of one whom He has permitted." Or it may be an exceptive in the accusative on this reading, or a disjunctive exception, in which case it is accusative in the Hijazi dialect and nominative in the Tamim dialect. In all these interpretations "man" refers to the intercessor. The "word that is approved" is, according to Ibn 'Abbas, "There is no god but Allah."

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "﴿what is before them and what is behind them﴾" refers to the created beings gathered, who are the followers of the caller. It has been said that it refers to the angels, and it has been said that it refers to people in general, not restricted to the gathering and following. The explanation of this phrase has already been given in the Verse of the Throne in al-Baqara. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to "ma" (what): "﴿and they do not encompass it﴾ in knowledge," that is, of His knowledge. The apparent sense is that "the faces" is general, meaning the faces of all creatures, and "the faces" was specified because the signs of humiliation first appear on the faces. Talq ibn Habib said: the intended meaning is the prostration of people upon their faces and the seven limbs. If he related that this will occur on the Day of Resurrection, then the verse is a report about it, and the meaning is sound; but if he meant in this world, then that is not consistent with the verses before and after it. Al-Zamakhshari said: by "faces" is meant the faces of the disobedient, and that when they witness on the Day of Resurrection disappointment, wretchedness and evil reckoning, their faces become "humbled," that is, abased and submissive, like the faces of captives, the prisoners; and similar is "﴿So when they see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed﴾" [al-Mulk: 27] and "﴿And faces that Day will be gloomy﴾" [al-Qiyama: 24]. As for "al-Qayyum," its discussion has already been given in al-Baqara.

﴿And he has failed﴾: that is, he has not succeeded, nor attained what he sought. Injustice (ẓulm) encompasses both polytheism (shirk) and sins, and the failure of each bearer of injustice is in proportion to the injustice he bore. So the failure of the polytheist is perpetual, while the failure of the sinful believer is restricted to a period of punishment, if he is punished. When al-Zamakhshari (al-Zamakhsharī) restricted the faces (wujūh) to the faces of the disobedient (ʿuṣāh), he said, regarding His words ﴿And he has failed, who bore injustice﴾, that it is an interjection (iʿtirāḍ), like your saying: "They failed and lost," so that the sentence falls between the disobedient and those who do righteous deeds. Thus, in his view, this is the counterpart (qasīm) of ﴿And faces shall be humbled﴾.

As for Ibn ʿAṭiyya, he made His words ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾ up to ﴿any oppression﴾ a parallel (muʿādil) to His words ﴿And he has failed, who bore injustice﴾, because he made ﴿And faces shall be humbled﴾ general in the faces of all creatures.

And ﴿of the righteous deeds﴾ means "some of the righteous deeds," since min (مِن) indicates partitive (tabʿīḍ). Injustice (ẓulm) is exceeding the limit in the greatness of one's misdeeds, and hadm is a reduction from one's good deeds. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās. Qatādah said: injustice is that one's share of another's sin be increased. Ibn Zayd said: injustice is that one is not recompensed for his deeds. It was also said: injustice is that one takes from his companion more than his right, and hadm is that one diminishes the right of his brother so that he does not give it to him in full, like the description of the defrauders (al-muṭaffifīn), who take more for themselves when they measure from others, and give less when they measure out to others. End.

Injustice (ẓulm) and hadm are close in meaning. al-Māwardī said: the difference is that ẓulm is withholding the whole right, and hadm is withholding part of it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 113–114:

The majority of readers recited ﴿فَلا يَخافُ﴾ [Ta-Ha: 112] as an indicative (*khabar*), meaning "so he does not fear." Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd recited *fa-la yakhaf* as a prohibition (*nahy*). (Wa-kadhalika) is conjoined to *kadhalika naqussu*, meaning: "And like that revelation, or as We revealed to you these verses containing the threat, We revealed the whole Qur'an in this manner, repeating in it the verses of threat, so that they would be in a state where what is desired from them is abandoning sins or doing good and obedience. The word *dhikr* (remembrance) is applied to obedience and worship." It was also said: "Just as We decreed these matters and made them truly a watchful guard over the servants, so We warned these people about their affair, and ﴿We revealed it as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ and We threatened in it with kinds ﴿of warning, so that they may﴾ according to the expectation and hope of evil (*tawaqquʿ al-sharr wa-tarajjihim*) ﴿fear﴾ God and fear His punishment, so that they believe and remember His blessings upon them. And what He warned them of, His painful punishment, is the interpretation of one group regarding His saying ﴿or it causes them to remember﴾. Another group said: its meaning is, or it brings them honor and preserves their faith as a remembrance among those who remain." It was also said: the meaning is, just as We encouraged the people of faith with promise, We warned the people of polytheism with threat. ﴿And We have diversified in it of the threats﴾ such as the flood, the Cry, the earthquake and transformation into animals. The promise was not mentioned because the verse was framed in the manner of a threat. ﴿So that they may be God-fearing﴾, meaning, that they may be in hope that fear (*ittiqaʾ*) of Him is placed in their hearts, or that they may fear that what befell those before them will befall them. ﴿Or it causes them to remember﴾, meaning admonition, thought and consideration. Qatada said: "*wara*ʿ" (scrupulousness). It was also said: He revealed the Qur'an so that they would become guarded against what is not fitting. ﴿Or it causes them to remember﴾, it calls them to acts of obedience. He attributed the hope of God-fearing (*taqwa*) to them, and the hope of the arousing of remembrance to the Qur'an, because *taqwa* is an expression for the absence of the performance of ugly acts, and that is a continuation of the original state of non-existence. So He did not attribute *taqwa* to the Qur'an, and He attributed the bringing about of remembrance to the Qur'an, because it is a matter that came into being after it had not existed. The apparent meaning is that *aw* here is for one of the two things. It was said: *aw* here is like it is in "sitting or Ibn Sirin," meaning, do not be devoid of either of them.

Al-Hasan recited ﴿aw yuhdithu﴾ with the *tha'* silent (sukun). ʿAbd Allah, Mujahid, Abu Haywa, al-Hasan in one narration, al-Jahdari and Salam recited *aw nuhdith* with *nun* and the *tha'* jussed (*jazm*). That is "*hamlu wasl ʿala waqf*" (treating continuation as pause), or the silencing of the letter of inflection (*harf al-iʿrab*) due to the heaviness of its vowel, like the verse of Jarir:

"Or the River Tiri, so the Arabs will not know you"

Since in what preceded there was the glorification of the Qur'an in His saying ﴿And We have certainly given you from Us a reminder﴾ [Ta-Ha: 99] and ﴿And thus We revealed it as an Arabic Qur'an﴾, He mentioned the greatness of His station, the Exalted, and then mentioned these two attributes: the attribute of the King (*al-Malik*), which includes subjugation, sovereignty and truth, and it is the attribute that is established for Him, since everyone who claims a god besides Him is false, especially the god they fashioned from ornaments, whose dominion is perishing and borrowed. Also previously mentioned was the attribute of His authority on the Day of Resurrection, the greatness of (p-282) His power, the humility of His servants and the goodness of His gentleness towards them. So it was fitting that He be exalted and described with the two attributes mentioned. And since the Qur'an and its revelation were mentioned, He said, by way of digression (*istitrad*), requesting of him to be deliberate in preserving the Qur'an: ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you﴾, meaning, be patient until the one who conveys the revelation to you has finished, and do not match your recitation with his recitation and delivery, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16]. It was also said: its meaning is, do not convey what was ambiguous from it until the clarification comes to you.

It was said: the cause of the verse is that a woman complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) that her husband had slapped her, so he said to her, "Between you both is retaliation." Then there was revealed ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 34]. And this verse came with the meaning of an order to be careful in judgment by the Qur'an. It was also said: when revelation came down to him, he ordered it to be written down for the time being, so he was ordered to wait until the meanings were explained to him and were settled in his mind. Al-Mawardi said: its meaning is, do not ask before the revelation comes to you. The people of Mecca and the bishop of Najran said, "O Muhammad, tell us about such and such, and we have set you a term of three days," so the revelation was delayed to him, and the saying spread among the Jews that Muhammad had been defeated. Then there was revealed ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾, meaning, with its descent. Abu Muslim said: ﴿And do not hasten﴾ in its recitation within yourself, or in its delivery to others, or in holding to its apparent meaning, or in informing others of what its apparent meaning requires: these are possibilities.

﴿Before its revelation is completed to you﴾, meaning its completion or its clarification: these are possibilities. The intended meaning then is that he should not appoint himself or anyone else over it until its completion or its clarification, or both, is made clear by revelation, because it is necessary to pause regarding the meaning, lest there occur after it an exception, a condition, or other specifiers. This hastiness was perhaps something he did through his own effort, peace be upon him. End. There is some summarization in it.

The majority recited ﴿yuqda ilayka﴾ in the passive voice, with *wahyuhu* (its revelation) as its raised subject. ʿAbd Allah, al-Jahdari, al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, Yaʿqub, Salam, al-Zaʿfarani and Ibn Miqsam recited *naqdi* with the first-person plural *nun* of majesty, the *ya'* opened, and *wahyahu* in the accusative. Al-Aʿmash recited it likewise, except that he silenced the *ya'* of *yaqdi*. The companion of al-Lawami' said: this is according to the dialect of those who do not allow the *ya'* to be opened in any circumstance when the letter before it is kasra and it falls at the end of a word.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 113–114:

The majority of readers recited ﴿فَلا يَخافُ﴾ [Ta-Ha: 112] as an indicative (*khabar*), meaning "so he does not fear." Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd recited *fa-la yakhaf* as a prohibition (*nahy*). (Wa-kadhalika) is conjoined to *kadhalika naqussu*, meaning: "And like that revelation, or as We revealed to you these verses containing the threat, We revealed the whole Qur'an in this manner, repeating in it the verses of threat, so that they would be in a state where what is desired from them is abandoning sins or doing good and obedience. The word *dhikr* (remembrance) is applied to obedience and worship." It was also said: "Just as We decreed these matters and made them truly a watchful guard over the servants, so We warned these people about their affair, and ﴿We revealed it as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ and We threatened in it with kinds ﴿of warning, so that they may﴾ according to the expectation and hope of evil (*tawaqquʿ al-sharr wa-tarajjihim*) ﴿fear﴾ God and fear His punishment, so that they believe and remember His blessings upon them. And what He warned them of, His painful punishment, is the interpretation of one group regarding His saying ﴿or it causes them to remember﴾. Another group said: its meaning is, or it brings them honor and preserves their faith as a remembrance among those who remain." It was also said: the meaning is, just as We encouraged the people of faith with promise, We warned the people of polytheism with threat. ﴿And We have diversified in it of the threats﴾ such as the flood, the Cry, the earthquake and transformation into animals. The promise was not mentioned because the verse was framed in the manner of a threat. ﴿So that they may be God-fearing﴾, meaning, that they may be in hope that fear (*ittiqaʾ*) of Him is placed in their hearts, or that they may fear that what befell those before them will befall them. ﴿Or it causes them to remember﴾, meaning admonition, thought and consideration. Qatada said: "*wara*ʿ" (scrupulousness). It was also said: He revealed the Qur'an so that they would become guarded against what is not fitting. ﴿Or it causes them to remember﴾, it calls them to acts of obedience. He attributed the hope of God-fearing (*taqwa*) to them, and the hope of the arousing of remembrance to the Qur'an, because *taqwa* is an expression for the absence of the performance of ugly acts, and that is a continuation of the original state of non-existence. So He did not attribute *taqwa* to the Qur'an, and He attributed the bringing about of remembrance to the Qur'an, because it is a matter that came into being after it had not existed. The apparent meaning is that *aw* here is for one of the two things. It was said: *aw* here is like it is in "sitting or Ibn Sirin," meaning, do not be devoid of either of them.

Al-Hasan recited ﴿aw yuhdithu﴾ with the *tha'* silent (sukun). ʿAbd Allah, Mujahid, Abu Haywa, al-Hasan in one narration, al-Jahdari and Salam recited *aw nuhdith* with *nun* and the *tha'* jussed (*jazm*). That is "*hamlu wasl ʿala waqf*" (treating continuation as pause), or the silencing of the letter of inflection (*harf al-iʿrab*) due to the heaviness of its vowel, like the verse of Jarir:

"Or the River Tiri, so the Arabs will not know you"

Since in what preceded there was the glorification of the Qur'an in His saying ﴿And We have certainly given you from Us a reminder﴾ [Ta-Ha: 99] and ﴿And thus We revealed it as an Arabic Qur'an﴾, He mentioned the greatness of His station, the Exalted, and then mentioned these two attributes: the attribute of the King (*al-Malik*), which includes subjugation, sovereignty and truth, and it is the attribute that is established for Him, since everyone who claims a god besides Him is false, especially the god they fashioned from ornaments, whose dominion is perishing and borrowed. Also previously mentioned was the attribute of His authority on the Day of Resurrection, the greatness of (p-282) His power, the humility of His servants and the goodness of His gentleness towards them. So it was fitting that He be exalted and described with the two attributes mentioned. **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 115–121 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And say: "My Lord, increase me in knowledge."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114] Muqatil said: that is, the Qur'an. It was also said: understanding. And it was said: memorization. This statement implies humility before God and gratitude to Him, given what is known of the order of learning: that is, "You taught me subtle purposes in the field of learning and a beautiful etiquette that I did not have, so increase me in knowledge." It was also said: God did not command His Messenger to seek increase in anything except knowledge.

(p-283) ﴿We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve.﴾ ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused.﴾ ﴿So We said, "O Adam, this is an enemy to you and to your wife. So let him not drive you both out of the Garden, for then you would be miserable.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is granted to you that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked.﴾ ﴿And that you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun."﴾ ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying, "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?"﴾ ﴿So they both ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves of the Garden. And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred.﴾ ﴿Then his Lord chose him, turned to him in forgiveness, and guided him.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122] ﴿He said, "Go down from it, all of you, as enemies to one another. But when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor be unhappy."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123] ﴿But whoever turns away from My remembrance, for him is a constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 124] ﴿He will say, "My Lord, why have You gathered me blind, when I was [previously] seeing?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 125] ﴿He will say, "Thus Our signs came to you, and you forgot them; and thus today you are forgotten."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 126] ﴿And thus do We recompense one who transgresses and does not believe in the signs of his Lord. And the punishment of the Hereafter is severer and more lasting.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 127]

The story of Adam has preceded in al-Baqarah, al-A'raf, al-Hijr and al-Kahf. Then He mentions it here in connection with what preceded: ﴿Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has already passed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 99]. Among this news is the story of Adam, so that his descendants may guard themselves against the whispering of Satan and be alert to his dangers. Whoever among them obeys Satan is reminded of what happened to their father Adam with him, and that his enmity was made clear to him, and yet he forgot what his Lord had covenanted with him. Also, when he was commanded to say ﴿My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114], part of that was the mention of the story of Adam and some of his circumstances in it that had not been mentioned before. Thus there was in that an increase of knowledge for him, upon him be peace.

The word 'ahd (covenant) means, according to the majority, a charge (wasiyyah). The apparent reading is that the omitted genitive after the phrase "min qablu" (before) is in the sense of "min qablu" (before) these people to whom threats have been expounded in the Qur'an, so that they may be mindful, and they are those who break God's covenant and abandon faith. Al-Hasan said: "min qablu" (before) refers to the Messenger and the Qur'an. It was also said: "min qablu" (before) means before he ate from the tree.

Al-Tabari said: the meaning is that these disbelievers, O Muhammad, turn away from My signs, oppose My messengers and obey Iblis; and their father Adam did this long ago. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is weak, because Adam being an example for the disbelievers who deny God is nothing; and Adam, upon him be peace, disobeyed only through ta'wil (interpretation), so in this there is a disparagement of him, upon him be peace. The apparent meaning of this verse is either that it is the beginning of a narrative with no connection to what precedes, or that its connection is to what was charged to Muhammad (ﷺ), that he should not hasten with the Qur'an. It presented to him a prophet before him who was charged and "forgot" (fa-nasiya), so that it would be stronger in warning and more forceful in charging Muhammad (ﷺ).

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is said in the commands and charges of kings: "The king advanced toward so-and-so, and was angered at him, and resolved upon him, and charged him." God, glory be to Him, connected the story of Adam to His saying ﴿And We have expounded in it some of the threats, so that they may be mindful﴾ [Ta-Ha: 113]. The meaning is: "I swear an oath, We certainly commanded your father Adam and charged him not to approach the tree, and We threatened him with being included among the wrongdoers if he approached it. And that was before their existence, before We threatened them. So he went against what he was forbidden, and he was threatened for committing it, and he did not heed the threat, just as they do not heed it. It is as if He is saying: the foundation of the affair of the children of Adam is upon that, and their lineage is firmly rooted in it." End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that "forgetting" here means abandonment, if he abandoned what he was charged with of guarding against the tree and eating its fruit. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is possible that what is meant by forgetting is its opposite, remembrance, and that he did not give the charge sincere care, did not make it firm by fixing it in his heart and controlling his self, so that forgetting arose from that (p-284). End of quotation. Others also said this. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: forgetting through heedlessness (dhuhul) is not possible here, because no punishment attaches to one who forgets. End of quotation.

Al-Yamani and al-A'mash read ﴿fa-nussiya﴾ with a dammah on the nun and a shaddah on the sin, meaning: Satan caused him to forget. "Al-'azm" means determination and resolve.

Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, [he had no resolve] in abstaining from eating, and in being firm in that, in a way that would make Satan despair of tempting him. The word "wujud" may be in the sense of knowledge, with its two objects being ﴿lahu 'azman﴾ (for him, resolve); or it may be the opposite of nonexistence, as if He said: a promise from Us ﴿lahu 'azman﴾ (for him, resolve). End of quotation.

It was said: ﴿And We found in him no resolve﴾ refers to disobedience, and this is derived from the view of those who said that he committed it through forgetting. It was said: [the resolve refers to] memorization of what he was commanded. It was said: patience in abstaining from the tree. It was also said: ﴿'azman﴾ (resolve) refers to caution regarding the manner of ijtihad (independent reasoning).

\* \*

The discussion of the parallel of His saying ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused﴾ has already occurred. The word "aba" (he refused) is a resumptive clause explaining that his not prostrating was from refusal and obstinacy. The apparent reading is that the complement of "aba" is omitted, and what is stated in the other verse is understood here: ﴿He refused to be among those who prostrate﴾ [al-Hijr: 31]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "aba" is a resumptive clause, as if it were the answer to one who asked: "Why did he not prostrate?" The better view is that no object is to be supposed for it, which is the prostration indicated by "isjudu" (prostrate); and that its meaning is that he showed refusal, held back, and was reluctant. End of quotation.

"Hadha" (this) is a reference to Iblis, and "'aduww" (enemy) is used for the singular, dual and plural. God, exalted be He, made Adam aware of Iblis's enmity toward him and his wife, so that they would be wary of him. Yet caution does not avail against the divine decree (qadar). The cause of the enmity, it is said, is that Iblis was envious: when he saw the signs of God's blessings upon Adam, he envied him and became his enemy. It was also said: the enmity arose from the incompatibility of their origins, since Iblis was from fire and Adam from water and clay.

﴿So let him not drive you both out﴾: the prohibition is addressed to him, but the intended addressees are others; that is, let no obedience to him occur from you both in his seduction, so that this would be the cause of your expulsion from the Garden. He attributed the expulsion to Satan, though the one who expels is God, exalted be He, because it was by his whispering that he did what resulted in the expulsion. ﴿Then you would be miserable﴾ (fa-tashqa) may be in the accusative, by supposing "an" after the prohibition, or in the nominative, on the reckoning "fa-anta tashqa" (then you are miserable). He attributed the misery to him alone, after the sharing with his wife in the expulsion, since he was the one addressed first and the intended subject of the speech, and because within the misery of the man is the misery of his family, and within his happiness is hers. So the speech is abbreviated by attributing it to him rather than her, while preserving the verse-ending (fasilah).

It was said: by misery he meant the toil of seeking sustenance, and that returns to the man. From Ibn Jubayr: a red bull was sent down to him, which he plowed with, so he would eat by the labor of his right hand and the sweat of his brow.

Shayba, Nafi', Hafs and Ibn Sa'dan read ﴿wa-innaka la tadha'u﴾ (and indeed you are not thirsty) with a kasrah on the hamzah of "inna." The majority read it with a fathah. The kasrah is coordinated with "inna laka" (indeed for you), and the fathah is coordinated with the verbal noun constructed from "an la tju'a" (that you not hunger); that is, "for you is the absence of your hunger and the absence of your thirst." It is permissible to coordinate "annaka" with "anna" because they share the verbal noun; if the kasrah-"inna" directly governed it, that would not be permitted, even though it is in its implied form. Do you not see that it is coordinated with the noun of "inna," which is "an la tju'a"? But in coordination what is not permitted in direct government is permitted. Since satiety, quenching, clothing and shelter are the things that are necessities for a human being, he limited the statement to them, because they are sufficient for him. In the Garden there are kinds of bliss and comfort in comparison to which these are as nothing: among them is safety from death, which spoils every pleasure; the sight of the Face of God, glory be to Him; His good pleasure, exalted be He, toward its people; and that there is no sickness, no sorrow, no pain, no old age, no decrepitude, no rancor, no anger, no impurity, no filth, no obligation, no grief, no fear, and no boredom. These four were mentioned in the form of negation to affirm their opposites, namely satiety, quenching, clothing and shelter; and their opposites were stated in the form of negation: hunger, nakedness, thirst and exposure to the sun, so that his hearing would be struck with the names of the kinds of wretchedness against which he was warned, until he would avoid the cause that brings them about, out of aversion to them.

\* \*

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the customary usage of speech is that hunger goes with thirst, and nakedness goes with exposure to the sun, because they are opposites: nakedness itself is cold, which harms, while heat does this to one exposed to the sun. This is a well-trodden method in the speech of the Arabs (p-285), of pairing the two. From it is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*As if I had never mounted a steed for pleasure, nor embraced a maiden with anklets,*
*Nor had I taken captive the free-born slave, nor said to my horses, "Charge again, a second charge after fleeing."*

Some men of letters went so far as to say that the two verses of Imru' al-Qays are a kind of pairing by affinity, and that riding horses for hunting and other pleasures suits the embracing of a maiden. End of quotation.

It was said: this reply is in proportion to the question. When God commanded Adam to dwell in the Garden, he said: "My God, is there for me in it what I eat? Is there for me in it what I wear? Is there for me in it what I drink? Is there for me in it what I shade myself with?" It was also said: it is a spiritual correspondence, so hunger is the emptiness of the inner self, nakedness the emptiness of the outer self, thirst the burning of the inner self, and exposure to the sun the burning of the outer self; thus he paired emptiness with fullness and burning with burning. It was also said: Imru' al-Qays combined in his two verses riding horses for pleasure and leisure with embracing a maiden for the pleasure obtained in both; and he combined taking captives with his saying to his horses "charge," because of the courage in both. Abu al-Tayyib was criticized for his saying:

*She stood, and there is no doubt in the death of one who stands; as if you were in the sheath of destruction, and he is asleep.*
*The heroes pass by you defeated, humbled; and your face is bright, and your smile is cheerful.*

He said: if I was wrong, then Imru' al-Qays was also wrong.

The discussion of ﴿fa-waswasa﴾ (then he whispered) has preceded, and the disagreement over its manner in al-A'raf. Here "waswasa" takes "ila" (to), and in al-A'raf it takes the lam. The construction with "ila" means that he delivered the whispering to him; the construction with the lam of attribution is said to mean "for his sake." When he whispered to him, he called him by his name so that he would be more attentive to him and more able to listen. Then he presented to him what he would encounter, with his saying ﴿Shall I direct you﴾ in the form of a question which suggests sincerity, and which induces acceptance by the one addressed, like Moses's saying ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18]; this is an offer containing counsel. Adam had been encouraged by God, exalted be He, toward lasting ease and an ordered livelihood with His saying ﴿So let him not drive you both out﴾, and so on. Iblis encouraged him toward lasting ease with his saying ﴿Shall I direct you?﴾; so he came to him from the direction in which God had encouraged him. In al-A'raf it is ﴿What your Lord has forbidden you from this tree﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]; and here it is ﴿Shall I direct you?﴾. The reconciliation between them is that his saying ﴿Shall I direct you?﴾ came before his saying ﴿What has your Lord forbidden you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]: when he saw his attentiveness and inclination toward what he had presented to him, he moved on to statement and restriction.

The meaning of ﴿the tree of eternity﴾ is: the tree whoever eats from it becomes immortal and gains a kingdom that never decays. This supports the reading of al-Hasan ibn Ali and Ibn Abbas, "unless you become two angels" (*malakayn*), with a kasra on the lam. ﴿So they ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves from the Garden.﴾ The discussion of this verse has already been covered in al-A'raf. ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray.﴾ ﴿Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122]

Al-Zamakhshari said, quoting Ibn Abbas: There is no doubt that Adam, may the blessings of God be upon him, did not comply with what God had prescribed for him, and he overstepped the bounds of obedience in this matter, and that is disobedience (*'isyan*). When he disobeyed, his action ceased to be right guidance and good, and so it was inevitably error (*ghayy*), since *al-ghayy* is the opposite of *al-rushd* (right guidance). However, the statement ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray﴾ is in this unqualified form and with this explicit wording, and the fact that it does not say "Adam slipped," "erred," or anything similar to the expressions used for lapses and oversights, contains kindness toward those who are responsible (*mukallafin*), a powerful deterrent, and a comprehensive admonition. It is as if they were told: Look and take heed how We rebuke the infallible Prophet (*al-nabi al-ma'sum*), the beloved of God, who cannot commit even a minor sin that does not repel, for his slip is reproached with such severity and in such a shocking expression. So do not be lax about the bad deeds and minor sins that you commit, let alone become bold enough to plunge into major sins. Some of them read *fa-ghawa* as *fa-sa'ima* ("he grew weary") from the great amount of eating. Although this is valid according to the dialect of those who change a kasra-marked *ya'* preceded by a vowel into an *alif*, saying *fana* and *baqa* for *fani* and *baqi*, namely the Banu Tayy, it is an evil interpretation. End of quotation.

* *

The Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: It is not permissible for any of us today to report this about him, peace be upon him, except when we mention it within the context of God's words or the words of His Prophet, peace be upon him. If one begins it on one's own initiative, it is not permissible for us regarding our nearer fathers who are similar to us, so how about our first, greatest, most honorable father, the Prophet who was foremost, whom God chose, accepted his repentance, and forgave him. Al-Qurtubi said: If this is impermissible regarding a created being, then reporting the attributes of God, such as the hand, the foot, the finger, the side, descending, and so on, is all the more deserving of prohibition, and it is not permissible to initiate any mention of such things except within the recitation of His Book or the Sunnah of His Messenger, peace be upon him. For this reason Imam Malik ibn Anas said: Whoever describes any attribute of the Essence of God, such as His words: ﴿And the Jews said, "God's hand is chained"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], and points with his hand to his neck, I will cut off his hand. The same applies to hearing and sight, which should be cut off from him, because he has likened God, glorified be He, to himself. (p-286)

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 115–121 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And say: "My Lord, increase me in knowledge."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114] Muqatil said: that is, the Qur'an. It was also said: understanding. And it was said: memorization. This statement implies humility before God and gratitude to Him, given what is known of the order of learning: that is, "You taught me subtle purposes in the field of learning and a beautiful etiquette that I did not have, so increase me in knowledge." It was also said: God did not command His Messenger to seek increase in anything except knowledge.

(p-283) ﴿We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve.﴾ ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused.﴾ ﴿So We said, "O Adam, this is an enemy to you and to your wife. So let him not drive you both out of the Garden, for then you would be miserable.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is granted to you that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked.﴾ ﴿And that you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun."﴾ ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying, "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?"﴾ ﴿So they both ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves of the Garden. And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred.﴾ ﴿Then his Lord chose him, turned to him in forgiveness, and guided him.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122] ﴿He said, "Go down from it, all of you, as enemies to one another. But when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor be unhappy."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123] ﴿But whoever turns away from My remembrance, for him is a constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 124] ﴿He will say, "My Lord, why have You gathered me blind, when I was [previously] seeing?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 125] ﴿He will say, "Thus Our signs came to you, and you forgot them; and thus today you are forgotten."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 126] ﴿And thus do We recompense one who transgresses and does not believe in the signs of his Lord. And the punishment of the Hereafter is severer and more lasting.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 127]

The story of Adam has preceded in al-Baqarah, al-A'raf, al-Hijr and al-Kahf. Then He mentions it here in connection with what preceded: ﴿Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has already passed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 99]. Among this news is the story of Adam, so that his descendants may guard themselves against the whispering of Satan and be alert to his dangers. Whoever among them obeys Satan is reminded of what happened to their father Adam with him, and that his enmity was made clear to him, and yet he forgot what his Lord had covenanted with him. Also, when he was commanded to say ﴿My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114], part of that was the mention of the story of Adam and some of his circumstances in it that had not been mentioned before. Thus there was in that an increase of knowledge for him, upon him be peace.

The word 'ahd (covenant) means, according to the majority, a charge (wasiyyah). The apparent reading is that the omitted genitive after the phrase "min qablu" (before) is in the sense of "min qablu" (before) these people to whom threats have been expounded in the Qur'an, so that they may be mindful, and they are those who break God's covenant and abandon faith. Al-Hasan said: "min qablu" (before) refers to the Messenger and the Qur'an. It was also said: "min qablu" (before) means before he ate from the tree.

Al-Tabari said: the meaning is that these disbelievers, O Muhammad, turn away from My signs, oppose My messengers and obey Iblis; and their father Adam did this long ago. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is weak, because Adam being an example for the disbelievers who deny God is nothing; and Adam, upon him be peace, disobeyed only through ta'wil (interpretation), so in this there is a disparagement of him, upon him be peace. The apparent meaning of this verse is either that it is the beginning of a narrative with no connection to what precedes, or that its connection is to what was charged to Muhammad (ﷺ), that he should not hasten with the Qur'an. It presented to him a prophet before him who was charged and "forgot" (fa-nasiya), so that it would be stronger in warning and more forceful in charging Muhammad (ﷺ).

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is said in the commands and charges of kings: "The king advanced toward so-and-so, and was angered at him, and resolved upon him, and charged him." God, glory be to Him, connected the story of Adam to His saying ﴿And We have expounded in it some of the threats, so that they may be mindful﴾ [Ta-Ha: 113]. The meaning is: "I swear an oath, We certainly commanded your father Adam and charged him not to approach the tree, and We threatened him with being included among the wrongdoers if he approached it. And that was before their existence, before We threatened them. So he went against what he was forbidden, and he was threatened for committing it, and he did not heed the threat, just as they do not heed it. It is as if He is saying: the foundation of the affair of the children of Adam is upon that, and their lineage is firmly rooted in it." End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that "forgetting" here means abandonment, if he abandoned what he was charged with of guarding against the tree and eating its fruit. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is possible that what is meant by forgetting is its opposite, remembrance, and that he did not give the charge sincere care, did not make it firm by fixing it in his heart and controlling his self, so that forgetting arose from that (p-284). End of quotation. Others also said this. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: forgetting through heedlessness (dhuhul) is not possible here, because no punishment attaches to one who forgets. End of quotation.

Al-Yamani and al-A'mash read ﴿fa-nussiya﴾ with a dammah on the nun and a shaddah on the sin, meaning: Satan caused him to forget. "Al-'azm" means determination and resolve.

Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, [he had no resolve] in abstaining from eating, and in being firm in that, in a way that would make Satan despair of tempting him. The word "wujud" may be in the sense of knowledge, with its two objects being ﴿lahu 'azman﴾ (for him, resolve); or it may be the opposite of nonexistence, as if He said: a promise from Us ﴿lahu 'azman﴾ (for him, resolve). End of quotation.

It was said: ﴿And We found in him no resolve﴾ refers to disobedience, and this is derived from the view of those who said that he committed it through forgetting. It was said: [the resolve refers to] memorization of what he was commanded. It was said: patience in abstaining from the tree. It was also said: ﴿'azman﴾ (resolve) refers to caution regarding the manner of ijtihad (independent reasoning).

\* \*

The discussion of the parallel of His saying ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused﴾ has already occurred. The word "aba" (he refused) is a resumptive clause explaining that his not prostrating was from refusal and obstinacy. The apparent reading is that the complement of "aba" is omitted, and what is stated in the other verse is understood here: ﴿He refused to be among those who prostrate﴾ [al-Hijr: 31]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "aba" is a resumptive clause, as if it were the answer to one who asked: "Why did he not prostrate?" The better view is that no object is to be supposed for it, which is the prostration indicated by "isjudu" (prostrate); and that its meaning is that he showed refusal, held back, and was reluctant. End of quotation.

"Hadha" (this) is a reference to Iblis, and "'aduww" (enemy) is used for the singular, dual and plural. God, exalted be He, made Adam aware of Iblis's enmity toward him and his wife, so that they would be wary of him. Yet caution does not avail against the divine decree (qadar). The cause of the enmity, it is said, is that Iblis was envious: when he saw the signs of God's blessings upon Adam, he envied him and became his enemy. It was also said: the enmity arose from the incompatibility of their origins, since Iblis was from fire and Adam from water and clay.

﴿So let him not drive you both out﴾: the prohibition is addressed to him, but the intended addressees are others; that is, let no obedience to him occur from you both in his seduction, so that this would be the cause of your expulsion from the Garden. He attributed the expulsion to Satan, though the one who expels is God, exalted be He, because it was by his whispering that he did what resulted in the expulsion. ﴿Then you would be miserable﴾ (fa-tashqa) may be in the accusative, by supposing "an" after the prohibition, or in the nominative, on the reckoning "fa-anta tashqa" (then you are miserable). He attributed the misery to him alone, after the sharing with his wife in the expulsion, since he was the one addressed first and the intended subject of the speech, and because within the misery of the man is the misery of his family, and within his happiness is hers. So the speech is abbreviated by attributing it to him rather than her, while preserving the verse-ending (fasilah).

It was said: by misery he meant the toil of seeking sustenance, and that returns to the man. From Ibn Jubayr: a red bull was sent down to him, which he plowed with, so he would eat by the labor of his right hand and the sweat of his brow.

Shayba, Nafi', Hafs and Ibn Sa'dan read ﴿wa-innaka la tadha'u﴾ (and indeed you are not thirsty) with a kasrah on the hamzah of "inna." The majority read it with a fathah. The kasrah is coordinated with "inna laka" (indeed for you), and the fathah is coordinated with the verbal noun constructed from "an la tju'a" (that you not hunger); that is, "for you is the absence of your hunger and the absence of your thirst." It is permissible to coordinate "annaka" with "anna" because they share the verbal noun; if the kasrah-"inna" directly governed it, that would not be permitted, even though it is in its implied form. Do you not see that it is coordinated with the noun of "inna," which is "an la tju'a"? But in coordination what is not permitted in direct government is permitted. Since satiety, quenching, clothing and shelter are the things that are necessities for a human being, he limited the statement to them, because they are sufficient for him. In the Garden there are kinds of bliss and comfort in comparison to which these are as nothing: among them is safety from death, which spoils every pleasure; the sight of the Face of God, glory be to Him; His good pleasure, exalted be He, toward its people; and that there is no sickness, no sorrow, no pain, no old age, no decrepitude, no rancor, no anger, no impurity, no filth, no obligation, no grief, no fear, and no boredom. These four were mentioned in the form of negation to affirm their opposites, namely satiety, quenching, clothing and shelter; and their opposites were stated in the form of negation: hunger, nakedness, thirst and exposure to the sun, so that his hearing would be struck with the names of the kinds of wretchedness against which he was warned, until he would avoid the cause that brings them about, out of aversion to them.

\* \*

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the customary usage of speech is that hunger goes with thirst, and nakedness goes with exposure to the sun, because they are opposites: nakedness itself is cold, which harms, while heat does this to one exposed to the sun. This is a well-trodden method in the speech of the Arabs (p-285), of pairing the two. From it is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*As if I had never mounted a steed for pleasure, nor embraced a maiden with anklets,*
*Nor had I taken captive the free-born slave, nor said to my horses, "Charge again, a second charge after fleeing."*

Some men of letters went so far as to say that the two verses of Imru' al-Qays are a kind of pairing by affinity, and that riding horses for hunting and other pleasures suits the embracing of a maiden. End of quotation.

It was said: this reply is in proportion to the question. When God commanded Adam to dwell in the Garden, he said: "My God, is there for me in it what I eat? Is there for me in it what I wear? Is there for me in it what I drink? Is there for me in it what I shade myself with?" It was also said: it is a spiritual correspondence, so hunger is the emptiness of the inner self, nakedness the emptiness of the outer self, thirst the burning of the inner self, and exposure to the sun the burning of the outer self; thus he paired emptiness with fullness and burning with burning. It was also said: Imru' al-Qays combined in his two verses riding horses for pleasure and leisure with embracing a maiden for the pleasure obtained in both; and he combined taking captives with his saying to his horses "charge," because of the courage in both. Abu al-Tayyib was criticized for his saying:

*She stood, and there is no doubt in the death of one who stands; as if you were in the sheath of destruction, and he is asleep.*
*The heroes pass by you defeated, humbled; and your face is bright, and your smile is cheerful.*

He said: if I was wrong, then Imru' al-Qays was also wrong.

The discussion of ﴿fa-waswasa﴾ (then he whispered) has preceded, and the disagreement over its manner in al-A'raf. Here "waswasa" takes "ila" (to), and in al-A'raf it takes the lam. The construction with "ila" means that he delivered the whispering to him; the construction with the lam of attribution is said to mean "for his sake." When he whispered to him, he called him by his name so that he would be more attentive to him and more able to listen. Then he presented to him what he would encounter, with his saying ﴿Shall I direct you﴾ in the form of a question which suggests sincerity, and which induces acceptance by the one addressed, like Moses's saying ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18]; this is an offer containing counsel. Adam had been encouraged by God, exalted be He, toward lasting ease and an ordered livelihood with His saying ﴿So let him not drive you both out﴾, and so on. Iblis encouraged him toward lasting ease with his saying ﴿Shall I direct you?﴾; so he came to him from the direction in which God had encouraged him. In al-A'raf it is ﴿What your Lord has forbidden you from this tree﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]; and here it is ﴿Shall I direct you?﴾. The reconciliation between them is that his saying ﴿Shall I direct you?﴾ came before his saying ﴿What has your Lord forbidden you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]: when he saw his attentiveness and inclination toward what he had presented to him, he moved on to statement and restriction.

The meaning of ﴿the tree of eternity﴾ is: the tree whoever eats from it becomes immortal and gains a kingdom that never decays. This supports the reading of al-Hasan ibn Ali and Ibn Abbas, "unless you become two angels" (*malakayn*), with a kasra on the lam. ﴿So they ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves from the Garden.﴾ The discussion of this verse has already been covered in al-A'raf. ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray.﴾ ﴿Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122]

Al-Zamakhshari said, quoting Ibn Abbas: There is no doubt that Adam, may the blessings of God be upon him, did not comply with what God had prescribed for him, and he overstepped the bounds of obedience in this matter, and that is disobedience (*'isyan*). When he disobeyed, his action ceased to be right guidance and good, and so it was inevitably error (*ghayy*), since *al-ghayy* is the opposite of *al-rushd* (right guidance). However, the statement ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray﴾ is in this unqualified form and with this explicit wording, and the fact that it does not say "Adam slipped," "erred," or anything similar to the expressions used for lapses and oversights, contains kindness toward those who are responsible (*mukallafin*), a powerful deterrent, and a comprehensive admonition. It is as if they were told: Look and take heed how We rebuke the infallible Prophet (*al-nabi al-ma'sum*), the beloved of God, who cannot commit even a minor sin that does not repel, for his slip is reproached with such severity and in such a shocking expression. So do not be lax about the bad deeds and minor sins that you commit, let alone become bold enough to plunge into major sins. Some of them read *fa-ghawa* as *fa-sa'ima* ("he grew weary") from the great amount of eating. Although this is valid according to the dialect of those who change a kasra-marked *ya'* preceded by a vowel into an *alif*, saying *fana* and *baqa* for *fani* and *baqi*, namely the Banu Tayy, it is an evil interpretation. End of quotation.

* *

The Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: It is not permissible for any of us today to report this about him, peace be upon him, except when we mention it within the context of God's words or the words of His Prophet, peace be upon him. If one begins it on one's own initiative, it is not permissible for us regarding our nearer fathers who are similar to us, so how about our first, greatest, most honorable father, the Prophet who was foremost, whom God chose, accepted his repentance, and forgave him. Al-Qurtubi said: If this is impermissible regarding a created being, then reporting the attributes of God, such as the hand, the foot, the finger, the side, descending, and so on, is all the more deserving of prohibition, and it is not permissible to initiate any mention of such things except within the recitation of His Book or the Sunnah of His Messenger, peace be upon him. For this reason Imam Malik ibn Anas said: Whoever describes any attribute of the Essence of God, such as His words: ﴿And the Jews said, "God's hand is chained"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], and points with his hand to his neck, I will cut off his hand. The same applies to hearing and sight, which should be cut off from him, because he has likened God, glorified be He, to himself. (p-286)

It was said: this reply is in proportion to the question. When God commanded Adam to dwell in the Garden, he said: "My God, is there for me in it what I eat? Is there for me in it what I wear?
