It was also said: it is a spiritual correspondence, so hunger is the emptiness of the inner self, nakedness the emptiness of the outer self, thirst the burning of the inner self, and exposure to the sun the burning of the outer self; thus he paired emptiness with fullness and burning with burning. It was also said: Imru' al-Qays combined in his two verses riding horses for pleasure and leisure with embracing a maiden for the pleasure obtained in both; and he combined taking captives with his saying to his horses "charge," because of the courage in both. Abu al-Tayyib was criticized for his saying:

*She stood, and there is no doubt in the death of one who stands; as if you were in the sheath of destruction, and he is asleep.*
*The heroes pass by you defeated, humbled; and your face is bright, and your smile is cheerful.*

He said: if I was wrong, then Imru' al-Qays was also wrong.

The discussion of ﴿fa-waswasa﴾ (then he whispered) has preceded, and the disagreement over its manner in al-A'raf. Here "waswasa" takes "ila" (to), and in al-A'raf it takes the lam. The construction with "ila" means that he delivered the whispering to him; the construction with the lam of attribution is said to mean "for his sake." When he whispered to him, he called him by his name so that he would be more attentive to him and more able to listen. Then he presented to him what he would encounter, with his saying ﴿Shall I direct you﴾ in the form of a question which suggests sincerity, and which induces acceptance by the one addressed, like Moses's saying ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18]; this is an offer containing counsel. Adam had been encouraged by God, exalted be He, toward lasting ease and an ordered livelihood with His saying ﴿So let him not drive you both out﴾, and so on. Iblis encouraged him toward lasting ease with his saying ﴿Shall I direct you?﴾; so he came to him from the direction in which God had encouraged him. In al-A'raf it is ﴿What your Lord has forbidden you from this tree﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]; and here it is ﴿Shall I direct you?﴾. The reconciliation between them is that his saying ﴿Shall I direct you?﴾ came before his saying ﴿What has your Lord forbidden you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]: when he saw his attentiveness and inclination toward what he had presented to him, he moved on to statement and restriction.

The meaning of ﴿the tree of eternity﴾ is: the tree whoever eats from it becomes immortal and gains a kingdom that never decays. This supports the reading of al-Hasan ibn Ali and Ibn Abbas, "unless you become two angels" (*malakayn*), with a kasra on the lam. ﴿So they ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves from the Garden.﴾ The discussion of this verse has already been covered in al-A'raf. ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray.﴾ ﴿Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122]

Al-Zamakhshari said, quoting Ibn Abbas: There is no doubt that Adam, may the blessings of God be upon him, did not comply with what God had prescribed for him, and he overstepped the bounds of obedience in this matter, and that is disobedience (*'isyan*). When he disobeyed, his action ceased to be right guidance and good, and so it was inevitably error (*ghayy*), since *al-ghayy* is the opposite of *al-rushd* (right guidance). However, the statement ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray﴾ is in this unqualified form and with this explicit wording, and the fact that it does not say "Adam slipped," "erred," or anything similar to the expressions used for lapses and oversights, contains kindness toward those who are responsible (*mukallafin*), a powerful deterrent, and a comprehensive admonition. It is as if they were told: Look and take heed how We rebuke the infallible Prophet (*al-nabi al-ma'sum*), the beloved of God, who cannot commit even a minor sin that does not repel, for his slip is reproached with such severity and in such a shocking expression. So do not be lax about the bad deeds and minor sins that you commit, let alone become bold enough to plunge into major sins. Some of them read *fa-ghawa* as *fa-sa'ima* ("he grew weary") from the great amount of eating. Although this is valid according to the dialect of those who change a kasra-marked *ya'* preceded by a vowel into an *alif*, saying *fana* and *baqa* for *fani* and *baqi*, namely the Banu Tayy, it is an evil interpretation. End of quotation.

* *

The Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: It is not permissible for any of us today to report this about him, peace be upon him, except when we mention it within the context of God's words or the words of His Prophet, peace be upon him. If one begins it on one's own initiative, it is not permissible for us regarding our nearer fathers who are similar to us, so how about our first, greatest, most honorable father, the Prophet who was foremost, whom God chose, accepted his repentance, and forgave him. Al-Qurtubi said: If this is impermissible regarding a created being, then reporting the attributes of God, such as the hand, the foot, the finger, the side, descending, and so on, is all the more deserving of prohibition, and it is not permissible to initiate any mention of such things except within the recitation of His Book or the Sunnah of His Messenger, peace be upon him. For this reason Imam Malik ibn Anas said: Whoever describes any attribute of the Essence of God, such as His words: ﴿And the Jews said, "God's hand is chained"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], and points with his hand to his neck, I will cut off his hand. The same applies to hearing and sight, which should be cut off from him, because he has likened God, glorified be He, to himself. (p-286)

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 115–121 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And say: "My Lord, increase me in knowledge."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114] Muqatil said: that is, the Qur'an. It was also said: understanding. And it was said: memorization. This statement implies humility before God and gratitude to Him, given what is known of the order of learning: that is, "You taught me subtle purposes in the field of learning and a beautiful etiquette that I did not have, so increase me in knowledge." It was also said: God did not command His Messenger to seek increase in anything except knowledge.

(p-283) ﴿We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve.﴾ ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused.﴾ ﴿So We said, "O Adam, this is an enemy to you and to your wife. So let him not drive you both out of the Garden, for then you would be miserable.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is granted to you that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked.﴾ ﴿And that you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun."﴾ ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying, "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?"﴾ ﴿So they both ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves of the Garden. And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred.﴾ ﴿Then his Lord chose him, turned to him in forgiveness, and guided him.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122] ﴿He said, "Go down from it, all of you, as enemies to one another. But when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor be unhappy."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123] ﴿But whoever turns away from My remembrance, for him is a constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 124] ﴿He will say, "My Lord, why have You gathered me blind, when I was [previously] seeing?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 125] ﴿He will say, "Thus Our signs came to you, and you forgot them; and thus today you are forgotten."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 126] ﴿And thus do We recompense one who transgresses and does not believe in the signs of his Lord. And the punishment of the Hereafter is severer and more lasting.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 127]

The story of Adam has preceded in al-Baqarah, al-A'raf, al-Hijr and al-Kahf. Then He mentions it here in connection with what preceded: ﴿Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has already passed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 99]. Among this news is the story of Adam, so that his descendants may guard themselves against the whispering of Satan and be alert to his dangers. Whoever among them obeys Satan is reminded of what happened to their father Adam with him, and that his enmity was made clear to him, and yet he forgot what his Lord had covenanted with him. Also, when he was commanded to say ﴿My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114], part of that was the mention of the story of Adam and some of his circumstances in it that had not been mentioned before. Thus there was in that an increase of knowledge for him, upon him be peace.

The word 'ahd (covenant) means, according to the majority, a charge (wasiyyah). The apparent reading is that the omitted genitive after the phrase "min qablu" (before) is in the sense of "min qablu" (before) these people to whom threats have been expounded in the Qur'an, so that they may be mindful, and they are those who break God's covenant and abandon faith. Al-Hasan said: "min qablu" (before) refers to the Messenger and the Qur'an. It was also said: "min qablu" (before) means before he ate from the tree.

Al-Tabari said: the meaning is that these disbelievers, O Muhammad, turn away from My signs, oppose My messengers and obey Iblis; and their father Adam did this long ago. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is weak, because Adam being an example for the disbelievers who deny God is nothing; and Adam, upon him be peace, disobeyed only through ta'wil (interpretation), so in this there is a disparagement of him, upon him be peace. The apparent meaning of this verse is either that it is the beginning of a narrative with no connection to what precedes, or that its connection is to what was charged to Muhammad (ﷺ), that he should not hasten with the Qur'an. It presented to him a prophet before him who was charged and "forgot" (fa-nasiya), so that it would be stronger in warning and more forceful in charging Muhammad (ﷺ).

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is said in the commands and charges of kings: "The king advanced toward so-and-so, and was angered at him, and resolved upon him, and charged him." God, glory be to Him, connected the story of Adam to His saying ﴿And We have expounded in it some of the threats, so that they may be mindful﴾ [Ta-Ha: 113]. The meaning is: "I swear an oath, We certainly commanded your father Adam and charged him not to approach the tree, and We threatened him with being included among the wrongdoers if he approached it. And that was before their existence, before We threatened them. So he went against what he was forbidden, and he was threatened for committing it, and he did not heed the threat, just as they do not heed it. It is as if He is saying: the foundation of the affair of the children of Adam is upon that, and their lineage is firmly rooted in it." End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that "forgetting" here means abandonment, if he abandoned what he was charged with of guarding against the tree and eating its fruit. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is possible that what is meant by forgetting is its opposite, remembrance, and that he did not give the charge sincere care, did not make it firm by fixing it in his heart and controlling his self, so that forgetting arose from that (p-284). End of quotation. Others also said this. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: forgetting through heedlessness (dhuhul) is not possible here, because no punishment attaches to one who forgets. End of quotation.

Al-Yamani and al-A'mash read ﴿fa-nussiya﴾ with a dammah on the nun and a shaddah on the sin, meaning: Satan caused him to forget. "Al-'azm" means determination and resolve.

Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, [he had no resolve] in abstaining from eating, and in being firm in that, in a way that would make Satan despair of tempting him. The word "wujud" may be in the sense of knowledge, with its two objects being ﴿lahu 'azman﴾ (for him, resolve); or it may be the opposite of nonexistence, as if He said: a promise from Us ﴿lahu 'azman﴾ (for him, resolve). End of quotation.

It was said: ﴿And We found in him no resolve﴾ refers to disobedience, and this is derived from the view of those who said that he committed it through forgetting. It was said: [the resolve refers to] memorization of what he was commanded. It was said: patience in abstaining from the tree. It was also said: ﴿'azman﴾ (resolve) refers to caution regarding the manner of ijtihad (independent reasoning).

\* \*

The discussion of the parallel of His saying ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused﴾ has already occurred. The word "aba" (he refused) is a resumptive clause explaining that his not prostrating was from refusal and obstinacy. The apparent reading is that the complement of "aba" is omitted, and what is stated in the other verse is understood here: ﴿He refused to be among those who prostrate﴾ [al-Hijr: 31]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "aba" is a resumptive clause, as if it were the answer to one who asked: "Why did he not prostrate?" The better view is that no object is to be supposed for it, which is the prostration indicated by "isjudu" (prostrate); and that its meaning is that he showed refusal, held back, and was reluctant. End of quotation.

"Hadha" (this) is a reference to Iblis, and "'aduww" (enemy) is used for the singular, dual and plural. God, exalted be He, made Adam aware of Iblis's enmity toward him and his wife, so that they would be wary of him. Yet caution does not avail against the divine decree (qadar). The cause of the enmity, it is said, is that Iblis was envious: when he saw the signs of God's blessings upon Adam, he envied him and became his enemy. It was also said: the enmity arose from the incompatibility of their origins, since Iblis was from fire and Adam from water and clay.

﴿So let him not drive you both out﴾: the prohibition is addressed to him, but the intended addressees are others; that is, let no obedience to him occur from you both in his seduction, so that this would be the cause of your expulsion from the Garden. He attributed the expulsion to Satan, though the one who expels is God, exalted be He, because it was by his whispering that he did what resulted in the expulsion. ﴿Then you would be miserable﴾ (fa-tashqa) may be in the accusative, by supposing "an" after the prohibition, or in the nominative, on the reckoning "fa-anta tashqa" (then you are miserable). He attributed the misery to him alone, after the sharing with his wife in the expulsion, since he was the one addressed first and the intended subject of the speech, and because within the misery of the man is the misery of his family, and within his happiness is hers. So the speech is abbreviated by attributing it to him rather than her, while preserving the verse-ending (fasilah).

It was said: by misery he meant the toil of seeking sustenance, and that returns to the man. From Ibn Jubayr: a red bull was sent down to him, which he plowed with, so he would eat by the labor of his right hand and the sweat of his brow.

Shayba, Nafi', Hafs and Ibn Sa'dan read ﴿wa-innaka la tadha'u﴾ (and indeed you are not thirsty) with a kasrah on the hamzah of "inna." The majority read it with a fathah. The kasrah is coordinated with "inna laka" (indeed for you), and the fathah is coordinated with the verbal noun constructed from "an la tju'a" (that you not hunger); that is, "for you is the absence of your hunger and the absence of your thirst." It is permissible to coordinate "annaka" with "anna" because they share the verbal noun; if the kasrah-"inna" directly governed it, that would not be permitted, even though it is in its implied form. Do you not see that it is coordinated with the noun of "inna," which is "an la tju'a"? But in coordination what is not permitted in direct government is permitted. Since satiety, quenching, clothing and shelter are the things that are necessities for a human being, he limited the statement to them, because they are sufficient for him. In the Garden there are kinds of bliss and comfort in comparison to which these are as nothing: among them is safety from death, which spoils every pleasure; the sight of the Face of God, glory be to Him; His good pleasure, exalted be He, toward its people; and that there is no sickness, no sorrow, no pain, no old age, no decrepitude, no rancor, no anger, no impurity, no filth, no obligation, no grief, no fear, and no boredom. These four were mentioned in the form of negation to affirm their opposites, namely satiety, quenching, clothing and shelter; and their opposites were stated in the form of negation: hunger, nakedness, thirst and exposure to the sun, so that his hearing would be struck with the names of the kinds of wretchedness against which he was warned, until he would avoid the cause that brings them about, out of aversion to them.

\* \*

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the customary usage of speech is that hunger goes with thirst, and nakedness goes with exposure to the sun, because they are opposites: nakedness itself is cold, which harms, while heat does this to one exposed to the sun. This is a well-trodden method in the speech of the Arabs (p-285), of pairing the two. From it is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*As if I had never mounted a steed for pleasure, nor embraced a maiden with anklets,*
*Nor had I taken captive the free-born slave, nor said to my horses, "Charge again, a second charge after fleeing."*

Some men of letters went so far as to say that the two verses of Imru' al-Qays are a kind of pairing by affinity, and that riding horses for hunting and other pleasures suits the embracing of a maiden. End of quotation.

It was said: this reply is in proportion to the question. When God commanded Adam to dwell in the Garden, he said: "My God, is there for me in it what I eat? Is there for me in it what I wear? Is there for me in it what I drink? Is there for me in it what I shade myself with?" It was also said: it is a spiritual correspondence, so hunger is the emptiness of the inner self, nakedness the emptiness of the outer self, thirst the burning of the inner self, and exposure to the sun the burning of the outer self; thus he paired emptiness with fullness and burning with burning. It was also said: Imru' al-Qays combined in his two verses riding horses for pleasure and leisure with embracing a maiden for the pleasure obtained in both; and he combined taking captives with his saying to his horses "charge," because of the courage in both. *She stood, and there is no doubt in the death of one who stands; as if you were in the sheath of destruction, and he is asleep.*
*The heroes pass by you defeated, humbled; and your face is bright, and your smile is cheerful.*

He said: if I was wrong, then Imru' al-Qays was also wrong.

Al-Yamani and al-A'mash read ﴿fa-nussiya﴾ with a dammah on the nun and a shaddah on the sin, meaning: Satan caused him to forget. "Al-'azm" means determination and resolve.

Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, [he had no resolve] in abstaining from eating, and in being firm in that, in a way that would make Satan despair of tempting him. The word "wujud" may be in the sense of knowledge, with its two objects being ﴿lahu 'azman﴾ (for him, resolve); or it may be the opposite of nonexistence, as if He said: a promise from Us ﴿lahu 'azman﴾ (for him, resolve). End of quotation.

It was said: ﴿And We found in him no resolve﴾ refers to disobedience, and this is derived from the view of those who said that he committed it through forgetting. It was said: [the resolve refers to] memorization of what he was commanded. It was said: patience in abstaining from the tree. It was also said: ﴿'azman﴾ (resolve) refers to caution regarding the manner of ijtihad (independent reasoning).

\* \*

The discussion of the parallel of His saying ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused﴾ has already occurred. The word "aba" (he refused) is a resumptive clause explaining that his not prostrating was from refusal and obstinacy. The apparent reading is that the complement of "aba" is omitted, and what is stated in the other verse is understood here: ﴿He refused to be among those who prostrate﴾ [al-Hijr: 31]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "aba" is a resumptive clause, as if it were the answer to one who asked: "Why did he not prostrate?" The better view is that no object is to be supposed for it, which is the prostration indicated by "isjudu" (prostrate); and that its meaning is that he showed refusal, held back, and was reluctant. End of quotation.

"Hadha" (this) is a reference to Iblis, and "'aduww" (enemy) is used for the singular, dual and plural. God, exalted be He, made Adam aware of Iblis's enmity toward him and his wife, so that they would be wary of him. Yet caution does not avail against the divine decree (qadar). The cause of the enmity, it is said, is that Iblis was envious: when he saw the signs of God's blessings upon Adam, he envied him and became his enemy. It was also said: the enmity arose from the incompatibility of their origins, since Iblis was from fire and Adam from water and clay.

﴿So let him not drive you both out﴾: the prohibition is addressed to him, but the intended addressees are others; that is, let no obedience to him occur from you both in his seduction, so that this would be the cause of your expulsion from the Garden. He attributed the expulsion to Satan, though the one who expels is God, exalted be He, because it was by his whispering that he did what resulted in the expulsion. ﴿Then you would be miserable﴾ (fa-tashqa) may be in the accusative, by supposing "an" after the prohibition, or in the nominative, on the reckoning "fa-anta tashqa" (then you are miserable). He attributed the misery to him alone, after the sharing with his wife in the expulsion, since he was the one addressed first and the intended subject of the speech, and because within the misery of the man is the misery of his family, and within his happiness is hers. So the speech is abbreviated by attributing it to him rather than her, while preserving the verse-ending (fasilah).

It was said: by misery he meant the toil of seeking sustenance, and that returns to the man. From Ibn Jubayr: a red bull was sent down to him, which he plowed with, so he would eat by the labor of his right hand and the sweat of his brow.

Shayba, Nafi', Hafs and Ibn Sa'dan read ﴿wa-innaka la tadha'u﴾ (and indeed you are not thirsty) with a kasrah on the hamzah of "inna." The majority read it with a fathah. The kasrah is coordinated with "inna laka" (indeed for you), and the fathah is coordinated with the verbal noun constructed from "an la tju'a" (that you not hunger); that is, "for you is the absence of your hunger and the absence of your thirst." It is permissible to coordinate "annaka" with "anna" because they share the verbal noun; if the kasrah-"inna" directly governed it, that would not be permitted, even though it is in its implied form. Do you not see that it is coordinated with the noun of "inna," which is "an la tju'a"? But in coordination what is not permitted in direct government is permitted. Since satiety, quenching, clothing and shelter are the things that are necessities for a human being, he limited the statement to them, because they are sufficient for him. In the Garden there are kinds of bliss and comfort in comparison to which these are as nothing: among them is safety from death, which spoils every pleasure; the sight of the Face of God, glory be to Him; His good pleasure, exalted be He, toward its people; and that there is no sickness, no sorrow, no pain, no old age, no decrepitude, no rancor, no anger, no impurity, no filth, no obligation, no grief, no fear, and no boredom. These four were mentioned in the form of negation to affirm their opposites, namely satiety, quenching, clothing and shelter; and their opposites were stated in the form of negation: hunger, nakedness, thirst and exposure to the sun, so that his hearing would be struck with the names of the kinds of wretchedness against which he was warned, until he would avoid the cause that brings them about, out of aversion to them.

\* \*

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the customary usage of speech is that hunger goes with thirst, and nakedness goes with exposure to the sun, because they are opposites: nakedness itself is cold, which harms, while heat does this to one exposed to the sun. This is a well-trodden method in the speech of the Arabs (p-285), of pairing the two. From it is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*As if I had never mounted a steed for pleasure, nor embraced a maiden with anklets,*
*Nor had I taken captive the free-born slave, nor said to my horses, "Charge again, a second charge after fleeing."*

Some men of letters went so far as to say that the two verses of Imru' al-Qays are a kind of pairing by affinity, and that riding horses for hunting and other pleasures suits the embracing of a maiden. End of quotation.

It was said: this reply is in proportion to the question. When God commanded Adam to dwell in the Garden, he said: "My God, is there for me in it what I eat? Is there for me in it what I wear? Is there for me in it what I drink? Is there for me in it what I shade myself with?" It was also said: it is a spiritual correspondence, so hunger is the emptiness of the inner self, nakedness the emptiness of the outer self, thirst the burning of the inner self, and exposure to the sun the burning of the outer self; thus he paired emptiness with fullness and burning with burning. It was also said: Imru' al-Qays combined in his two verses riding horses for pleasure and leisure with embracing a maiden for the pleasure obtained in both; and he combined taking captives with his saying to his horses "charge," because of the courage in both. Abu al-Tayyib was criticized for his saying:

*She stood, and there is no doubt in the death of one who stands; as if you were in the sheath of destruction, and he is asleep.*
*The heroes pass by you defeated, humbled; and your face is bright, and your smile is cheerful.*

He said: if I was wrong, then Imru' al-Qays was also wrong.

When he whispered to him, he called him by his name so that he would be more attentive to him and more able to listen. Then he presented to him what he would encounter, with his saying ﴿Shall I direct you﴾ in the form of a question which suggests sincerity, and which induces acceptance by the one addressed, like Moses's saying ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18]; this is an offer containing counsel. Iblis encouraged him toward lasting ease with his saying ﴿Shall I direct you?﴾; so he came to him from the direction in which God had encouraged him. In al-A'raf it is ﴿What your Lord has forbidden you from this tree﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]; and here it is ﴿Shall I direct you?﴾. The meaning of ﴿the tree of eternity﴾ is: the tree whoever eats from it becomes immortal and gains a kingdom that never decays. This supports the reading of al-Hasan ibn Ali and Ibn Abbas, "unless you become two angels" (*malakayn*), with a kasra on the lam. ﴿So they ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves from the Garden.﴾ The discussion of this verse has already been covered in al-A'raf. ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray.﴾ ﴿Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122]

Al-Zamakhshari said, quoting Ibn Abbas: There is no doubt that Adam, may the blessings of God be upon him, did not comply with what God had prescribed for him, and he overstepped the bounds of obedience in this matter, and that is disobedience (*'isyan*). It is as if they were told: Look and take heed how We rebuke the infallible Prophet (*al-nabi al-ma'sum*), the beloved of God, who cannot commit even a minor sin that does not repel, for his slip is reproached with such severity and in such a shocking expression. So do not be lax about the bad deeds and minor sins that you commit, let alone become bold enough to plunge into major sins. Some of them read *fa-ghawa* as *fa-sa'ima* ("he grew weary") from the great amount of eating. Although this is valid according to the dialect of those who change a kasra-marked *ya'* preceded by a vowel into an *alif*, saying *fana* and *baqa* for *fani* and *baqi*, namely the Banu Tayy, it is an evil interpretation. End of quotation.

If one begins it on one's own initiative, it is not permissible for us regarding our nearer fathers who are similar to us, so how about our first, greatest, most honorable father, the Prophet who was foremost, whom God chose, accepted his repentance, and forgave him. Al-Qurtubi said: If this is impermissible regarding a created being, then reporting the attributes of God, such as the hand, the foot, the finger, the side, descending, and so on, is all the more deserving of prohibition, and it is not permissible to initiate any mention of such things except within the recitation of His Book or the Sunnah of His Messenger, peace be upon him. For this reason Imam Malik ibn Anas said: Whoever describes any attribute of the Essence of God, such as His words: ﴿And the Jews said, "God's hand is chained"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], and points with his hand to his neck, I will cut off his hand. The same applies to hearing and sight, which should be cut off from him, because he has likened God, glorified be He, to himself. (p-286)

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 115–121 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And say: "My Lord, increase me in knowledge."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114] Muqatil said: that is, the Qur'an. It was also said: understanding. And it was said: memorization. This statement implies humility before God and gratitude to Him, given what is known of the order of learning: that is, "You taught me subtle purposes in the field of learning and a beautiful etiquette that I did not have, so increase me in knowledge." It was also said: God did not command His Messenger to seek increase in anything except knowledge.

(p-283) ﴿We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve.﴾ ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused.﴾ ﴿So We said, "O Adam, this is an enemy to you and to your wife. So let him not drive you both out of the Garden, for then you would be miserable.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is granted to you that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked.﴾ ﴿And that you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun."﴾ ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying, "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?"﴾ ﴿So they both ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves of the Garden. And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred.﴾ ﴿Then his Lord chose him, turned to him in forgiveness, and guided him.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122] ﴿He said, "Go down from it, all of you, as enemies to one another. But when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor be unhappy."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123] ﴿But whoever turns away from My remembrance, for him is a constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 124] ﴿He will say, "My Lord, why have You gathered me blind, when I was [previously] seeing?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 125] ﴿He will say, "Thus Our signs came to you, and you forgot them; and thus today you are forgotten."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 126] ﴿And thus do We recompense one who transgresses and does not believe in the signs of his Lord. And the punishment of the Hereafter is severer and more lasting.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 127]

The story of Adam has preceded in al-Baqarah, al-A'raf, al-Hijr and al-Kahf. Among this news is the story of Adam, so that his descendants may guard themselves against the whispering of Satan and be alert to his dangers. Whoever among them obeys Satan is reminded of what happened to their father Adam with him, and that his enmity was made clear to him, and yet he forgot what his Lord had covenanted with him. Also, when he was commanded to say ﴿My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114], part of that was the mention of the story of Adam and some of his circumstances in it that had not been mentioned before. Thus there was in that an increase of knowledge for him, upon him be peace.

The word 'ahd (covenant) means, according to the majority, a charge (wasiyyah). The apparent reading is that the omitted genitive after the phrase "min qablu" (before) is in the sense of "min qablu" (before) these people to whom threats have been expounded in the Qur'an, so that they may be mindful, and they are those who break God's covenant and abandon faith. Al-Hasan said: "min qablu" (before) refers to the Messenger and the Qur'an. It was also said: "min qablu" (before) means before he ate from the tree.

Al-Tabari said: the meaning is that these disbelievers, O Muhammad, turn away from My signs, oppose My messengers and obey Iblis; and their father Adam did this long ago. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is weak, because Adam being an example for the disbelievers who deny God is nothing; and Adam, upon him be peace, disobeyed only through ta'wil (interpretation), so in this there is a disparagement of him, upon him be peace. The apparent meaning of this verse is either that it is the beginning of a narrative with no connection to what precedes, or that its connection is to what was charged to Muhammad (ﷺ), that he should not hasten with the Qur'an. It presented to him a prophet before him who was charged and "forgot" (fa-nasiya), so that it would be stronger in warning and more forceful in charging Muhammad (ﷺ).

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is said in the commands and charges of kings: "The king advanced toward so-and-so, and was angered at him, and resolved upon him, and charged him." It is as if He is saying: the foundation of the affair of the children of Adam is upon that, and their lineage is firmly rooted in it." End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that "forgetting" here means abandonment, if he abandoned what he was charged with of guarding against the tree and eating its fruit. The Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: It is not permissible for any of us today to report this about him, peace be upon him, except when we mention it within the context of God's words or the words of His Prophet, peace be upon him. If one begins it on one's own initiative, it is not permissible for us regarding our nearer fathers who are similar to us, so how about our first, greatest, most honorable father, the Prophet who was foremost, whom God chose, accepted his repentance, and forgave him. Al-Qurtubi said: If this is impermissible regarding a created being, then reporting the attributes of God, such as the hand, the foot, the finger, the side, descending, and so on, is all the more deserving of prohibition, and it is not permissible to initiate any mention of such things except within the recitation of His Book or the Sunnah of His Messenger, peace be upon him. For this reason Imam Malik ibn Anas said: Whoever describes any attribute of the Essence of God, such as His words: ﴿And the Jews said, "God's hand is chained"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], and points with his hand to his neck, I will cut off his hand. The same applies to hearing and sight, which should be cut off from him, because he has likened God, glorified be He, to himself. (p-286)

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 115–121 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And say: "My Lord, increase me in knowledge."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114] Muqatil said: that is, the Qur'an. It was also said: understanding. And it was said: memorization. This statement implies humility before God and gratitude to Him, given what is known of the order of learning: that is, "You taught me subtle purposes in the field of learning and a beautiful etiquette that I did not have, so increase me in knowledge." It was also said: God did not command His Messenger to seek increase in anything except knowledge.

(p-283) ﴿We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve.﴾ ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused.﴾ ﴿So We said, "O Adam, this is an enemy to you and to your wife. So let him not drive you both out of the Garden, for then you would be miserable.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is granted to you that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked.﴾ ﴿And that you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun."﴾ ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying, "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?"﴾ ﴿So they both ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves of the Garden. And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred.﴾ ﴿Then his Lord chose him, turned to him in forgiveness, and guided him.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122] ﴿He said, "Go down from it, all of you, as enemies to one another. But when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor be unhappy."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123] ﴿But whoever turns away from My remembrance, for him is a constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 124] ﴿He will say, "My Lord, why have You gathered me blind, when I was [previously] seeing?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 125] ﴿He will say, "Thus Our signs came to you, and you forgot them; and thus today you are forgotten."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 126] ﴿And thus do We recompense one who transgresses and does not believe in the signs of his Lord. And the punishment of the Hereafter is severer and more lasting.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 127]

The story of Adam has preceded in al-Baqarah, al-A'raf, al-Hijr and al-Kahf. Then He mentions it here in connection with what preceded: ﴿Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has already passed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 99]. Among this news is the story of Adam, so that his descendants may guard themselves against the whispering of Satan and be alert to his dangers. Whoever among them obeys Satan is reminded of what happened to their father Adam with him, and that his enmity was made clear to him, and yet he forgot what his Lord had covenanted with him. Also, when he was commanded to say ﴿My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114], part of that was the mention of the story of Adam and some of his circumstances in it that had not been mentioned before. Thus there was in that an increase of knowledge for him, upon him be peace.

The word 'ahd (covenant) means, according to the majority, a charge (wasiyyah). The apparent reading is that the omitted genitive after the phrase "min qablu" (before) is in the sense of "min qablu" (before) these people to whom threats have been expounded in the Qur'an, so that they may be mindful, and they are those who break God's covenant and abandon faith. Al-Hasan said: "min qablu" (before) refers to the Messenger and the Qur'an. It was also said: "min qablu" (before) means before he ate from the tree.

Al-Tabari said: the meaning is that these disbelievers, O Muhammad, turn away from My signs, oppose My messengers and obey Iblis; and their father Adam did this long ago. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is weak, because Adam being an example for the disbelievers who deny God is nothing; and Adam, upon him be peace, disobeyed only through ta'wil (interpretation), so in this there is a disparagement of him, upon him be peace. The apparent meaning of this verse is either that it is the beginning of a narrative with no connection to what precedes, or that its connection is to what was charged to Muhammad (ﷺ), that he should not hasten with the Qur'an. It presented to him a prophet before him who was charged and "forgot" (fa-nasiya), so that it would be stronger in warning and more forceful in charging Muhammad (ﷺ).

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is said in the commands and charges of kings: "The king advanced toward so-and-so, and was angered at him, and resolved upon him, and charged him." God, glory be to Him, connected the story of Adam to His saying ﴿And We have expounded in it some of the threats, so that they may be mindful﴾ [Ta-Ha: 113]. The meaning is: "I swear an oath, We certainly commanded your father Adam and charged him not to approach the tree, and We threatened him with being included among the wrongdoers if he approached it. And that was before their existence, before We threatened them. So he went against what he was forbidden, and he was threatened for committing it, and he did not heed the threat, just as they do not heed it. It is as if He is saying: the foundation of the affair of the children of Adam is upon that, and their lineage is firmly rooted in it." End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that "forgetting" here means abandonment, if he abandoned what he was charged with of guarding against the tree and eating its fruit. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is possible that what is meant by forgetting is its opposite, remembrance, and that he did not give the charge sincere care, did not make it firm by fixing it in his heart and controlling his self, so that forgetting arose from that (p-284). End of quotation. Others also said this. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: forgetting through heedlessness (dhuhul) is not possible here, because no punishment attaches to one who forgets. End of quotation.

Al-Yamani and al-A'mash read ﴿fa-nussiya﴾ with a dammah on the nun and a shaddah on the sin, meaning: Satan caused him to forget. "Al-'azm" means determination and resolve.

Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, [he had no resolve] in abstaining from eating, and in being firm in that, in a way that would make Satan despair of tempting him. The word "wujud" may be in the sense of knowledge, with its two objects being ﴿lahu 'azman﴾ (for him, resolve); or it may be the opposite of nonexistence, as if He said: a promise from Us ﴿lahu 'azman﴾ (for him, resolve). End of quotation.

It was said: ﴿And We found in him no resolve﴾ refers to disobedience, and this is derived from the view of those who said that he committed it through forgetting. It was said: [the resolve refers to] memorization of what he was commanded. It was said: patience in abstaining from the tree. It was also said: ﴿'azman﴾ (resolve) refers to caution regarding the manner of ijtihad (independent reasoning).

\* \*

The discussion of the parallel of His saying ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused﴾ has already occurred. The word "aba" (he refused) is a resumptive clause explaining that his not prostrating was from refusal and obstinacy. The apparent reading is that the complement of "aba" is omitted, and what is stated in the other verse is understood here: ﴿He refused to be among those who prostrate﴾ [al-Hijr: 31]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "aba" is a resumptive clause, as if it were the answer to one who asked: "Why did he not prostrate?" The better view is that no object is to be supposed for it, which is the prostration indicated by "isjudu" (prostrate); and that its meaning is that he showed refusal, held back, and was reluctant. End of quotation.

"Hadha" (this) is a reference to Iblis, and "'aduww" (enemy) is used for the singular, dual and plural. God, exalted be He, made Adam aware of Iblis's enmity toward him and his wife, so that they would be wary of him. Yet caution does not avail against the divine decree (qadar). The cause of the enmity, it is said, is that Iblis was envious: when he saw the signs of God's blessings upon Adam, he envied him and became his enemy. It was also said: the enmity arose from the incompatibility of their origins, since Iblis was from fire and Adam from water and clay.

﴿So let him not drive you both out﴾: the prohibition is addressed to him, but the intended addressees are others; that is, let no obedience to him occur from you both in his seduction, so that this would be the cause of your expulsion from the Garden. He attributed the expulsion to Satan, though the one who expels is God, exalted be He, because it was by his whispering that he did what resulted in the expulsion. ﴿Then you would be miserable﴾ (fa-tashqa) may be in the accusative, by supposing "an" after the prohibition, or in the nominative, on the reckoning "fa-anta tashqa" (then you are miserable). He attributed the misery to him alone, after the sharing with his wife in the expulsion, since he was the one addressed first and the intended subject of the speech, and because within the misery of the man is the misery of his family, and within his happiness is hers. So the speech is abbreviated by attributing it to him rather than her, while preserving the verse-ending (fasilah).

It was said: by misery he meant the toil of seeking sustenance, and that returns to the man. From Ibn Jubayr: a red bull was sent down to him, which he plowed with, so he would eat by the labor of his right hand and the sweat of his brow.

Shayba, Nafi', Hafs and Ibn Sa'dan read ﴿wa-innaka la tadha'u﴾ (and indeed you are not thirsty) with a kasrah on the hamzah of "inna." The majority read it with a fathah. The kasrah is coordinated with "inna laka" (indeed for you), and the fathah is coordinated with the verbal noun constructed from "an la tju'a" (that you not hunger); that is, "for you is the absence of your hunger and the absence of your thirst." It is permissible to coordinate "annaka" with "anna" because they share the verbal noun; if the kasrah-"inna" directly governed it, that would not be permitted, even though it is in its implied form. Do you not see that it is coordinated with the noun of "inna," which is "an la tju'a"? But in coordination what is not permitted in direct government is permitted. Since satiety, quenching, clothing and shelter are the things that are necessities for a human being, he limited the statement to them, because they are sufficient for him. In the Garden there are kinds of bliss and comfort in comparison to which these are as nothing: among them is safety from death, which spoils every pleasure; the sight of the Face of God, glory be to Him; His good pleasure, exalted be He, toward its people; and that there is no sickness, no sorrow, no pain, no old age, no decrepitude, no rancor, no anger, no impurity, no filth, no obligation, no grief, no fear, and no boredom. These four were mentioned in the form of negation to affirm their opposites, namely satiety, quenching, clothing and shelter; and their opposites were stated in the form of negation: hunger, nakedness, thirst and exposure to the sun, so that his hearing would be struck with the names of the kinds of wretchedness against which he was warned, until he would avoid the cause that brings them about, out of aversion to them.

\* \*

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the customary usage of speech is that hunger goes with thirst, and nakedness goes with exposure to the sun, because they are opposites: nakedness itself is cold, which harms, while heat does this to one exposed to the sun. This is a well-trodden method in the speech of the Arabs (p-285), of pairing the two. From it is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*As if I had never mounted a steed for pleasure, nor embraced a maiden with anklets,*
*Nor had I taken captive the free-born slave, nor said to my horses, "Charge again, a second charge after fleeing."*

Some men of letters went so far as to say that the two verses of Imru' al-Qays are a kind of pairing by affinity, and that riding horses for hunting and other pleasures suits the embracing of a maiden. End of quotation.

It was said: this reply is in proportion to the question. When God commanded Adam to dwell in the Garden, he said: "My God, is there for me in it what I eat? Is there for me in it what I wear? Is there for me in it what I drink? Is there for me in it what I shade myself with?" It was also said: it is a spiritual correspondence, so hunger is the emptiness of the inner self, nakedness the emptiness of the outer self, thirst the burning of the inner self, and exposure to the sun the burning of the outer self; thus he paired emptiness with fullness and burning with burning. It was also said: Imru' al-Qays combined in his two verses riding horses for pleasure and leisure with embracing a maiden for the pleasure obtained in both; and he combined taking captives with his saying to his horses "charge," because of the courage in both. Abu al-Tayyib was criticized for his saying:

*She stood, and there is no doubt in the death of one who stands; as if you were in the sheath of destruction, and he is asleep.*
*The heroes pass by you defeated, humbled; and your face is bright, and your smile is cheerful.*

He said: if I was wrong, then Imru' al-Qays was also wrong.

The discussion of ﴿fa-waswasa﴾ (then he whispered) has preceded, and the disagreement over its manner in al-A'raf. Here "waswasa" takes "ila" (to), and in al-A'raf it takes the lam. The construction with "ila" means that he delivered the whispering to him; the construction with the lam of attribution is said to mean "for his sake." When he whispered to him, he called him by his name so that he would be more attentive to him and more able to listen. Then he presented to him what he would encounter, with his saying ﴿Shall I direct you﴾ in the form of a question which suggests sincerity, and which induces acceptance by the one addressed, like Moses's saying ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18]; this is an offer containing counsel. Adam had been encouraged by God, exalted be He, toward lasting ease and an ordered livelihood with His saying ﴿So let him not drive you both out﴾, and so on. Iblis encouraged him toward lasting ease with his saying ﴿Shall I direct you?﴾; so he came to him from the direction in which God had encouraged him. In al-A'raf it is ﴿What your Lord has forbidden you from this tree﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]; and here it is ﴿Shall I direct you?﴾. The reconciliation between them is that his saying ﴿Shall I direct you?﴾ came before his saying ﴿What has your Lord forbidden you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]: when he saw his attentiveness and inclination toward what he had presented to him, he moved on to statement and restriction.

The meaning of ﴿the tree of eternity﴾ is: the tree whoever eats from it becomes immortal and gains a kingdom that never decays. This supports the reading of al-Hasan ibn Ali and Ibn Abbas, "unless you become two angels" (*malakayn*), with a kasra on the lam. ﴿So they ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves from the Garden.﴾ The discussion of this verse has already been covered in al-A'raf. ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray.﴾ ﴿Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122]

Al-Zamakhshari said, quoting Ibn Abbas: There is no doubt that Adam, may the blessings of God be upon him, did not comply with what God had prescribed for him, and he overstepped the bounds of obedience in this matter, and that is disobedience (*'isyan*). When he disobeyed, his action ceased to be right guidance and good, and so it was inevitably error (*ghayy*), since *al-ghayy* is the opposite of *al-rushd* (right guidance). However, the statement ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray﴾ is in this unqualified form and with this explicit wording, and the fact that it does not say "Adam slipped," "erred," or anything similar to the expressions used for lapses and oversights, contains kindness toward those who are responsible (*mukallafin*), a powerful deterrent, and a comprehensive admonition. It is as if they were told: Look and take heed how We rebuke the infallible Prophet (*al-nabi al-ma'sum*), the beloved of God, who cannot commit even a minor sin that does not repel, for his slip is reproached with such severity and in such a shocking expression. So do not be lax about the bad deeds and minor sins that you commit, let alone become bold enough to plunge into major sins. Some of them read *fa-ghawa* as *fa-sa'ima* ("he grew weary") from the great amount of eating. Although this is valid according to the dialect of those who change a kasra-marked *ya'* preceded by a vowel into an *alif*, saying *fana* and *baqa* for *fani* and *baqi*, namely the Banu Tayy, it is an evil interpretation. End of quotation.

* *

The Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: It is not permissible for any of us today to report this about him, peace be upon him, except when we mention it within the context of God's words or the words of His Prophet, peace be upon him. If one begins it on one's own initiative, it is not permissible for us regarding our nearer fathers who are similar to us, so how about our first, greatest, most honorable father, the Prophet who was foremost, whom God chose, accepted his repentance, and forgave him. Al-Qurtubi said: If this is impermissible regarding a created being, then reporting the attributes of God, such as the hand, the foot, the finger, the side, descending, and so on, is all the more deserving of prohibition, and it is not permissible to initiate any mention of such things except within the recitation of His Book or the Sunnah of His Messenger, peace be upon him. For this reason Imam Malik ibn Anas said: Whoever describes any attribute of the Essence of God, such as His words: ﴿And the Jews said, "God's hand is chained"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], and points with his hand to his neck, I will cut off his hand. The same applies to hearing and sight, which should be cut off from him, because he has likened God, glorified be He, to himself. (p-286)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 122–127:

﴿Then He chose him﴾, meaning He selected him and drew him near, and ﴿turned to him﴾, meaning He accepted his repentance. ﴿And guided him﴾, meaning He guided him to prophethood, or to the manner of repentance, or He guided him to his right course until he returned to remorse. The pronoun in ﴿Go down﴾ is a dual pronoun, and it is a command to Adam and Hawwa'; He made their descent a punishment for them. ﴿All of you﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the two of them. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Then He informed them, by His saying ﴿all of you﴾, that Iblis and the serpent would descend along with them, and He informed them that enmity would exist between them and their descendants until the Day of Resurrection. End of quotation.

But His saying ﴿all of you﴾ does not indicate that Iblis and the serpent descend with them, because ﴿all of you﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun of the two, meaning gathered together, and the pronoun in ﴿some of you to others﴾ is a plural pronoun. It was said: He means Iblis and his progeny, and Adam and his progeny. It was also said: He meant Adam and his offspring, and the enmity occurs between them, and the hatred due to the difference of religions and the scattering of opinions. It was said: Adam, Iblis and the serpent. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: The address is to Adam, peace be upon him, and because the two are two kinds, His saying ﴿Go down﴾ is correct; and because each of the two kinds includes multitude, His saying ﴿So when there comes to you from Me guidance﴾ is correct.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Since Adam and Hawwa', peace be upon them, are the two origins of humankind and the two causes from which they grew and branched out, they were treated as if they themselves were humankind, so they were addressed with the address given to humankind, and it was said ﴿So when there comes to you﴾ in the plural form. Its parallel is their attributing the verb to the cause while in reality it belongs to the one who causes. End of quotation. And ﴿guidance﴾ is the law of Allah. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: Allah guaranteed for whoever follows the Qur'an that he will not go astray in this world nor be wretched in the Hereafter, then he recited ﴿Whoever follows My guidance will not go astray, nor will he be distressed.﴾ The meaning is that wretchedness in the Hereafter is the punishment of those who went astray in this world from the path of religion; so whoever follows the Book of Allah, carries out its commands and refrains from its prohibitions, is saved from straying and from its punishment. It is related from Ibn Jubayr: Whoever recites the Qur'an and follows what is in it, Allah protects him from error and shields him from the evil of reckoning. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: This verse indicates that what is meant by the guidance which Allah Most High mentioned is following the proofs, and following them is not complete unless one reasons by them and acts by them; whoever is in this state, Allah Most High has guaranteed that he will not go astray and will not be wretched in the Hereafter, because He Most High will guide him to Paradise. It was said: ﴿He will not go astray, nor be wretched﴾ refers to this world. If it is said: One blessed with the guidance of Allah may still suffer wretchedness in this world. We say: What is meant is that he will not go astray in religion, nor be wretched because of religion; if it occurs through some other cause, there is no harm. End of quotation.

* *

When He Most High mentioned those who follow guidance, He followed it with the threat against those who turn away from His remembrance, and "remembrance" applies to the Qur'an and to all the divine books. "Dank" (ḍank) is a verbal noun which is used as a description for the masculine, the feminine, the singular, the dual and the plural, and its meaning is hardship and distress of life, of dwellings, of battlegrounds and the like. From it is the saying of 'Antara:

Indeed, death, if it were to be given a form, would take my form when they alight in a narrow dwelling.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: This verse was revealed concerning al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Asad al-Makhzumi, and what is meant is the squeezing of the grave, in which his ribs are interlaced. Al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Kalbi said: It is the constriction in the Hereafter in Hell, for their food therein is ḍarī' and zaqqum, and their drink is ḥamīm and ghislin, and they neither die therein nor live. 'Ata' said: The dank life is the life of the disbeliever, because he is not certain of reward and punishment. Ibn Jubayr said: He is stripped of contentment so that he is never satisfied. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and al-Suddi said: It is the punishment of the grave, and Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, related it from the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Jawhari said: The dank life is in this world, and the meaning is that the disbeliever, even if his state and wealth are expansive, has with him greed, hope, and torment by worldly matters and desire, and the impossibility of pure living because of that, so that his life becomes dank. A group said: ﴿dank﴾ means by eating what is forbidden.

It is inferred that the dank life is before the Day of Resurrection from His saying ﴿and We will raise him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾, and His saying ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting﴾; it is as if He mentioned one kind of punishment, then mentioned that the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting. Al-Zamakhshari endorsed the view of the majority and said: The meaning of that is that with religion comes submission, contentment, and reliance upon Allah and upon His allotment, so its adherent spends what He has provided him with generosity and ease, and he lives a good life, as the Most High said: ﴿So We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [al-Nahl: 97]. But the one who turns away from religion is controlled by greed, which never ceases to drive him toward increasing worldly gain, and he is dominated by stinginess, which clenches his hand from spending; so his life is dank and his state is dark. End of quotation.

Al-Hasan read ﴿ḍankī﴾ with the feminine alif and without tanwin, and with imala; its form is an adjective on the pattern fa'lā from ḍank. The majority read ﴿ḍankan﴾ with tanwin, and the fatḥa on the kaf is the fatḥa of i'rab. The majority read (wa-naḥshuruhu) with a nun, and a group among them, Aban ibn Taghlib, read it with a sukun on the rā', so it may be a lightening, or it may be a jussive by conjunction with the position of ﴿fa-inna lahu ma'ishatan ḍankan﴾, because it is the answer of the condition; and it is as if it were said: ﴿Whoever turns away from My remembrance, there will be for him a dank life﴾ and ﴿We will raise him﴾. A similar case is ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray, there is no guide for him, and He leaves them﴾ [al-A'raf: 186] in the reading of one who reads sukun on ﴿wa-yadharhum﴾. A group read ﴿wa-yaḥshuruhu﴾ with the yā'. And it was read ﴿wa-yaḥshuruh﴾ with a sukun on the hā' according to the pausal form, as al-Zamakhshari said. Ibn Khalawayh related this reading from Aban ibn Taghlib, and the best way to explain it is according to the dialect of Banu Kilab and 'Uqayl, for they make such a hā' quiescent. It was also read ﴿li-rabbihi la-kanud﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 6]. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿blind﴾ is blindness of sight, as He said: ﴿and We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind﴾ [al-Isra': 97]. It was also said: blind of insight. Ibn 'Atiyya said: If this were so, the disbeliever would not perceive that, because he died blind of insight and is raised in that state. Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Muqatil, Abu Salih, and it is related from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿blind﴾ means blind to his proof; he has no proof by which he is guided. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: He is raised seeing, then when he reaches the place of gathering he is ﴿blind﴾. It was said: ﴿blind﴾ regarding the means of averting punishment from himself, like the blind man who has no way to deal with what he cannot see. It was said: ﴿blind﴾ to everything except Hell. Al-Jubba'i said: What is meant by his being raised ﴿blind﴾ is that he is not guided to anything. Ibrahim ibn 'Arafa said: Whatever Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentions in His Book and censures, He means blindness of the heart, as He said: ﴿For indeed it is not the eyes that are blinded, but the hearts which are in the breasts are blinded﴾ [al-Hajj: 46].

Al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Kalbi said: It is the constriction in the Hereafter in Hell, for their food therein is ḍarī' and zaqqum, and their drink is ḥamīm and ghislin, and they neither die therein nor live. 'Ata' said: The dank life is the life of the disbeliever, because he is not certain of reward and punishment. Ibn Jubayr said: He is stripped of contentment so that he is never satisfied. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and al-Suddi said: It is the punishment of the grave, and Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, related it from the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Jawhari said: The dank life is in this world, and the meaning is that the disbeliever, even if his state and wealth are expansive, has with him greed, hope, and torment by worldly matters and desire, and the impossibility of pure living because of that, so that his life becomes dank. A group said: ﴿dank﴾ means by eating what is forbidden.

It is inferred that the dank life is before the Day of Resurrection from His saying ﴿and We will raise him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾, and His saying ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting﴾; it is as if He mentioned one kind of punishment, then mentioned that the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting. Al-Zamakhshari endorsed the view of the majority and said: The meaning of that is that with religion comes submission, contentment, and reliance upon Allah and upon His allotment, so its adherent spends what He has provided him with generosity and ease, and he lives a good life, as the Most High said: ﴿So We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [al-Nahl: 97]. But the one who turns away from religion is controlled by greed, which never ceases to drive him toward increasing worldly gain, and he is dominated by stinginess, which clenches his hand from spending; so his life is dank and his state is dark. End of quotation.

Al-Hasan read ﴿ḍankī﴾ with the feminine alif and without tanwin, and with imala; its form is an adjective on the pattern fa'lā from ḍank. The majority read ﴿ḍankan﴾ with tanwin, and the fatḥa on the kaf is the fatḥa of i'rab. The majority read (wa-naḥshuruhu) with a nun, and a group among them, Aban ibn Taghlib, read it with a sukun on the rā', so it may be a lightening, or it may be a jussive by conjunction with the position of ﴿fa-inna lahu ma'ishatan ḍankan﴾, because it is the answer of the condition; and it is as if it were said: ﴿Whoever turns away from My remembrance, there will be for him a dank life﴾ and ﴿We will raise him﴾. A similar case is ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray, there is no guide for him, and He leaves them﴾ [al-A'raf: 186] in the reading of one who reads sukun on ﴿wa-yadharhum﴾. A group read ﴿wa-yaḥshuruhu﴾ with the yā'. And it was read ﴿wa-yaḥshuruh﴾ with a sukun on the hā' according to the pausal form, as al-Zamakhshari said. Ibn Khalawayh related this reading from Aban ibn Taghlib, and the best way to explain it is according to the dialect of Banu Kilab and 'Uqayl, for they make such a hā' quiescent. It was also read ﴿li-rabbihi la-kanud﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 6]. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿blind﴾ is blindness of sight, as He said: ﴿and We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind﴾ [al-Isra': 97]. It was also said: blind of insight. Ibn 'Atiyya said: If this were so, the disbeliever would not perceive that, because he died blind of insight and is raised in that state. Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Muqatil, Abu Salih, and it is related from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿blind﴾ means blind to his proof; he has no proof by which he is guided. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: He is raised seeing, then when he reaches the place of gathering he is ﴿blind﴾. It was said: ﴿blind﴾ regarding the means of averting punishment from himself, like the blind man who has no way to deal with what he cannot see. It was said: ﴿blind﴾ to everything except Hell. Al-Jubba'i said: What is meant by his being raised ﴿blind﴾ is that he is not guided to anything. Ibrahim ibn 'Arafa said: Whatever Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentions in His Book and censures, He means blindness of the heart, as He said: ﴿For indeed it is not the eyes that are blinded, but the hearts which are in the breasts are blinded﴾ [al-Hajj: 46].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 20, verses 122–127:

﴿Then He chose him﴾, meaning He selected him and drew him near, and ﴿turned to him﴾, meaning He accepted his repentance. ﴿And guided him﴾, meaning He guided him to prophethood, or to the manner of repentance, or He guided him to his right course until he returned to remorse. The pronoun in ﴿Go down﴾ is a dual pronoun, and it is a command to Adam and Hawwa'; He made their descent a punishment for them. ﴿All of you﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the two of them. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Then He informed them, by His saying ﴿all of you﴾, that Iblis and the serpent would descend along with them, and He informed them that enmity would exist between them and their descendants until the Day of Resurrection. End of quotation.

But His saying ﴿all of you﴾ does not indicate that Iblis and the serpent descend with them, because ﴿all of you﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun of the two, meaning gathered together, and the pronoun in ﴿some of you to others﴾ is a plural pronoun. It was said: He means Iblis and his progeny, and Adam and his progeny. It was also said: He meant Adam and his offspring, and the enmity occurs between them, and the hatred due to the difference of religions and the scattering of opinions. It was said: Adam, Iblis and the serpent. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: The address is to Adam, peace be upon him, and because the two are two kinds, His saying ﴿Go down﴾ is correct; and because each of the two kinds includes multitude, His saying ﴿So when there comes to you from Me guidance﴾ is correct.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Since Adam and Hawwa', peace be upon them, are the two origins of humankind and the two causes from which they grew and branched out, they were treated as if they themselves were humankind, so they were addressed with the address given to humankind, and it was said ﴿So when there comes to you﴾ in the plural form. Its parallel is their attributing the verb to the cause while in reality it belongs to the one who causes. End of quotation. And ﴿guidance﴾ is the law of Allah. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: Allah guaranteed for whoever follows the Qur'an that he will not go astray in this world nor be wretched in the Hereafter, then he recited ﴿Whoever follows My guidance will not go astray, nor will he be distressed.﴾ The meaning is that wretchedness in the Hereafter is the punishment of those who went astray in this world from the path of religion; so whoever follows the Book of Allah, carries out its commands and refrains from its prohibitions, is saved from straying and from its punishment. It is related from Ibn Jubayr: Whoever recites the Qur'an and follows what is in it, Allah protects him from error and shields him from the evil of reckoning. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: This verse indicates that what is meant by the guidance which Allah Most High mentioned is following the proofs, and following them is not complete unless one reasons by them and acts by them; whoever is in this state, Allah Most High has guaranteed that he will not go astray and will not be wretched in the Hereafter, because He Most High will guide him to Paradise. It was said: ﴿He will not go astray, nor be wretched﴾ refers to this world. If it is said: One blessed with the guidance of Allah may still suffer wretchedness in this world. We say: What is meant is that he will not go astray in religion, nor be wretched because of religion; if it occurs through some other cause, there is no harm. End of quotation.

* *
